News.title: Disgraced Huw Edwards gives tell-all interview in new documentary – as Channel 4 blasted for platforming convicted paedo
News.content:
Next

DISGRACED ex-BBC presenter Huw Edwards is being featured in a new Channel 4 documentary – sparking fury on social media.

Edwards, 65, was handed a six-month suspended sentence in 2024 for possessing 41 vile images of kids, some as young as seven.



But the new documentary, which will air on December 1, is billed as “a stark exploration of a disgraced public figure in the aftermath of a shocking fall from grace”.

The doc – which was filmed over the course of nearly a year – will follow vile Edwards at home in rural Wales, far from London and the high-profile career he brought crashing down after his criminal conviction.



In the trailer for Channel 4’s Huw Edwards – Guilty, the paedophile ex-BBC presenter reacts angrily when asked to explain his crimes.

Edwards, who appears with a large gash down one side of his face, is asked: “What do you think you were doing?”

He replies: “You want me to analyse what I was doing? I mean, seriously? I’d lost the plot!”

But the controversial documentary has now seen Channel 4 accused of “giving airtime to a predator”.



The trailer has sparked anger from the public across social media today with campaigners fearing he will use it to paint himself in a more sympathetic light.

The Sun understands that Channel 4 staffers are also believed to be angry at the decision to give a platform to a paedophile.

Emma Jane Taylor, founder of sexual abuse charity Project 90-10, said: “Why would anyone want to read about a registered sex offender’s ‘poor me’ story? What about listening to the victims?

“And why he is entitled to a platform? Remember, every one of those images represents a real child who has been harmed.

“Accountability matters but so do the victims, and what troubles me is that this is all about Edwards and not the children exploited in those images, how they were harmed, how it has affected their families.”



Disgraced Edwards has already attempted to rehabilitate his public image by launching a personal Substack in which he blamed his mental health.

Meanwhile, Rachel Rebecca Halliwell, whose 12-year-old daughter Semina took her own life after reporting being raped, said: “Channel 4 platforming convicted child sex offender Huw Edwards in ”Huw Edwards – Guilty” is outrageous.

“Why reward predators with airtime? Stop normalising this.”

Broadcaster and political columnist Sangita Myska also blasted the release of the trailer.

She said on X, formerly Twitter: “The rehabilitation Huw Edward’s reputation via a ‘personal journey’ documentary is contemptible.



“He’s a sex offender. What the hell is Channel 4 thinking?”

Another social media user said: “Edwards should be in a cell not on our TV screens.”

Channel 4 said: “The film is an uncomfortable portrayal of what happens when a previously beloved public figure betrays the trust of the people and asks what accountability really means in the wake of a serious criminal conviction.”

It comes after the mother of the teenager groomed by the star said she is appalled that the disgraced broadcaster is being given a platform to present his side of the story.

The mum, who first blew the whistle on Edwards, told The Sun on Sunday earlier this year: “It’s absolutely disgusting Channel 4 has given a convicted paedophile a platform.



“I don’t understand what he has to say — or what his side of the story really is. Who wants to hear that? And why would they agree to it?”

The former news anchor’s downfall was the subject of a Channel 5 drama in March.

The presenter – portrayed by Doc Martin star Martin Clunes – hinted he was considering a tell-all chat in a self-pitying statement issued ahead of its broadcast.

Edwards was best known for presenting the BBC’s News At Ten for decades, delivering some of the biggest stories to the British public including Queen Elizabeth II’s death.

His downfall came after our bombshell report in July 2023 alleged that a “top BBC star” had paid a teenager for sexual pictures, and days later his wife named him as the presenter at the centre of the scandal.



Edwards resigned in April 2024 and was charged in June that same year after a Metropolitan Police probe was triggered by our in-depth investigation.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A month later, he admitted making indecent images of children and having 41 photographs on WhatsApp, including seven of the most serious type.

He was handed a six-month prison sentence, suspended for two years.

News.title: Supply teacher dies at school after suffering serious medical emergency while teaching – as college closes
News.content:
SCHOOL TRAGEDY Supply teacher dies at school after suffering serious medical emergency while teaching – as college closes







Next

A TEACHER has died after suffering a serious medical emergency while teaching.

The supply teacher was rushed to hospital in an air ambulance after falling ill at a school in Sheffield.

Handsworth Grange Community Sports College has since confirmed their death following the episode yesterday.

Emergency services scrambled to the school and a helicopter landed on the playing field before escorting the patient to Northern General Hospital.





The school remains closed following the tragedy.

In a letter to parents, Bev Matthews, the Chief Executive Officer of Minerva Learning Trust which runs the school said: “It is with great sadness that we can confirm that the member of supply teaching staff who experienced a medical emergency whilst teaching at the school on 25 November 2026 has sadly passed away.

“Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with their family, friends and colleagues at this extremely difficult time.

“This has been a deeply upsetting incident for everyone affected. Pupils and staff witnessed the response to a serious medical emergency, and we recognise the impact this will have on our school community.

“Specialist support is being made available to pupils and staff and will continue over the coming days and weeks.”

She continued: “We would like to thank the emergency services and medical professionals who attended the scene so quickly.

“I would also like to thank our staff for the care and professionalism they have shown throughout this difficult situation.”

“Thank you as well to the many parents and carers who have sent kind and supportive messages. They have meant a great deal to our staff.



“Out of respect for the individual’s family, we will not be releasing any further personal details at this time. We kindly ask that their privacy is respected.”

The Handsworth Grange Road school had already planned INSET days for Friday, November 27, and Monday, November 30.

“That means pupils will not be back in class until Tuesday, December 1.

News.title: We were left with 26ft crater in our street after secret tunnels collapsed… are YOU in a UK sinkhole hotspot?
News.content:
Next

AS residents of the peaceful Surrey town of Godstone slept they had no idea that their ordinary looking High Street was caving in.

To their horror they woke the following morning to find a giant 26ft sinkhole had opened up, revealing a vast underground network of Victorian mining tunnels beneath their feet.



Had it happened during the day, or a mere few metres away, it could have been devastating.

Sami Bristow, who runs Blossoms coffee shop, recalled that bizarre day back in February 2025.



Sami, 33, explained: “I woke up to all these messages saying the road had opened up. I saw the street had been cordoned off but we were shocked by the size of it.

“This was a disaster waiting to happen.”

The huge collapse, which rocked the local community, unearthed eerie eight-metre deep abandoned tunnels.

In the 1800s Godstone had a thriving sand mining industry, its fine silver sand was valued for its high quality – making it ideal for glass and gardening purposes.

“I’d always known about the caves underneath Godstone, my Gran used to speak about them and it’s quite a well known fact that they are spread underneath the town,” says Sami.

“I feel like the majority of people who live in Godstone know about the caves.



“I’ve never been down there, I’m not a fan of small, dark spaces but I know a few people have been when they’re open to the public.”

When the Godstone mines were abandoned their location was forgotten – none of the mines were mapped or recorded so engineers who raced to the sink hole that morning had no idea of the extent or depth or direction of the tunnels.

The only way to find out was to dig a vast network of bore holes.

Dozens of families were evacuated from their homes, some for months, while water supplies were cut off and the High Street was closed to traffic for almost two years.

Tonight a new BBC documentary Why Sinkholes Collapse investigates why the problem is getting worse, what causes the ground beneath our feet to give way and why these dangerous and dramatic collapses are becoming an increasing threat to towns and cities across the globe.



Ripon, in North Yorkshire, has been dubbed the sinkhole capital of the UK, with seven major collapses in 30 years caused by soluble gypsum under the road structure.

The British Geological Survey (BGS) also names the Mendips, Peak District, Chilterns, Dorset, Hampshire and Cheshire’s salt areas as susceptible areas.

Godstone High Street finally reopened to traffic in July 2026 after engineers had filled the hole with a special type of concrete which could flow into every nook and cranny. It had been closed for 18 months.



Engineer David White explained: “Initially we found an awful lot of sand which was incredibly frustrating but by the end of the first week we found a fairly significant void beneath the highway.

“We were then able to introduce CCTV cameras eight metres deep and found manmade tunnels. It was quite sobering that no one had seen these tunnels for over 100 years.”

To find out how far the tunnels extended they inserted a special camera into the ground, and after eight long months of investigation they built up a 3D model of the entire tunnel network.

In total, the team discovered 100m of tunnels beneath the High Street, all north of the sink hole. And to work out where the sand had gone they drilled dozens more boreholes into the ground.



“At the end of it we had a very small area of resurfacing but beneath that an area of 190 holes drilled down to a depth of ten metres and about 1100 tonnes of grout injected into them – and nobody will ever see that,” added David.

Although sink holes are becoming increasingly frequent and impacting communities around the world, Sami feels this one could have been avoided.

“If the roads had been better maintained and regulated it might not have happened,” she said.

“You hear about catastrophic sink holes in Thailand that get fixed quicker than this one just outside London.”



And Sami says she lost a huge amount of business as customers needed to take a three mile diversion around the town.

They were left in the dark over how long the repairs would take.

She added: “People aren’t going to drive that far out of their way for a coffee, they were staying on the other side of the sink hole.



“It was incredibly frustrating because they kept saying it was going to reopen to through traffic, but then it was delayed repeatedly and nobody could tell us what was taking so long.

“I’d go and talk to the engineers but to be honest you never get any answers. We’d ask how long? How long? And it would always just be, we don’t know.

“It got to the stage where it was pointless asking questions because you just wouldn’t be successful, it was annoying.

“I still had a business to run, rent and bills to pay.

“I lost the equivalent of a full time wage, which when you put it into context is a big loss because we had to lose a person and I ended up working all the shifts with my sister Nicky because we just couldn’t afford to pay another wage.



“We were still relatively new and it was a big loss.”

Like many locals, Sami fears this could happen again: “I absolutely worry about that,” she said.

“I feel that because the caves are so vast they really need to keep a closer eye on things, especially the water pipes because if it happens again it will cause more devastation and Godstone will be a laughing stock.

“I haven’t seen the engineers back here since work finished, and it needs regular maintenance. Without it people who live by the sink hole will be constantly worried, it’s something that will always be on your mind.



“We haven’t been told this will never happen again and it’s having an ongoing effect. There are so many properties on the market but they can’t sell them because who is going to buy a house knowing it could happen again.

“Now I’m always keeping an eye out for dips in the road which is the first sign it might give way.

“There is a noticeable dip on the A22 just outside of the town now, you can feel it as you drive over, that road has definitely suffered some damage as a result of all the extra traffic and big lorries that went that way while the High Street was closed.

“My shop has been there since 1917 so it’s well built, thankfully. But you have to ask the question, why was there so much building work allowed on top of those caves?”

News.title: Royal Navy Command HQ plunged into lockdown after ‘bomb threat’ as armed cops and sniffer dogs descend on base
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

‘BOMB’ PROBE Royal Navy Command HQ plunged into lockdown after ‘bomb threat’ as armed cops and sniffer dogs descend on base







Next

THE Royal Navy headquarters was plunged into lockdown over a bomb hoax today.

Armed police and sniffer dogs raced to HMS Excellent after a threat was called in at around 9.45am.



The site was declared safe around three hours later.

Police are investigating who made the threat but sources insisted it was too early to know if it was a hostile state.



The base on Whales Island in Portsmouth Harbour is home to the Navy’s Command Headquarters and several training teams.

It follows thousands of sinister hoaxes disrupting schools across Europe earlier this month.



More than 7,500 schools have been targeted in Italy, Germany, Denmark, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Part of the Whale Island base was evacuated while other staff were ordered to shelter in place.

The Sun understands the threat referred to a specific part of the island.

A source said: “There was a threat made. We responded.



“A search was carried out of the area indicated. They concluded it was all safe.”

They added: “Who made the call is under investigation.”

A Royal Navy spokesperson today said: “Police and Ministry of Defence personnel are currently responding to a security incident at HMS Excellent in Portsmouth.

“The safety of personnel and the public is our priority. People are asked to avoid the area while the incident is ongoing.

“We will provide further information in due course.”



The Navy Command Headquarters (NCHQ) is responsible for the direction and management of the Navy in the UK.

News.title: Moment mum tells cop ‘it’s your word against mine’ before falsely accusing him of sexually assaulting her during arrest
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment a lying mum told a cop “it’s your word against mine” before falsely accusing him of sexually assaulting her.

Sophie Hodgkinson had been arrested following a car crash when she made a string of chilling threats against the officer.



She branded him a “n***e” and told him: “You’re getting done for touching a woman, do you understand that?”

Bodycam also showed the mum, 31, claiming the cop had “touched my f***y” as she called him a “little dirty perv”, Kent Online reports.



When a second officer in the police car pointed out she was being recorded, Hodgkinson replied: “I don’t give a f***.

“You touched my f***y when you was trying to arrest me, you dirty c***.”

Turning to the first officer, she continued: “Your word against mine – what are you going to do about it?”

Rather than dropping her lies, Hodgkinson, of Folkestone, lodged a formal complaint accusing the officer of sexually assaulting her both at her home and at the station.

The police officer was placed under investigation over the lie – with a court hearing a “cloud of suspicion still hovers” above him.

Hodgkinson has now been jailed for 18 months after admitting perverting the course of justice by making a false allegation of sexual assault against the officer.



In a victim impact statement, the officer described the ordeal as “by far the worst conduct he has dealt with in six years of policing”.

The court heard Hodgkinson had been arrested in August 2025 after fleeing the scene of a crash.

While being taken to Canterbury Police Station, she made the sickening claims.



In a subsequent written complaint, she alleged the officer had “manhandled her inappropriately” and groped her during the arrest.

Hodgkinson wrote: “I felt so exposed. It made me feel so uncomfortable.

“I kept asking for my skirt to be pulled down, and no officer did right away.”

Despite her claims being quickly dismissed, the officer remained under investigation during the criminal proceedings against Hodgkinson.

Sentencing, Judge Taylor said the allegations could have had devastating consequences for him.



He added: “It could have been career-ending. It could have been marriage-ending.

“Your complaint could have taken a frontline officer off duty for a considerable period of time.”

The court heard Hodgkinson has two previous convictions for five offences, including battery against a serving police officer in 2009 and possession of a prohibited weapon in 2020.

Investigating officer PC Charlotte Carey said: “Reports of sexual offences are taken extremely seriously and are subject to a thorough investigation, which in this case, swiftly established the facts and exposed the lies told by Hodgkinson.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Making a false allegation of this nature is a serious criminal offence, which in this case not only subjected a victim to considerable distress and trauma, and was an insult to genuine victims who need our support, it also sought to undermine the integrity of the police.



“I’m pleased the court has recognised the impact of Hodgkinson’s actions and imposed a custodial sentence, holding her accountable for the harm she caused.”

News.title: Britain and America must fight for the special relationship our wartime heroes gave their lives to forge
News.content:
In a Thanksgiving message, US Ambassador Warren Stephens pays tribute to the heroes who fought for our freedom

WARREN STEPHENS Britain and America must fight for the special relationship our wartime heroes gave their lives to forge







Next

IT is a fitting coincidence of history that Thanksgiving falls every year in the same month as Veterans Day, or Remembrance Day here in the UK.

Thanksgiving is a time when Americans gather around the globe to give thanks for the blessings and freedoms we enjoy.



We remember those who came before us, and those who overcame great difficulties to establish the American nation.

This year, I could think of few individuals more deserving of our thanks than thosewho gave their lives fighting for our freedom.



The United States and United Kingdom fought side by side in two world wars, but it was the second that really cemented our partnership.

And thanks to Winston Churchill, gave it a name: the “special relationship.”



From 1941 onwards, Britain and America began training, planning, and sharinginformation on an unprecedented scale. Personal relationships formed at all levels, from our leaders to our citizens. That cooperation continues to this day.

On this Thanksgiving Day, I am grateful to the individuals who got off the sidelines to fight for their country and for our special relationship.

We must continue to fight for – and invest in – that partnership today.

I think of heroes like Billy Fiske: the Olympic gold medal-winning bobsled championfrom Chicago, who left a comfortable life to fight with the Royal Air Force in the Battle of Britain.



Billy was motivated by his hatred of Hitler, and his love for the friends he made travelling in Europe, studying in Cambridge, and living in London.

Sadly, he also became the first American to die in the Battle of Britain. After taking enemy fire, Billy managed to land his heavily damaged aircraft, but died in the hospital days later from the burns he sustained.

At Billy’s funeral, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill sent personal a note andflowers to his widow, Rose Fiske.

Later that day – perhaps with Billy in mind – Churchill delivered one of his most famous lines: “Never was so much owed by so many, to so few.”

Today, we remain truly grateful for the sacrifice of “The Few.” Without their bravery and skill, Britain may have fallen to the Nazis and D-Day as we know it would never have happened.



I also give thanks for the heroes whose names we never heard. Like Virginia Hall, who overcame enormous obstacles to fight with her friends in Europe.

Virginia was born to a successful business owner in Maryland, but left behind an easylife to see the world and serve her country.

After rejection from the Us foreign service, Virginia found work in Europe andjoined the ambulance corps in Nazi-occupied France.

Despite a prosthetic leg from a hunting accident, Virginia drove thousands of injured troops across France under the watchful eye of their German occupiers.

Her bravery drew the attention of Britain’s new Special Operations Executive, who recruited her services to wage a campaign of sabotage and subterfuge across Europe.



Before long, Virginia had a network of 1,500 male and female agents under her command: an unthinkable feat for a woman in the 1940s.

Virginia’s work during the war, with both British and American intelligence, earned her a Distinguished Service Cross – the United States’ second highest military decoration. She was the only civilian woman to receive this honor.

But when President Roosevelt offered a public award ceremony, Virginia declined in order to continue serving her country undercover. She remained unknown to the public until her death in 1982.

These two wartime heroes – Billy Fiske and Virginia Hall – capture the very best of our special relationship.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Both performed tremendous acts of heroism, forsaking safety and comfort to defendtheir friends and their freedoms. And there are many more examples like them.



As America’s 250th year draws to a close, I give thanks for the special relationshipestablished during World War Two – by brave individuals like Billy Fiske and Virginia Hall – and that those bonds forged in war continue to this day.

News.title: Dad, 36, & man, 26, killed in horror helicopter crash after chopper smashed into hillside minutes after takeoff
News.content:
Next

A DAD and former US marine has been identified as one of the victims of a horror helicopter crash.

Christopher Lamaku, 36, died when a Robinson R22 chopper plunged into a hillside on Monday morning in Temecula, California.



The father was killed alongside passenger Steven Madrid, 26, from Yuma, Arizona, when the aircraft dropped out of the air just minutes after take off.

Christopher, from Escondido, served as a reserve police officer before joining US Marines and becoming a pilot.





He leaves behind a wife and their young child.

The Riverside Flight Academy gave an emotional tribute to the dad, describing him as “a dedicated Marine, a committed Police Officer, a skilled Pilot and a dear friend”.

It wrote: “Your courage, service and love for flying will always be remembered.”

The helicopter took off from French Valley Airport at 9.17am local time, plummeting to the ground 12 minutes later, according to the FAA.



Emergency services rushed to the site of the crash near Oak Mountain Winery and Altisima Winery.

Fire crews reportedly had to fight their way through thick brush to get to the wreck of the chopper, which was around 200ft up the hillside.



Both occupants of the aircraft were pronounced dead at the scene.

Horrifying video showed the aircraft’s mangled wreckage lying in dense forest.

The Federal Aviation Administration said: “A Robinson R22 helicopter crashed into a hillside in Temecula, California, around 9.30am local time Monday, November 23.”

Riverside County Sheriff’s Office said: “Deputies were dispatched to the area of De Portola Road and Oak Mountain Road regarding a reported air emergency.



“Upon arrival, deputies located a helicopter crash and two subjects who were pronounced deceased at the scene.”

Riverside County Airports Director Angela Jamison said the “entire aviation community is feeling the weight of this tragedy”.

She added: “We are deeply saddened by this tragic accident. Our hearts go out to the families and loved ones of those involved.”

It is currently unclear why the aircraft smashed into the hillside.

The National Transportation Safety Board has launched a probe to investigate the cause of the horror crash.

It comes after two people were killed in October when a medical helicopter with five on board crashed into the ocean of Catalina Island, LA.

News.title: Charity created in memory of Princess Diana & backed by William & Harry is placed into administration after going bust
News.content:
CHARITY BUST Charity created in memory of Princess Diana & backed by William & Harry is placed into administration after going bust







Next

A CHARITY set up in memory of Princess Diana is to close down – after running out of money.

The Diana Award – which has been backed by both Harry and William – has gone into administration.



The international award was set up to honour young people and launched in honour of Diana by former PM Gordon Brown in 1999.

It comes just less than a year before the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death in Paris.



The charity said in a statement: “Twenty-seven years ago, the Diana Awards were created to honour Diana, Princess of Wales and her belief that young people had the power to change their community, their country and the world.

“We are proud to have shone a spotlight on a generation of young people.





“Over 50,000 young people have received the prestigious Diana Award and the charity has worked with thousands more through programmes to power the impact created by these inspirational young leaders on the lives of those around them.”

They continued: “It is with heavy hearts that we announce The Diana Award charity has been placed into Administration, after independent advice made clear that the charity can no longer continue to meet its obligations.

“This is not the outcome any of us wanted. We thank everyone who has supported this charity over the years and, above all, the young people whose achievements have always been at the heart of it.

“Their achievements matter, and nothing about today’s decision changes that.

Prince William expressed his sadness at the news the charity was shutting down.



He said: “ The Diana Award has recognised and encouraged thousands of young people who are changing the world for the better.

“I want to thank everyone whose dedication and hard work helped make that possible over so many years.”

Last year Harry and William both sent congratulatory letters to winners.

As a charity it received grants from bodies including The National Lottery and fundraising.

In honour of Diana’s belief: “Young people have the power to change the world”, the awards recognise young leaders, fundraisers, campaigners and peer mentors aged 9-25.



In a ceremony earlier this month, 200 recipients from 44 countries were recognised for their dedication to social action.

The Prince of Wales also spoke at the 2024 ceremony where he paid tribute to Diana for the 25th anniversary of the awards.

He said his mother taught him that “everyone has the potential to give something back”.

William said: “I know that she would have been honoured to see a charity in her name doing such inspirational work to uplift young people from all corners of the globe.”

He added that his mother taught him that “everyone in need deserves a supporting hand in life”.



He said: “That legacy is something that both Catherine and I have sought to focus on through our work, as have the 50,000 young people who have received a Diana Award over the past 25 years.

“I am so proud to see this belief of my mother’s manifested in the amazing young people receiving the Legacy Award tonight.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In the same ceremony, Harry told the winners in a “casual” video chat: “Thank you, very much, for inspiring so many others and at the same time protecting my mother’s legacy.

“I really appreciate that. And, again, well done on this fantastic group of individuals.”

News.title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
News.content:
The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.

The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.

Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".

"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."

This is a reference to the so-called "Boris Wave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.

That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.

In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".

Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.

"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."

News.title: UK reservists contacted as 'threat environment' rises, Streeting says
News.content:
The Ministry of Defence has written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment", Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.

It comes after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said.

"You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," Streeting told Today.

"We saw last Friday a very serious incident â the incursion into Polish airspace by Russian missiles, we've seen state-sponsored terrorism waged by Russia across Europe, we've obviously had incidents concerning Iran around RAF bases here in the UK.

"And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks."

He added: "Because the more ready we are the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war, that is my goal, that is the goal of this government."

Streeting told BBC Breakfast that "if, God forbid, this country did find itself at war" and there was then an inquiry, the Ministry of Defence would be criticised if the government had not kept its records up-to-date."

The Telegraph reported that the letters offered opportunities to volunteer, external for training and exercises.

This is not a case of pressing the panic button for imminent war, but more one of good housekeeping.

When Britain went to war in Iraq in 2003 the MoD had a poor grasp of who might be available to serve, what current skills they had and what their up-to-date contact details were. So they obviously don't want to be in that situation if there is a national crisis in the future that triggers a mobilisation.

Twenty three years on, the Ukraine war has changed everything. It's brought a hot war to the very borders of Nato, it's exposed the dangers of having too few troops available, but most of all it has changed the nature of warfare.

People who have spent their adult lives never touching a weapon can turn out to be extraordinarily skilled drone operators, those with a talent for electronics, radio and signals work have a vital role to play in electronic warfare.

So this exercise by the government, probably long overdue, is about knowing who can do what and where they can be contacted.

Justin Crump, a former Army officer and now CEO of the business intelligence firm Sibylline, told the BBC: "Ukraine has shown us the importance of mobilising civilian skills and approaches in modern warfare. This is a first step, and an overdue one in many ways, with the effort likely to increase through early 2027. [It is] very much a part of deterrence and not an intention to use people".

He said veterans - a sometimes misleading term for men and women who are often in peak physical shape and fitness - that he has contacted have generally responded positively to the move. "After all", he said, "they signed up to help before, but want to make sure their enhanced skills and talents are valued".

The MoD's decision to contact ex-military personnel comes after news that the UK has signed an Â£8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which the defence secretary said would help get the country "warfighting ready".

Meanwhile, Streeting also praised the Duke of Sussex's "patriotic spirit" after the former soldier said he would rejoin the armed forces again if needed.

Asked whether there could be a role for Harry, the defence secretary told Today: "I'm always happy to talk to him about how we can work together, whether that's through his Invictus Games, which does a brilliant job supporting our veterans and giving them opportunities to take part in those amazing and inspiring competitive sporting events, but he does have experience to bring to bear."

Streeting praised the "service he's given to our country" and the fact he had spoken about his "willingness and readiness to serve".

"I think that's exactly the sort of patriotic spirit we're looking for," he said.

"I think it's that sort of patriotic spirit we'll find throughout our strategic reserve."

Last week, Harry, who spent a decade in the forces and served on the front line in Afghanistan, said: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

News.title: Expect fewer frosts and more hot days as UK seasons shift, says Met Office
News.content:
The UK's seasons are changing, with fewer winter frosts and more hot summer days, according to new analysis from the Met Office.

Across the UK, the number of winter days with an air frost â when the air temperature falls to 0C or below â was around a quarter lower in the decade to 2025 than during the period from 1961 to 1990.

In southern England, the reduction was around a third while the average number of UK summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled.

The Met Office says climate change has led to these seasonal shifts.

"Our summer is getting wider and our winter is getting smaller," says Dr James Pope, climate scientist at the Met Office.

"The driver of this is that the whole global climate is warming. And that impacts on the UK.

"Some areas went from their wettest ever winter to a severe drought via a record-breaking summer for the whole country."

The changing conditions have affected wildlife and led some farmers to grow different crops.

News.title: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage
News.content:
The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.

The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.

Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".

But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.

The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings.

The BBC said the partnership includes:

A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecasts

Met Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather app

More local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presenters

More "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climate

There will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.

Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".

News.title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
News.content:
Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.

Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

News.title: Government's antisemitism adviser opens investigation into BBC
News.content:
The government's antisemitism adviser has launched an investigation into the BBC over allegations of a "hostile work environment" for Jews.

Lord Mann told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he had decided to open the investigation "because there seems to be a growing feeling of discomfort among Jewish staff".

He said: "If that's true, and that's what I'm going to attempt to find out, and if that is widespread, then that's a really serious problem that has to be addressed. And I don't hear and see that being addressed, and at a senior level."

The BBC said it takes "any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously â there is no place for it at the BBC".

The corporation said it had introduced compulsory antisemitism training for all staff, and said "we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have".

The BBC statement added that it is "determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted".

Lord Mann, who was appointed by former Prime Minister Theresa May as an independent adviser on antisemitism in 2019, external, said anyone contacting him would have "total anonymity guaranteed".

"I have no agenda against the BBC," he told Today, calling himself "an entirely blank sheet of paper".

"Some of the things that I'm being told have been quite disturbing sometimes, how little the senior manager of the BBC seem to get it, and so I'm opening this up," he said.

"Look, there is a problem. The question is - is the problem just a few people? Is it a problem that's easily solved? But if it's an institutional problem, that's much deeper and more difficult to solve. It may be. I'll report the facts."

The former MP said he had previously "made suggestions" to the corporation after he had "repeatedly met" Jewish staff.

He said the things "the BBC has done to try and sort things out have not worked".

His agenda was "ensuring the BBC meets its charter obligations", saying "people are fearful... of expressing their concerns internally, that's the problem".

Lord Mann's remit as the government's independent adviser on antisemitism includes "to engage proactively with the Jewish community and institutions".

He said he plans to have his investigation "totally completed and reported to the BBC and the government before Easter".

He previously conducted a review into antisemitism and racism in the NHS, which was commissioned by the health secretary and which reported in June.

The Guardian recently reported, external that BBC deputy director general Rhodri Talfan Davies said he did not accept that an independent inquiry into antisemitism was needed.

"We have very, very robust processes â we review them regularly," he told members of the Broadcasting Press Guild earlier this month.

"Of course in any large organisation there can be instances of discrimination, which you deal with when they arise, but there is no evidence of any systemic issue within the BBC that would merit anything like that.

"I don't believe there is institutional discrimination of any sort in the BBC, but I think as an organisation you always have to look harder and review how you go about identifying issues, and that work is never done."

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said in a statement that it welcomed the review into "deeply concerning" experiences of Jewish staff at the BBC.

"The BBC is an important national institution and should be setting the gold standard for an inclusive workplace and impartial broadcasting," it said.

"We stand ready to support both Lord Mann and the BBC in addressing these concerns, rebuilding confidence within the Jewish community and ensuring that the BBC sets an example for other broadcasters to follow."

Last month, Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon said the BBC had given her a Â£400,000 payout after she raised antisemitism concerns.

The BBC said it did not uphold allegations of antisemitism but accepted there were "shortcomings" in how it treated Kon, which had a "personal impact" on her. The corporation did not specify what the shortcomings were.

In January, the BBC apologised for its use of language during coverage of Holocaust Memorial Day, saying programmes should have referred to "six million Jewish people" having been murdered by the Nazi regime, rather than "six million people" or "six million mostly Jewish people".

Last September, the BBC's broadcast of Bob Vylan's controversial set at Glastonbury broke editorial guidelines in relation to harm and offence, with the corporation's complaints unit ruling that some comments could "fairly be characterised as antisemitic". The band denied being antisemitic.

News.title: Queen's University clear Jason Arday co-authored paper over plagiarism concerns
News.content:
Research by academic Jason Arday, who was accused of plagiarism before his death, has been cleared by one of the institutions that was investigating him.

Queen's University Belfast (QUB) began looking into Jason Arday's work after he resigned from his University of Cambridge roles.

The university had published a paper on its academic research site co-authored by Arday and other academics from Queen's in 2021.

In a statement, a spokesperson for QUB said: "Having reviewed the matter, we are satisfied that the paper meets the appropriate academic standards and have no concerns regarding its publication."

Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest black professor in 2023, was found dead in Battersea on 14 August, having resigned as a professor of sociology of education the week prior.

The 41-year-old's death followed weeks of media coverage over plagiarism allegations and questions about his achievements. He denied the claims. An inquest into his death is under way.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the death of the former professor as "a tragedy on so many levels".

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher and self-defined "race realist".

Cofnas has previously written that black people are less intelligent than other groups and would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment" under a meritocratic system.

He claimed on the online publishing platform Substack that he had put Arday's work through a plagiarism detection software, which found that "many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source".

Following Arday's death, Cofnas was suspended from his post at Ghent University, after it launched an investigation into him "for discriminating against" the former Cambridge professor. He was later handed a three-month teaching ban.

Public figures and friends of Arday had called for a public inquiry into media coverage surrounding the former professor before his death.

Labour MP Diane Abbott and actress Jameela Jamil were among 30,000 signatories of a letter to the prime minister, which claims Arday's death followed "two weeks of relentless harassment".

The University of Cambridge launched a two-part independent review examining the support available to Arday before his death, as well as the wider context of his time at the university.

Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.

Other institutions including Glasgow University, Durham University and Queen's University Belfast all began investigating Arday's work or his appointments to various positions.

Back in August, Queen's University said it was "looking into" a paper, published in 2021, on the impact of what was taught in universities on "Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic (BAME) learners" and "academics of colour".

The paper was called "Attempting to break the chain: Reimaging inclusive pedagogy and decolonising the curriculum within the academy".

News.title: The US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned
News.content:
"Patriarchy is in accordance with the way God made the world." That is the view of Pastor Doug Wilson, a conservative minister who the US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth calls his mentor.

Speaking to the BBC from his base in Moscow, Idaho, Wilson explained his view that a society led by men is "a very great blessing". It's a perspective Christians who disagree with him say is based on a fundamentalist understanding of the Bible, which promotes the subjugation of women.

A self-described Christian nationalist, Wilson believes the US should be a theocracy, with gay sex criminalised, abortion outlawed, and people of other faiths unable to hold public office.

In the past he has delivered a sermon on "The Lost Virtue of Sexism," arguing that the Bible says women should be excluded from leadership of the church, and certain roles in civic affairs. And as part of his views on the division between the sexes, he would like the 19th Amendment of the US constitution, which granted women the right to vote, to be repealed, something his detractors say is anti-democratic.

The vast majority of Christians support women's right to vote, and dismiss his message as misogynistic and extreme.

Rev. Canon Dana Colley Corsello, the vicar at the Washington National Cathedral, rejects Wilson's understanding of what the Bible says about women's roles.

"In my mind, there is no biblical precedent or standing for what [Wilson has] proposed," she told the BBC.

"I'm married, I have a husband, I have children. My husband and I are complete equals in everything we do."

But while Wilson still represents a fringe perspective amongst Christians in the US, some of his views have been gaining support.

The denomination he co-founded, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), has around 150 churches in the US. It's a drop in the ocean compared to the 350,000 or so other Christian congregations the US. But Wilson says membership continues to rise.

His influence has grown in part because of his connection to Pete Hegseth. The Secretary of Defence is a "proud member" of a CREC affiliated church, a Pentagon spokesperson told the BBC, adding that the "secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson's writings and teachings".

Wilson says the two have "a warm relationship", although he stresses it is "largely a pastoral one, not a political one". Wilson has led prayer services at the Pentagon, including one in mid-November.

Joining Wilson on stage, Pete Hegseth said "thank you for your leadership, for your mentorship, for the things you've started, the truth you've told, your willingness to be bold."

Hegseth worships at the Washington, DC branch of Wilson's network of churches. And there are other members of the current administration that worship there too, according to Wilson.

News.title: UK signs £8bn deal to ensure submarines are 'warfighting ready'
News.content:
The UK has signed an Â£8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said would help get the country "warfighting ready".

The five-year deal, awarded to defence firm Babcock, will create 3,000 new jobs and around 2,500 apprentice and graduate roles mainly across Plymouth, Clyde and Bristol, the MoD said.

It will allow the Royal Navy to "work around the clock to get our submarines back out to sea" and see naval base services modernised, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it demonstrated his commitment to "keeping the public safe" and "providing opportunities to "get young people into work".

"We're providing opportunities to get young people into work, to bring jobs to communities in Plymouth, Clyde and beyond, and to boost growth across the UK," the prime minister added.

Streeting said: "We're not going to repeat the mistakes of the past, where investment in our nuclear capability was delayed.

"Even when we have to move funding from other departments, we will prioritise our nuclear deterrent and getting Britain warfighting ready."

Speaking to BBC Breakfast during a visit to HMNB Devonport on Thursday, the defence secretary described the investment as a "win for the Navyâ¦ for jobs and the taxpayer."

He said the structure of the contract incentivises Babcock to produce results, adding "the more productive they are, the more they earn but if they fall short, then they don't get paid as much".

Streeting was also asked about reports that 100,000 military reservists who previously served in the armed forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

"What we're doing today is contacting our strategic reserves to make sure their contact details are up to date and we have those details to hand and this is all part of our readiness picture," he said.

The funding is part of a wider Â£26bn investment into the UK's naval bases announced earlier this year.

First Sea Lord, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said it will allow the Navy to "tackle delays that hold us back" by "getting submarines through maintenance quicker and back where they belong: beneath the waves".

Harry Holt, Babcock's chief executive, said: "We are very proud at Babcock of the critical support that we provide to the Royal Navy, in particular our unwavering support to the continuous at sea deterrent â the UK's highest defence priority."

News.title: Double jeopardy killer recommended for release from prison
News.content:
A murderer who became the first person tried after a change to the 800-year-old double jeopardy law has been recommended for release from prison.

William Dunlop, now 63, strangled Julie Hogg, 22, in Billingham, County Durham, in 1989 and hid her mutilated body behind a bath panel which was discovered by her mother more than two months later.

The Parole Board has recommended he be released after his fourth application to review his case. A panel had recommended Dunlop's transfer to open prison multiple times but three justice secretaries had intervened.

In response to the result, Hogg's son Kevin called the Parole Board "not fit for purpose".

The 22-year-old's murder was "accompanied by the brutal sexual degradation of [her] body", the Old Bailey judge said at Dunlop's sentencing, which came in 2006 after Julie Hogg's family campaigned for the legal change so he could be charged with the same crime twice.

Kevin Hogg said: "You know them victim personal statements? They mean absolutely nothing â nothing whatsoever and that's been proven time and time again."

News.title: Drivers over 70 face eye tests every three years under new plans
News.content:
Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans.

Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks.

Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over.

To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required.

Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence.

The change follows a consultation which launched early last year, set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers.

Under the current rules, over 70s have to renew their licence every three years, but only have to self-certify that their sight.

Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, which represents older people, said it was "discriminatory to just pick an age out of the hat and say 'everybody over 70 has to go through this, but nobody else does'".

But he said the group is not opposed in principle to regular eye tests for older drivers.

The changes being considered were first reported by the Daily Mail, external.

News.title: Heathrow third runway plans 'should be grounded'
News.content:
The report said the climate test was examined in the context of the recent advice from the Climate Change Committee.

The results showed the west London airport's expansion would not be compatible with the UK's carbon budgets or net-zero targets, it said.

The committee said both the air quality test and the noise test should be strengthened, adding that there was a lack of certainty over the cost of expansion that could affect the prices paid by airlines and passengers.

It also raised concerns over a lack of extensive plans to improve public transport, such as new rail lines into Heathrow from the west and south.

"If a third runway is to get off the ground, then government also needs to strengthen the air quality test and noise tests, develop plans for improving public transport and bottom out how much it will cost airlines and passengers to use an expanded Heathrow," Cadbury said.

She also called for "robust analysis" to set out what would happen if decarbonisation goals were missed.

"Expansion should not go ahead at any price, or at any cost to society or the environment," the report said.

News.title: Nuclear test veterans speak to BBC about 'search for justice'
News.content:
Nuclear test veterans and their relatives have reacted to the prime minister's announcement of an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

Andy Burham said a panel will assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s on troops, adding that the process will be treated with the "utmost seriousness".

The BBC heard reaction from veterans and their families as part of Newsnight's 'Nuclear Test Veterans: The Newsnight Special'.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.

You can watch the full Newsnight special on BBC Two or on BBC iPlayer.

News.title: 'Top Gear is back': Gordon Ramsay announced as new host
News.content:
TV chef Gordon Ramsay is to lead the new presenting line-up on BBC motoring show Top Gear, which is being revived four years after it was last on air.

In a clip announcing the new host, Ramsay is seen racing with the show's character the Stig as he shouts: "Top Gear is back."

Ramsay will take the driving seat alongside as yet unnamed co-presenters when the show starts filming next year. It will return to screens in 2028.

The long-running programme has been off air since 2022, when co-host Andrew Flintoff suffered serious facial and rib injuries after his open-topped three-wheeled car overturned at the show's test-track.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Simon Jack: Is Poundland's US owner to blame for its collapse?
News.content:
The blame game for the demise of Poundland is in full swing.

The number one target is US-based Gordon Brothers who bought the discount chain for Â£1 and have taken nearly Â£20m out of the business already.

Gordon Brothers stand to get paid back a further Â£22.5m, as their share of an existing Â£30m loan is set to be one of the first debts that the administrators will have to pay out of the proceeds of any sale of the business in whole or in part.

The team running Poundland blame the owners for strangling their ability to turn the business around, saying that their access to Poundland's own cash was restricted, leaving them unable to fully restock ahead of the crucial Christmas period.

They point to improving sales over October as proof the business had a future.

MPs also laid into the US firm with members of the Business Committee accusing it of "predatory capitalism" and "asset stripping".

News.title: Every day is living hell, says dad of boy, 2, murdered by grandparents
News.content:
A father who raised concerns about the grandparents who murdered his two-year-old son says that every day without him has been "living hell".

Ethan Ives-Griffiths died on 16 August 2021 after suffering a "catastrophic" head injury at his grandparents' home in Garden City, Flintshire.

Michael Ives, 49, and Kerry Ives, 47, were jailed for life in 2025. Ethan's mum, Shannon Ives, 29, was jailed for 12 years for causing or allowing his death and child cruelty.

A review into Ethan's death found that his father, Will Griffiths, raised concerns about his safety, but they were not acted on, and opportunities to protect Ethan were missed by multiple agencies.

Griffiths said he believed his son would "still be alive today" if his concerns had been acted upon.

"I wasn't being heard," he said, adding he was "still stuck in 2021" and unable to move past the day Ethan died.

"I haven't felt like I've lived. I've just been existing, waiting for everything to come out slowly."

Griffiths said it "disgusted" him that the police "didn't listen" when he told them he believed Ethan and his other children were not safe around the grandparents.

"They made threats and they've shown in every way, shape and form since day one they are a threat to my children," he said.

News.title: Government promised Peter Mandelson ‘light touch’ vetting on conflicts of interest, new files show
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Peter Mandelson was promised a “light touch” approach over his potential conflicts of interest by the government despite officials raising numerous concerns over his former clients and shares in a lobbying firm, new bombshell files reveal.

The latest tranche of files on the scandal surrounding the former US ambassador’s sacking, released on Thursday, also reveal that the disgraced peer failed to sell his shares in the firm Global Counsel, despite being expected to do so.

Lord Mandelson was sacked last September over his relationship with a paedophile financier, after emails showed he sent supportive messages to Jeffrey Epstein even as he was facing jail for sex offences.

open image in gallery Lord Mandelson was sacked as US ambassador due to his links with Jeffrey Epstein (James Manning/PA) ( PA )

No 10 said the emails revealed “materially different” information from what was known when Lord Mandelson was appointed to the key role of ambassador.

The scandal played a significant role in the eventual resignation of Sir Keir, with questions raised about how much the then-premier knew about their ties when he made the appointment.

On Thursday, prime minister Andy Burnham vowed to tackle the “vested interests” he said contributed to the scandal surrounding, promising “political reform” as part of his 10-year plan.

Lord Mandelson was arrested earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office, following claims he leaked sensitive government information to Epstein. He denies wrongdoing.

The documents show that the head of the Foreign Office Sir Olly Robbins was concerned Mandelson did not sell his shares in Global Counsel.

A letter sent last March, after Mandelson was already in post, shows that the Foreign Office thought the “ideal” solution to prevent a conflict of interest would be for Global Counsel to buy Mandelson out.

However, it adds, the company has not made an offer “Lord Mandelson considers commensurate with the fair value” of the shares.

Sir Olly later wrote to Mandelson setting out “a process we [could] agree on … that protects you against perceptions of benefitting GC in some way while in public office and for the (hopefully short) period you remain a significant shareholder”.

Sir Olly added: “If this looks sensible to you, I will sign and send and we can get this up and running in a light touch way.”

The files also show that while in office Lord Mandelson sent sent a copy of his speech to a director of the lobbying firm, who told him to tone down “parts of your apologia of the Trump administration”.

open image in gallery Mandelson sent supportive messages to Jeffrey Epstein as he was facing jail for sex offences ( US Department of Justice )

Mandelson later replied: “Thanks. I will look at changes.” He also added that he would “soften” the language on China.

The speech included a call for a US-UK technology partnership to win a battle with China he said would shape this century.

The documents also show the Labour grandee weighing in on Sir Keir’s reshuffle days before he was sacked as ambassador.

In an Aexchange of WhatsApps on September 5 2025 between Mandelson and Sir Keir’s chief of staff at the time, Morgan McSweeney, he tells Mr McSweeney to “solve your Darren issue” – referring to former chief secretary to the prime minister Darren Jones.

He also wrote: “Are you taking peter Kyle away….?” and asked where Mr McSweeney was, telling him: “I am in upstairs meeting room”.

open image in gallery Sir Olly Robbins, the former top civil servant at the Foreign Office, suggested a process to police conflicts of interest ‘in a light touch way’ (Dominic Lipinski/PA) ( PA Wire )

The messages were exchanged three days after the first batch of Epstein filed released by US lawmakers.

Days later, September 9 2025, the US government released documents which showed Mandelson describing Epstein as “my best pal”, and sent him other supportive messages, even as Epstein faced jail for sex offences.

He was sacked as US ambassador on September 11 amid growing pressure on the then-prime minister to remove him from office.

This story is being updated.

News.title: Tube strikes live: Lines shut and severe delays as Londoners face travel chaos
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

When are the tube strikes?

Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Severe disruption across the Tube network is affecting travellers across London today as drivers walk out for 24 hours, causing widespread delays and cancellations across the entire Underground network.

Thursday, 26 November marks the first of eight 24-hour walkouts by some Tube drivers as the Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT) calls on its members to strike in retaliation against plans to change their working patterns.

Strikes do not officially start until midday today, but services have already been reduced, while the entire Circle line has also been suspended ahead of the official kick-off. The Metropolitan line has also been partially suspended between Baker Street and Aldgate.

There have also been significant delays across the Tube network this morning during rush hour, with other TfL services such as the Elizabeth line also seeing more crowds than usual.

Bike rental companies also expect an increase in demand today and are positioning bikes where riders may need them most.

While some trains will still operate, disruption is expected across the Tube network.

After 9pm, Transport for London (TfL) says no Tube services are expected to run, but they should resume around 7am on Friday, 27 November.

While the strike officially ends at 12pm on Friday, normal services are not expected back until 6pm that day.

News.title: Santa gave me a lapdance at London’s most outrageous Christmas show
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The point at which I realised that Sophie’s Surprise Christmas Party at Underbelly’s Soho theatre wasn’t your average saccharine, schmaltzy holiday show is no longer clear to me.

It might have been when a juggler in a tight-fitting Christmas jumper shouted to “put on something festive” and the unmistakable sounds of Sean Paul blared out over the speaker; it might have been when Scrooge got a member of the audience up on stage and convinced them to draw on abs with a magic marker, turn their T-shirt into a crop top and start jumping to retrieve a digestive biscuit from a fishing rod using only their mouth. It had definitely happened by the time a camp, be-muscled “Jesus” whipped off his robes and started doing a high-octane acrobatic routine on an aerial contraption shaped like a cross to the pumping beat of Madonna’s “Just Like a Prayer”, clad only in a spangly loin cloth and crown of thorns.

The creation of Three Legged Race Productions, this new show is a Christmas follow-up to the Nineties-inspired Sophie’s Surprise 29th, in which circus meets risque comedy and cabaret alongside a healthy dose of audience participation. The biggest example of the latter is the selection, at each performance, of a random audience member to play the eponymous Sophie. The night I attended, I was lucky enough to nab this hallowed role.

open image in gallery Throwing shapes: Performers achieve impressive acrobatic displays on the dinky stage ( Roger Robinson )

Well, I say “lucky”. It certainly felt that way to me. For my performance-shy plus one, it would have been their literal worst nightmare. Thankfully, the cast didn’t mix us up as they led me, not her, onto the small, in-the-round stage to kick off the show.

It adds a whole new element of excitement to proceedings – not quite knowing what might be asked of me next – although it’s all designed to be as straightforward as possible, and no special skills are required other than being able to follow simple instructions like “stand here” and “sit there”. (The level of participation does, admittedly, ramp up somewhat as the show progresses, building to a stunt with a unicycle that necessitates a high level of trust – and a stiff drink afterwards.)

open image in gallery Helen earns her stripes as 'Sophie' ( Helen Coffey )

Sophie – aka me – is only up a few times during the show and otherwise gets to chill in the audience with the other punters. The extremely loose “plot” involves Sophie having lost her (literal) Christmas spirit; how that relates to me sitting in a chair getting a lapdance off a small but extremely buff Santa, Magic Mike-style, while he gyrates to Genuwine’s “Pony” (and keeps saying to me, rather disconcertingly, “Yeah, mama!”), is anyone’s guess. I’m cringing/giggling too hard to care.

The first half gets off to a slightly sluggish start – partly because of the choice of segments themselves, partly because, to put it bluntly, the audience is still too buttoned-up and sober at the rather early 7pm start time – but there’s a real gear change post-interval as things get more rowdy, raucous and fun. One minute we’re watching a woman dressed as a robot being swung round by the neck by her male counterpart on roller skates at a frankly alarming speed; the next, a naked man on a unicycle is trying (and failing) to dress himself without flashing his nether regions; the next, Scrooge’s dead wife performs a strangely moving routine using aerial silks to Jeff Buckley’s “Hallelujah”.

open image in gallery Jesus and an inexplicable Playboy bunny take to the air to show the real meaning of Christmas ( Roger Robinson )

It passes by in a whirlwind of laughter, adrenaline and gasps of amazement, and in the blink of an eye I’m back up onstage taking a somewhat undeserved bow with the rest of the outrageously talented cast. Drinking in the applause, I feel like my inability to execute an advanced tumbling routine or accurately catch a custard cream on my foot no longer matters: now, I am one of them.

I greet my adoring fans as we shuffle out of the theatre and tell them the score – no, I’m not a professional actor (yet!); yes, I was just a regular audience member who stepped up when power was thrust upon her. Some look envious, while an equal number look relieved. I, as it turns out, feel utterly exhilarated. In a world saturated with twee, mawkish festive fare, it turns out that seeing Jesus doing a spinning aerial duet with a half-naked Playboy bunny is just the tonic I needed to experience the real meaning of Christmas this year.

Sophie’s Surprise Christmas Party is playing at Underbelly Soho Boulevard in London until 10 January. Tickets from £23.50.

Authorities scrambled to a bomb threat at the Royal Navy’s headquarters in Portsmouth on Thursday.

The threat was made against HMS Excellent in a telephone call.

However, searches by police and Ministry of Defence personnel identified no threat at the base.

An investigation into the incident is ongoing.

As well as being the Royal Navy HQ, the base is also home to the navy’s Defence Diving School and the Phoenix Damage Repair Instructional Unit.

A Royal Navy spokesperson told The Independent: “The security incident at HMS Excellent has now concluded following a search Police and Ministry of Defence Personnel.

“The base remains fully operational and investigations into the incident are continuing.”

Sky News reported that a cordon was put in place at the site, which is located on Whale Island in the city.

News.title: Gordon Ramsay becomes grandfather as daughter Holly welcomes baby girl with Adam Peaty
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Holly Ramsay-Peaty, the daughter of celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay and Tana Ramsay, has given birth to her first child with husband Adam Peaty.

The 26-year-old announced the news on Instagram on Thursday, revealing her new daughter’s name: “Daphne June Ramsay-Peaty, Welcome to the World.”

“You’ll forever be our beautiful baby girl and George’s baby sister,” she continued in the caption. “Thank you to all the Doctors, Nurses and Midwives who made sure we were safe, healthy and happy - we will forever be grateful.”

Peaty, 31, shares son George from his previous relationship with Eirianedd Munro. The pair split in August 2022.

Holly announced she was pregnant on Instagram in June, six months after she and Peaty married in a star-studded ceremony at Bath Abbey. Their engagement was announced in September 2024, after Peaty proposed during a holiday in Crete.

open image in gallery Holly Ramsay-Peaty announced the birth of her daughter on Instagram ( Instagram )

open image in gallery Gordon Ramsay is officially a grandfather less than a year after he walked his daughter down the aisle ( PA Wire )

The gold medal-winning athlete reportedly met Holly through her sister Tilly when they both participated in the BBC dancing programme Strictly Come Dancing in 2021.

Their wedding, however, followed reports of a family feud. According to the Daily Mail, the dispute escalated after Peaty’s mother, Caroline, was reportedly not invited to Holly’s hen do.

The Sun also reported that Peaty’s parents had described Gordon as “a big bully” who had “pushed them too far”.

Gordon Ramsay vehemently dismissed these claims as “absolute nonsense”.

He told the newspaper: “I’m certainly not a bully. I think when you send personal chauffeur cars up to Nottingham to invite this incredible family down to enjoy their party – by the way Holly and Adam were hosting that party, Caroline and Mark (Peaty’s parents), Tana (Ramsay’s wife) and I were guests – (it’s) appalling to even suggest there was any bullying. That’s absolute nonsense.”

He continued: “Secondly, opening up my door, welcoming them into the family, at the end of the day there was a lot of friction going on before all that and so there was some stuff that they needed to sort it out, and so it was sad to see that barrage of negativity that was self-propelled by them. I think once you start enjoying that kind of press attention and you revel in it, you’re sort of feeding the beast.”

Gordon and Tana are also parents to Megan, 28, Jack, 26, Tilly, 25, Oscar, seven, and Jesse, two.

Gordon paid tribute to Holly last week as she was forced to miss his Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony.

He told the crowd: “The Ramsay household is getting bigger. We welcome our first grandchild in a couple of days from now.”
