Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

After his statement, Justice Adewunmi-Oshin permitted the trustees to serve Form 48 and other court documents on him through substituted service.

The judge approved three methods: publication in a widely circulated newspaper, pasting the documents at a conspicuous spot at his last known Lagos address, and electronic delivery.

Justice Adewunmi-Oshin issued the ex parte order on 18 November, barring Mr Odukoya from claiming the position of the church’s senior pastor and spiritual head, either directly or through proxies.

The order also prohibits him from disrupting the church’s activities, interfering with its governance or obstructing its operations.

The Incorporated Trustees of The Fountain of Life Church instituted the case under suit number LD/0126PRA/2026.

They told the court that Mr Odukoya had ceased to hold the position after the late Taiwo Odukoya purportedly appointed a successor under the church’s constitution.

The judge permitted the trustees to initiate the proceedings under the Lagos State High Court’s pre-action protocol and ordered them to serve Mr Odukoya with the originating processes and other accompanying documents.

The court, however, preserved his right to challenge the order or respond to the substantive claims once the trustees serve him.

Backstory

The court proceedings stem from a growing leadership crisis at the church, which Taiwo and Bimbo Odukoya established in 1992.

A group identifying itself as the church’s trustees announced Mr Odukoya’s removal and appointed Rotimi Okpaise as interim spiritual and administrative leader.

The trustees also published a purported succession video in which the late founder named Adekunle Areogun as his preferred successor and assigned Mr Odukoya an administrative role.

Mr Odukoya and his supporters rejected the announcement and insisted that he remained the church’s senior pastor.

He later filed a separate suit at the Federal High Court in Lagos to challenge the decision, naming his sister, Tolu Odukoya, and several trustees as respondents.

He is asking the court to invalidate the trustees’ resolutions and declare his removal unconstitutional under the church’s governing document.

Mr Odukoya had not reacted to the arrest order as of press time.

A review of his Facebook page, however, showed a post announcing the church’s “Thursday Showers” service.

World.title: Oborevwori’s aide resigns over Uduere killings, alleges intimidation of opposition
World.content:
A Senior Special Assistant to Delta State Governor Sheriff Oborevwori, Tonia Gbemre, has resigned her appointment over the killing of six people at a campaign rally in Uduere community, Ughelli North Local Government Area, and alleged persistent intimidation of opposition supporters in the state.

Ms Gbemre announced her decision in a resignation statement she subsequently shared on her Facebook page, expressing anger and disappointment over the killings and what she described as the government’s failure to adequately protect lives and guarantee citizen safety.

Her resignation comes amid mounting concerns over political violence in Delta State following Monday’s attack on supporters of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) during a campaign tour by former Deputy Senate President Ovie Omo-Agege, the party’s candidate for Delta Central Senatorial District in the 2027 elections.

The court on Tuesday nullified Mr Omo-Agege’s nomination as the NDC senatorial candidate.

The police confirmed that six people died in the attack, revising the initial casualty figure of four announced by Mr Omo-Agege’s campaign organisation.

Among those killed were Moses Anaughe, a former member of the Delta State House of Assembly, and Efemena Umukoro, popularly known as Comrade Akima, a prominent Urhobo youth activist.

In her resignation statement, Ms Gbemre questioned why young Nigerians should lose their lives because of their political affiliations or their decision to support candidates of their choice.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I am a mother. I cannot continue to watch our children being killed just because of politics. I cannot work under a government where human life is not treated as important,” she said.

She also accused political actors in the state of persistently intimidating, harassing and abusing opposition members and supporters seeking to exercise their democratic rights by campaigning for candidates outside the ruling political establishment.

Ms Gbemre said she could no longer remain in an administration that, in her view, was not doing enough to protect citizens, particularly as political activities intensify ahead of the 2027 general elections.

She called on Mr Oborevwori to take responsibility for the security of residents, stressing that the protection of lives and property should take precedence over political interests.

She also urged the governor to caution local government chairpersons, political leaders and community stakeholders against actions capable of preventing opposition parties from freely organising political activities and mobilising supporters.

The resignation adds to the growing political fallout from the Uduere killings, which have triggered demands for accountability and raised fresh concerns about the safety of political actors and supporters in the state.

On Wednesday, the Speaker of the Delta State House of Assembly, Dennis Guwor, condemned the killings and called for a thorough investigation, warning political actors against violence, intimidation and lawlessness ahead of the 2027 elections.

Governor Oborevwori had also visited Uduere following the attack and directed security agencies to apprehend those responsible.

The police said they have commenced an investigation into the incident, while allegations concerning the identities and roles of those responsible remain under investigation.

Ms Gbemre’s resignation and subsequent videos condemning the killings have further amplified calls for the state government to address concerns about political violence and guarantee the rights of opposition supporters.

World.title: The odds moved while you were making coffee — what probably happened?
World.content:
At 9:15, the home win costs 2.10. By lunch it is 1.84.

Annoying, if you liked the first number.

There is no message explaining what happened. Just a shorter price, a reshuffled market and, possibly, three people in the group chat claiming they saw it coming. While the bizbet promosyon kodu conditions sit open in another tab, the match price quietly drops from 2.10 to 1.84. No, your memory has not failed.

Why? There are a few suspects.

Somebody may be missing

Team information does not arrive in one neat package. A local reporter notices that a forward missed training. Later, the club bus arrives without him. The official line-up appears much later.

By then, the price may have gone.

The effect depends on the player. One missing winger in a deep squad might barely trouble the market; take away the goalkeeper and both centre-backs, though, and traders have something less comfortable to price.

There are false alarms as well. A player is absent from an open session because he worked indoors. Social media decides he is injured. Twenty minutes later, another reporter says he is fine.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

And the odds? They may jump twice.

Or everybody backed the famous shirt

Money moves prices too.

Picture a popular club playing away against an unfashionable opponent. Some bettors recognise the badge, remember last weekend’s win and stop their research there. As the same selection fills more slips, bookmakers may cut its price.

Was that clever money? Not necessarily.

The rough trail might look like this:

Time checked Home Draw Away Morning 3.60 3.30 2.05 Early afternoon 3.80 3.40 1.92 Near kick-off 4.05 3.55 1.80

Here, the away side keeps getting shorter. That is all the table can honestly confirm. The names behind the bets—and their reasons—remain hidden.

Were they right? The match has not started yet.

Look around before following the move

The number changes. Fine. Now find out what was happening around the same time.

Useful checks include:

a confirmed starting eleven;

a late injury or suspension update;

a change of venue or difficult weather;

similar movement across the wider market;

the exact time the price began to shift.

Timing can give a clue. Movement straight after line-ups are published probably has something to do with the names on that sheet. A slow change throughout the day may be ordinary betting pressure.

Or a mixture of both. Football rarely labels the evidence for us.

One isolated move deserves a closer look. A service may have responded to activity on its own platform while the wider market remained stable. If several prices move together, there may be a broader reason for the change.

The old price is not yours yet

Seeing 1.95 on screen does not secure 1.95.

Leave the selection untouched for a few minutes and the confirmation box may now say 1.88. Depending on the chosen account setting, the changed price could require another tap or be accepted without one.

So pause.

After reaching the account through bizbet giriş güncel, a bettor should read the accepted price on the final slip rather than rely on a screenshot taken before submission. The receipt is the record. An open tab is only an open tab.

Suppose the stake is 100 units:

At 1.95, a win returns 195.

At 1.88, it returns 188.

The profit falls from 95 to 88.

Nothing mysterious there. Seven units disappeared because the accepted odds were shorter.

Shorter does not mean safe

This is the trap, honestly.

Once a price falls far enough, the team begins to look more likely to win simply because everybody can see the fall. People join late. The number shortens again. Now the movement itself feels like proof.

It is not.

The favourite can concede from a corner after four minutes. The supposedly injured striker can start. A leaked line-up can be fake. All perfectly possible.

Odds contain information, opinion and the bookmaker’s margin, with public behaviour mixed through the lot.

Watch them if you find the movement useful. Compare morning and closing prices, sure.

But do not turn a shrinking number into a promise. The market gets no place on the scoresheet.

World.title: Plateau Attack: Death toll rises to 19
World.content:
By Golok Nanmwa

JOS — The death toll from an attack on Tafi-Gana (Cando Zrreci), a community in Jebbu Miango, Bassa Local Government Area of Plateau State, has risen to 19 following the death of three persons who were rushed to hospital after the incident.

The attack reportedly occurred on Wednesday night, November 25, and continued into the early hours of Thursday, November 26, 2026, throwing the community into confusion, fear and panic.

A resident of the community, Moses Monday, who confirmed the casualty figure on Thursday, said 16 bodies were recovered at the scene, while three other victims died after being taken to hospital.

Monday said: “This is evil. I can confirm that 16 bodies have so far been recovered at the spot, with an additional three who died after they were taken to the hospital. These evil men will not rest.”

Another resident, Nuhu Fidelis, who also confirmed the attack, described it as another assault on a neighbouring community in Jebbu Miango.

Fidelis said: “Yes, in the early morning of today, Thursday. Last night, November 25, 2026, a Christian neighbouring village, Tafi-Gana (Cando Zrreci), in Jebbu Miango, Bassa LGA, Plateau State, was attacked again. Many innocent people lost their lives.”

He condemned the killings and called on the government and security agencies to take urgent measures to protect residents.

Another resident, Paul Nehemiah, who said he lost a close relative in the attack, described the killings as wicked and unprovoked, adding that residents had been living in fear following repeated attacks.

Nehemiah said: “We are tired of burying our people. These are farmers, women and children who did nothing to anyone. How long will this continue? We are calling on the government to rise up and save us.”

Rita Joseph, whose family fled the village during the attack, said community members could no longer sleep peacefully because of persistent security threats.

She said: “We ran into the bush with our children.”

The residents appealed to the Plateau State Government, the Federal Government and security agencies to deploy more personnel to Miango and surrounding communities to prevent further attacks.

They also urged the authorities to take decisive action to bring the perpetrators to justice and restore confidence among residents.

Efforts to obtain comments from the Plateau State Police Command spokesman, SP Alfred Alabo, and his counterpart at Operation Enduring Peace, Captain Polycarp Chinonso Oteh, were unsuccessful, as they had yet to respond to inquiries by our correspondent as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: Tinubu housing projects deliver over 26,000 units, 525,100 jobs, APC-PCC says
World.content:
President Tinubu

…As MOFI implements N1 trillion mortgage programme

By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA: The All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council APC-PCC said on Thursday thst the President Bola Tinubu administration has facilitated the financing and delivery of over 26,000 housing units and generated 525,100 real estate construction jobs nationwide in the past three years.

Spokesperson of the council, Dele Alake, made the claim in a statement issued in Abuja.

According to the statement, the Ministry of Finance Incorporated MOFI, through the MOFI Real Estate Investment Fund (MREIF), has provided more than N158 billion in mortgage financing to 2,269 homebuyers as of October 31, 2026.

The statement said the fund financed properties valued at more than N279 billion, while 695 housing units have received offtake guarantees, “creating a ready market for private-sector property development”.

It said 6,620 properties have been listed on the fund’s platform, with 21 financial institutions providing mortgage services across 28 states and all six geopolitical zones.

MREIF, a N1 trillion housing finance programme sponsored by MOFI, commenced operations on March 17, 2025, to expand access to affordable mortgages and mobilise private investment in the housing sector.

The statement said beneficiaries can access mortgage loans at an interest rate of 9.75 per cent per annum, with repayment periods of up to 20 years and a minimum equity contribution of 10 per cent.

It added that the fund raised an initial N250 billion, made up of N150 billion in concessionary Federal Government funding and N100 billion in private commercial investment.

“To enable more Nigerians to own homes, President Tinubu’s administration recognises that affordable mortgage loans, reasonably priced developer financing, and local production of building materials are crucial to reducing housing costs and expanding construction activities,” the statement said.

On construction, the council said the Federal Ministry of Housing and Urban Development is building 10,328 housing units at different stages of completion under the Renewed Hope Cities and Estates Programme.

These include 2,744 units at the Renewed Hope City in Abuja, 2,000 in Kano and 2,084 in Lagos, while another 3,500 units are being developed under the Renewed Hope Estates Programme across 14 states.

The Federal Housing Authority FHA, it said, is delivering 3,341 units, including 1,550 units for armed forces personnel in Jabi, Abuja. The Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria FMBN accounts for another 11,294 housing units, comprising 9,076 units financed between 2024 and 2025 and 2,218 units delivered in the first quarter of 2026.

According to the statement, the ministry’s housing projects are estimated to have generated 258,200 employment opportunities, while FMBN’s interventions have generated 226,900. It said FMBN disbursed more than N120 billion in housing and mortgage loans in 2025.

The council said the Federal Government has also introduced the Renewed Hope Social Housing Programme, which targets 77,400 housing units across the 774 Local Government Areas (LGAs).

“So far, the fund has catalysed the conditions needed to deliver housing at scale through financial institutions, capital markets, and the building materials sector, while deepening Nigeria’s mortgage market,” the statement said.

World.title: FIFA confirms cyberattack, says hackers stole personal, business data
World.content:
Infantino

By Adegboyega Adeleye

FIFA has confirmed a criminal cyberattack that exposed a limited amount of personal and business information, while files linked to its abandoned World Cup stake-sale plan were not accessed.

According to Reuters, a person with direct knowledge of the incident said less than 0.1 per cent of FIFA’s total data was affected and no files from the FIFA Forward Enterprise project were accessed.

“FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information,” a FIFA spokesperson told Reuters.

The football governing body condemned the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data, calling it “a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy”.

FIFA did not disclose when the attack took place, how many people or organisations were affected, or what business information was accessed. It also did not say whether any data had appeared online or where it may have been published.

FIFA scrapped plans in July to sell private investors a stake in a new unit that would manage its events, including the World Cup. The proposal aimed to raise up to $4.2 billion by selling a 20 per cent stake.

World.title: Meet Nigeria’s Damilola Bolarinde, crowned Miss International Africa 2026
World.content:
By Enitan Abdultawab

Nigerian beauty queen Damilola Bolarinde has been crowned Miss International Africa 2026 after representing the country at the 64th edition of the Miss International pageant in Tokyo, Japan.

The continental title was announced on Thursday, November 26, a day after the grand finale held on November 25, which featured 73 contestants from different countries.

Bolarinde, popularly known as Queen Dammy, secured a place among the Top 20 contestants but did not advance to the Top 10. Her performance at the competition earned her the Miss International Africa title.

The achievement adds to her growing profile in the Nigerian beauty pageant industry, having represented Lagos State at the 2025 Miss Universe Nigeria competition, where she emerged first runner-up behind Anambra State representative, Onyinyechi Basil.

In April 2026, Bolarinde won the Face of Hope pageant, earning the right to represent Nigeria at the Miss International competition as Miss International Nigeria 2026.

She defeated contestants representing Anambra and Rivers states, who finished as first and second runners-up, respectively, at the event held on April 19 at the Eko Convention Centre in Lagos.

Meanwhile, Elizaveta Kuznetsova of Moldova won the overall Miss International 2026 crown, becoming the first contestant from her country to claim the title.

Brittany Feeney of the United Kingdom finished as first runner-up, while Laura Glozarová of the Czech Republic came third.

Victoria Kosasieputri of Indonesia and Khánh Như Lê of Vietnam completed the Top Five, finishing fourth and fifth, respectively.

Bolarinde’s continental recognition marks another milestone in her pageant career and adds Nigeria to the list of countries represented among the award recipients at the international competition.

World.title: Ever Joj Gold, KimmelFX, Baracai, SohCahToa Payout BDC and Others to Benefit as CBN Approves $1 Million Cash Sales to BDCs
World.content:
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has approved an increase in the amount of foreign currency banks can sell in physical cash to Bureau De Change (BDC) operators, allowing eligible operators to access up to $1 million in cash.

The new directive, which takes effect Wednesday, November 25, 2026, represents a significant adjustment to the previous arrangement, under which banks were permitted to sell a maximum of $150,000 weekly to BDCs, with only 25% of the allocation available for physical cash withdrawals.

Under the revised arrangement, the entire approved allocation can now be accessed in cash, potentially improving the availability of physical foreign currency in Nigeria’s retail foreign exchange market.

CBN Releases List of BDC Operators to Banks

The list released by the CBN to banks includes several Bureau De Change operators across the country, among them Ever Joj Gold Bureau De Change Limited, KimmelFX Bureau De Change Limited, Baracai Bureau De Change Limited and SohCahToa Payout BDC, alongside other operators.

The document contains the names of the listed operators across different locations in Nigeria.

The development provides further insight into the operators covered by the latest adjustment to the foreign exchange cash allocation framework.

CBN Intervention Expected to Support FX Market Liquidity

The CBN’s decision represents a notable intervention aimed at improving the supply of physical foreign currency to the retail market.

By allowing the full approved allocation to be accessed in cash, the policy could ease some of the supply constraints previously faced by BDC operators and improve access to foreign currency for individuals and businesses with legitimate cash requirements.

The apex bank is also expected to provide additional cash liquidity to banks where necessary to facilitate the transactions.

The intervention comes amid renewed pressure on the Naira and increased demand for foreign exchange towards the end of the year.

The CBN Governor, Olayemi Cardoso, had previously attributed the recent pressure on the Naira to seasonal factors, including portfolio investors adjusting their positions, domestic businesses positioning against possible foreign exchange movements and increased spending ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The Naira closed at N1,396.50/$ at the official foreign exchange market on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, representing a depreciation from the N1,393/$ recorded the previous trading day.

The CBN’s latest intervention is a welcome step towards strengthening foreign exchange availability, improving market liquidity and supporting the operations of authorised BDC operators. Its sustained impact will depend on effective implementation and continued access to foreign currency supply.

World.title: Opposition coalition confirms Monday summit, to adopt 3 key documents
World.content:
By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA: The Coalition for Democracy has confirmed that the Second Summit of Nigeria’s opposition political parties will hold on Monday in Abuja, with participating parties expected to adopt three foundational documents.

The coalition is a multiparty platform pioneered by the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and Social Democratic Party (SDP).

In a statement signed by Salihu Moh. Lukman on behalf of the coalition parties, it said the decision was reached on Wednesday night at the seventh meeting of its Central Leadership Committee.

The statement said the leaders reached the decision “following extensive deliberations on the state of the nation, the prevailing political environment and the earlier resolution to suspend campaign activities on day of the Summit”.

The leaders, however, made it clear that the suspension does not end inter-party engagement.

“The leaders agreed that the suspension of campaign activities does not preclude the continuation of consultations and engagements among opposition political parties on matters of common interest, including electoral integrity, democratic participation and institutional reform,” the statement said.

The documents to be considered and adopted are the National Covenant for Democratic Renewal, the Framework for Opposition Unity and the National Reform Programme. They were developed by working groups made up of representatives of the constituent parties after the inaugural summit of August 31, 2026.

According to the statement, “the documents set out proposed mechanisms for inter-party cooperation and a framework for addressing national governance challenges.”

The coalition leaders also reaffirmed their commitment “to working collectively to safeguard the integrity of the electoral process and protect the sanctity of the ballot across the country”.

The coalition invited other opposition political parties to participate in the summit and “contribute to the ongoing consultations”.

Three personalities will address the summit on the theme, “The Doctrine of a Necessary Democratic Opposition”. They are the Alaago of Kajola Alago, Ileshan, HRH Oba Oladipo Olaitan; Prof. Ango Abdullahi; and Chief S. N. Okeke.

The statement said the summit is expected to bring together “national leaders of opposition political parties, elected representatives, former public officeholders, civil society leaders, representatives of the media, and observers from foreign diplomatic missions in Nigeria”.

World.title: 2027: We’ll protect voters, INEC, parties, others — FG
World.content:
Ribadu

– You can’t sign peace accord in Abuja and fund terror in states, INEC tells parties

– Says nine states hit by violence, lists effects on electoral process

– Faults rule requiring presiding officers’ order before police can arrest electoral offenders

By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA — The Federal Government has assured voters, politicians, electoral officials and political parties of adequate protection before, during and after the 2027 general election.

The National Security Adviser (NSA), Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, gave the assurance on Thursday at the Strategic Election Security Conference, jointly convened in Abuja by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA).

“The duty of government and the security agencies is to protect voters, electoral officials and the wider population before, during and after the election. We will protect you. We will protect the voters. We will protect politicians. And even after the election, we will make sure there is no violence,” he declared.

He said the administration of President Bola Tinubu was “committed to providing the security necessary for peaceful, transparent and credible elections”.

Ribadu pledged that security agencies would act impartially, noting that their constitutional independence “must be protected and respected, especially now that we have a professor of law heading INEC”.

“Security agencies will discharge their responsibilities impartially and in accordance with the law,” he added.

On emerging threats, he singled out social media, describing it as a major source of misinformation and false narratives.

“Social media is a big problem. It creates false narratives and misinformation, causing problems among people. One individual, sitting somewhere in a village, could say something that triggers trouble,” he said.

He also warned against the conduct of politicians desperate to gain power, saying, “Sometimes they become desperate. There is almost nothing they may not do.”

The INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, SAN, warned political parties against signing peace accords in Abuja while allegedly sponsoring violence in the states.

“Signing peace accords in Abuja while tolerating or financing thuggery in the states is a contradiction our democracy can no longer afford,” he said.

Amupitan said that since open campaigns began in August 2026, Nigeria had witnessed “a disturbing escalation in political intolerance, incendiary rhetoric, and coordinated physical attacks” on campaign convoys, town hall gatherings, party offices and supporters in nine states: Lagos, Edo, Ekiti, Enugu, Ebonyi, Delta, Cross River, Oyo and Benue.

He said the attacks were not limited to party supporters, adding that INEC leadership, staff and ad hoc workers had also been harassed, intimidated and physically attacked by supporters and agents of political parties, both within Nigeria and abroad.

“We will neither be intimidated nor blackmailed into compromising our neutrality, and every attack on INEC personnel, facilities, or materials will be met with the full weight of the law,” he said.

He added that accountability “does not end with the foot soldiers who throw stones or wield weapons”, stressing that “party leadership bears moral and political responsibility for the conduct of its candidates, campaign councils, and youth wings”.

The INEC chairman identified three major consequences of the violence for the electoral process, beginning with voter suppression.

“When bullets replace ballots and rallies end in bloodshed, ordinary citizens stay home, effectively disenfranchising millions of peaceful Nigerians,” he said.

The second concern, he said, was the safety of the more than 1.41 million ad hoc personnel, most of them National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members, to be deployed across 177,299 polling units.

“No parent or institution will willingly deploy young Nigerians into environments where political thugs operate with impunity,” he said.

He identified the third consequence as the impact of pre-election violence on the post-election environment.

“Pre-election violence conditions the political climate for post-election rejection,” he said, warning that collation centres could become flashpoints.

Amupitan said the stakes extended beyond Nigeria to the West African sub-region, noting that the country accounts for more than half of its population. He said a peaceful election would serve as “the primary anchor of regional stability and constitutional order”.

On enforcement, the INEC chairman faulted a provision in the Regulations and Guidelines for the Conduct of Elections, 2026, which he said requires security agents to obtain instructions from presiding officers or other INEC officials before arresting electoral offenders.

“This dichotomy has hampered the efficiency of the law enforcement agents to arrest and investigate electoral offenders,” he said.

He noted that the regulations also empower security agents to prevent violence and activities capable of disrupting elections, and called for the issue to be addressed through a code of conduct and a proposed legal framework for the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES).

Amupitan said the Electoral Act 2026 increased penalties for electoral offences to fines of up to N5 million or 12 months’ imprisonment for individuals, and up to N10 million for political parties committing first-time breaches.

He added that Section 148 of the Act empowers INEC legal officers and appointed counsel to prosecute offenders directly once case files are transmitted by the police and other relevant agencies.

“INEC is fully prepared to discharge its prosecutorial mandate, and our legal teams are ready to review case files from recent violent incidents across the federation.

“When political actors see prominent sponsors and foot soldiers swiftly arrested, arraigned, and convicted under the 2026 Act, the incentive for violent campaigns will evaporate,” he said.

Amupitan said the presidential and National Assembly elections would hold on Saturday, January 16, 2027, while governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections would take place on Saturday, February 6, 2027.

He also announced that INEC would conduct a nationwide mock accreditation and result transmission exercise on Saturday, November 28, urging security commanders to treat it as a full-scale rehearsal.

World.title: Abia Missing Nurse: Rights group, S’East youths demand answers over alleged police release
World.content:
– Demand probe, immediate rescue of Chiamaka

– Raise alarm over criminal gangs allegedly operating under guise of Keke, shuttle bus operators

By Steve Oko

UMUAHIA — A human rights organisation, the African Centre for Human Advancement and Resource Support (CHARS-Africa), and the Coalition of South East Youth Leaders (COSEYL) have demanded urgent intervention and a transparent investigation into the disappearance of Fortunate Chiamaka, a nursing graduate of Abia State University, Uturu, amid allegations that she was released from police custody before the arrival of a family member.

The groups, in separate statements, expressed concern over the circumstances surrounding Chiamaka’s disappearance, saying she reportedly went missing on Monday, November 23, 2026, after leaving home for afternoon duty at Abia State Specialist Hospital, Umuahia.

She was suspected to have been abducted on her way to work by a criminal syndicate commonly known as ‘One Chance’, whose members reportedly operate commercial tricycles and shuttle buses.

Chiamaka, who graduated from ABSU earlier this year, is currently undergoing an internship at Abia State Specialist Hospital, Umuahia, and lives with her parents at Amuzukwu, Umuahia.

The development has raised fresh concerns following allegations by her father, Mr Phillip Aku, that his daughter was earlier found in a confused and disoriented condition around Umuekaa, Isiala Ngwa South, by a Good Samaritan who reportedly took her to a police station for protection.

However, rather than keep her in protective custody until her family could be contacted, the police allegedly released her on the grounds that they had no facility to keep her.

When her father eventually arrived at the Umuekaa police station on Tuesday, officers reportedly could not produce her. Instead, they allegedly asked him for financial assistance to fuel their vehicle for a search.

CHARS-Africa described the reported circumstances as deeply troubling, insisting that a police facility entrusted with protecting vulnerable persons must guarantee their safety, dignity and fundamental human rights.

The organisation called on the Nigeria Police Force to urgently clarify the circumstances surrounding her disappearance, disclose her last known whereabouts and take immediate steps to locate her and ensure her safe return.

It also demanded a transparent investigation into the incident and accountability for anyone found culpable, while urging the authorities to protect the missing woman’s identity and privacy.

“Seeking protection in a government facility must never become a pathway to disappearance,” the group said, stressing that the safety of every citizen was a collective responsibility.

Similarly, COSEYL expressed outrage over the alleged circumstances surrounding Chiamaka’s disappearance, describing the reported handling of the matter as a potential failure of duty and betrayal of public trust if established.

The youth coalition questioned how a woman reportedly found in a vulnerable and disoriented condition could be taken to a police station and subsequently disappear without her identity being established or her family contacted.

It demanded answers from the Abia State Police Command on who authorised her alleged release, whether her presence and custody were documented, and what measures were taken to identify her or ensure her safety.

COSEYL called for an independent and transparent investigation into the incident, insisting that officers found culpable should face appropriate disciplinary and legal consequences.

The group also urged Governor Alex Otti to personally intervene and direct the deployment of all necessary security resources to locate Chiamaka. It called for collaboration among the police, Department of State Services (DSS) and other security agencies to intensify the search.

Beyond the missing nurse’s case, COSEYL raised concerns over alleged criminal syndicates operating under the guise of commercial tricycle and shuttle bus operators to lure, hypnotise, rob and abduct unsuspecting members of the public.

It urged the state government, police and other security agencies to launch intelligence-driven operations to identify and dismantle criminal networks allegedly exploiting commercial transportation in Umuahia and other parts of Abia.

The coalition called for stricter enforcement of transport regulations, proper identification of operators, regular security patrols and intelligence gathering around motor parks, bus stops and vulnerable routes.

It further advocated stronger community policing, functional emergency response mechanisms and collaboration among security agencies, transport unions and community leaders to address public safety concerns.

Both organisations urged residents of Umuahia, Isiala Ngwa South and neighbouring communities to remain vigilant and provide credible information that could help locate Chiamaka.

Anyone with useful information about her whereabouts was encouraged to contact her family on 07034907745 or report to the nearest police station.

The groups expressed solidarity with Chiamaka’s father, Phillip Aku, and the family, insisting that the case must not be swept under the carpet or allowed to fade from public attention.

They maintained that citizens must be able to seek protection from security agencies without fear of being exposed to further danger, stressing that the state has a duty to protect lives and ensure accountability.

World.title: Ozokwor Brings Story Of Nigeria’s Woman King, Ahebi Ugbabe, to Abuja Stage
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Michael Olugbode in Abuja

Veteran actress Patience Ozokwor is set to lead a theatrical exploration of the extraordinary life of Ahebi Ugbabe, a woman who rose to become a king in colonial-era southeastern Nigeria, as a musical stage drama brings her largely unusual political story to the Abuja audience on December 5.

The production, titled Ahebi: The Woman King, is produced by MOO Entertainment and will be staged at the NAF Conference Centre, Abuja, with performances scheduled for 7 p.m. and 9 p.m.

Born in Enugu-Ezike, present-day Enugu State, Ahebi occupied an exceptional position in the traditional political history of her community. At a time when leadership and political authority were largely reserved for men, she rose to become a warrant chief and subsequently a king, navigating the complex power relations between indigenous institutions and the colonial administration.

Her remarkable ascent challenges conventional narratives about gender and traditional authority in Igbo society, while raising important questions about political ambition, identity and the structures through which power was negotiated in colonial Nigeria.

Written by Ikechukwu Erojikwe and Chinonso Udeh, and directed by Erojikwe, the production combines drama, music, dance and traditional performance elements to recreate Ahebi’s life and the political circumstances surrounding her rise.

Ozokwor takes the titular role, supported by Grace Okonkwo, Boma Ilamina-Eremie, Emeka Uba, Hopez, Emmanuel Eyaba, Ozichukwu Kanu and Michael Eneje.

According to the creative team, the decision to bring Ahebi’s story to the stage followed historical research undertaken by Udeh and Aba Lambert Mmaduabuchi in 2017.

Udeh, the producer, and Erojikwe said the project was conceived to draw greater attention to an important historical personality whose life provides a compelling basis for examining the intersections of gender, culture and political authority.

The production has also benefited from the support of creative practitioners and institutions. Kolanut Gallery, managed by Ifesinachi Nwanyanwu, provided rehearsal space for the cast and crew, while the AMEMUSO Choir joined the project despite its existing performance commitments.

Music is a significant feature of the production, with songs, traditional rhythms and choreography complementing the dramatic reconstruction of Ahebi’s experience.

Beyond the extraordinary fact that a woman occupied a position traditionally associated with men, Ahebi’s story presents a more complex historical narrative involving her relationship with colonial authority and the indigenous political establishment.

Her rise was not simply a straightforward challenge to patriarchal traditions. It also reflected the ways individuals could negotiate, exploit and exercise authority within the political arrangements of their time.

Consequently, Ahebi: The Woman King seeks to move beyond presenting its central character merely as a symbol of women’s emancipation, examining instead the contradictions and complexities of a woman who broke established gender boundaries while operating within the power structures of her era.

The production is scheduled for December 5 at the NAF Conference Centre, Abuja.

World.title: Community Leaders Applaud DSS Operatives for Thwarting Kidnap Attempt in Lafia
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

…Three suspects arrested

Linus Aleke in Abuja

Community leaders in Lafia Local Government Area of Nasarawa State have commended the Department of State Services (DSS) for its sustained efforts to combat kidnapping and other violent crimes in the area.

The leaders praised the DSS for its timely intervention in thwarting a recent kidnapping attempt in the Isa Mustapha Agwai area of Lafia metropolis, describing the operatives as dedicated and professional in the discharge of their duties.

Chief Yahaya Mohammed, the Mai-Angwa of Farin Kasa community, who spoke on behalf of the leaders, expressed confidence in the DSS, noting that its operatives responded within minutes of receiving the distress call.

According to him, “Around midnight, some unidentified gunmen invaded our community and attempted to abduct residents. We immediately alerted DSS operatives, who swiftly arrived at the scene. The operatives exchanged gunfire with the abductors.’

He said the presence of the operatives had restored the community’s hope and confidence in the security arrangements, while acknowledging the collaboration among security agencies in the state.

“The DSS operatives were also supported by community vigilantes in the area,” he said.

Mohammed further appealed to security agencies to ensure that all suspects apprehended in connection with the incident were dealt with decisively in accordance with the law.

Meanwhile, the DSS has taken three suspects into custody in connection with the foiled attack. They are Hassan Musa, 19; Muhammadu Sani Idris, 20; and Sale Umaru Zangba, 47.

Zangba, a cleaner at a primary healthcare centre in the area, allegedly confessed to treating one of the suspects who sustained gunshot wounds during the foiled attack, the source added.

“The DSS has been working tirelessly to reduce criminal activities, and Nasarawa State has recorded significant successes,” the source noted.

He further disclosed that barely three weeks earlier, DSS operatives had arrested one Bello Abdullahi, a suspected arms courier, who was allegedly on his way to deliver weapons to bandits in Kebbi State.

In a related development, a suspected kidnapper was arrested while collecting ransom from a female resident of Nasarawa State.

“These suspects, like others, will face the full wrath of the law,” the source affirmed.

World.title: More Than Moral Voices: Why Climate Finance Needs Faith-Based Delivery Partners
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Godman Akinlabi

Climate commitments are only as meaningful as the institutions and systems capable of delivering them. The conclusion of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, offers an opportunity to examine the distance between global climate ambition and the realities confronting communities across developing countries. Financing remains critical, but money alone cannot build resilience, strengthen infrastructure or protect livelihoods. These outcomes depend on capable institutions, effective partnerships and locally grounded solutions that translate commitments into measurable impact.

This calls for broader recognition of the role faith-based organisations can play in the climate response. Beyond moral influence and advocacy, many have established institutions, community infrastructure, extensive networks and years of experience delivering social interventions. Properly equipped and supported, they can help translate climate finance into practical, accountable and community-centred action.

In my previous article, ‘Climate Change: Our Responsibility to Future Generations’, I examined every generation’s responsibility to safeguard the conditions for long-term prosperity. Climate change affects livelihoods, healthcare, education, infrastructure, economic opportunity and community resilience. At The Elevation Church, this commitment to investing in the future of the communities we serve is expressed through our Legacy Ministry, which provides the institutional platform for exploring how existing community development work can contribute to climate action. The conversation therefore extends beyond what faith-based organisations believe about stewardship to what their institutions can credibly deliver and how their community presence can support measurable, climate-aligned outcomes.

The Climate Finance Gap Requires Capable Delivery Institutions

The financing challenge remains considerable. The United Nations Environment Programme’s 2026 Adaptation Gap Report estimates that developing countries will require approximately US$305 billion annually by 2035 for adaptation, while international public adaptation finance from developed to developing countries reached only US$28.2 billion to US$31.7 billion in 2024.

However, the financing gap is not the only challenge. Available capital must be translated into credible projects, effective implementation and measurable community outcomes. Financing must reach well-designed projects, institutions able to execute them and communities where interventions can be sustained.

A climate-resilient hospital needs sound infrastructure, reliable energy, water systems, trained personnel and maintenance. A flood-resilient community needs drainage, responsible land-use planning, early-warning systems, preparedness and institutions able to coordinate action. An organisation may attract financing yet struggle to achieve impact without sound project preparation, technical expertise, governance, operational capacity and accountability.

For Africa, development priorities such as energy, healthcare, agriculture, transport and employment must account for climate risks, resilience, inclusion and sustainability.

Faith-based organisations can contribute because many operate where these priorities are urgent. Churches, mosques and other faith institutions run schools, healthcare facilities, shelters, community centres and social programmes. They support vulnerable households, mobilise volunteers, develop young people and maintain relationships formal development structures may struggle to establish. Yet community presence alone does not qualify an organisation for climate finance. Trust must be matched by technical competence, transparent governance, sound financial controls, safeguards and measurable outcomes.

From Community Trust to Institutional Climate Readiness

Faith-based organisations have an opportunity to move beyond being recognised solely as moral advocates and develop the capacity to participate meaningfully in climate finance and implementation. A promising intervention must become a properly defined project, with identifiable beneficiaries, technical specifications, implementation arrangements, cost estimates, financing requirements, environmental and social safeguards, and measurable outcomes.

Baselines and performance indicators must be established, and results monitored through credible reporting. Financial accountability must show how resources are received, allocated, monitored and accounted for. Governance must be clear, beneficiary information protected, and projected outcomes distinguished from independently verified results. These requirements enable partners and financiers to assess the credibility, viability and impact of proposed interventions.

Partnerships are equally critical because no single institution has every capability required to deliver climate solutions at scale. Governments provide policy direction and public infrastructure; development finance institutions and investors bring capital; technical organisations provide project design, engineering and measurement expertise; philanthropic institutions can support interventions that may not generate commercial returns; and community organisations contribute local knowledge, relationships and implementation experience.

Faith-based institutions must be prepared to contribute to this ecosystem, not operate outside it. Their community relationships and infrastructure can create valuable opportunities, but these must be developed with the technical, financial and institutional partners required for credible outcomes. Community trust can provide access and local understanding, while technical competence, governance and project readiness help turn that trust into investable, accountable interventions.

At The Elevation Church, this thinking informs our proposed Elevation Impact & Climate Finance Initiative (EICFI), developed with Carbonivity Limited as our technical and climate-finance architecture partner. The initiative seeks to organise selected elements of our Legacy Ministry ecosystem into a transparent pipeline of climate-aligned, measurable and finance-ready community development projects.

It provides a framework for assessing where existing programmes, facilities and community relationships can support credible climate interventions, with the technical expertise, financing structures, safeguards and accountability required for implementation. Existing social development infrastructure can provide a foundation for climate action where a demonstrable climate-related contribution can be established.

Legacy Ministry: The Vehicle for Climate-Aligned Community Impact

The Legacy Ministry is The Elevation Church’s vehicle for investing in the future of the communities it serves. It brings together our commitment to enduring social impact, community development, leadership, health, education and opportunity. Climate action carries the same responsibility to preserve the future, ensuring that progress today does not compromise tomorrow’s opportunities.

Through the proposed EICFI architecture, we are exploring how this commitment can extend into climate-aligned community development through four interconnected pilot areas, to be executed through the Legacy Ministry.

1. Sustainable and climate-smart legacy infrastructure. We are exploring assessments of selected community facilities, schools and healthcare assets for renewable energy, energy efficiency, water, sanitation and sustainable waste systems. The aim is to strengthen the reliability and environmental performance of infrastructure already serving communities, reduce environmental vulnerabilities and improve the resilience of facilities.

2. Circular economy and green enterprise. Waste management is an environmental challenge, but it also creates opportunities for enterprise and employment. Community collection, sorting, recycling and resource recovery, supported by qualified operators, can help develop viable businesses, particularly for young people and women. These models can connect environmental improvement with livelihoods and more sustainable communities.

3. Community resilience, education and inclusive livelihoods. Climate preparedness, environmental literacy, relevant skills and economic opportunity help communities respond to changing conditions. Existing platforms such as Find Your Voice Global and the Pistis Life and Leadership Institute can contribute through youth development, leadership capacity, mentorship and opportunity mobilisation. They can help strengthen the knowledge and skills communities need to respond to environmental and economic change, where interventions establish a clear climate-related contribution.

4. UBOMI climate-smart community health. UBOMI, the medical and surgical outreach of the Pistis Foundation, provides free consultations, surgeries, dental and eye care to underserved communities in Lagos, Ibadan and beyond. Healthcare depends on reliable electricity, safe water, sanitation, appropriate cold-chain systems and resilient clinical infrastructure. Assessing these needs through a climate lens can identify ways to improve continuity of care, resource efficiency and facility resilience while reducing environmental vulnerabilities.

These pilot areas reflect an important principle: existing social development infrastructure can provide a foundation for carefully designed climate interventions. The task is to identify genuine climate-aligned opportunities, develop them to appropriate technical and financial standards, and establish partnerships capable of delivering measurable results.

Healthcare, scholarships, shelter and poverty reduction remain valuable social interventions in their own right. They should be classified as climate-aligned only where a demonstrable connection to mitigation, adaptation, resilience, resource efficiency or an inclusive transition exists. The objective is not to retrofit a climate label onto every programme, but to identify credible opportunities and develop them with the rigour required.

The proposed EICFI architecture is working towards an indicative US$5 million catalytic funding mobilisation ambition over 24 months, alongside a follow-on project pipeline ambition of US$15 million to US$20 million. These are mobilisation and project-development targets, not funds already secured. Achieving them will require credible project preparation, institutional partnerships, appropriate financing instruments and rigorous validation.

Financing must reflect each intervention’s nature. Community healthcare and child protection may require philanthropic support and grants; infrastructure improvements may suit concessional financing or asset-based investment; and commercially viable recycling and green enterprise activities may attract recoverable or private capital following proper appraisal. The aim is not to turn every social programme into an investment proposition, but to ensure the right capital reaches the right projects and supports their intended outcomes and long-term sustainability.

Beyond Advocacy: Building the Capacity to Deliver

With COP31 concluded, the wider development community must pay greater attention to institutions capable of connecting global ambition with local implementation. Faith-based organisations should not be confined to moral voices in climate conversations when their infrastructure, relationships, programmes and networks may offer valuable pathways for delivery.

This opportunity must be approached with discipline. Community trust must be supported by institutional competence, social programmes by credible governance, and ambitions by projects that withstand technical scrutiny and demonstrate measurable value. Faith-based organisations must collaborate beyond familiar institutional boundaries because climate change does not respect religious, geographical or organisational divisions. Solutions must be inclusive, and benefits must reach people according to need rather than religious affiliation.

The Legacy Ministry represents The Elevation Church’s investment in the future of the communities we serve. The proposed EICFI architecture offers an opportunity to extend that commitment into the climate conversation by assessing and developing selected programmes and infrastructure into climate-aligned interventions capable of attracting appropriate partnerships and financing. These ambitions remain subject to project preparation, technical assessment, validation and implementation.

The direction is clear: strengthen the institutions, systems and partnerships required to protect progress and extend its benefits into the future. Meaningful climate action must be rooted in the capacity to deliver.

The Global South’s financing gap cannot be closed by capital alone. It requires credible institutions, project developers, technical partners, financiers and community organisations working together. Faith-based organisations belong in this ecosystem because of the institutions they have built, the communities they serve and the capacity they can develop. Their participation must be earned through readiness, partnerships and accountability.

In my previous reflection, I argued that a generation cannot call itself progressive if its prosperity undermines the conditions for future prosperity. Climate action gives that responsibility practical expression: preserving the future and building institutions capable of sustaining progress.

Global commitments matter, but their true value will be determined by what communities experience. The future depends on the institutions we strengthen, communities we invest in, partnerships we build and lives we improve. That is the work of legacy. This work must start today. It is a responsibility we share.

Godman Akinlabi is a renowned leadership expert, author, and the Global Lead Pastor of The Elevation Church. He is widely recognised as a leading voice on leadership, purpose, and personal transformation.

* Akinlabi is the Global Lead Pastor, The Elevation Church

World.title: Osubi Airport Holds Full-Scale Emergency Simulation In Delta
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Sylvester Idowu in Warri

The management of Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN), Alfred Diete-Spiff Airport, Osubi, on Tuesday, conducted a simulation air crash rescue operation to assess its readiness in responding to air crashes and other emergencies.

The authority has also restated its total commitment to tackling emergency situations, noting that its collaboration within and outside the sector would go a long way in enhancing its readiness to comply with the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) recommended practices.

The exercise, which commenced at about 1:30pm, simulated an aircraft crash that left several passengers with varying degrees of injuries, triggering an emergency response by the airport’s emergency management team and external assisting agencies, including Delta Procare Hospital, Nigerian Navy Hospital, Delta State Fire Service, Nigeria Red Cross, Port Health Service of the NPA, Nigerian Navy Air Station (Fire Service) Renaissance Fire (Shell) and Nigerian Civil Defence.

The simulation was designed to assess the airport’s preparedness, test the efficiency of emergency response procedures and evaluate the level of collaboration among relevant agencies during aviation emergencies.

Despite the large-scale simulation, which held at the airside of the Osubi Airport, normal airport operations were not disrupted.

That was the second simulation to be conducted since 1999 when the airport was established and first after FAAN took over the operatorship of the airport.

Speaking with journalists after the exercise, the Airport Manager, Winston Egwuatu, expressed satisfaction with the conduct of the exercise, assuring the audience that some of the lapses noticed in the simulation would be addressed going forward.

He noted that the exercise was designed to expose operational gaps and provide an opportunity to address them before an actual emergency occurs.

Egwuatu acknowledged that there was no perfect simulation, but noted that the objective was to test personnel, equipment and established emergency response procedures.

“There is no simulation exercise that is perfect. It was actually meant to test the preparedness of both the officers who are going to be deployed, the materials and also the procedures.

“The purpose of this is to identify the gaps and close them, so that when it is deployed, we will deploy better,” Egwuatu said.

He disclosed that observers from the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) had identified areas requiring improvement, particularly in personnel training and retraining, noting that the aviation industry was dynamic and required continuous adaptation.

On equipment, the airport manager said Osubi Airport had recorded significant improvements from its previous status as an airstrip, but acknowledged the need for more operational vehicles and modern firefighting tankers.

“Within the ambit of the resources available to the management of the airport, we have done very well. This airport used to be an airstrip, but now it is operating as an airport. That means there have been some level of upgrade.

“However, there is need for improvement as regards operational vehicles and state-of-the-art fire tankers to meet the time that we find ourselves now,” he said.

Egwuatu said the airport management would take the observations from the exercise in good faith, adding that a comprehensive report would be prepared to guide corrective measures and escalate requests requiring higher-level intervention.

He emphasised the importance of personnel mastering their respective responsibilities, warning that confusion during an actual aircraft accident could undermine rescue efforts.

“Like the training, we need to master our roles because when an accident occurs, it can become chaotic. So we need to master our roles,” he said.

On the need to improve response time among external emergency agencies, Egwuatu said continuous engagement and sensitisation remained critical to building effective collaboration.

According to him, assisting agencies could not be compelled to respond, but sustained engagement would help them appreciate the importance of timely intervention.

“It is in the interest of everybody to deploy, all of us who have the wherewithal to not just respond but respond timely. Because that timely response is critical. It can save the life of someone,” he said.

He disclosed that stakeholders hold regular meetings, the latest about two weeks before the exercise, during which video clips were shown and the responsibilities of participating agencies explained.

The airport manager commended the participating organisations, host communities and other stakeholders for their cooperation, describing their turnout as encouraging.

Earlier, while addressing participants, Egwuatu said the exercise was necessary because aviation emergencies could occur without warning and airports were required by regulations to maintain effective emergency response systems.

He also explained that FAAN hoped to produce a video documentary of the full-scale exercise for educational purposes and to help improve emergency preparedness across the aviation sector.

The Airport On-Scene Commander, Ambrose Idisi, also appreciated the participating organisations for responding to the exercise, noting that they were part of the Osubi Airport community planning committee and had been informed ahead of the simulation.

He said the committee regularly engaged stakeholders on emergency preparedness and their respective responsibilities.

In their separate assessments, representatives of the collaborating agencies commended the airport management and emergency response team.

“They did their best. Coordination needs to be looked into, and there is the need to do a proper check before deploying the ambulances used for any operation,” he said.

A representative of the Nigerian Navy commended the alertness and promptness of personnel during the exercise, while the Nigeria Police Force also praised the participating agencies for their response.

Similarly, Mr. Charles of the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (NSIB) disclosed that his team received information about the simulated crash at 2:34pm and arrived at the scene seven minutes later.

He said the team was subsequently briefed by the On-Scene Commander, describing the exercise as an important demonstration of the need for preparedness in the aviation industry.

The Delta State Fire Service and Delta Procare also commended the airport management and other participants for their efforts.

One of the NCAA observers, Maureen Amewhule, who monitored activities from the fire watch room, commended the alertness and professionalism displayed by airport personnel.

She also praised the Nigerian Navy for its prompt response and professionalism in evacuating simulated victims.

Amewhule recommended additional training for medical personnel, stronger synergy among the agencies and regular stakeholder meetings to ensure that everyone understood their respective roles and responsibilities.

Another NCAA observer, Mr. Okrinade Ahmed, described the exercise as a well-simulated emergency response but observed that the Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) was absent and called for more collaborations.

He also advised the airport management to carefully select simulation locations that would allow assisting agencies to demonstrate and meet the expected emergency response time.

The airport management, however, assured the audience that observations from the exercise would be documented and escalated to the appropriate authorities, while deficiencies within its operational capacity would be addressed.

The exercise was widely adjudged successful and impressive by industry experts.

The full-scale emergency simulation is a regulatory requirement of the NCAA, aimed at testing airport emergency preparedness and ensuring that relevant personnel and assisting agencies can respond effectively to aircraft accidents and other emergencies.

World.title: Ex-Paramount Executive Unveils LivDot to Take Nigerian Events Global
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Funmi Ogundare

Former Paramount Skydance Africa Country Manager, Bada Akintunde-Johnson, recently unveiled LivDot, a live-event streaming and creator-commerce platform designed to connect Nigerian event organisers, artists and content creators with global audiences and unlock new revenue opportunities.

The platform, which combines live streaming, digital payments, production services and a marketplace for vetted photographers and videographers, will enable event organisers to distribute content globally, either free of charge or through paid access.

Akintunde-Johnson said the initiative was aimed at removing the limitations imposed by physical venues on the audience reach and commercial potential of live entertainment.

He explained that while a sold-out concert with a capacity of 5,000 people traditionally marks the end of its ticketing opportunities, LivDot could enable organisers to sell 50,000 or more streaming tickets to audiences across Nigeria, Africa and the diaspora.

“For too long, the reach and economics of live events have been defined by the walls of the venue. We want to change that. A sold-out room should be the floor of an event’s audience and earning potential, not the ceiling,” he stated.

As part of its market entry strategy, LivDot is preparing to stream a series of concerts and live experiences exclusively during the forthcoming Detty December season.

The lineup includes concerts by BNXN, formerly known as Buju, on December 19; Fola on December 20; Oxlade on December 21; and Ruger on December 22, alongside other headline performances.

Other events scheduled for the platform include, ‘The Worship Project’, by The Fountain of Life Church on December 12; Saheed Osupa and ‘Friends White Party’, on December 25; as well as the Digital Product Growth Summit.

The platform is also targeting Nigerians in the diaspora who wish to participate in the country’s December entertainment activities without the cost and logistics of travelling home.

Akintunde-Johnson said LivDot would make it possible for Nigerians living in cities such as London, Houston and Toronto to experience concerts and other live events in Lagos in real time.

“Imagine being in London, Houston or Toronto and being able to experience the energy of Detty December concerts in real time. For fans who cannot make the trip, we are curing your fear of missing out by making Lagos’s live entertainment accessible to you wherever you are,” he said.

He noted that the platform would also create opportunities for African artists to engage international audiences more frequently without having to depend solely on occasional performances at major venues abroad.

According to him, musicians could organise performances in Nigeria and sell affordable digital tickets to fans across the world, using LivDot’s production, streaming and payment infrastructure to deliver the experience.

He added that the model could support intimate performances, exclusive sessions, album listening events and other fan engagement activities, enabling artists to earn directly from international audiences while strengthening their relationships with supporters.

“Artists should be able to perform more often, on their own terms, and earn directly from fans around the world. We want to make that commercially practical,” he said.

Beyond music concerts, Akintunde-Johnson said the platform was designed to serve a broader range of events, including birthday celebrations, weddings, comedy shows, cultural festivals, fashion shows and conferences.

He said the platform would help organisers reach people who, despite their interest, might be unable to attend events physically, thereby converting unmet audience demand into additional revenue.

Akintunde-Johnson, whose career spans entertainment and media brands including MTV Base, BET, Nickelodeon and comedy central in Nigeria, said LivDot would continue to expand partnerships with brands, show promoters, artists, event planners, production companies and other industry stakeholders.

He said the platform’s ambition was to ensure that the location of an event and the capacity of its venue no longer determined the size of its audience or the scale of its commercial opportunities.

World.title: 58% of GBV Survivors in Nigeria Never Seek Help, PPDC Raises Alarm
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Folalumi Alaran in Abuja

The Public and Private Development Centre (PPDC) has raised the alarm over the high number of women experiencing gender-based violence who never seek help, revealing that 58 per cent of women who suffered physical or sexual violence in Nigeria neither sought assistance nor told anyone about their experiences.

The organisation also expressed concern over the low rate of legal accountability for reported cases, calling for stronger survivor protection, institutional accountability and improved access to justice.

PPDC’s Head of Communications and Knowledge Management, Nnenna Eze, disclosed this on Wednesday at a screening of ‘Sanctuary’, a film by Chavala Yaduma, organised in collaboration with HomeVida Media and Films in Abuja to mark the 2026 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence.

Citing the 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey, Eze said 21 per cent of women aged 15 to 49 had experienced physical or sexual violence, while 58 per cent of those affected had neither sought help nor disclosed their experiences to anyone.

She also cited Federal Ministry of Women Affairs and Social Development figures indicating that 2,755 cases of gender-based and intimate partner violence were recorded between January and April 2026, but only four per cent had reached legal accountability.

She said the figures exposed the gap between reporting violence and securing justice, stressing that ending gender-based violence required more than public campaigns.

According to her, survivors must be supported when they speak out, while institutions must ensure that perpetrators are held accountable.

Eze said the screening was part of HomeVida, PPDC’s film-for-change initiative, which uses storytelling to promote social awareness and behavioural change.

She disclosed that the initiative had, over the past 10 years, trained more than 1,000 filmmakers, supported over 35 short films and secured the broadcast of two films on Africa Magic.

During the post-screening discussion, panellists identified institutional failures, harmful social attitudes and inadequate survivor support as major obstacles to addressing gender-based violence in Nigeria.

One of the panellists, reflecting on the country’s legal framework, said the existence of laws against sexual violence had not translated into adequate protection because of the attitudes of some people responsible for enforcing them.

Recalling her advocacy for the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act, she criticised practices in which families pressure survivors to marry their perpetrators to protect family reputation.

She said justice must go beyond having laws on paper to ensuring that institutions enforce them and hold offenders accountable.

Another panellist called for a deliberate change in how boys are raised, warning that childhood attitudes towards power, control and rejection could contribute to gender-based violence in adulthood.

She urged parents and guardians to teach boys emotional intelligence, responsibility and respect for personal boundaries rather than reinforce beliefs that men must always dominate or that persistence can override consent.

The discussion also highlighted the vulnerability of survivors when those accused of abuse are public officials or law enforcement personnel.

A panellist associated with the Dorothy Javazah Foundation said its crisis shelter provided accommodation for approximately 10 days, while transitional sheltering could last between two and three months.

She, however, questioned the adequacy of existing support systems for underage survivors and women with children, stressing that individual organisations could not address systemic failures without government intervention.

Earlier, Programmes and Research Officer at PPDC and HomeVida Media and Films, Abdulmuizz Oyekola, said the organisation complemented its film initiatives with annual research reports and outreach programmes in schools and universities.

He described gender-based violence as a collective responsibility and called on government to strengthen institutions, including the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), improve access to justice and provide adequate recovery services for survivors.

Oyekola said ‘Sanctuary’, which portrays a girl struggling with abuse by a religious leader and her efforts to seek help, was intended to encourage survivors to speak out and challenge harmful social practices.

The screening featured stakeholders including Hassana Maina, Shamaki Dalton, Chavala Yaduma, Omeje Richard and Dorothy Njemanze.

The 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence runs from November 25 to December 10 annually.

World.title: Plateau Bloodbath: 16 Killed in Midnight Raid on Bassa Community
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Yemi Kosoko in Jos

Grief engulfed Tafi Gana community in Bassa Local Government Area of Plateau State after gunmen launched a deadly midnight attack that left no fewer than 16 persons dead and four others injured.

The attackers reportedly stormed the hamlet of Kyie Ihwien near Jebbu Miango at about 11:30 p.m. on Wednesday, shooting indiscriminately and unleashing terror on sleeping residents.

The Irigwe Development Association (IDA) said the assailants, armed with assault rifles and other dangerous weapons, carried out the attack under the cover of darkness before fleeing the area.

Among those killed were women, youths and children, including a 10-year-old boy and a 13-year-old teenager, in what community leaders described as one of the deadliest attacks on the area in recent times.

Confirming the incident, the traditional ruler of the area, Nggwe Gado Dama, said security agencies, including personnel from the Divisional Police Headquarters in Bassa and Operation Enduring Peace, had been alerted and were at the scene.

The IDA condemned the killings and urged residents to remain calm and avoid reprisals, while calling on security agencies to track down the perpetrators and ensure justice for the victims.

The association also expressed sympathy to the bereaved families and the entire Irigwe nation, praying for the repose of the souls of the victims and comfort for those affected by the tragedy.

The latest massacre is expected to renew concerns over the persistent wave of violence in Plateau communities, where recurring attacks have continued to claim lives and displace residents.

As families mourned their loved ones, the community appealed for urgent government intervention to halt the cycle of bloodshed and restore lasting peace to the area.

World.title: Olukayode Ajulo: Attorney-General As Guardian Of Constitutionalism And Architect Of Justice Sector Reform
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

An appraisal of constitutional advocacy, landmark litigation, public service and the transformation of justice administration in Ondo State

By Hamza Nuhu Dantani

Introduction

There are offices in government whose stature is defined by the magnitude of the powers they wield; there are others whose greatness is measured not by the exercise of power, but by the wisdom, discipline and restraint with which it is deployed. The office of the Attorney-General occupies a singular place in the latter category. It is an office where power must be tempered by principle, political expediency subordinated to constitutional fidelity, and the imperatives of governance constantly reconciled with the demands of justice. For the Attorney-General, the ultimate test of public service is not merely how effectively government exercises its authority, but how faithfully that authority is restrained by the Constitution, guided by the rule of law and deployed in the service of justice. It is, therefore, an office where the greatest expression of power may sometimes lie in the courage to refrain from exercising

An Attorney-General is not merely the government’s advocate. He is also a guardian of the constitutional boundaries within which government must operate. He must defend the State without becoming an instrument of arbitrary power and protect the legitimate interests of the executive without undermining the independence of other institutions. The responsibility is not simply to ensure that government wins its cases, but to ensure that government remains governed by law.

This principle finds expression in the observation of the United States Supreme Court in Berger v. United States (1935): “But, while he may strike hard blows, he is not at liberty to strike foul ones.” Under Sections 195 and 211 of the 1999 Constitution, the Attorney-General of a State occupies a position of considerable constitutional responsibility. It is against this background that the sterling tenure of Dr. Olukayode Abraham Ajulo, OON, SAN, as Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Ondo State deserves examination.

The discerning leadership of Governor Lucky Orimisan Aiyedatiwa deserves particular commendation in this interrogation.
