"I want to tell Kenyans to stop harassing IEBC. IEBC does not have votes. The votes belong to the people of Kenya," he said.

The President maintained that his administration was focused on delivering development, challenging the Opposition to explain its alternative plans on electricity connectivity, education, healthcare and infrastructure.

He questioned what the Opposition considered its development agenda, dismissing what he described as recycled political slogans and simplistic promises.

The President particularly took issue with promises centred on providing porridge to Kenyans, questioning whether such pledges could constitute a credible national development agenda.

He urged voters to interrogate the policies and development track records of politicians seeking their support instead of being swayed by political rhetoric and personal attacks.

The latest attack marks an escalation in political exchanges between Ruto and his rivals as competing camps intensify mobilisation ahead of the 2027 General Election.

It also comes amid efforts by Gachagua and other Opposition figures to consolidate their political formations and build a formidable challenge to Ruto's re-election bid, with Western Kenya emerging as a key battleground.

World.title: Wafd Party deputy leader demands accountability and overhaul of hazardous transport following Al-Warraq tragedy
World.content:
The vice president of the Al-Wafd Party, Senator Hazem al-Gendy, emphasized that the devastating Al-Warraq Ring Road blaze—which claimed roughly 31 lives and left 21 injured according to Ministry of Health and Population figures—must not be treated as a passing traffic incident.

Calling the incident a painful humanitarian tragedy, he stressed the lives of citizens cannot be treated as mere statistics and the right of grieving families and society at large to know the full truth cannot be delayed.

In a statement issued on Thursday, al-Gendy asserted that safeguarding citizens must remain a state priority.

He noted that this catastrophe necessitates a rigorous review of how petroleum products and hazardous materials are transported across the country.

He urged authorities to verify the road-worthiness of tankers and transport vehicles, ensure strict compliance with technical standards and preventive safety rules, require transport companies to enforce safety protocols and GPS tracking systems, and step up monitoring along heavily congested arteries—restricting hazardous freight movement near residential areas to designated routes and off-peak hours.

Calls for transparent prosecution findings

The senator demanded full transparency in releasing the Public Prosecution’s investigation findings, identifying any operational shortcomings, and holding accountable anyone proven negligent in operating, maintaining, or overseeing the tanker – strictly under the law and without exception.

At the same time, al-Gendy also commended President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s directives to deliver swift medical care to the injured and extend support to victims’ families, alongside the government’s rapid response to contain the fallout.

He also saluted the civil defense personnel, ambulance crews, medical teams, and ordinary citizens who stepped in to rescue survivors.

A binding highway safety plan

Al-Gendy concluded his statement by calling for a binding safety plan with a clear timeline across highways and major traffic corridors to prevent similar disasters from recurring.

“Honoring the souls of those we lost does not come through grief alone,” he said, “but through serious action so that this tragedy is never repeated.”

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Economy continues to grow despite global challenges – PM
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said the Egyptian economy continues to achieve growth despite prevailing global conditions, stressing that the government is focused on maintaining the stability of economic activities and ensuring uninterrupted production to strengthen the economy’s resilience in the face of challenges.

Speaking at a press conference held on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, at the government headquarters in the New Capital to announce amendments to the executive regulations of Companies Law No. 159 of 1981, Madbouly noted that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had announced the completion of the eighth and final review of its cooperation program with Egypt.

He added that a meeting of the IMF Executive Board is expected to be held before mid-December to discuss the review.

On efforts to reduce public debt, the prime minister said the government is working toward clear and ambitious debt-reduction targets and has already taken tangible steps in that direction. He added that implementation plans and further measures for the coming period would be announced in due course, reflecting the state’s clear approach to addressing the debt issue.

World.title: Egypt set to raise entry fees for key archaeological sites starting April 2027
World.content:
The Egyptian Travel Agents Association (ETAA) announced new admission fee adjustments for several archaeological landmarks, following approval by the Supreme Council of Antiquities (SCA) board during its 39th session on November 9.

The updated ticket prices are scheduled to take effect on April 1, 2027.

Updated entry fees for Habu Temple in Luxor

The price hike applies to Habu Temple on Luxor’s West Bank—covering both Habu Temple and the Temple of Thoth—with the new rates set as follows:

Foreign visitors: LE 300

LE 300 Foreign students: LE 150

LE 150 Egyptian visitors: LE 40

LE 40 Egyptian students: LE 20

Ticket increases for the Pyramid of Khafre

The SCA also approved higher admission rates for foreign visitors entering the Pyramid of Khafre, setting the new prices at:

Foreign visitors: LE 500

LE 500 Foreign students: LE 250

Discount for tour operators

The board of the SCA approved extending the 25 percent discount granted to travel agencies on bulk ticket purchases for the Hurghada Museum through June 30, 2027, subject to standard administrative procedures.

Edited translation from Al-Masry al-Youm

World.title: Egypt reaffirms full support for Eritrea’s sovereignty, territorial integrity
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt’s full support for Eritrea’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity. He made the remarks during a meeting on Wednesday,November 25,2026 with Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Ambassador Nader Zaki said Abdelatty praised the growing momentum in Egyptian-Eritrean relations, reiterating the importance of continuing to strengthen bilateral cooperation.The meeting also addressed the latest regional developments in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea.

Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt’s firm position in support of the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries in the region, as well as the preservation of their national institutions, rejecting foreign interference in their internal affairs.

The two ministers agreed to build on the outcomes of the consultative summit held in El Alamein last October, in a way that contributes to achieving stability and development in the region.

World.title: Egyptian, Qatari FMs discuss bilateral ties, regional developments
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty received on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, Qatari Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al-Thani, as part of ongoing consultations and coordination between the two countries and exchanges of high-level visits aimed at strengthening bilateral relations and discussing regional developments.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Nader Zaki said the meeting opened with both sides underscoring the depth of fraternal relations and close ties between the two countries, as well as their shared commitment to further strengthening cooperation and coordination across various fields in pursuit of mutual interests.

The two ministers also discussed ways to advance economic relations between Egypt and Qatar, building on the notable progress achieved recently. They stressed the importance of expanding economic partnerships, increasing trade exchange and boosting mutual investments, particularly in light of the considerable potential and promising opportunities available in both countries.

The meeting also addressed current regional developments, including the latest developments in the crisis involving Iran.

The two sides reviewed intensive mediation efforts undertaken by Egypt and Qatar, in coordination with regional and international partners, to de-escalate tensions and contain the situation. They stressed the importance of prioritizing dialogue and political solutions to preserve regional security and stability.

They also exchanged views on developments in Libya and Sudan.

World.title: Egypt, Chevron review development plans for Cyprus’ Aphrodite gas field
World.content:
The Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources and global energy company Chevron held a joint workshop, under the auspices of Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawi, to review the latest developments in the development of Cyprus’ Aphrodite natural gas field and its planned connection to Egypt’s infrastructure, as well as discuss the project’s technical and regulatory requirements, with a focus on process safety.

In a statement on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, the ministry said the workshop was part of its efforts to strengthen cooperation with international partners, maintain coordination to advance the project and ensure the application of the highest safety standards throughout its various stages.

Participants included Mohamed al-Bagouri, Head of the Central Administration for Legal Affairs at the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, Islam Bassiouni, EGAS Executive Managing Director for Operations, Basel Allam, Chevron’s Country Manager for Cyprus, Chris Clover, Technical Safety Engineering Advisor, and Nicoletta Achilleos, Regulatory Affairs and Risk Management Advisor at Chevron’s global headquarters in Houston, who joined via video conference, alongside senior officials and experts from both sides.

The workshop reviewed the current status of discussions on the Aphrodite field development project and examined the procedural, technical and regulatory requirements related to its facilities. These included the classification of Major Hazard Facilities (MHF), the technical assessments supporting this classification, notification requirements and submission procedures before the relevant regulatory authorities.

Participants also identified the next steps and coordination mechanisms between the two sides’ working teams to complete the necessary procedures.

Discussions also focused on process safety requirements.

Al-Bagouri stressed the importance of adhering to Minister Badawi’s directives prioritizing process safety, describing it as an inherent responsibility and an internal commitment before being a requirement imposed by international conventions and laws, particularly in cross-border projects.

Bassiouni said process safety was a key pillar of successful natural gas development and production projects, adding that compliance with technical requirements and safety standards enhances project implementation efficiency and ensures sustainable operations.

For his part, Allam said Chevron applies international best practices in identifying, assessing and managing risks to ensure the safety of facilities and equipment and protect workers and the surrounding environment.

Discussions also addressed the importance of developing and implementing comprehensive preventive and periodic maintenance programmes for equipment and facilities, improving operational asset efficiency, and ensuring their readiness and safe, continuous operation.

Participants further stressed the need to comply with occupational health, safety and environmental (HSE) standards and implement process safety management systems to reduce operational risks, prevent accidents and enhance the reliability and sustainability of operations.

The workshop also underscored the importance of continued technical and regulatory coordination between the Egyptian Natural Gas Holding Company (EGAS) and Chevron, as well as exchanging expertise and leveraging both sides’ technical and technological capabilities to support the completion of requirements for connecting the Aphrodite field to Egypt’s infrastructure and advancing the project in line with the highest safety and operational efficiency standards.

World.title: Authorities arrest driver behind deadly Al-Warraq blaze
World.content:
The Public Prosecution announced in an official statement that authorities have apprehended the driver responsible for causing the catastrophic fuel tanker crash and fire along the Ring Road in Giza’s Al-Warraq district.

Egypt’s Ministry of Health and Population announced late Wednesday that the death toll from the devastating fire has reached 31 fatalities, with 21 others injured.

Investigations pinpoints the suspect

According to the statement, the arrest follows an ongoing investigation into the collision and subsequent inferno involving a petroleum tanker in Al-Warraq.

Through witness testimonies, on-site inspections, and forensic examinations of the crash scene, investigators identified and located the motorist behind the tragedy.

During questioning, prosecutors confronted the suspect with witness findings and technical evidence from the scene.

He confessed to causing the crash while driving along the Ring Road from al-Marg toward Al-Haram at 110 km/h with his father in the vehicle.

The suspect admitted that while weaving between traffic lanes and overtaking other vehicles, the front left side of his car struck the rear right side of the fuel tanker.

He lost control of the steering wheel and swerved to the far right of the roadway, while one of the tanker’s tires blew out—causing the truck to slam into a concrete barrier, overturn, leak gasoline, and then erupt into flames.

The Public Prosecution continues to interrogate the suspect to establish the full sequence of events and determine the extent of his criminal liability, while overseeing damage assessments, loss inventories, and follow-up legal measures.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Netanyahu gets major legal boost as court casts doubt on corruption case
World.content:
Jerusalem — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s yearslong corruption trial took a significant turn in his favor on Wednesday as judges recommended that prosecutors drop charges in the most serious of the three cases against him and reconsider a second case.

In televised remarks later Wednesday, Netanyahu said the recommendations amount to a vindication and declared, “This trial needs to end immediately.”

Speaking at the Israeli parliament, or Knesset, the prime minister said: “It took 10 years of terrible suffering for me, my wife and my sons for the truth to finally be revealed to everyone. Who will give us back those years, during which my sons couldn’t go out to a restaurant or walk around the city?”

Netanyahu’s political allies also immediately celebrated the decision. “After years of persecution against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the time has come to put an end to a trial that was tainted from the outset, divides Israeli society, and exacts a heavy price from the country,” Defense Minister Israel Katz, a Netanyahu ally, said in a statement on X.

Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman, who is presiding over the trial of Israel’s longest-serving leader, indicated to Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara in a hearing that a conviction of Netanyahu in what’s known as Case 4000 is unlikely and the case should be dropped.

“It seems to us that the bribery charge presents considerable difficulties,” the court said, according to a spokesperson. “There is serious doubt as to whether the evidentiary foundation supports this allegation.”

In this case, prosecutors alleged that Netanyahu gave regulatory benefits worth more than 1 billion shekels (approximately $300 million) to his friend, millionaire Shaul Elovitch, whose telecommunications company Bezeq owned the Walla! news website.

Netanyahu faced a charge of bribery and another charge of fraud and breach of trust in this case.

The court emphasized that its recommendations in these cases were not final decisions or a judgment in the corruption trial, but the statements alone are nevertheless an enormous win for Netanyahu.

In his remarks in response to the recommendations, Netanyahu repeated Wednesday that he is prepared to form a unity government with the parliamentary opposition. Netanyahu’s political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, is maneuvering to form a government that would oust the prime minister and his far-right partners after nearly four years in power.

Caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during the parliamentary meeting of the Israeli parliament (Knesset) in Jerusalem on November 25, 2026. Knesset

Verdict or ‘appropriate plea agreement’

Justice Minister Yariv Levin shared one of Netanyahu’s old social media posts in which he said, “There will be nothing because there is nothing,” which became one of Netanyahu’s catchphrases when the cases began.

Baharav-Miara, who does not normally attend the trial, was summoned by the court to attend Wednesday’s hearing. The attorney general said she would “carefully review” all of the court’s recommendations with the prosecution team.

“There are only two ways to bring the case to a conclusion: a verdict or an appropriate plea agreement that reflects the nature of the acts and offenses,” she said during the hearing.

The court also recommended reconsidering Case 2000, in which prosecutors had alleged that Netanyahu sought favorable coverage in one of Israel’s top newspapers in exchange for limiting the circulation of one of that paper’s main rivals. Netanyahu faced the charge of fraud and breach of trust in this case.

“We have serious doubts as to whether the conduct described in the indictment actually constitutes a criminal offense,” the court said bluntly.

In the final case, known as Case 1000, the court urged Netanyahu’s attorneys to come to an agreement with prosecutors. In this case, Netanyahu is charged with fraud and breach of trust over allegations that he received gifts such as cigars and champagne from overseas businessmen. But this case was viewed as far less serious than Case 4000, and it would be a major political victory for Netanyahu if it’s the only one left standing.

The court said it seemed that Case 1000 could be “brought to a conclusion.”

Netanyahu was indicted in Jerusalem District Court in January 2020. At the time of the announcement, he was in the US visiting President Donald Trump during his first term. Hours after the indictment came down, Trump unveiled what would become known as his “Deal of the Century” to solve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

The indictment made Netanyahu the first sitting Israeli prime minister to appear in court as a defendant. The criminal trial, which began in May 2020, has lasted through several wars, multiple elections and two US presidents. Netanyahu began testifying in the trials in December 2024.

But the saga began earlier. Police said there was sufficient evidence to indict Netanyahu in February 2018.

From the beginning, Netanyahu proclaimed his innocence, deriding the prosecution as a political witch hunt.

Last December, Netanyahu formally requested a pardon. In a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog, he said the trial had become “a focal point of fierce controversy” for which he bears “broad public and more responsibility, with an understanding of the overall ramifications of these events.” In the one-page letter, Netanyahu did not admit guilt or commit to anything about his political future.

One month earlier, Trump wrote his own letter to Herzog asking him to grant Netanyahu a full pardon.

“While I absolutely respect the independence of the Israeli Justice System, and its requirements, I believe that the ‘case’ against Bibi, who has fought alongside me for a long time, including against the very tough adversary of Israel, Iran, is a political, unjustified prosecution,” Trump wrote in the letter.

In Israel, only the president has the authority to issue a pardon.

Netanyahu’s main rivals, who seek to oust him after the election in late October, have yet to issue a statement following the court hearing.

Max Saltman in New York contributed to this report.

World.title: Mercy Corps Rebrands as Prosper Global After 24 Years in Liberia
World.content:
Organization Says Name Change Will Not Affect Ongoing Programs, Donor-Funded Projects or Partnerships as It Pledges Stronger Focus on African Leadership and Community-Driven Development

MONROVIA – International humanitarian and development organization Mercy Corps has officially rebranded as Prosper Global, marking a new chapter in its more than two-decade presence in Liberia while reaffirming its commitment to community-led development, economic empowerment and resilience.

The transition, announced Tuesday, November 24, in Monrovia, forms part of the organization’s global rebranding initiative aimed at strengthening its focus on locally driven solutions, African leadership and sustainable economic opportunities for vulnerable communities.



Despite the change in name and visual identity, Prosper Global said its mission, programs, partnerships and donor-funded projects in Liberia would continue without disruption.

The organization, which began operations in Liberia in 2002, has worked alongside government institutions, local communities, civil society organizations and private-sector actors to address development challenges and improve livelihoods.

Over the years, its interventions have covered youth employment, education, food security, economic inclusion, renewable energy, governance, climate resilience and humanitarian response.

Speaking at the transition ceremony held at the Royal Grand Hotel in Monrovia, Melaku Yirga, Prosper Global’s Vice President for Africa, said Liberia occupies a special place in the organization’s history in West Africa.



He noted that the organization’s work in the country over the past two decades has been shaped by the resilience, aspirations and leadership of Liberians.

Yirga said the transition presents an opportunity to build on that legacy by strengthening local leadership and supporting development solutions that reflect the priorities and needs of communities.

“While our name may be changing, our commitment to Liberia and our longstanding partnerships remain as strong as ever,” he said.

Among the organization’s major interventions in Liberia are the Ebola Community Action Plan (E-CAP), Economic Recovery from Ebola for Liberia (EREL), Promoting Sustainable Partnerships for Economic Recovery (PROSPECTS), Liberia Employment and Entrepreneurship Program (LEEP), and Liberia Empowerment through Attendance, Reading and Nutrition (LEARN).

Through these initiatives, the organization has supported youth employment and entrepreneurship, improved agricultural productivity, strengthened education outcomes and promoted social inclusion.

Meanwhile, Ambassador Charles A. Snetter, who represented the Minister of State for Presidential Affairs, Samuel A. Stevquoah, welcomed the organization’s new identity and commended its contributions to Liberia’s development over the years.

Snetter particularly highlighted the challenges confronting young Liberians graduating from universities and other institutions of higher learning, questioning how they would secure employment and establish sustainable livelihoods in an increasingly challenging economic environment.

He encouraged young people to engage organizations such as Prosper Global to learn about available programs and opportunities that could help them acquire relevant skills, establish businesses and achieve economic independence.

He also recalled President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr.’s repeated emphasis on youth empowerment, noting that the government remains concerned about the welfare, economic prospects and future of young Liberians.

Snetter congratulated Prosper Global on its transition and encouraged the organization to sustain and expand its development interventions across the country.

Speaking on behalf of international partners, Foday C. Bayoott of the Embassy of Ireland acknowledged Mercy Corps’ contributions to Liberia over the past two decades, particularly in promoting economic opportunities, resilience and inclusive development.

Bayoott emphasized that sustainable development requires placing local communities at the center of decisions and solutions that affect their lives.

He encouraged Prosper Global to build on the foundation established under Mercy Corps, strengthen existing partnerships and continue investing in climate resilience, inclusive development and community empowerment.

He also reaffirmed Ireland’s interest in continued collaboration with the organization and congratulated its leadership and staff on the new identity.

Under its new name, Prosper Global said it would continue working with communities throughout Liberia to expand economic opportunities for young people, improve food security and educational outcomes, strengthen resilience to climate and economic shocks, and advance inclusive and sustainable development in line with national priorities.

The organization maintained that the transition reflects its belief that lasting development depends on strong partnerships, local leadership and evidence-based approaches that address the root causes of poverty, vulnerability and exclusion.

About Prosper Global

Prosper Global, formerly Mercy Corps, is an international humanitarian and development organization working with communities affected by climate change, conflict and crises.

In Liberia, the organization partners with government institutions, civil society organizations, local communities and private-sector actors to strengthen resilience, expand economic opportunities, improve food security and education systems, and advance locally led development solutions.

World.title: Boakai Bets His Legacy on US$5.7 Billion MIDA, Promising Light and Roads Without New Debt
World.content:
Monrovia – President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has put his presidency behind a single agreement.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Speaking publicly for the first time on the US$5.7 billion Master Infrastructure Development Agreement (MIDA) with Bea Mountain Mining Corporation (BMMC), the President cast Wednesday’s signing as a turning point for the country.



“Today marks a historic day for Liberia as we lay the foundations for tomorrow,” Boakai said, according to prepared remarks obtained by FrontPageAfrica. “As I have always said, it is time that we ‘Think Liberia, Love Liberia, and Build Liberia.’ And this is being demonstrated here today.”

It is the boldest move of his administration: a bet that one company-backed deal can do what decades of donor programs have not, and give Liberia reliable power and roads that connect every region.

Two Problems, One Deal

Boakai framed MIDA as a direct attack on what he called “two longstanding binding constraints that limit Liberia’s growth”: the lack of electricity and the lack of roads.



On power, the numbers he presented are significant. Four new plants are expected to add 270 megawatts, more than three times the capacity of Mount Coffee, the country’s main hydro plant. The President said the system could eventually “support over 1000 megawatts down the road.”

He presented the VIA and SP-4 dams as the answer to the dry-season blackouts that have long frustrated Liberians and businesses. Together they would hold “around 10 billion cubic meters of water, so that the lights stay on all year round, even in the dry season.”

New transmission lines and grid upgrades are meant “to ensure that the power generated is transmitted beyond Monrovia,” he said. The 14 road and bridge projects, he added, fit his ARREST Agenda “to ensure that development reaches every region of our country.”

“Da What Will We Eat?”

Boakai anticipated the most common Liberian question about any large deal: what is in it for ordinary people?

“I know some will ask, ‘Da What will we Eat?'” he said. “The fact is, this Agreement holds more for every Liberian.”

His answer was concrete. He promised steadier power so “children [can] study at night” and families can store food for longer; clinics and hospitals that “keep their machines running”; and “power for the welder, the tailor, the barber, and the shopkeeper, without the daily cost of generator fuel.” He also pointed to market access for farmers and “thousands of new jobs and skills for our young people.”

The message was clear: MIDA is presented not only as an engineering project but as a kitchen-table promise.

Answering the Debt Question

The President also faced the issue head-on. A day earlier, former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf had warned on ELBC Radio that the US$5.7 billion “has to be paid back” and urged an independent African Development Bank review.

“There have also been concerns about debt to Liberia under this Agreement and how we will pay for it as a country,” Boakai acknowledged.

His answer is the core of the bet. “Leveraging the rise in gold price,” he said, the government has arranged with BMMC “to ring-fence new revenue streams from the Corporation beginning 2027 to pay for the cost of all projects.” Government talking points add that BMMC “will continue to contribute to the Consolidated Account” and that these are “entirely new revenue sources.”

To reassure doubters, Boakai noted that BMMC has agreed to a US$500 million bridge financing facility “to ensure the projects do not run out of money and stall during the construction period.”

In short, the President is saying that Liberia can build without borrowing in the traditional sense, by using a gold windfall that did not exist before.

The Promise and the Clock

Boakai ended with a firm commitment. “My promise is this: we will deliver within five years, with the Biomass plant and transmission lines completed in just two years. In short, MIDA will build the economic backbone of a modern Liberia.”

That promise defines the gamble. The two-year projects would arrive around late 2028, ahead of the October 2029 elections, and give the President visible results to show voters. The dams and the full road program are due by about 2031, after his term ends in January 2030. His legacy will depend on work his successor must complete.

What Has to Go Right

For Boakai’s bet to pay off, several things must hold:

• Gold must stay strong. The financing explicitly depends on “the rise in gold price.”

• Delivery must be fast. Two dams, four plants, three transmission corridors and 14 road projects in five years is extremely ambitious.

• The money must add up. Government documents give the cost as both “more than US$5.45 billion” and “about US$5.7 billion.”

• Trust must be built. Sirleaf’s call for independent technical review, and her question about whether the President is getting “the right information,” still need an answer.

Sirleaf does not oppose the goals. “We want more roads; we want more lights,” she said, “but we have to be careful.”

The Stakes

If MIDA delivers, Boakai could be remembered as the President who switched on the lights in the counties and finally connected the country by road, something his supporters would say no post-war leader managed. If it stumbles, the deal could follow him into the 2029 campaign and well beyond.

Either way, the President has made his choice clear. As he put it on Wednesday: “This is being demonstrated here today.”

World.title: Rights Groups Warn Senate War Crimes Court Bill Could Undermine Independence, Urge Court by November 2027
World.content:
Monrovia – A coalition of human rights organizations has called on the Liberian Senate to revisit a provision that would give the country’s Supreme Court final appellate authority over the proposed Special War Crimes Court for Liberia (SWACCOL), warning that it could damage the court’s independence and credibility.

By Rodney D Sieh

The groups made the recommendation in a joint statement submitted to the Senate Judiciary Committee’s public hearing on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, on the Senate’s harmonized bill, “An Act to Establish a Special War Crimes Court for Liberia.”



The statement was issued on behalf of The Advocates for Human Rights, the Center for Justice and Accountability (CJA), the Civil Society Human Rights Advocacy Platform, Civitas Maxima, the Global Justice and Research Project, the Global Justice Center and Human Rights Watch.

Supreme Court Concern

The groups noted that, unlike some earlier proposals, the Senate bill gives the Liberian Supreme Court the last word on appeals. While they recognized the Supreme Court’s constitutional role, they said the arrangement “could affect the Court’s independence, impartiality and effectiveness or appearance thereof.”

The concern, they said, is “heightened by longstanding and well documented challenges facing the domestic justice system, including in relation to its capacity and independence.”



The coalition urged lawmakers to keep a majority international panel of judges serving alongside Liberian judges, and to consult experts who helped set up other hybrid courts, including the Special Criminal Court in the Central African Republic, the Extraordinary African Chambers in Senegal and the Special Tribunal for The Gambia.

“Let Us Maintain This Momentum”

Despite their concerns, the groups strongly backed the push for a court and urged all legislative committees to move “without delay,” with the aim of establishing the court by November 2027, in line with the Executive’s stated timeline.

“Our call is simple: let us maintain this momentum,” the statement said, adding that Liberia now has “a real chance to secure accountability for grave crimes committed during the country’s civil wars.”

They noted that Liberia will hold the rotating presidency of the UN Security Council in December, saying that advancing the bill now “would demonstrate Liberia’s leadership on justice and accountability.”

The groups cited war crimes trials of Liberians in France and Switzerland as proof that such crimes can be prosecuted, adding that “survivors rightly expect to see justice delivered at home.”

Other Concerns

The coalition raised several other issues with the bill:

• Timeframe: The bill reaches back to crimes committed from 1979. The groups recommended a later start date tied more closely to the outbreak of war in 1989, which they said would be “more feasible for the Court to manage.”

• Child offenders: The bill appears to allow prosecution of people who were aged 15 to 18 when the alleged crimes took place. The groups urged lawmakers to exclude anyone under 18 at the time, in line with international standards.

• Genocide: Since Liberia’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) found that genocide was not committed during the wars, the groups suggested lawmakers consider whether including the crime is necessary.

• Definition of gender: The bill limits gender to “the two sexes, male and female.” The groups recommended dropping the definition entirely, as with comparable terms such as race in the Rome Statute, and relying on interpretation in line with international law.

• Victims: They welcomed provisions on victims’ participation and reparations but called for a clearer definition of “victim” and “harm,” and suggested reparations could be handled by a separate body, similar to the ICC’s Trust Fund for Victims.

• Investigative unit: They said the Independent Investigative Unit for Liberia (IIU-L), as a separate institution, should be governed by its own legal framework rather than the court’s statute.

• UN role: The bill provides for extensive UN participation, which the groups support, but they said this should be “confirmed and worked through” before the statute is adopted.

What They Welcomed

The groups praised the bill for including key international law principles: that official position offers no immunity, that following superior orders is no defense, limits on amnesties, and strong fair-trial protections.

They also welcomed the inclusion of sexual and gender-based crimes, including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage and reproductive violence, as well as requirements for gender parity and at least 10 years of relevant experience for judges.

The statement credited the TRC, whose final report recommended a war crimes court, the Liberian National Bar Association’s 2021 draft statute, and the Office for the Establishment of War and Economic Crimes Court for Liberia (OWECC) for laying the groundwork.The groups urged the Senate plenary, House committees and the Joint Plenary of the Legislature to continue holding public hearings and consulting victims, civil society and legal experts as the bill moves forward.

World.title: Liberia: Jewel Howard Taylor Seeks Separate Trial, Wants Judge Feika Removed from US$317M Cocaine Case
World.content:
MONROVIA – Former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor has launched two legal challenges in the US$317 million cocaine trafficking case, asking Criminal Court ‘C’ to separate her trial from those of 19 co-defendants and seeking the recusal of presiding Judge Ousman F. Feika.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The two motions, filed as pretrial proceedings commenced on Wednesday, November 25, introduce fresh legal questions in one of Liberia’s most closely watched drug-related prosecutions.



In one application, Taylor’s lawyers are seeking severance, which would allow her to stand trial separately from the other 19 defendants indicted in connection with the alleged international cocaine trafficking operation.

In a separate motion, the defense is asking Judge Feika to withdraw from presiding over the case, placing his continued participation in the proceedings before the court for consideration.

The applications present two distinct procedural questions: whether Taylor should face a separate trial and whether Judge Feika should continue presiding over the matter.

The specific grounds advanced by the defense in support of the motions will be central to the court’s determination. Neither application, however, amounts to a dismissal of the charges or establishes wrongdoing by the prosecution or the presiding judge.



Two Motions, Two Legal Challenges

The motion for severance seeks to remove Taylor from the joint prosecution involving 20 individuals accused of various roles in the alleged trafficking operation.

If granted, the application would allow the former Vice President to face a separate trial rather than proceed alongside the other defendants.

The second application seeks Judge Feika’s recusal, effectively asking him to relinquish control of the proceedings.

Although the motions raise different legal issues, their combined implications could significantly affect the direction and pace of the prosecution.

A ruling on severance would determine whether Taylor’s case proceeds independently, while a decision on recusal would determine whether Judge Feika remains assigned to the matter.

The court must consider the merits of both applications before the substantive trial can proceed.

From Airport Arrest To High-Profile Prosecution

Taylor’s legal battle follows her arrest on August 19 at Roberts International Airport, where security authorities stopped her as she prepared to travel to Accra, Ghana, to attend a women’s forum.

Following hours of questioning at Liberia National Police headquarters, former Justice Minister Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh announced that she had been formally charged with several offenses, including drug trafficking, criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation, criminal solicitation, and money laundering.

She was subsequently detained at the Monrovia Central Prison.

However, citing concerns about her health, Judge Feika granted her compassionate medical release on September 4, placing her under strict home detention at her residence.

Her legal team later filed a bail application seeking to remove the restrictions imposed under the medical release arrangement.

On September 24, Judge Feika denied the application, maintaining the restrictions while the criminal proceedings continued.

The court subsequently ordered the permanent seizure of electronic devices recovered from her court-designated residence following allegations that she had violated the conditions of her medical release.

The Us$317 Million Cocaine Discovery

The prosecution stems from the July 21, 2026 seizure of approximately 3,971 kilograms of suspected cocaine at a compound along Cement Road in the VOA Community, Duazon, Margibi County.

Authorities estimated the shipment’s value at approximately US$317 million, making it one of the largest cocaine seizures in Liberia’s history.

Two foreign nationals, identified as Srdan Seles and Johann David Garces Grajales, were arrested at the scene.

The discovery triggered a wider investigation involving individuals from the security, aviation, and business sectors, as investigators examined allegations of an organized network transporting cocaine through Liberia for onward shipment to international markets.

On October 7, a Montserrado County grand jury returned a 55-page indictment naming 20 individuals, including Taylor.

Among the prominent Liberians indicted are Gerald Foley Smith, former Deputy Director for Administration of the National Security Agency, and Mark Quiah, former Deputy Director for Operations of the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority.

Other defendants include Nikola Ivancic, whom prosecutors identified as an alleged principal in the trafficking network; Croatian nationals Mihovil Vrovac and Taras Zadereiko; and several other Liberian and foreign nationals accused of various roles in the alleged operation.

The indictment contains multiple charges, including unlicensed possession, importation, transportation and exportation of controlled substances, illicit trafficking, criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation, criminal solicitation, and money laundering.

What The State Alleges Against Taylor

According to the prosecution, Taylor was introduced to individuals linked to the suspected trafficking network while serving as Vice President.

The indictment alleges that she met some of the foreign nationals through Sheik Bashiru Kante, whom prosecutors describe as an intermediary between her and members of the alleged network.

Prosecutors further allege that Taylor traveled to Dubai to meet individuals associated with the operation and received financial benefits totaling approximately US$162,000.

The payments identified in the indictment include US$27,000 for travel, US$45,000 described as a shopping gift, US$75,000 allegedly donated to her Jewel Starfish Foundation, and another US$15,000 allegedly transmitted through Kante in August 2026.

The State also relies on WhatsApp voice recordings it attributes to Taylor, alleging that the communications form part of its evidence concerning her relationship with members of the suspected network.

Taylor has denied the allegations, while her legal representatives have questioned the prosecution’s evidence and the basis for linking her to the alleged trafficking operation.

In earlier comments to FrontPage Africa, her lawyer, Cllr. Gbawou Kowou, argued that the allegations against his client rely heavily on the account of Sheik Bashiru Kante, who is himself among those indicted.

Legal Questions Before The Court

The two defense applications have placed separate legal issues before Criminal Court ‘C’.

The severance motion raises questions about whether the allegations and evidence involving the other defendants should be considered in a joint proceeding with Taylor’s case.

The recusal application, meanwhile, challenges Judge Feika’s continued participation in the proceedings.

A recusal request must be determined on its specific legal and factual grounds. Its filing does not, in itself, establish judicial bias or misconduct.

Similarly, seeking a separate trial does not amount to an admission of guilt, an acquittal, or a dismissal of the charges.

The court must determine whether the defense has established sufficient grounds to warrant either request before the case advances to a substantive determination.

For the prosecution, the challenge remains establishing the alleged connections among the defendants and proving the individual criminal responsibility of each accused person.

For Taylor’s defense, the immediate legal objectives are to secure a separate proceeding for the former Vice President and have Judge Feika removed from presiding over the case.

Taylor, who served as Vice President under former President George Manneh Weah, maintains her innocence and remains entitled to the constitutional presumption of innocence unless proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

As the US$317 million cocaine case enters another critical phase, the court’s handling of the two applications could shape the next direction of the prosecution and determine the procedural course through which the former Vice President will face the charges.

World.title: Arthur Energy Africa Meets MME Deputy Minister, Announces Workers’ Arrival Ahead of May 2027 St. John Hydro Project Construction
World.content:
Monrovia, Liberia – Arthur Energy Africa (AEA), developer of the proposed St. John Hydropower Project, has held a meeting with the Deputy Minister of Energy at the Ministry of Mines and Energy (MME), Charles Umehai, and his team as part of ongoing efforts to advance the implementation of the project.

By Victoria G Wesseh

During the meeting, representatives of Arthur Energy Africa informed the Ministry that the company’s workers have arrived in Liberia and are preparing for the commencement of construction activities, which are expected to begin in May 2027.



The meeting also served as a follow-up on the project’s progress and an opportunity for the company to reaffirm its commitment to working closely with the Ministry to advance the development of the hydropower initiative.

Speaking during the meeting, Deputy Minister for Energy Charles Umehai said the Government of Liberia remains committed to expanding electricity generation and improving access to reliable power across the country.

Minister Umehai disclosed that Arthur Energy Africa, with support from Liberian and international professionals, is currently conducting field assessments along the St. John River Basin in Bong and Grand Bassa Counties.

According to him, the assessments include topographical surveys, environmental and social impact data collection, geological and geotechnical surveys, as well as sampling activities.



He explained that these activities form part of the ongoing preparatory work for the St. John Hydropower Project, which is expected to support the establishment and operation of several hydropower stations along the river.

The Deputy Minister noted that the assessments and other preparatory activities will continue as the project progresses toward implementation.

He further emphasized that the government is positioning itself to improve the living conditions of citizens through increased electricity generation and infrastructure development.

Umehai described Liberia as a country with significant potential in the energy market, noting that the government welcomes investments and initiatives that will contribute to expanding national electricity generation capacity.

He added that the St. John Hydropower Project is expected to play a significant role in strengthening Liberia’s energy sector, increasing electricity generation, improving access to reliable power, and supporting the country’s broader national development agenda.

World.title: Keynote Speaker Calls for Innovation, Ethical Leadership and Entrepreneurship, Urging Graduates to Apply Their Knowledge to Solving Liberia’s Development Challenges
World.content:
MONROVIA – Starz University has graduated 294 students at its ninth convocation and commencement ceremony, with keynote speaker Dr. Thomas Nimene Tweh Jr. challenging the graduates to transform their academic knowledge into practical solutions through technological innovation, entrepreneurship and ethical leadership.

By Patience Jones

The ceremony, held Tuesday, November 24, brought together members of the university’s Board of Trustees, administrators, faculty, government officials, parents, guardians and other distinguished guests to celebrate the achievements of the Trailblazer Class of 2025/2026.



According to the university, the graduating class comprised 266 undergraduate and 37 graduate students who received degrees in various academic disciplines.

Delivering the keynote address under the theme, “From Knowledge to Impact: Shaping Liberia’s Future Through Innovation and Leadership,” Tweh stressed that academic qualifications alone cannot transform a nation unless graduates apply their knowledge to address real-world challenges.

“Knowledge is important, but knowledge by itself does not build a nation. People who apply knowledge are the ones that build a nation,” he said.

He encouraged the graduates to look beyond academic certificates and traditional employment opportunities, urging them to embrace entrepreneurship, innovation and community service as pathways to national development.



Drawing from his personal experiences, Tweh recounted his humble beginnings in Trowein, New Kru Town, where he sold polo, Kool-Aid, doughnuts and meat pies to support his family before becoming a taxi driver.

He also recalled spending approximately 10 years as a refugee in Ghana following Liberia’s civil war, where he shined shoes and played musical instruments to survive before relocating to the United States. There, he pursued further education, established businesses and explored professional opportunities.

Using his personal journey to inspire the graduates, Tweh reminded them that their backgrounds should not determine the limits of their ambitions.

“Never allow the circumstances of your beginning to convince you that they are the boundaries of your future,” he told them.

Turning to emerging technological opportunities, Tweh identified artificial intelligence, digital finance and information technology as areas graduates could explore to help address Liberia’s development challenges.

He particularly emphasized the need for innovative approaches to improving education in rural communities, expanding healthcare access, strengthening agricultural production and connecting local farmers to markets.

“But technology alone will not develop Liberia. We must develop the people who can use technology intelligently and responsibly to solve Liberian problems,” he said.

On leadership, Tweh cautioned against the tendency to measure leadership solely by political appointments, public offices or positions of authority.

“We have spent too much time equating leadership with position. Leadership is not about being served, it is about serving,” he stated.

He further warned graduates against sacrificing their integrity in pursuit of wealth and professional advancement, stressing that character, honesty and personal responsibility must remain central to their definition of success.

By Patience Jones

“Success without character is ultimately failure wearing expensive clothing,” Tweh declared.

The keynote speaker also highlighted his contributions to education through the Nimene-Tweh Foundation, which provides scholarships and educational opportunities to Liberian students.

He concluded by reminding the graduates that the true value of their education would ultimately be determined by the contributions they make to society.

“Your degree is your achievement. But your impact will be your legacy. And the Liberia you help build will be your contribution to generations yet unborn,” he added.

Meanwhile, Starz University Founder and Chairman of the Board of Trustees, Ambassador Latim Dathong, urged the graduates to become entrepreneurs, innovators and responsible citizens capable of creating opportunities and contributing meaningfully to Liberia’s development.

In his commencement message, Dathong challenged the graduates to move beyond waiting for employment and instead explore opportunities to establish businesses, create jobs and develop solutions to societal problems.

“Liberia needs you. Our nation needs young people who are prepared to create businesses, develop technology, solve problems, serve their communities, and lead with integrity,” he said.

He also encouraged them to demonstrate courage, humility and integrity in their professional and personal lives, emphasizing that success should be measured not only by individual accomplishments but also by contributions to others.

“Success is not only about what you achieve for yourself; it is also about what you are able to give back to others,” Dathong added.

For his part, Starz University President Dr. Isaac Usung challenged the graduates to pursue professional excellence, embrace technological innovation and translate their academic training into meaningful contributions to their workplaces, families and communities.

“Your degree is a qualification, but what you do with it will define your legacy,” Usung said.

He also recognized the sacrifices made by parents, guardians, faculty members and university staff in supporting the graduates throughout their academic journeys.

Representing the undergraduate class, valedictorian Unison Nagbeh Meantuo emphasized resilience, ethical leadership and national responsibility, urging his colleagues to become problem solvers rather than merely holders of academic certificates.

“Liberia needs competent professionals. Liberia needs ethical leaders. Liberia needs entrepreneurs who create opportunities,” Meantuo said.

He encouraged his fellow graduates to remain committed to lifelong learning, protect their integrity and pursue their aspirations despite the challenges they may encounter.

Meanwhile, Graduate School Class President Yassah Saway Baysah shared her personal journey of overcoming depression, family responsibilities and academic setbacks following the death of her mother.

Baysah also disclosed that she had established a nonprofit initiative that has empowered more than 200 women through village savings and loan programs, operating four branches across Montserrado County.

Reflecting on the difficulties she encountered while pursuing her education, Baysah emphasized that perseverance and determination were essential to overcoming life’s challenges.

“Success is not measured by how easy the journey was. Success is measured by the courage to keep going when every reason to quit stood before us,” she said.

She encouraged her fellow graduates to remain resilient, pursue their professional ambitions and use their education and skills to create opportunities for others.

World.title: Liberia: LPRC MD Denies Unauthorized US$30M Loan, Puts Storage Expansion Cost at US$35M
World.content:
Amos Tweh Tells Senate Project Will Be Financed Through US$15M in Internal Resources and US$20M Loan, Says Expansion Is Critical to National Energy Security

MONROVIA – Managing Director of the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company (LPRC), Amos Tweh, has denied allegations that the state-owned entity secured a US$30 million loan without legislative approval to construct petroleum storage tanks, telling the Liberian Senate that the actual project investment is valued at US$35 million and will be financed through a combination of internal resources and external borrowing.

By Obediah Johnson

Tweh appeared before the Senate Plenary on Tuesday, November 24, following a citation issued by lawmakers seeking clarification on reports that the LPRC had obtained a loan to finance the construction of Petroleum Storage Terminal (PST) tanks without the Legislature’s consent.



Appearing before the Senate, Tweh explained that the US$35 million investment covers a comprehensive modernization and expansion of the company’s Petroleum Storage Terminal, rather than the construction of storage tanks alone.

He said the project is intended to expand national petroleum storage capacity while introducing modern infrastructure and operational systems to strengthen Liberia’s ability to manage petroleum supplies.

Project to Add 50,000 Metric Tons of Storage Capacity

According to Tweh, the expansion will provide an additional 50,000 metric tons of petroleum storage capacity across three major fuel categories.



The proposed infrastructure includes two Premium Motor Spirit (PMS) tanks, each with a capacity of 12,500 metric tons, providing a combined storage capacity of 25,000 metric tons.

The project will also include one Automotive Gas Oil (AGO) tank with a capacity of 20,000 metric tons and one Jet A-1 aviation fuel tank with a capacity of 5,000 metric tons.

In addition, a dedicated firewater storage tank with a capacity of 2,155 metric tons will be constructed.

Tweh said the modernization project goes beyond storage facilities to include automated petroleum pumping and measurement systems, marine vessel back-loading facilities, road tanker loading infrastructure and modern fire protection systems.

Other components include coastal protection and land reclamation works, administrative and operational support buildings, as well as associated civil, mechanical and electrical infrastructure.

US$15M Internal Resources, US$20M Loan

Addressing concerns about the financing arrangement, Tweh disclosed that the project would be funded through two major sources.

He said the LPRC would contribute approximately US$15 million from its internally generated resources, representing 42.86 percent of the total investment, while the remaining US$20 million, or 57.14 percent, would come through loan financing.

Tweh maintained that the company’s substantial internal contribution demonstrates management’s commitment to responsible investment while limiting its external borrowing requirements.

However, the Senate’s concern centered on whether the proposed borrowing had received the necessary legislative authorization.

Tweh said the LPRC remains committed to transparency, accountability, responsible borrowing and statutory compliance, adding that management was prepared to provide lawmakers with the relevant legal, financial, procurement and contractual documents for scrutiny.

LPRC Seeks to Strengthen National Energy Security

Defending the strategic importance of the project, Tweh said the uninterrupted availability of petroleum products remains fundamental to Liberia’s national security, economic stability and sustainable development.

He noted that transportation, electricity generation, mining, agriculture, manufacturing, healthcare and other essential public services depend heavily on reliable petroleum supplies.

Tweh recalled that upon assuming leadership of the LPRC in 2024, management made a commitment to President Joseph Nyuma Boakai that gasoline shortages would become a thing of the past.

He said the commitment has informed management’s decisions, particularly in the areas of direct petroleum importation, expansion of state-owned storage facilities and strengthening national energy security.

According to Tweh, the LPRC currently accounts for approximately 34 percent of Liberia’s total petroleum storage capacity, with the remaining capacity largely controlled by private-sector operators.

While acknowledging the importance of private-sector participation, he argued that the limited storage capacity under state ownership restricts the government’s ability to independently safeguard national petroleum supplies during emergencies and international disruptions.

He cited geopolitical instability in the Middle East, potential disruptions to international shipping routes and Liberia’s heavy dependence on imported petroleum products as reasons the country must strengthen its petroleum storage infrastructure.

Tweh also referenced reported petroleum supply challenges in neighboring countries, including fuel shortages and long queues at filling stations, as evidence of the importance of maintaining adequate national reserves.

He argued that the affordability of petroleum products becomes less meaningful when the products themselves are unavailable to consumers.

“It is therefore imperative that the Government of Liberia, through LPRC, possess adequate state-owned petroleum storage infrastructure to facilitate the establishment and effective management of a National Strategic Petroleum Reserve,” he said.

He added that such infrastructure, supported by appropriate national reserve policies and inventory arrangements, would strengthen Liberia’s resilience against international supply disruptions, global market shocks and national emergencies.

Petroleum Demand Rises by 59.4%

Tweh further justified the expansion by pointing to what he described as significant growth in Liberia’s national petroleum demand.

He disclosed that petroleum demand increased by approximately 59.4 percent between 2023 and 2025, underscoring the need to expand the country’s storage infrastructure to accommodate growing consumption.

Upon completion of the project, he projected that the LPRC’s share of national petroleum storage capacity would increase from approximately 34 percent to 48 percent.

He said the expansion would significantly improve the government’s ability to safeguard national petroleum supplies and respond to potential emergencies.

Tweh maintained that the investment goes beyond the commercial interests of the LPRC and represents a strategic national undertaking aimed at strengthening energy security, economic resilience and emergency preparedness.

Management Pledges Transparency

Concluding his presentation, Tweh reaffirmed the LPRC’s commitment to transparency, accountability, responsible borrowing, statutory compliance and prudent management of public assets.

He welcomed the Senate’s scrutiny of the project and said management was prepared to provide all relevant documentation, including legal, statutory, financial, procurement, contractual and institutional records, to facilitate an informed assessment.

The Senate’s inquiry places the financing and approval process for the US$35 million modernization project under legislative scrutiny, particularly the proposed US$20 million loan component.

The question of whether the borrowing and associated project arrangements received the required legislative authorization remains central to the concerns raised by lawmakers.

World.title: Liberia: ‘Regulation Must Not Become Restriction’ — PUL President Confronts LTA Over Radio Rules
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE, Liberia — The President of the Press Union of Liberia (PUL), Julius Kanubah, has cautioned the Liberia Telecommunications Authority (LTA) against turning broadcasting regulations into instruments of restriction and censorship, warning that excessive regulatory controls could undermine press freedom and democratic accountability in Liberia.

By Patience M. Jones

Kanubah said while the media community recognizes the need for effective regulation of the country’s broadcasting sector, such measures must not create an atmosphere of fear, uncertainty, or intimidation among radio broadcasters.



He made the statement on Monday, November 23 while delivering the keynote address at the opening of a two-day FM Radio Regulations Stakeholders’ Sensitization Workshop organized by the LTA and implemented by Howe Trainers and Associates (HTA) at the Paynesville City Hall.

Speaking under the theme:, “Towards a Regulatory Framework that Protects Both Order and Freedom,” the PUL president emphasized that regulation must be grounded in transparency, fairness, consultation, and respect for constitutional freedoms.

“Regulation must never become synonymous with restriction. And I like the fact the Director of National Communications Bureau at the Ministry of Information, Mrs. Agatha Thompson-Venn, said it must not be synonymous with censorship,” Kanubah declared.

He stressed that the media community is not opposed to regulation, acknowledging that the airwaves are a limited national resource requiring technical standards, proper frequency management, and professional broadcasting practices.



However, he maintained that regulatory authorities must prioritize legitimacy and stakeholder confidence rather than rely primarily on sanctions and enforcement.

According to Kanubah, radio remains Liberia’s most accessible communication medium, particularly for rural communities where newspapers have limited circulation and internet connectivity remains a challenge.

He described radio as more than a commercial enterprise, noting that it serves as a public good and a critical democratic institution through which citizens access information on governance, elections, public health, education and national development.

The PUL President also referenced President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s recent description of journalism and media work, particularly radio broadcasting, as a public service.

Kanubah warned that any regulatory framework that fails to recognize the public interest role of broadcasting risks weakening the very democratic principles it is intended to support.

PUL Raises Concerns Over Licensing, Fees and Due Process

The PUL president outlined several concerns requiring urgent attention from the LTA, including the transparency of licensing and renewal procedures, the financial burden of regulatory compliance, due process, and the protection of freedom of expression.

He argued that radio stations investing in equipment, personnel, content production, and community engagement deserve predictable and objective licensing procedures.

According to him, unnecessary delays, unclear requirements, and inconsistent decisions could discourage investment and create uncertainty within the broadcasting industry.

He also expressed concern over the financial difficulties confronting community radio stations, particularly those operating in rural Liberia with limited donor support and resources.

Kanubah warned that excessive regulatory costs could force some of these stations out of operation, thereby depriving thousands of Liberians of access to essential public information.

On due process, he insisted that broadcasters accused of violating regulations must be given opportunities to respond to allegations and access fair and independent appeal mechanisms before administrative actions are imposed.

He further cautioned against regulatory interference with legitimate criticism, investigative journalism, and public debate.

While acknowledging broadcasters’ responsibility to avoid incitement, misinformation, and harmful content, Kanubah maintained that democratic societies must allow scrutiny and accountability rather than silence dissenting voices.

Demands Eight Reforms from LTA

Moving beyond criticism, Kanubah presented eight practical recommendations aimed at improving regulatory compliance and strengthening relations between the LTA and broadcasting stakeholders.

Among his proposals is the establishment of a permanent Broadcasting Stakeholders Forum that would bring together radio station owners, journalists’ associations, community broadcasters, and civil society organizations for quarterly consultations.

He said regular engagement would help address challenges before they escalate into disputes and prevent the regulator from engaging stakeholders only when introducing new regulations or responding to problems.

Kanubah also called on the LTA to publish simplified regulatory guidelines explaining licensing requirements, renewal procedures, compliance obligations, technical standards, sanctions, and appeal processes.

To support his argument, he referenced a 2021/2022 research assessment conducted by Internews, which, according to him, found that more than 30 community radio stations participating in the project did not meet the LTA’s regulatory requirements despite already operating.

He said the findings demonstrate the need for clearer regulatory guidance to help broadcasters understand and meet their obligations.

“Many stations, particularly in rural areas, struggle to interpret complex legal and regulatory language. Clear guidance would improve compliance and transparency,” he noted.

The PUL President also proposed a graduated compliance framework that would prioritize advisory notices, corrective action plans, technical support, and written warnings before resorting to administrative sanctions.

He argued that such an approach would encourage radio stations to correct violations without unnecessarily threatening their operations.

Additionally, Kanubah called for a comprehensive review of licensing and regulatory fees affecting community radio stations, proposing a differentiated fee structure that considers the financial realities of small, nonprofit broadcasters.

He further urged the LTA to establish clear timelines for processing licensing applications and renewals, publicly communicate reasons for denied, suspended, or revoked licenses, and strengthen independent appeals mechanisms.

On professional development, he encouraged the Authority to collaborate with the PUL, media training institutions, and development partners to provide broadcasters with technical training, regulatory compliance education, digital broadcasting knowledge, spectrum management awareness, and emerging technology skills.

He also called for the development of a national digital broadcasting roadmap to address digital migration, online broadcasting, streaming services, artificial intelligence in media, and cross-platform broadcasting standards.

Warns Against Excluding PUL from Regulatory Process

In one of his strongest messages, Kanubah called for a new regulatory relationship between the LTA and broadcasters, insisting that effective regulation cannot be achieved without the meaningful participation of the media community.

He said the success of the LTA should not be measured by the number of radio stations it sanctions but by the number of stations it helps become compliant, sustainable, professional and independent.

“The future of broadcasting in Liberia requires a new compact between regulators and broadcasters. One grounded in mutual respect. One based on transparency rather than suspicion. One built on dialogue rather than directives,” he stated.

Kanubah also emphasized that independent media and effective regulation should not be treated as opposing forces but as essential partners in democratic development.

He called for the institutional involvement of the Press Union in future regulatory consultations, warning that the Union should not be sidelined in decisions affecting the broadcasting industry.

Acknowledging Howe Trainers and Associates for implementing the workshop in partnership with the LTA, Kanubah disclosed that he had held discussions with the company’s Chief Executive Officer and Managing Consultant, Aris Leviticus Howe, regarding opportunities for broader engagement.

He expressed hope that the PUL would be actively involved in organizing future stakeholder consultations rather than being treated merely as a participant or invited speaker.

“The LTA must not avoid or ignore the PUL in such a process,” he stressed.

Kanubah maintained that the LTA, the Ministry of Information, the Press Union of Liberia, and other relevant stakeholders must work collectively if the country is to establish an effective and accountable broadcasting regulatory system.

He concluded by reaffirming the media community’s readiness to work with the Authority while making clear that the Union would continue to challenge regulatory decisions that threaten constitutional freedoms.

“For in the end, a free and responsible media is not a threat to national development. It is one of its strongest foundations,” Kanubah declared.

World.title: Govt to launch the National Anticipatory Action Framework 2026 -20230
World.content:
The Disaster Risk Management Division National Coordinator, Norman Chipakupaku, has announced that Zambia will tomorrow Friday, November 27, 2026, launch the National Anticipatory Action Framework 2026–2030 ahead of the anticipated 2026/2027 El Niño phenomenon.

Mr Chipakupaku said the framework is designed to shift Zambia’s approach to disaster management from responding to emergencies after they occur to taking proactive measures before disasters strike.

He said the framework is expected to support the government’s Grow Zambia Agenda by safeguarding agricultural productivity, food security, infrastructure and livelihoods against climate-related disasters.

Speaking during the National Anticipatory Action Dialogue Platform in Lusaka, Mr Chipakupaku said anticipatory action is critical to protecting the country’s development gains and ensuring that climate shocks do not undermine national economic transformation.

He said the framework would ensure that early warning information translates into timely action, particularly in vulnerable communities.

Mr Chipakupaku said the 2023/2024 El Niño-induced drought exposed weaknesses in the country’s disaster preparedness, despite early forecasts indicating the likelihood of below-normal rainfall.

He said the drought affected millions of Zambians, significantly reduced agricultural production, strained water resources and disrupted electricity generation.

Mr Chipakupaku said the experience demonstrated the need for government institutions and other stakeholders to act on early warning information before disasters escalate into national emergencies.

He said the framework aligns with the Grow Zambia Agenda, which prioritises economic transformation, increased agricultural productivity, food security, job creation and inclusive growth.

Mr Chipakupaku said protecting communities, infrastructure and livelihoods against disasters would help ensure that public resources are directed towards development rather than costly emergency response and recovery efforts.

He cited 211 bridges that could potentially be affected by flooding, warning that damage to critical infrastructure could disrupt economic activities and national development.

Mr Chipakupaku said the framework would also strengthen coordination among government ministries, cooperating partners, provincial and district structures, the private sector and humanitarian organisations.

He said the National Anticipatory Action Framework is not merely a policy document but a national commitment to making preparedness a permanent feature of Zambia’s governance system.

Mr Chipakupaku said the framework would be implemented under the theme “Anticipate, Integrate and Act,” calling on all stakeholders to take collective responsibility for identifying risks and responding before they develop into disasters.

Speaking at the same event, United Nations Resident Coordinator Beatrice Mutali, represented by Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Representative Geoffrey Chomba, commended the Government for launching the National Anticipatory Action Framework.

Ms Mutali reaffirmed the United Nations’ commitment to supporting Zambia in mitigating disaster risks associated with the anticipated 2026/2027 El Niño phenomenon.

World.title: Youths in Rufunsa embark on waste recycling initiative
World.content:
Youths in Chintimbwe Ward of Rufunsa District have embarked on a waste recycling initiative aimed at complementing government’s efforts in promoting proper waste management and environmental protection.

The initiative, spearheaded by Anseu Eco Innovations, a group of youths in the area, involves collecting discarded plastics and cardboard boxes which they take to recyclers outside the district.

ZANIS reports that Project Founder, Gloria Mabena, observed that improper disposal of waste materials such as plastics and cardboard boxes was a growing concern in most of the communities including schools and offices because of the negative impact on the environment and the potential spread of diseases.

Ms Mabena said collecting the waste and recycling such materials could contribute to national development and the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by creating economic opportunities and promoting sustainable waste management practices.

“Waste materials should not merely be viewed as unwanted products but as valuable resources that could be transformed into useful products through recycling and economic benefit for the country,” Ms Mabena stated.

She further added that the team is looking forward to becoming a hub of waste management where recyclers can trade.

Meanwhile, some youths and elderly members of the community have welcomed the initiative, saying it would help promote a cleaner and healthier environment.

Susan Chimusanya said the community has realised that collecting waste such as plastics and card boxes has an economic value not only to the people but the nation.

“Such efforts are important in addressing waste management challenges and also encouraging us the residents to take responsibility in keeping our surroundings clean,” Ms Chimusanya said.

Christopher Mwanza, also a resident in the area, said the project by Anesu has kept most of the youths busy with collecting plastic wastes and card boxes which they gather and later sell to recyclers in Lusaka.

World.title: Chongwe’s Nakatindi Ward Councilor elected Deputy Mayor
World.content:
Chongwe’s Nakatindi Ward Councilor, Sitali Akashi, has been elected as Deputy Mayor of Chongwe following an unopposed nomination.

Chongwe Municipal Council, Town Clerk, Carol Mkandawire, swore in Mr Akashi during the first full council meeting held at Chongwe Municipal Council Chambers.

Ms Mkandawire says Mr Akashi went unopposed as the local authority did not receive any other nominations by close of November 23rd, 2026 which was the set deadline for nominations.

Mr Akashi thanked his fellow councilors for electing him as Deputy Mayor.

He stated that he is looking forward to working with the Mayor and various stakeholders to uplift the livelihood of people in the area and also contributing towards advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Akashi assured that he will work with all the councilors regardless of their political affiliation to deliver desired development to Chongwe.

“I will work with all our councilors including those from opposition and independent ones because our duty is to serve the people of Chongwe and develop the area which can only be attained with unity of purpose,” Mr Akashi said.

He thanked members of the United Party for National Development (UPND) for supporting and encouraging him to contest for the Deputy Mayoral seat.

Meanwhile, Chongwe Mayor, Frederick Sashi, has congratulated Mr Akashi for being elected as Deputy Mayor.

Mr Sashi wished his newly elected deputy well as he undertakes his duties.
