World.title: Over 3,590 farmers in Milenge redeem inputs
World.content:
Over 3,590 farmers in Milenge District have fully redeemed their farming inputs under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP) for the 2026/2027 farming season out of 4,601 registered beneficiaries.

Milenge Agriculture Marketing Officer, Kennedy Munthali, has also disclosed that 33 farmers had partially redeemed their inputs, while 291 had not yet collected their supplies.

Mr Munthali said the district has 16 active agro-dealers operating across the district to facilitate farmers’ access to inputs and ensure efficient redemption.

“This time around, we have 16 active agro-dealers scattered around the district,” Mr Munthali said.

He further noted that over 3,880 farmers had been automatically added to the Authority to Deposit (ATD) system by virtue of selling their maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA).

Mr Munthali explained that the automatic inclusion of farmers who supplied maize to FRA had contributed to the number of beneficiaries captured on the system under the programme.

He also urged farmers who had not yet redeemed their inputs to collect their supplies from the available agro-dealers in readiness for the current farming season.

World.title: Government reaffirms commitment to ending child marriage
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its commitment to ending child marriage and protecting the rights of children through strengthened legislation, public awareness and partnerships aimed at keeping girls in school.

Speaking during a media engagement breakfast ahead of the special screening of the feature film LUTE in Lusaka, Gender Division Permanent Secretary at Cabinet Office, Mainga Kabika said government remains committed to addressing child marriage, which continues to deprive many girls of their childhood, education and opportunities.

Ms Kabika explained that the fight against child marriage requires collective efforts from government, cooperating partners, civil society organizations and the media to address the social and economic factors contributing to the practice.

She further explained that the Gender Division is working with partners, including the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), Yash Foundation and Centripetal Media Productions, to raise awareness and strengthen interventions aimed at ending child marriage.

Ms Kabika noted that the government enacted legislation in December 2023, setting 18 years as the minimum legal age for marriage under both customary and statutory law.

She added that the national GBV toll-free line 944 provides support and emergency response services to victims, while the ongoing review of the Anti-Gender-Based Violence Act is expected to strengthen protection mechanisms.

Meanwhile, United Nations Population Fund [Highlight end] , (UNFPA) Country Representative, Seth Broekman said child marriage remains a major concern, with nearly one in four young women in Zambia aged 20 to 24 having been married before turning 18 years old .

Mr Broekman highlighted that although Zambia had made progress in reducing child marriage, with prevalence declining from 43.3 percent in 1992 to 23.9 percent in 2024, significant disparities remain across districts.

He stated that keeping girls in secondary school significantly reduces their chances of entering into child marriage, making education one of the strongest interventions in protecting their future.

He said the film LUTE provides an opportunity to highlight the realities faced by girls and encourage society to protect their right to education and make decisions about their own futures.

Mr Broekman said the engagement is also part of activities commemorating the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, being observed under the theme, “Ensure justice, protect survivors, and end impunity.”

And Yash Foundation Director, Aditi Patel said the organisation had supported the production of LUTE as part of efforts to promote girls’ education and empowerment.

Ms Patel disclosed that all proceeds generated from the movie would go towards supporting children’s education.

She further stated that the initiative seeks to use the power of cinema to create meaningful social impact by raising awareness about child marriage, poverty and the barriers that prevent girls from completing their education.

Ms Patel appealed to corporates, business leaders and development partners to support the initiative by promoting the film and helping extend its message beyond Zambia.

World.title: Multi-sports facility centre on the cards in Ndola
World.content:
Ndola’s Bwana Mkubwa Member of Parliament Warren Mwambazi has announced plans to establish a multi-sports facility centre through the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to promote youth development, nurture talent and address social challenges affecting young people in the constituency.

Mwambazi said the initiative follows the implementation of more than 45 projects in health, education and water between 2021 and 2026, adding that there is now need to invest in projects specifically targeting the youth.

The lawmaker said the proposed facility will accommodate football, basketball, volleyball, netball and badminton, with four seven-a-side football pitches allowing eight teams to play simultaneously, alongside an indoor hall for mixed martial arts, karate, judo and boxing.

Mwambazi said the centre will also include counselling services to address drug and substance abuse and mental health challenges, an art gallery to promote and commercialise local artistic talent, as well as a music recording studio.

“We want to have four seven-aside football pitches. We want to have playing fields for volleyball, basketball, netball and badminton,” he said in Ndola.

He said architectural drawings have already been prepared, with an architect and project manager engaged to develop the concept before it is presented to the local authority and other stakeholders for consideration and support.

Mwambazi said the facility will further establish grassroots sports academies to identify and nurture talent in different disciplines while providing young people with constructive activities and opportunities to keep them away from drug and alcohol abuse.

World.title: More seats, but whose interests? The constitutional mandate of Zambia’s proportional representation MPs
World.content:
In their maiden parliamentary speeches, some of the country’s new proportional representation MPs called for removing presidential term limits, raising troubling questions about their understanding of their constitutional mandate.

Holding seats intended to amplify the voices of women, young people, and persons with disabilities, these legislators should lead in holding the executive to account and translating political representation into meaningful policy outcomes.

Following the August 2026 general elections, the country entered a new chapter in its democratic evolution. The Fourteenth National Assembly welcomed, for the first time, forty Members of Parliament (MPs) holding seats under the proportional representation electoral system, as provided for in Article 68(1)(b) of the Constitution: twenty women, fifteen youths and five persons with disabilities.

The expansion was intended to address a persistent democratic deficit: the underrepresentation of these groups in the chamber where national laws are made and public resources allocated. Yet, in the opening months of the First Session, a troubling question has emerged: do proportional representation (PR) MPs fully understand their constitutional role?

Amid the pressing concerns of women entrepreneurs, unemployed graduates and citizens facing inaccessible public infrastructure, some PR MPs have championed a vastly different cause: the removal of presidential term limits. One such intervention came from United Party for National Development (UPND) youth PR MP Mr Mwanto Kabaso during his maiden speech on 3 November 2026.

The Government, through Minister of Information and Media Elvis Nkandu, subsequently stated that reopening the issue of presidential term limits was not government policy. The dispute raises a fundamental question about the distinction between serving the Constitution and serving the perceived wishes of political power.

Three issues matter: what proportional representation means, how the country’s electoral system distributes power, and what Article 63 of the Constitution demands of MPs in overseeing the executive.

At its core, proportional representation (PR) is an electoral principle built on a simple premise: representation should broadly reflect the distribution of electoral support. Under first-past-the-post (FPTP), the system traditionally used for the country’s constituency seats, the candidate with the most votes wins the seat, even without securing an absolute majority.

Smaller political formations and minority viewpoints may consequently be underrepresented; historically marginalised groups can also face barriers to winning constituency contests. PR seeks to reduce such distortions by distributing seats broadly in proportion to electoral support, subject to the applicable formula and eligibility rules.

In a party-list system, seats are allocated to parties and filled from candidate lists. The timing of list submission and whether voters can influence the choice of individual candidates depend on the particular electoral rules.

Crucially, the method of obtaining a PR seat does not diminish the parliamentary status of its holder. PR MPs are not simply party-list delegates whose primary duty is to reward those who selected them. They are full Members of the National Assembly.

Their representative responsibility is twofold: to serve the national interest alongside constituency MPs and to bring the perspectives of historically underrepresented groups into legislative, policy, and budget deliberations. This aligns with Articles 45 and 61, which emphasise inclusive representation and the exercise of legislative authority on behalf of the people, respectively.

Section 2 of the Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2025, enacted from Bill 7, describes National Assembly elections in Article 47(2) as a mixed-member proportional representation (MMPR) system. In comparative electoral terminology, however, the label is inaccurate.

For example, in New Zealand’s MMPR system, the proportional tier compensates for disproportionality in constituency results. If a party receives 40 per cent of the relevant party vote, its overall seat entitlement is ordinarily calculated on that basis, with list seats used to make up any shortfall after constituency seats are counted, subject to the system’s rules.

Zambia’s model does not do this. The original Bill 7 envisaged a separate PR ballot, but at the Committee Stage on 15 December 2025 an amendment introduced allocation by presidential votes, now embodied in Article 47(4).

Under Articles 47 and 68, 226 constituency seats are decided by FPTP, while the forty reserved PR seats are distributed separately according to presidential electoral support. Section 36B and the First Schedule to the Electoral Process (Amendment) Act No. 12 of 2026 implement that allocation through category-specific quotas based on valid presidential votes in the initial ballot.

Constituency seats already won are not deducted from a party’s PR entitlement. The two tiers operate in parallel. We have, in substance, a mixed-member majoritarian (MMM), or parallel, electoral system with reserved demographic seats, notwithstanding the constitutional label.

The Inter-Parliamentary Union likewise classifies the 2026 system as mixed-member majoritarian.

Why does this distinction matter? The MMPR label suggests overall proportionality, whereas a dominant party can win a large share of both constituency and reserved seats without the latter correcting the former.

Moreover, section 36C of the 2026 amendment requires parties to submit candidate lists within seven days after seats are allocated. The Electoral Commission of Zambia verifies candidates’ eligibility and publishes the names under sections 36C and 36G.

Thus, voters influence the allocation of PR seats through their presidential votes, but it is the parties, not the electorate, which select the individuals to fill them. Voters do not vote on a party list submitted before the election.

Article 72(2)(d) and (e) provides for loss of office upon resignation from or expulsion by the sponsoring party, subject to constitutional safeguards. Section 36H(2) of the 2026 amendment also allows a sponsoring party to recall its PR MP at any time during the parliamentary term. Without a geographical constituency of their own, PR MPs may face acute pressure to conform to party expectations.

That vulnerability matters because executive oversight is a central function of the National Assembly. Under Article 63, the National Assembly is neither a cheering squad for State House nor a rubber stamp for Cabinet proposals.

Article 63(2) requires it to oversee executive functions by promoting equity in national resource distribution, appropriating public funds and scrutinising expenditure (including defence, constitutional and special expenditure). It also requires the House to approve public debt before it is contracted, and to approve international agreements and treaties before accession or ratification.

In a presidential system where the executive exercises substantial appointment and budgetary authority, the National Assembly is a vital institutional counterweight. Through portfolio committees, budget oversight and the work of the Public Accounts Committee, MPs can hold the executive accountable on behalf of citizens. The Parliamentary Legal Committee also plays a distinct role in scrutinising legislation for constitutional compliance.

For PR MPs, this oversight responsibility has an especially practical dimension. Consider what it could mean for the groups whose inclusion the reserved seats were designed to advance.

For the twenty women PR MPs, it means interrogating the release and use of women’s economic empowerment funds, scrutinising maternal healthcare budgets and holding ministries accountable for responses to gender-based violence.

For the fifteen youth PR MPs, it means examining expenditure on skills development, questioning procurement barriers faced by young entrepreneurs and demanding transparent job-creation indicators. For the five PR MPs representing persons with disabilities, it means scrutinising infrastructure legislation and budgets for accessible public buildings, and monitoring social protection disbursements.

The real test is turning representation into policy impact. PR MPs can use budget sittings, committee inquiries, parliamentary questions, and Auditor-General findings to press for gender-, youth- and disability-responsive allocations.

They should follow the money from appropriation to release, expenditure, and service delivery, asking ministries to publish disaggregated results: who benefited, where, and with what outcomes? For example, a maternal health allocation should translate into staffed facilities; youth skills funding into accessible training and employment opportunities; and infrastructure expenditure into buildings persons with disabilities can use.

Committee recommendations should specify corrective action and invite follow-up on implementation. Article 65 reserves the introduction of Money Bills to ministers, so MPs must pursue funding changes through lawful budget oversight, recommendations, and engagement with the executive. The measure of success is not just a larger allocation, but better services and demonstrable policy change.

When PR MPs neglect this detailed legislative oversight work in favour of partisan grandstanding, they undermine the justification for increasing constituency seats from 156 to 226 and introducing forty PR seats, with associated implications for public expenditure.

Concerns about legislators subordinating their constitutional role to political expediency predate the Fourteenth National Assembly. They were also evident in the dispute surrounding Bill 7 in 2025.

When Bill 7 was introduced and passed in December 2025, civil society organisations, legal scholars, and governance watchdogs raised concerns about its substance and the constitutional reform process. Contested proposals included increasing constituency seats and removing term limits for mayors and council chairpersons.

Critics contended that fundamental changes required broad, consensus-driven public participation rather than legislative arithmetic. The initial consultation process was successfully challenged in the Constitutional Court, and a technical committee undertook consultations before the Bill returned to Parliament.

Nevertheless, critics continued to question the process, and the House passed the Bill on 15 December 2025. The episode raises an enduring concern about treating the supreme law as political convenience rather than a national covenant.

The recent calls to remove presidential term limits must be viewed in this light. Article 106(3) provides that a person who has twice held office as President is ineligible for election to that office again, read together with the term-counting rules in Article 106(6).

That safeguard exists for a reason. Across post-independence Africa, presidential term limits have served as an institutional barrier against the personalisation of power, entrenched patronage, and democratic backsliding.

MPs enjoy parliamentary freedom of speech under Article 76 and may discuss constitutional reform. Advocating an amendment is not a constitutional violation. Yet there is profound irony when legislators brought into Parliament to strengthen representation of marginalised citizens prioritise removing a constitutional limit on executive power.

In a healthy democracy, strong institutions and predictable transfers of power safeguard rights. Weakening executive accountability risks making women, young people, and persons with disabilities more dependent on executive goodwill than institutional guarantees.

The country’s experiment with reserved PR seats is still young. Its forty MPs have a unique opportunity to transform how Parliament engages with citizens who have historically felt invisible in Lusaka.

Realising that promise requires a mindset shift within Parliament and among citizens. First, parliamentary leadership and civil society must invest in constitutional induction beyond procedural standing orders.

MPs must internalise that, although their political parties select them to fill PR seats, their constitutional responsibility is to the people of Zambia. Article 61 makes clear that legislative authority derives from the people and must be exercised to protect the Constitution and promote democratic governance.

Second, Zambians must hold PR MPs to measurable performance standards. They should be judged not by how loudly they praise executive leadership on the House floor, but by the budget priorities they champion, the questions they put to ministers, the recommendations they pursue through committees and the tangible policy improvements they help secure for women, young people and persons with disabilities.

Proportional representation was introduced to strengthen voices too often unheard. If those entrusted with that mandate mistake executive sycophancy for legislative duty, the country would have enlarged its Parliament without enlarging the substance of its democracy.

By Prof Cephas Lumina

Source: The Mast

World.title: Councils Must Draft Growth Plans Aligned to Grow Zambia Agenda, Says Hichilema
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has directed local authorities across Zambia to draw up clear economic growth strategies in line with government’s development plan. He said councils must move beyond routine administration and become active drivers of investment, enterprise and jobs under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The Head of State said councils played a critical role in carrying out the agenda. He described it as anchored on increased production, economic expansion, job creation and wealth creation for all citizens.

His message was delivered in a speech read on his behalf by Minister of Local Government and Rural Development Gift Sialubalo. The occasion was the 70th annual conference of the Local Government Association of Zambia (LGAZ), which ran together with the 23rd conference of the Alliance of Mayors and Municipal Leaders on HIV/AIDS in Africa (AMICAAL).

The gathering was held under the theme “Building Prosperous Communities Through Local Economic Development and Inclusive Governance.” The President’s instruction to the councils assembled was direct.

“I urge all local authorities to develop a clear economic growth strategy aligned with Government’s development plan,” President Hichilema said.

Mr Hichilema said the theme spoke directly to the nation’s aspirations. He stressed that Zambia could only prosper when local communities experienced meaningful economic development.

The UPND leader said councils held a strategic position in the country’s development architecture. They should therefore look beyond their traditional administrative duties and take up a more active role in growing the economy.

He spelt out what that role should look like in practice. “You are not merely providers of public services; you are also agents of investment, facilitators of enterprises, and catalysts of development,” the President said.

Mr Hichilema noted that investors often met government first through local authorities. That made it important for councils to present themselves as institutions that attract investment and promote economic development.

He urged each local authority to identify and exploit its comparative advantages in sectors such as agriculture, mining, tourism, manufacturing, forestry and trade. Doing so, he said, would turn local potential into economic opportunities for residents.

The Head of State made clear that central government could not carry the agenda on its own. He said implementation required the active participation and collaboration of every council in the country.

“The Grow Zambia Agenda can only succeed when all local authorities become active partners in driving economic growth,” President Hichilema said.

He then set out a list of practical tasks for councils. He challenged them to improve land management, facilitate industrialisation and create business-friendly environments that support small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

Mr Hichilema also called on local authorities to promote investment, widen employment opportunities and back entrepreneurship, particularly among young people and women. He added that councils should embrace green growth and ensure that their budgets are gender responsive, in the interest of inclusive development.

The call was welcomed by the conference leadership. Presiding chairperson Mr Maurice Mbolela commended President Hichilema for recognising local authorities as important partners in national development.

Mr Mbolela pledged that councils would continue working with government to improve service delivery and promote sustainable economic growth.

Lusaka Mayor Chitambala Mwewa said the gathering showed a shared commitment to strengthening local governance and improving service delivery at grassroots level.

With the President’s directive on record, each council is now expected to produce its own economic growth strategy aligned with the national development plan. Those strategies should be built on the sectors where each district holds a natural edge.

World.title: ZCTU flags funding gaps in 2027 national budget statement
World.content:
THE Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU) has accused Treasury of failing to allocate resources for job creation to support Cabinet’s recently adopted job-creation policies.

ZCTU secretary-general flagged the issue in his analysis of Finance minister Mthuli Ncube’s 2027 national budget, saying the budget was silent on the National Employment Policy (2026-2030) and the National Formalisation Strategy. Both policies were approved by Cabinet in April this year.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: TB treatment success tops 90%, but shrinking aid puts gains at risk
World.content:
AN estimated 26,000 people developed tuberculosis (TB) in Zimbabwe in 2025, and about 22,200 of them were diagnosed and put on treatment, Health and Child Care deputy minister Sleiman Kwidini has said.

Speaking at the official launch of the Zimbabwe National Tuberculosis Conference 2026 in Harare on Wednesday, Kwidini warned that the shrinking external funding base could reverse the gains made in taming the disease.

Kwidini said the country’s TB treatment success rates were above 90% for both drug-sensitive and drug-resistant TB.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Prosecutors launch GBV awareness campaign
World.content:
THE National Prosecuting Authority of Zimbabwe (NPAZ) has rolled out an awareness campaign to sensitize the public on gender-based violence (GBV).

The programme kicked off at the national launch of the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence in Murehwa on Wednesday.

During the launch, prosecutors explained court procedures and the legal protections that Zimbabwean law gives to GBV survivors.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Air Zimbabwe resumes London flights with new partner
World.content:
AIR Zimbabwe resumes its Harare London Gatwick flights today with a Portuguese supplied aircraft, after Spanish lessor Plus Ultra pulled out this week, leaving passengers stranded.

The airline has signed a wet-lease agreement with Portugal’s EuroAtlantic Airways for an Airbus A330-300 after its Plus Ultra arrangement collapsed. Mutapa Investment Fund chief executive John Mangudya confirmed the deal to media on Wednesday night.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Mzondo named Team Zimbabwe captain and flag bearer for AUSC Region 5 Youth Games
World.content:
YOUTH Olympic champion Ropafadzo Mzondo has been appointed captain and flag bearer of Team Zimbabwe for the 12th AUSC Region 5 Youth Games in Mozambique.

The 17-year-old will lead the delegation and carry the national flag at the opening ceremony, an honour that reflects a remarkable few months. At the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games he won gold in the men’s 200 metres in 21,04 seconds, Zimbabwe’s first ever medal at the Youth Olympics.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Gotal gets her Mighty Warriors together for FIFA window camp
World.content:
Mighty Warriors head coach Stella Gotal has named a 28-player squad for a training camp in the FIFA window, giving her more time with the group after the defeat to Malawi ended the team’s Los Angeles 2028 Olympic qualifying campaign.

Time together has been the main limit on Gotal’s work. She is still in the early weeks of her tenure and the squad is spread across home clubs and teams abroad, so a camp gives her one of the few chances to work on her ideas.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 26, 2026
World.content:
Fuel Tanker Explosion on Cairo Highway Kills 31 People

At least 31 people were killed and 21 others injured when a fuel tanker overturned and caught fire on a busy highway in Cairo, Egypt. The fire in the Warraq neighborhood, which also burned several nearby cars, left victims suffering from burns and smoke inhalation. The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, was on the highway when a high-voltage cable fell on its path, and the driver lost control. The incident is being investigated by authorities. Emergency services have since cleared the wreckage and reopened the highway. The health ministry deployed 39 ambulances to assist victims, while hospitals treated those injured in the fire.

South African President Ramaphosa Wins Phala Phala Court Battle



South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal challenge against a parliamentary independent panel report that found he had a case to answer over the theft of $580,000 from his Phala Phala farm. The Western Cape High Court declared the report unlawful and set it aside in its entirety, ruling that the panel had exceeded its mandate and made legal errors. The decision effectively removes the basis for the current impeachment process. However, the opposition parties may challenge the verdict. The judgment does not find any wrongdoing. The scandal, which emerged in 2022, has continued to hang over Ramaphosa's presidency despite several investigations clearing him of any wrongdoing.

Nigeria Seizes 1.5 Tonnes of Meth in Cartel-Linked Lab Raid

Nigerian authorities have arrested five Mexican nationals and a local businessman following the discovery of an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory in Enugu State. More than 1.5 tonnes of the drug, valued at $227 million, were seized. The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said that the operation followed a seven-month international investigation. The suspects are allegedly linked to a wider drug trafficking network involving Mexican cartel specialists and Nigerian collaborators. Nearly seven tonnes of chemicals and industrial equipment were also recovered. This marks the fourth suspected cartel-linked meth laboratory uncovered in Nigeria in recent months. The agency said the latest arrests bring to 10 the number of suspected Mexican meth production specialists detained in the country in recent months.

EU Extends Mozambique Military Mission to 2028

The European Union has extended its Military Assistance Mission in Mozambique until December 2028. It has allocated €17.17 million to support the country's fight against Islamist insurgents in Cabo Delgado. The funding will cover the period from January 2027 to December 2028, under a decision adopted by the Council. The mission will continue training, mentoring and advising Mozambican armed forces in military planning, intelligence, logistics and operational readiness, but will not participate directly in combat. The extension aims to strengthen the country's ability to independently plan and sustain military operations while promoting human rights and civilian protection. The renewed mandate follows a September strategic assessment that found continued EU support necessary to build sustainable capabilities within Mozambique's armed forces.

Egypt, Sudan Agree on Post-War Reconstruction

Egypt and Sudan have agreed to prioritise Sudan's post-war reconstruction, expand economic cooperation and strengthen coordination on Red Sea security. During talks in Cairo, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Sudanese Prime Minister Kamal Idris reaffirmed their support for Sudan's sovereignty and rejected attempts to militarise the strategic waterway. They insisted that its governance belongs to coastal states. The two sides also underscored the importance of respecting freedom of navigation in the Red Sea while rejecting attempts to "militarize the waterway or take unilateral actions that infringe on the sovereignty of its coastal states." The discussions also covered the voluntary return of Sudanese nationals, the repatriation of prisoners and efforts to restore Sudan's participation in African Union institutions. Idris also called for an inclusive intra-Sudanese dialog to build national consensus, address humanitarian concerns and lay the groundwork for reconciliation.

Close 

AI Fears Mount Ahead of Nigeria's 2027 Elections

Nigeria's electoral commission is investigating suspected AI-generated images and other irregularities in the country's preliminary voter register, ahead of the 2027 general elections, raising concerns about electoral credibility and preparedness. The irregularities reported included manipulation of facial features, duplicated identities, and dead voters' names. The Independent National Electoral Commission has established a special unit to monitor AI-related threats and deepfakes, as experts warn artificial intelligence could fuel disinformation, manipulate voters and erode public trust in the electoral process. Concerns were heightened by the history of online misinformation during elections in Nigeria and a record-low voter turnout of 27% in 2023.

World.title: South Africa: More Arrests Expected in Tembisa Hospital Scandal - South African News Briefs - November 26, 2026
World.content:
press review

More Arrests Expected in Tembisa Hospital Corruption Scandal

The Special Investigating Unit (SIU) has said that further arrests are expected in the alleged R2 billion Tembisa Hospital corruption scandal, involving businessmen accused of siphoning funds from the facility, reports EWN. The update comes as businessman Hangwani Maumela seeks to recover his Ferrari, which was preserved by the SIU. The State's curator sold the car for R10.1 million. The SIU is also engaging with alleged syndicate member Rudolf Mazibuko. Businessman Stefan Govindraju and his alleged accomplices are set back in court in February 2027.

Ramaphosa Extends TRC Cases Inquiry to 2027



President Cyril Ramaphosa has extended the term of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) Cases Inquiry to March 31, 2027, reports SABC News. The deadline to submit its final report to Ramaphosa has also been extended to May 31 next year. The Presidency said that the third extension is necessary to allow more witnesses to testify before the inquiry, chaired by Justice Sisi Khampepe, concludes its work. The inquiry is investigating alleged efforts to obstruct the prosecution of apartheid-era crimes.

ConCourt Weighs Alternatives to Medical Negligence Payouts

The Constitutional Court is considering whether victims of state medical negligence should be allowed alternatives to once-off lump-sum compensation payments, reports EWN. The Eastern Cape Department of Health and other applicants are challenging a Supreme Court of Appeal ruling that overturned an order allowing victims to receive healthcare services instead. The department argued that large payouts place pressure on public healthcare finances. The court is set to hear arguments opposing the appeal.

World.title: Africa: Push for Safer Surgery to Reduce Maternal Deaths
World.content:
Nigeria faces one of the world's highest maternal mortality rates.

Many of these deaths can be prevented, but delays in the identification or treatment of emergencies during obstetrics will soon transform potential problems into tragedies. Emergency surgical care, particularly in the event of a caesarean section, can mean the difference between life and death for mothers and their newborns. In low- and middle-income countries, women are up to 100 times more likely to die after a caesarean than in wealthy nations.

As countries work towards the global target of fewer than 70 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030, closing the surgical care gap must become a greater health priority.

"I don't believe in doing nothing. Let us do something."



In Kano, Dr Olusegun Samuel Spaine has witnessed the struggles of mothers and health workers. He once donated his own blood in a desperate attempt to save a mother experiencing a life-threatening childbirth complication. Despite his efforts, she died.

"It remained with me because that was the first patient I lost on the operating table," he said.

Spaine said shortages of equipment and limited resources often make it difficult for healthcare workers to respond quickly to obstetric emergencies, forcing teams to balance the urgency of treatment against patient safety. "When you have a patient that you need to take care of immediately, and there's this delay one way or the other, it's very frustrating," he said.

"We don't want to lose the patient's life, and we don't want to take unnecessary risks," said Spaine.

Dr Geoff Ibbotson, Executive Director of the Global Surgery Foundation (GSF), said that the gaps run from community awareness and antenatal care to safe birthing in well-staffed facilities and follow-up after delivery. "Safe caesarean section is one of the biggest gaps, and it is where our work focuses," he said.

"A caesarean section is meant to save two lives. It can only do that if it is safe."

John Schaeffler, President of the GE HealthCare Foundation, which supports the work, said that urgency is why surgery should not be treated as a specialist extra. "For a woman experiencing an obstetric emergency, there's nothing optional about it," he said. He pointed out that in Africa and other parts of the world, surgical care is usually provided in larger cities, while practitioners and equipment are lacking in rural and less accessible areas where a surgical intervention is most likely to save a life.

"We believe that a woman's chances of surviving childbirth should never depend on where she lives or whether her local hospital has the resources to save her," said Schaeffler.

"Surgical care requires more than equipment."

Schaeffler said that one of the biggest challenges in global health is that surgery depends on far more than equipment: trained staff, reliable infrastructure and the means to keep standards high. He said the funding for these needs is often fragmented or insufficient.

Through GSF's SURGfund, the GE HealthCare Foundation brings together funding partners to strengthen surgical services in areas where needs are greatest. He said that in Nakuru, Kenya, this support is helping clinicians adopt safer surgical practices, monitor patient outcomes and share their expertise with colleagues. He said the aim was to make these improvements part of everyday hospital operations, ensuring mothers and families have better access to safe surgery.

"By investing in both the people delivering care and the systems supporting them", he said, "we can help make safe surgery more accessible to the mothers and families who depend on it."

Schaeffler said building lasting local capacity requires foundations and private-sector partners to strengthen healthcare systems rather than focus on individual interventions.

"The real measure of philanthropy is its lasting impact," he said. "That's why we're helping healthcare systems become stronger and more self-sufficient, so they can provide quality care for generations to come."

He said this requires understanding the daily challenges facing healthcare professionals, including limited access to training and equipment, infrastructure gaps and difficulties providing safe emergency care, while identifying existing practices that work and areas where additional support could have the greatest impact. He said that as international health funding becomes less predictable, this approach is more important than ever. "Investing in the system holistically allows for sustained improvements that will serve communities well into the future," he said.

The funding squeeze has hit many organisations hard.

A news survey by PMNCH, covering partner organisations in 67 countries, shows that nearly 80% are dealing with reduced or uncertain funding. Meanwhile, 77% say global disruptions have moderately to severely affected their ability to advance the health and rights of women, children and adolescents. The survey also found that 69% have already been forced to scale back, temporarily suspend or permanently close programmes.

The findings point to a growing crisis in service delivery, as organisations struggle to maintain programmes, reach vulnerable communities and sustain essential health services amid financial uncertainty.

Ibbotson acknowledged that funding cuts have affected many organisations but said GSF had seen an increase in funding, which he attributed to its collaborative funding model and partnerships with organisations such as the GE HealthCare Foundation.

"There is a real appetite, because surgical care, and safe caesarean section care in particular, is so clearly a neglected area with great potential for impact, and we are now seeing the results of these investments," he said.

The projects GSF supports are now expanding to more facilities in Nigeria, Kenya and Nepal.

However, Ibbotson said the programme is designed to ensure local healthcare professionals take ownership of improvements through training, mentorship and the transfer of skills to other teams.

In Kano, the initiative is led by the Association for Clinical and Professional Health Advancement (ACEPHAP) at Bayero University, in partnership with the Kano State Ministry of Health. GSF mobilises funding from several partners and accompanies the teams through mentoring and quality improvement. "They own, and they deliver the training, and it is then their choice whether to continue it," he said.

"The costs to do this are minimal because the skills are incorporated into the usual routines, and therefore there are really no additional ongoing costs. The cost of not continuing is far greater," said Ibbotson.

Strong teamwork and coordination deliver impact

GSF reports a 45% drop in newborn mortality and surgical complications across its Nigerian programmes. Similar efforts in Kenya have reported a 72% reduction in newborn mortality, further highlighting the potential impact of strengthening surgical services.

"Strong teamwork and coordination deliver impact," said Ibbotson.

A new operating theatre without a trained team is useless, and sometimes dangerous.

Ibbotson said the results in Kano demonstrate the importance of strengthening existing healthcare teams through better coordination, teamwork and training. The gains came from teams already working in those hospitals, not from new buildings. New operating theatres are welcome, he said, but "a new operating theatre without a trained team is useless, and sometimes dangerous."

He said that unsafe surgery is increasingly linked to maternal deaths and to injuries such as fistula. He cited a national study in Malawi which found that 52% of maternal deaths following childbirth occurred after caesarean sections, despite the procedure accounting for about one in six hospital births in the study.

"We're seeing encouraging results in both countries," added Schaeffler.

Caesarean sections can save lives, he said, but complications such as severe bleeding, hemorrhaging and infections following surgery can put mothers at serious risk, sometimes requiring emergency treatment or prolonged hospitalization. In the most serious cases, these complications can be fatal.

In Kenya, GSF has reported a 45% reduction in newborn unit admissions, while in Nigeria, surgical site infections following Caesarean sections have fallen by nearly half. But the impact goes beyond individual procedures, he said. In Kenya, clinicians who have completed their training are now helping train the next cohort, allowing their knowledge and experience to benefit more patients.

"The lesson for scaling this work is that we can't simply replicate the same model everywhere. We need to work with local healthcare professionals and governments to understand each community's needs and incorporate successful practices into their health systems," said Schaeffler.

He said that the ultimate measure of success was ensuring improved care became standard practice across hospitals.

Ibbotson said the model could be expanded to other countries, provided it was adapted to their local healthcare needs, adding that the same approach is also working in Nepal.

He said that additional funding through SURGfund could help extend the programmes to more locations. GSF has expanded its supported projects over the past year and is prepared for further growth.

Close 

Hub-and-spoke model

Ibbotson explained that the hub-and-spoke model is designed to extend surgical skills and mentorship beyond major teaching hospitals to more remote facilities. "The key is to get these skills out to the more remote areas, where the people are and where access is limited. This will show the biggest impact," he said.

In Kano, two hospitals act as hubs that mentor the teams in eight other hospitals. This builds a strong community in which teams can support each other. "We strongly recommend not working in isolation but as part of a supportive community," he said. "The hubs can support the spokes, and even spokes support each other. That will deliver success. We focus on the more remote areas, not the big teaching hospitals."

He said African governments must take primary responsibility for financing and prioritising surgical care, with external organisations supporting locally led health systems rather than replacing government efforts.

"The ultimate responsibility remains with governments," he said. "This is not a cost; it is an investment. Lives will be saved, disabilities will be avoided, and communities will grow stronger, which strengthens the economy. It is a win-win investment."

He sees reasons for hope.

Ibbotson said that surgical care has been largely ignored by global health actors over the past several decades, and nine out of ten people in low- and lower-middle-income countries still cannot access basic surgical care. "But there is now an increasing awareness that surgical care systems are the backbone of the entire health system, particularly at the district hospital level, where the lion's share of the patients are treated," he said.

He added that local teams have shown how quickly care can become safer when they are trained and supported through a platform and funding that give them stability.

"If we can change the current situation and ensure that safe surgical care is available across Africa, then communities will have a better chance to thrive. What we are seeing at the project sites gives me hope, because the model is replicable," he said. "What is working in Kano and Nakuru can work in district hospitals across Africa. We are ready to grow it."

World.title: Kenya: President Ruto Signs Law Outlawing Traditional Settlements of Sexual Offences
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has signed into law legislation barring the use of traditional dispute resolution mechanisms to settle sexual offence cases, requiring such cases to be handled through the formal court system.

The new law invalidates agreements reached outside the judicial process, including settlements through traditional practices such as maslaha, amid concerns that informal arrangements allow perpetrators to escape prosecution while victims are denied justice.

The Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act, 2025, sponsored by Garissa County Woman Representative Udgoon Siyad Kuno, also requires sexual offence cases to be heard on a day-to-day basis and concluded within six months from the date a plea is recorded.



The legislation further prohibits the withdrawal of sexual offence complaints through coercion, intimidation or inducement of victims, while barring courts from discontinuing proceedings solely because parties have reached an out-of-court settlement.

The law follows concerns that traditional dispute resolution arrangements have been used to resolve serious criminal offences, including rape and defilement, outside the formal justice system.

During the presentation of the Bill at State House, government officials said the measure was intended to prevent perpetrators from evading accountability through informal settlements.

"Things like maslaha, which are largely practised in part of Kenya, are now outlawed," an official said while explaining the legislation to the President.

He added that the Director of Public Prosecutions would not be able to withdraw sexual offence cases on the basis that parties had reached an agreement through traditional dispute resolution.

The National Council on the Administration of Justice (NCAJ), chaired by the Chief Justice, backed the legislation, arguing that alternative dispute resolution in sexual offence cases could allow offenders to escape justice while exposing victims to further victimization.

Officials said the six-month timeline was intended to address delays in the determination of sexual offence cases, which can prolong the suffering of survivors and undermine access to justice.

The legislation is anchored on the constitutional right to expeditious administration of justice under Article 50 and the provisions governing the administration of justice under Article 159.

The President also assented to the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Bill, 2023, which introduces measures to strengthen public awareness and prevention of sexual offences.

The law requires nationwide public education and awareness campaigns on sexual offences and available legal remedies, while directing the education sector to establish programmes protecting the right to education of survivors, including girls who become pregnant following sexual violence.

Close 

The measures seek to ensure that victims are not excluded from education because of sexual violence or its consequences.

President Ruto said the two laws would promote a better understanding of the provisions and limitations of the law and strengthen the country's response to sexual offences.

World.title: Africa: CAS Verdict Puts CAF Leadership Under Pressure As Experts Demand Accountability
World.content:
The Court of Arbitration for Sport's (CAS) decision to reinstate Senegal as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations has triggered strong reactions from Nigerian football administrators and stakeholders, with some describing the ruling as a major embarrassment for the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and a defining test of its credibility.

Former chairman of the Gombe State Football Association, Ahmed Shuaibu Gara Gombe, said the verdict had far-reaching implications for both CAF and CAS, warning that the continental body's leadership could face questions over the controversial decision to strip Senegal of the title.

Speaking with LEADERSHIP Sports, Gara Gombe described the ruling as a defining moment for CAS, arguing that its authority, neutrality and credibility as the highest adjudicating body in global sports would depend largely on its ability to enforce its decisions.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He noted that international institutions often faced challenges when their decisions conflicted with the interests of member countries, adding that the Senegal-Morocco dispute would test the willingness of football authorities to respect the jurisdiction of CAS.

"If this stands, that means the authority in global sports affairs as the policeman or the Supreme Court of global sports affairs is then assured and sealed, because this is a serious test case for CAS," he said.

Gara Gombe warned that any failure to enforce the ruling could undermine the court's legitimacy and credibility in international sports administration.

Turning his attention to CAF, he described the development as an embarrassment for the continental governing body, insisting that the decision to overturn the outcome of the final could have serious consequences for its leadership.

He argued that if CAF's decision to award the title to Morocco had been overturned, those responsible should be held accountable, adding that calls for resignation, including at the presidential level, might not be out of place.

Also reacting, former General Secretary of the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF), Ambassador Fanny Amun, criticised the haste with which the decision to reverse Senegal's victory was taken, describing it as a controversial precedent for football administration.

Amun, who spoke with LEADERSHIP Sports, said football administrators must exercise caution when making decisions with far-reaching consequences, particularly after a match has been concluded and a winner declared on the pitch.

He argued that although there might have been lapses during the final, CAF should have handled the matter more carefully rather than take a decision that generated widespread controversy.

"Some decisions you don't take in haste. The reversal of the AFCON victory is controversial forever. This one is not a good reference point," he said.

The former NFF scribe maintained that Senegal had already secured victory on the pitch and celebrated as champions before the subsequent administrative decision to hand the title to Morocco.

He likened the controversy to football moments that become permanent reference points in the history of the game, arguing that administrators should understand the implications of overturning decisions after matches have been concluded.

Amun added that the experience should serve as a lesson to football administrators on the need to avoid hasty decisions, irrespective of their perceived competence or authority.

Meanwhile, chairman of the Advocacy for Nigeria Football Reform Initiative, Prince Harrison Jalla, described CAF's initial decision to award the trophy to Morocco as a shameful development that had embarrassed African football.

Jalla said African football stakeholders and supporters had widely condemned what he described as boardroom politics, insisting that Senegal were the rightful champions based on the outcome of the match.

Close 

He maintained that the CAS ruling had reinforced the principle that decisions taken by referees during football matches should be respected.

"It's a shame and embarrassment to CAF as a continental body, but African football stakeholders and fans outrightly condemned the CAF shameful decision to hand the AFCON trophy to Morocco in their boardroom politics. Senegal are the true champions on the field of play," he said.

On whether Morocco would be required to return the trophy following the CAS verdict, Jalla expressed uncertainty, questioning whether Senegal had returned the trophy to CAF after the initial decision.

The reactions come amid renewed scrutiny of CAF's handling of the dispute, with the CAS ruling restoring Senegal's status as 2025 AFCON champions and raising fresh questions about decision-making and accountability within African football administration.

World.title: Nigeria: Gunmen Open Fire At Peter Obi's Rally in Edo

The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi in the midst of the people of Edo State in Benin City

The latest attack comes a few days after gunmen suspected to be political thugs killed six people, including a former state lawmaker, at an NDC rally in the neighbouring Delta State.

The police command in Edo State says it has intensified efforts to apprehend three gunmen who opened fire during a rally by presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, in Benin on Wednesday.

The command said the assailants, who arrived in a black Toyota Hilux, opened fire on people at the scene after encountering police operatives stationed at the Benin airport exit gate.

Eno Ikoedem, the command's spokesperson, disclosed this in a statement in Benin.



Ms Ikoedem, an assistant superintendent of police, said the gunmen made a U-turn after sighting the police operatives and opened fire before fleeing the scene.

She said one person, identified as Aimionkhale Micheal, sustained gunshot injuries to his thighs and was rushed to hospital, where he was receiving medical attention.

According to the spokesperson, the Commissioner of Police in Edo, Patrick Daaor, visited the scene and later went to the hospital to assess the victim's condition.

She said Mr Daaor also deployed additional personnel to the rally venue and hospital to prevent further attacks.

Ms Ikoedem added that tactical operatives had been mobilised, while strategic locations were alerted to track and apprehend the fleeing suspects.

"The commissioner has directed the Deputy Commissioner of Police in charge of the State Criminal Investigation Department to conduct a thorough investigation in collaboration with eyewitnesses.

"The command condemns the shooting and warns individuals and groups against actions capable of threatening public safety or disrupting the peace of the state, particularly during the ongoing political activities," she said.

Ms Ikoedem, however, urged residents to remain calm, continue their lawful activities and provide credible information that could assist the investigation.

She assured the public that all necessary measures were being taken to apprehend those responsible for the attack.

The latest attack comes a few days after gunmen suspected to be political thugs killed six people, including a former state lawmaker, at an NDC rally in the neighbouring Delta State.

World.title: Egypt: Over 30 Dead After Fuel Truck Overturns Near Cairo
World.content:
The accident occurred on the packed Ring Road in Giza near Cairo. Dozens of ambulances responded to the crash, and Egyptian health authorities say the death toll could rise.

A fuel truck overturned on a packed highway in Giza, Egypt, on Wednesday, killing 31 people and injuring 21 more, according to Egyptian authorities.

What do we know so far?

The fuel tanker crash ignited a massive blaze on Ring Road in Giza's Waraq district. The Ring Road encircles the greater Cairo metropolitan area.



Egyptian Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were transported to nearby hospitals and added that the death toll could rise further. He said 39 ambulances are responding to the accident.

A massive fire broke out after the accident, with rescue workers pulling people from their vehicles. A large crowd gathered in the densely populated Waraq neighborhood amid the rescue efforts.

The blaze left at least 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, charred.

An investigation has been launched into the crash, according to Egypt's public prosecutor. DNA tests are being carried out to identify badly burned victims of the blaze.

Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his deepest condolences and sympathy to the victims and directed relevant authorities to provide necessary support to the families of the victims and the injured.

Italy, Algeria extend condolences to victims

Other countries also reacted to the crash in Giza.

Italian Foreign Affairs Minister Antonio Tajani said he extended his "deepest solidarity to the victims' families," Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty "and to the Egyptian people, whom I count as friends, at this tragic time."

Algerian Ambassador to Egypt Mohamed Sofiane Berrah also said the Embassy of Algeria in Cairo extended "its deepest condolences and heartfelt sympathy to the sisterly Arab Republic of Egypt."

Car accidents are frequent in Egypt due to poor road conditions, reckless driving and lax enforcement of safety rules.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigeria's Upcoming Election Marred by Rising AI Disinformation
World.content:
As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).



Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Close 

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Parents of potential first Gen Z saint share daughter's powerful final message of hope
World.content:

The parents of a Doylestown, Pennsylvania, teenager who could become the Catholic Church's first Gen Z saint are sharing their daughter's powerful message of hope, recalling how she remained steadfast in her faith while braving a terminal brain tumor diagnosis.

"I will not despair. I will choose hope," Maria Middleton told her parents just two weeks after her diagnosis.

Her father, Brian Middleton, recounted the conversation Tuesday on "The Story with Martha MacCallum." Brian, along with his wife, Susan, joined the show to reflect on their daughter's legacy and the movement to canonize her as a saint.

GEN Z FLOCKING TO CATHOLIC CHURCHES IN NYC FOR YOUTH GROUPS, SOCIAL EVENTS AMID CONVERSION BOOM

"Maria made a decision that she wasn't going to cling to life, that she was going to spend it in self-transcendent service to others," Brian said, recalling his daughter's determination to not let her diagnosis define her remaining time.

"Two weeks after she was diagnosed, we asked her how she was doing. And she said, 'Mom and Dad, regardless of the circumstances of my life, my mission and purpose remain the same, and it's to know, love and serve God... my emotions will rise and fall, but my faith is not an emotion. It's a commitment and I will not despair. I will choose hope,'" he added.

"Her faith was so well integrated into her life that her decisions were always based on what was good, what was true, what was beautiful," Susan chimed in.

"That's how Maria navigated through life, always going back and saying to herself, and we found this in her journal... 'Only what God thinks matters.'"

FULTON SHEEN BECAME A TV SENSATION PREACHING FAITH, MORALITY AND WARNINGS MICHAEL KNOWLES SAYS STILL RESONATE

Maria died in 2020 at just 18 years old, approximately 20 months after being diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor. Her commitment to faith and serving others has since drawn widespread attention, prompting Catholic leaders to take a preliminary step toward her possible canonization.

On Nov. 17, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops voted to advance Middleton's cause for canonization, marking an early step in a process that could eventually see her recognized as the Catholic Church's first Gen Z saint.

The move comes a little over one year after Pope Leo canonized the first millennial saint, St. Carlo Acutis.

For her parents, the growing movement to recognize Maria as a saint reflects the lasting impact of her message, which they say continues to resonate with people around the world.

"In this world of despair, she's become a patroness of hope because of the way that she lived her life. In this world with anxiety, suicide, and depression, Maria made a decision that she was going to live out her life on a daily basis. She chose gratitude over anger," Brian said.

"But the thing that's undeniable is the impact that Maria has had on so many lives around the world... in this age of despair, she's a light of hope."

World.title: A look at how the Trumps spend their Thanksgiving holiday through the years
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

In keeping with tradition, President Donald Trump marked his sixth Thanksgiving in the executive office with the White House’s annual Turkey Pardon ceremony on Tuesday.

His plans for Thanksgiving Day this year remain unannounced — but previous holidays offer a preview of how the president likes to spend the day honoring those who can't be at home for the uniquely American holiday due to service to the country.

Last year Trump spent Thanksgiving at Mar-a-Lago participating in his favorite pass time — golf. But he also used the time in what is known as the "Winter White House" to call Maj. Gen. Dave Gardner, commander of the 101st Airborne Division and Joint Task Force–Southern Border by video conference and talk with troops deployed along the southern border.

TRUMP AND DANA WHITE HONOR MARINE CORPS BAND WITH SIX-FIGURE CHECKS IN FIRST EVENT ON NEW HELIPAD

First lady Melania Trump spent the days ahead of the holiday in 2025 visiting Camp Lejeune and Marine Corps Air Station New River with Second Lady Usha Vance on Nov. 19. They met with military families and made Thanksgiving crafts with children.

In 2020, during the final Thanksgiving of his first term, Trump remained at the White House and made calls to six deployed military units representing every branch of the armed forces, including troops in Kuwait and sailors aboard the USSWinston Churchill in the Red Sea.

Trump famously took a secret trip to Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan on Nov. 28, 2019, where he served turkey, posed for photos and thanked American troops for their sacrifices amid the ongoing war in the Middle East, which not even two years later in August 2021 was brought to an end by then-President Joe Biden.

"There's nowhere I'd rather celebrate this Thanksgiving than right here with the toughest, strongest, best, and bravest warriors on the face of the Earth," Trump told the troops at the time.

"And you don't even know how much the people of our country love and respect you."

TRUMP SAYS US MAY RECOVER ALL THE EQUIPMENT LEFT BEHIND IN AFGHANISTAN BY BIDEN ADMIN

The visit came as roughly 12,000 American troops remained in Afghanistan more than 18 years after the U.S. invasion.

During the visit, Trump met with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani to discuss efforts to end the war and told American troops that the Taliban wanted to reach a deal with the United States. He said his administration was reducing America's military presence in Afghanistan while pursuing a political solution to the more than 18-year conflict.

Trump spent Thanksgiving 2018 in Florida having a traditional dinner with his family, including Melania and his children and grandchildren.

He also held a video call with deployed troops before visiting Coast Guard members at Station Lake Worth Inlet with his wife, where the first couple thanked them for their service and hurricane rescues.

After that holiday in 2018, Melania and then-Second Lady Karen Pence assembled comfort kits for deployed troops at American Red Cross headquarters.

CFP SELECTION COMMITTEE HAS OFFICIALLY DISCREDITED ITSELF WITH LATEST RANKINGS

First? How they've handled the Hoosiers this season, and particularly the last few weeks.

Just three polls ago, Indiana was ranked No. 4 by the selection committee. After not playing for a bye week, they dropped all the way to No. 9. That was bizarre enough, considering again, they didn't play. The committee's excuse for this was that all of the Hoosiers' Big Ten opponents lost in the same week, devaluing their strength of schedule. We'll come back to that.

After the bye week, Indiana beat the then-No. 18 team, the USC Trojans, at home by two scores. It moved up just one spot to No. 8. Ahead of this week's poll, the Hoosiers lost on the road to overtime to a team now ranked in the selection committee's own poll. They dropped six spots. Six. So it didn't play, beat a top-15 team by two scores, lost on the road in overtime to a ranked team, and dropped from No. 4 to No. 14. This would never happen to a team from say, another conference that enjoys enhanced protection from consequences.

When the Georgia Bulldogs lost, at home, to an unranked Auburn team, they dropped four spots in the AP Top 25. Yes, the AP poll uses a different set of voters, but it's indicative of the different standards applied to different conferences.

BIG TEN FACES ONE-BID NIGHTMARE IN CFP RANKINGS AS SEC EYES FOUR BIDS AND BIG 12 COULD THRIVE

What makes the Indiana ranking even more, shall we say, confusing, is how it compares to say, Alabama. The committee had a golden opportunity to keep their standards consistent when all of Alabama's SEC wins lost in the same week between the second and third polls. Had they applied the same logic to the Tide as they did with Indiana, they'd have dropped multiple spots. They didn't move at all.

This week presented another opportunity for consistency. All of Alabama's SEC wins lost again, except for Mississippi State who beat FCS Tennessee Tech 34-16, which may or may not have counted as a Quality SEC Win™. Alabama dropped just three spots. They're now No. 6, while the Hoosiers are eight places behind them at No. 14. With the same record.

Now, there are multiple ways to evaluate records, strength of schedule and overall resume. But the committee seemingly prioritizes how teams perform against their own rankings. This is a terrible idea that inevitably creates circuitous logic, but it's how they've chosen to operate. Ok, fine.

Taking them at their word, here's how Alabama has done against teams currently ranked in the CFB playoff top-25:

Lost 20-17 to No. 1 Georgia at home

Lost 26-10 to No. 5 Tennessee on the road

That's it. This is the strength of schedule that boosts the Tide's resume, in the committee's mind, to worthy of being eight spots ahead of Indiana with the same record. Surely though, Indiana must have played an easy schedule that justifies such a lower spot in the poll...right?

Well, for comparison, here's how the Hoosiers have done against currently ranked teams:

Won 20-17 at No. 25 Nebraska

Lost 19-15 to No. 21 Ohio State at home (with Julian Sayin)

Won 27-13 over No. 15 USC at home

Lost 27-24 (OT) at No. 24 Washington

So they've played two more games against ranked opponents, and what do you know? They actually won two of those games! Their two losses have come by a combined seven points, including one to a top-5 quality Ohio State team with its starting quarterback healthy. That came down to one of the last plays of the game.

We can also look at ESPN's SP+ to point out how absurd the disparity is. While the perception is that Indiana's played an easy schedule, because of its non-conference opponents, nobody makes that claim about the No. 1 Georgia Bulldogs. Even though Georgia, by an objective analytics-driven measurement, has played an easier schedule than Indiana. And a similarly week non-conference slate.

Here's how the two schedules compare in SP+ rankings:

Indiana

No. 67 North Texas

No. 117 Western Kentucky

FCS

Georgia

No. 97 Georgia Tech

No. 117 Western Kentucky

FCS

Interesting. Also per SP+, Indiana's schedule ranks as the 38th hardest in the country. Georgia is 44th. Alabama is 14th, so harder than the Hoosiers, but again, they have the same record. The difference does not justify an eight spot differential. Heck, Miami's played a tougher schedule than Georgia, yet they somehow sit at No. 7 in the poll behind not one, not two, but three two-loss SEC teams. Despite the same number of losses, and its one loss coming down to a controversial incomplete pass call late in the fourth quarter on the road to a top-5 team. Not Auburn.

In fact, speaking of SEC teams getting the benefit of the doubt, Tennessee's strength of schedule is just 22nd, and they're 1-1 against teams currently ranked in the top-25. Their non-conference schedule, like Georgia's and Indiana's, is embarrassingly bad. They beat up on Furman 56-9, the same awful Georgia Tech team 45-24, and Kennesaw State 42-9. Its loss to South Carolina looks worse than Indiana's two losses now, and they have fewer wins over ranked teams. Why is it nine spots ahead of Indiana with a relatively comparable schedule?

The answer, as always, is perception. And selection committee chair Hunter Yurachek confirmed that in his typically embarrassing post-poll interview. When asked why the switch between Tennessee and Alabama, Yurachek basically said the committee just felt like it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"When we first ranked Alabama at No. 3 two weeks ago, the resume looked different than it did when we started the ranking process this week. So much so that the committee felt that both Texas and Notre Dame deserved to be ranked ahead of Alabama," he told Rece Davis. "And then you couple that with a UCLA loss, and the Indiana loss, and then a Tennessee win against LSU, Tennessee moves up to a point where they’re now directly comparable to Alabama. You got the head-to-head, Tennessee over Alabama. And that’s the switch where you have Texas at 3 now, Notre Dame at 4, Tennessee at 5, and Alabama at 6."

Why does beating an unranked 6-5 LSU team make Tennessee comparable to Alabama? What has Alabama actually accomplished besides losing its two toughest games of the year?

When asked about Indiana, he gave an even more rambling and incoherent answer.

"For the last six weeks, Indiana's had six one-score games. Three out of the last four have been in overtime. And until Saturday, they had found a way to win those games," he said.

This is wrong. Indiana beat USC 27-13 roughly 10 days ago. Does the committee not know the outcomes of the games? Because that is factually incorrect. Unfortunately for America, he wasn't done there.

"But Saturday, they did not," he continued. "They fell behind the team like a Texas Tech with one loss and then they were in direct comparison with their counterparts in the Big 10 in Oregon and Iowa. You got both of those teams. Oregon has won four games in a row. Iowa has also won four games in a row. Oregon has a win at Ohio State. Iowa lost at home to Ohio State."



Why was Indiana only in direct comparison to other Big Ten teams? Do the two-loss SEC teams not exist? Or is the committee so hopelessly inept and biased that they think two-loss Alabama and Tennessee simply can't be compared to the Big Ten because they're in the mighty SEC and play in big stadiums or something? Four of Indiana's last six games have been against teams currently ranked in the top-25, so why would it be surprising they were close? Though again, it did beat USC by two scores, which Yurachek got wrong.

Does he and the committee also think beating OSU without Julian Sayin is the same as beating it with him? Because Oregon's win was after his injury, and Iowa and Indiana's losses were before the injury. Incompetence all the way down.

Or maybe they're just mad because Cignetti continues to call out the committee's obvious bias.
