Tennessee lost one of its last four games, and their three ensuing wins have come over teams that are a combined 0-9 in their last nine. In fact, Tennessee's resume SP+ is No. 10, while Indiana is No. 11 and UCLA is No. 9. Tennessee is ranked nine spots ahead of Indiana and four spots ahead of UCLA. Guess that doesn't matter though! Cause SEC!

What these inconsistencies and illogical arguments boil down to is that the committee believes losses in the SEC shouldn't matter much. They believe that the SEC deserves preferential treatment it hasn't earned, particularly considering that conference's atrocious record in the playoff the past three seasons. There's a very real chance the Big Ten, which undoubtedly has a stronger middle class than the SEC this year, only gets one team in the tournament. While the SEC will get four. And we already know that the SEC conference championship game can't hurt the loser, a ridiculous fact Joey Galloway thankfully brought up on ESPN's show, to great consternation and disappointment from Rece Davis and Heather Dinich.

Ranked wins don't matter, objective resumes don't matter, the only thing that matters is perception. Which is why this poll will continue to be a discrediting embarrassment.

World.title: Dak Prescott's 1,000-yard, 11-touchdown surge over three games makes Cowboys heavy Thanksgiving favorites
World.content:
Happy Thanksgiving to all you turkeys out there. I hope your plate is full, your turkey is moist, the stuffing is aplenty, and most of all, that we make a ton of money today. By the time this game comes on, you probably will be either about to start your dinner or heading to the in-laws for the next meal.

What could be better today? Well, a win in this game would be a bit of help, and let’s see if we can get that with the Eagles and Cowboys.

The Philadelphia Eagles were impressive on Sunday, and that’s saying something. The team has been a bit of a disaster this season, specifically with Jalen Hurts and his injury situation. They come into today’s game with a 3-7 record and are probably just trying to play spoiler for any opponent at this point in their season. They aren’t mathematically eliminated from the postseason or anything, but they might as well be. And that’s taking into consideration the win they had Sunday.

Before we go and say that Joe Milton III is the answer at quarterback, let’s just admit that the Steelers aren’t exactly a great team. They are fine, but a really bad first quarter did Pittsburgh in for the game. The Eagles only scored six points the remainder of the game, and the Steelers outscored them 16-6 from the start of the second quarter on. A win is a win, but I don’t think want anyone thinking the Eagles have figured something out.

The good news for them is that they at least put up some points against a defense that is certainly better than what Dallas has to offer.

EAGLES QB JOE MILTON SHARES THAT HE SAYS HIS DAUGHTER'S NAME TO CALM NERVES BEFORE THROWING A DEEP BALL

The Dallas Cowboys are basically just running back what they did last season. I hate to bash the team because I was pretty high on them before the season started, but their only method of victory is to have Dak Prescott go bonkers and throw for a million yards and 10 touchdowns a game.

Obviously, I’m exaggerating here, but he does have almost exactly 1,000 passing yards and 11 touchdowns over the past three games. If he had any semblance of a defense this season, he might be in the MVP conversation as I predicted before the year.

BUT… he doesn’t. His defense is awful. They are ranked near the bottom in passing and rushing yards allowed, and they are giving up a ton of points. It means Prescott has to be near perfect for them to win. Even when he was close against the 49ers, they still lost by six because the defense couldn’t give him any help. Dallas is a fun team to watch, but it has to be frustrating for true fans of the club.

COWBOYS STAR QUINNEN WILLIAMS REPEATS SIX WORD ANSWER 12 TIMES IN PRESSER AFTER MAJOR COACHING CHANGE

Prescott and the Cowboys have already beaten the Eagles once this season. They went into Philadelphia and won 38-21. I’m not really sure why they aren’t bigger favorites in this one, outside of maybe because Philly looked a bit better with Milton under center. I like the Cowboys to cover the -8.5 in this game, and I think their team total is a good look as well. Prescott has been playing great lately and has already shown he can rack up points against the Eagles' defense.

A win from Philly last week also makes me think they will stumble this week. Sometimes a bad team just wants to get a win and then rests a bit the next week. Give me the Cowboys -8.5 and give me their team total over.

World.title: Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen set up for another shootout as Chiefs face Bills on Thanksgiving
World.content:
I don’t know if you know this or not, but we are at the main course of your Thanksgiving Day with this game.

Sure, you could’ve finished and might be in a food coma by the time this game kicks off, but the NFL has done a great job of giving us one game that we absolutely cannot miss late in the day. Any time the Chiefs and the Bills take each other on, it is must-see television, and that’s precisely what we get this week.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Kansas City Chiefs are one of the best teams in football again. They are coming off yet another win – a 34-7 drubbing of the Arizona Cardinals. I do think it is fair to ask if the Chiefs are actually good, or just taking advantage of an easy schedule.

Their eight wins have been over Denver, Indianapolis, Miami, Las Vegas, Los Angeles (Chargers), New York (Jets), Atlanta, and Arizona. Outside of Denver, whom they played at home and in the first week of the season, there isn’t one quality win in that group. In fact, none of those teams have winning records.

So, are the Chiefs actually good? Maybe. Patrick Mahomes has played much more like Patrick Mahomes in the past two games, throwing for 672 yards over the two games and eight touchdowns. We know he doesn’t really have a deep receiving corps, but he is making it work. I’ve harped about this for years, but Rashee Rice, Josh Downs, and Xavier Worthy are the options, and I don’t think any of them would be a true No. 1 on almost any other team.

Travis Kelce sporadically looks good, but you can’t really count on it. Kenneth Walker III is a difference-maker at running back, but he has been out the past two weeks, and they really need him to give the Bills defense something different to worry about.

The Buffalo Bills are still one of the best teams in football, and they still have their Superman, Josh Allen.

The Swiss Army Knife quarterback is arguably the best running back in football – certainly for short yardage and goal-to-go situations. He is the reason they win games, and hasn’t really been the reason for their lone loss this year. Even in the loss to the Patriots, the lone blemish on the Bills' season, he had one interception, but threw for one touchdown and ran for another. The Bills defense just couldn’t seem to stop Drake Maye – essentially the only team this season to struggle against him.

Perhaps it is worth considering if the Bills have beaten anyone this year, if I’m going to knock the Chiefs schedule. They’ve beaten Houston, Detroit, Los Angeles (both), Las Vegas, Baltimore, Minnesota, New York (Jets), and Miami. Detroit is a good team, but they got them at home.

The Rams are a solid team, but they did play them at least without Myles Garrett. The Vikings defense was still solid in their game, but got no offensive help and forced them to trade for Kirk Cousins after the game. Certainly their schedule has been harder than Kansas City’s, though.

THANKSGIVING WEEK BETTING GUIDE 2026: NFL THANKSGIVING, RIVALRY WEEK, NBA CUP, NHL AND COLLEGE HOOPS PICKS

Any time these two squads get together, you expect fireworks. Since 2020, they’ve played 10 times (including playoffs), and the series is tied 5-5, but in the regular season the Bills are 5-1 against the Chiefs. Which means … the Chiefs are 4-0 against them in the playoffs. In the ten games, the scores have been: 49, 61, 51, 51, 37, 44, 78, 58, 62, and 43. I think we'll see two quarterbacks do their thing tonight and treat us to a shootout. Give me the over 50.5.

World.title: Judge blocks FCC review of ABC station licenses for now
World.content:
The Walt Disney Co. secured a temporary restraining order Wednesday blocking the Federal Communications Commission from moving forward with an unusually early review of ABC’s broadcast-station licenses, which the media company has called an attack on free speech by the Trump administration.

U.S. District Judge Loren L. AliKhan’s decision is the latest turn in the legal battle between Disney and the FCC, the federal agency that regulates the broadcast airwaves. Disney filed a lawsuit against the FCC in August, calling the early license review an “existential threat” to the First Amendment.

The FCC “wants to stop, censor [and] control” what ABC can broadcast, Disney lawyer Beth Wilkinson told AliKhan at a hearing on Oct. 6. Wilkinson characterized FCC Chairman Brendan Carr’s actions as a series of “unending threats and retaliation.”

The FCC’s lawyers argued at the hearing that the U.S. District Court does not have jurisdiction in the matter, accusing ABC of trying to circumvent the federal regulatory process.

In her order Wednesday, the judge wrote that she concluded Disney was “likely to succeed on their retaliation claim” against the FCC.

The order blocks the agency “from taking any continuing or further action against Plaintiffs in relation to the early license renewal proceedings before the Federal Communications Commission.”

She also denied a request by the FCC to dismiss Disney’s lawsuits against the agency.

“This is not a close case,” AliKhan wrote, adding that the ABC stations “have a weighty interest” in vindicating their right to free speech without retaliation.

“Chairman Carr has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders,” AliKhan wrote. The judge’s opinion and order referenced multiple social media posts by Trump in which he was critical of ABC. “Starting with expressions of hostility, President Trump has set his sights on Plaintiff ABC for several years now.”

In response to a request for comment, an FCC spokesperson said: “While we appreciate the district court denying in part Disney’s request for preliminary injunctive relief, the portion of the decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law — as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear.

“The FCC looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations,” the agency spokesperson added.

In a statement, an ABC News spokesperson cheered the temporary restraining order as an “important victory for the First Amendment.”

The courtroom confrontation stems from the FCC’s April 28 order directing Disney’s eight owned-and-operated TV stations to file their broadcast license renewals ahead of schedule. The licenses were not due to come up for renewal until 2028 at the earliest.

Carr has said that order was tied to the agency’s investigation into Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices. It came a day after Trump called on ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over a joke he had made about first lady Melania Trump.

AliKhan addressed the sequence of events following Kimmel’s joke, writing that “against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr’s call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings.”

The FCC is also reviewing whether ABC’s “The View” broke a requirement that broadcast stations give equal time to political candidates for the same office. Disney has argued that the talk show qualifies as a “bona fide news” program, meaning it is exempt from the equal-time rule.

In a phone interview with NBC News after Disney filed suit, Carr said he believed Disney’s challenge to the FCC’s order was a “meritless case.” In remarks at the agency’s open commission meeting last week, Carr said the suit was filed “in the wrong court” at “the wrong time.”

ABC Owned Television Stations, a division of Disney Entertainment Television, operates stations in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia, Houston, San Francisco, the Raleigh-Durham area, and Fresno, California.

Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat on the FCC, said in a statement that AliKhan’s decision “shows that this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights.”

“Every broadcaster facing this pressure should take note and choose courage over capitulation because, as I’ve said from the beginning, the First Amendment is on their side,” Gomez added.

World.title: A rising political star in China is the latest victim of Xi’s purge
World.content:
He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials. But now Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s influential politburo, appears to be the latest senior official brought down by President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge.

The hammer unexpectedly came down on Chen in the form of a two-line bulletin on the Xinhua news agency Tuesday: He is “suspected of serious violations of Party discipline and law and is currently under disciplinary review and supervisory investigation” — a common euphemism for corruption crackdowns on ruling Communist Party officials under Xi.

Public announcements such as these usually mark the end of a political career in China. Chen has made no public statement.

He is the fourth politburo member to be purged in less than two years, part of a broader crackdown that has swept aside top military leaders as Xi consolidates power. He is set to extend his rule next year, at a party congress that is held once every five years and looms over the preceding months.

But Chen’s abrupt downfall took many close observers of China by surprise, given his profile and career path would usually point to a bright future.

“He was potentially going to the highest level, which would be the standing committee. And I think from a lot of Western observers, people thought he had even better prospects,” Damien Ma, the Singapore-based director of the Carnegie China think tank, told NBC News.

Xi’s pursuit of loyalty

Some analysts have speculated that Xi, increasingly viewed as likely to rule for life, may have been purging a viable replacement. Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said however that Chen was “someone who could rise further but not as a successor.”

Chen, a 62-year-old technocrat known as a friend of foreign business and an advocate for AI, was an environmental scientist who studied in London and swiftly rose through the party’s ranks. He served as China’s environmental minister, Beijing’s mayor and the party secretary in Shanghai — a post once held by Xi and widely considered a stepping stone to bigger things.

Just last month, Chen hosted Apple Chairman Tim Cook, welcoming the U.S. tech giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths” and bring more products to the city, a financial and cultural hub that has long served as a connection between China and the international community.

In his last public appearance last week, during a tour of a shipping facility, Chen called for advancing the industry’s digital transformation.

By Wednesday, Chen’s name has been removed from some official websites. A webpage on the Shanghai government site showing that meeting with Cook is now showing a 404 message, or not found.

Chen Jining and Sen. Chuck Schumer in Shanghai in 2023. Aly Song / AFP via Getty

Chen is just the latest senior official in the crosshairs of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign and emphasis on party discipline, which analysts say is as much about loyalty as it is about reform.

“It is a warning to all technocrats, as Chen was a rising star among technocrats and had no apparent failures in a technocratic way. So, message is: adhere to strict party discipline and demonstrate unquestionable loyalty to Xi or else,” Tsang said.

The party’s Central Committee, which has about 200 mostly male leaders, vowed to “ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive” at its closed-door gathering, the fifth plenum, last month.

“What they’ve been building as part of this discipline machine over the last 15 years is to kind of implement their sort of internal operating system of how they deal with, let’s say, bad eggs within the party,” Ma, of Carnegie China, said.

“The top leadership is normalizing this anti-corruption, this self-cleansing,” Ma said. “It is now a normal part of what the party expects, and they’re trying to embed that over time and down to every single level,” he added.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping, right, and Zhang Shengmin, second left, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing in March. Kevin Frayer / Getty ]

The Chinese government has not announced any charges against Chen, who was the youngest member of the country’s elite decision-making body. The 24-member Politburo was unveiled in 2022 but is now down to 21 members after the purges. Last month, top general Zhang Shengmin was elevated to the body in a rare addition.

Chen’s undoing comes a year before the party’s top leadership is reshuffled at the 21st Communist Party Congress, when Xi is expected to solidify control even further and cement another five-year term at the helm of the country.

From London to Shanghai

Born in 1964, Chen studied at the prestigious Tsinghua university, long a major pipeline for senior party officials and where he served as president from 2012 to 2015. His name has now been removed from Tsinghua’s online list of former presidents.

After studying at Tsinghua in the 1980s, he moved for a decade to Britain, where he obtained a doctorate from Imperial College London in 1993.

Chen returned to Tsinghua’s environmental science and engineering department in 1998 before being named the university’s president in 2012, according to an official biography.

He’s authored dozens of papers, including on carbon emission reduction and water quality monitoring.

The relatively young Chen would ride around campus on his bike and built a reputation for pushing institutional reforms in his three years at the helm of the university, according to an article in People’s Digest, a magazine affiliated with the People’s Daily, the community party’s official newspaper.

The article, titled “From University President to Cabinet Minister,” was published in 2015, the same year he was picked to lead the Environmental Protection Ministry. In 2017, Chen became mayor of the capital, Beijing, where he oversaw the 2022 Winter Olympics during the Covid pandemic.

World.title: FedEx cargo plane runs off MIA runway, causing brief ground stop
World.content:
A FedEx cargo plane ran off a runway at Miami International Airport amid wind and rain Wednesday night, prompting a temporary ground stop during one of the busiest travel days of the year.

According to an FAA advisory, departures bound for Miami were grounded until at least 9:45 p.m. Preliminary reports indicate a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 cargo plane went off the runway, prompting the halt in incoming air traffic.

The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said it responded to the runway at MIA at approximately 8:40 p.m. and found the cargo plane.

Neither of the two people on board was injured, and responding emergency crews from both the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office and Miami-Dade Fire Rescue reported no signs of fire or smoke.

MIA posted on X, confirming the incident happened at Runway 26R and that all runways were closed except for Runway 9R.

A FedEx aircraft overran Runway 26R at Miami International Airport at approximately 8:40 p.m. All runways are closed except for runway 9R. @MiamiDadeFire units have responded, and there are no reported injuries. Passengers scheduled to travel tonight are encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport. We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations. — Miami Int'l Airport (@iflymia) November 26, 2026

Minutes before flights were set to resume, the FAA also posted on X about the incident, confirming that the FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 had departed from Frederick W. Smith International Airport in Memphis.

Wet weather investigated as a possible cause for the incident



At the time of the incident, rainy conditions had reduced visibility to 7 miles, with a 13-mph tailwind reported at the airfield.

An airport employee who witnessed the aftermath and asked not to be named said the crew appeared to struggle to slow the aircraft on the wet pavement before it veered onto the grass.

"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," the employee said.

The worker noted that the overrun occurred on the airport's shortest runway, raising renewed concerns following a September Amazon cargo plane crash that killed five people.

The brief ground stop Wednesday left some Thanksgiving travelers waiting for hours before flight operations resumed.

"I'm kind of shocked," traveler Dennis Pastorizo said. "I didn't think that a delivery plane would cause a two-hour delay for a flight to the other side of the country, especially on one of the busiest [travel days] of the year."

FedEx issued a statement to CBS News Miami about the incident that says:

"FedEx Flight 910 from Memphis to Miami experienced an issue upon landing Wednesday evening at Miami International Airport. We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."

The FAA announced Wednesday night that it is investigating the incident.

World.title: Ukraine says it downed a Russian jet-powered drone with a laser
World.content:
Ukraine has used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered attack drone for the first time, a senior military adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday, marking a potentially significant development in the country's effort to defend cities from Russia's daily aerial attacks.

The interception was carried out using the Blysk laser air defense system, which was developed and manufactured by Ukrainian defense technology firm Carmine Sky. Technology for laser air defense systems is being developed as part of the wider Private Air Defense program, Zelenskyy's adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said in a statement.

About 100 companies across Ukraine have joined the government-backed private air defense initiative.

Russia started deploying jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine earlier this year. The weapons travel faster, making them harder to intercept than the more common propeller-driven attack drones.

In June, Ukraine was only intercepting about 57% of the jet-powered drones, reflecting a significant vulnerability as Ukrainian forces had been shooting down about 90% of the conventional Russian attack drones.

Russia has increasingly used its Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit group, told CBS News in September that Russia was likely to produce some 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 drones during that month alone, and it projected those numbers would grow each month.

A downed Russian Geran-4 turbojet-powered one-way attack drone is displayed at the National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War, in Kyiv, Ukraine, Oct. 29, 2026. Danylo Antoniuk/Ukrinform/Future Publishing/Getty

The laser interception reported by Beskrestnov this week gives some insight into Ukraine's mounting efforts to adapt both its offenses and defenses as Russia's weapons and tactics evolve.

Ukraine has pioneered battlefield drone technology, and it has started building partnerships to export that knowledge and its hardware around the world. In October, Ukrainian forces carried out a world-first aerial drone medical evacuation from the front line.

Ukraine started testing laser air defense systems over the summer. According to Beskrestnov, the Blysk system was used to protect critical infrastructure, though he declined to give more specifics.

He said a number of Ukrainian companies, including Carmine Sky, are working to develop laser technology, but he cautioned that "it is still too early to talk about serial production of the laser."

"Tests are underway, during which lasers protect critical infrastructure facilities," he said.

World.title: Fuel tanker explosion kills 31 on Egyptian highway
World.content:
Cairo — A massive fire on an Egyptian highway killed 31 people and injured 21 others after a car slammed into a fuel tanker truck at high speed, Egypt's Public Prosecution office said Thursday.

The driver has been arrested, according to the statement. At least 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, were destroyed in the fire.

The prosecutor said the suspect admitted causing the accident while driving around 70 miles per hour on a major highway in the Al-Warraq district of Giza, which is part of the Greater Cairo area.

A fire burns at the site where a vehicle carrying petroleum products overturned and caught fire on a major ring road in Al-Warraq district of Giza, Egypt, Nov. 25, 2026, in a screengrab obtained from social media video. Habiba Abd El Aziz/REUTERS

The driver said he was changing lanes and overtaking vehicles when the front-left side of his car struck the rear-right side of the tanker, according to the prosecutor's statement, "causing the steering wheel to slip from his hands and his car to veer off course."

When the car hit the truck, one of the truck's tires exploded, causing it to overturn and slam into a concrete barrier.

Gasoline then leaked from the tanker and caught on fire. Images of the blaze on social media showed multiple vehicles on fire as flames and smoke billowed into the night sky.

The prosecutor said the suspect was being questioned to establish the circumstances of the accident and assess any criminal responsibility.

"It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire," Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic behind the accident, told The Associated Press. "It was a shocking scene."

Sameer told the AP he saw at least eight bodies being removed from charred vehicles.

Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi expressed his condolences to the victims of the crash.

In a statement on X, Egypt's health ministry said 39 ambulances took part in the rescue operation.

While fatal traffic accidents are common in Egypt, the sheer scale of the incident has prompted calls for greater accountability. Last year, nearly 6,000 people died in road traffic accidents across Egypt, according to official data.

World.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed for 1st time in history
World.content:
For the first time in history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed due to weather, Macy's said Wednesday.

The 100th annual parade will now kick off Saturday at 8:30 a.m.

The historic move comes as a powerful coastal storm is set to impact the area Thursday.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we've made the decision to move the celebration due to expected severe weather," Macy's said in a statement. "Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday."

"Created by Macy's colleagues since 1924 as a gift to our city and nation, our parade has brought magic into the hearts of millions and have created cherished memories that have spanned generations," Will Coss, executive producer and vice president of Macy's Branded Entertainment, said at a press conference Wednesday. "This year we marked our 100th march, a milestone built on creativity, celebration and tradition. While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our participants and spectators is and always will be our top priority."

A balloon of Buzz Lightyear rests under protective netting during the inflation of Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade balloons on the Upper West Side on Nov. 25, 2026. TIMOTHY A. CLARY /AFP via Getty Images

"We know that our city is the greatest city in the world, and we also know that in our city, nothing comes easily, and you have to plan for every possibility," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "And while we were looking forward to celebrating Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade tomorrow, extreme weather has forced us to reschedule for Saturday instead."

Mamdani pointed to the "heavy storm" expected Thursday, with wind gusts up to 65 mph possible, along with potential flash flooding.

"Now I know many New Yorkers, myself included as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow," Mamdani said. "I know that this change of plan will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first. And on Saturday, when balloons climb into the sky, every New Yorker and everyone visiting, will be able to take in a show that is both truly spectacular and also safe."

"By moving the parade to Saturday when weather conditions are much more favorable, we can give New Yorkers the celebration that they've been looking forward to without compromising on safety," NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Wednesday night declared a state of emergency for New York City, along with Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties.

"We're expecting heavy rain and strong winds that could create dangerous travel conditions," she wrote on social media.

The watchword for the mayor's office, the NYPD and Macy's is safety, and there's ample reason for concern. Past parades have seen balloons tear, deflate or collide with overhead wires.

In 1997, high winds pushed several balloons out of control. The Cat in the Hat balloon struck a lamppost near Central Park West, which brought down a heavy fixture, injuring four spectators. A woman suffered a fractured skull and coma. Barney and the Pink Panther balloons also ran into trouble and had to be deflated.

In 1993, Sonic the Hedgehog was driven by high winds into a lamppost, injuring spectators and an NYPD officer. Dudley the Dragon hit a lamppost in Columbus Circle in that same parade, ending glass showering down on the crowd.

In 1971, balloons were grounded because of high winds, but even during COVID, the parade went on.

The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade balloons were inflated on Nov. 25, 2026, but were later deflated again after anticipated severe weather forced organizers to postpone the parade. Chopper 2

"Our colleagues, our volunteers, our participants - we've spent over two years working on this very parade. This parade has been built with love, with creativity. Since 1924 we've had an opportunity to create memories, to bring joy to millions of people here in New York City. That is our top priority. We're saddened by this shift, but we're optimistic about our opportunity to deliver the most spectacular 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, the best and biggest parade in our history," Coss said. "We look forward to sharing it with all of New York and everyone else across the nation."

The operational challenges involved in shifting the date of the parade are substantial. The parade involves plenty of marching bands and other performers who had been expecting the event on Thursday, and now will need to make alternative arrangements.

Coss said they are in communication with all parade participants, including those who have come from out of state.

"We are optimistic that we're going to be able to maintain the parade that we set out to produce and to deliver to New York City on Thanksgiving," he said. "There's still some logistics to be worked out, but everyone understands what we're up against and is rallying behind us to create the best and most successful 100th parade."

There will not be a second Inflation Celebration event before Saturday's parade, Coss added.

"[The balloons] have to be prepared, which is a weeks-long process that's going to get condensed to about 24 hours, so the team's going to be hard at work preparing for Saturday," he said, "so by the time we're ready to deliver back to New York City, it's really about inflating and getting ourselves stepped off for a successful parade on Saturday."

Workers deflate a balloon after the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026, in New York. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura

Tisch added that the NYPD will have to call in over 1,000 officers who were previously scheduled to be off on Saturday to work the parade.

"Our NYPD officers always step up for New York City, and Saturday will be no different," Tisch said.

She added that some officers who were scheduled to work overtime shifts for the parade on Thursday were told they were no longer needed and can spend Thanksgiving with their families.

Meanwhile, the mayor said due to the rescheduling, he will not be able to attend the parade because he is undergoing surgery Friday for his torn Achilles tendon.

The parade was previously suspended from 1942 to 1944 during World War II when officials needed the helium used to inflate the balloons for the war effort. It has never been postponed due to weather.

World.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
World.content:
North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture

toggle caption i Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.

Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.

Sponsor Message

KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.

Sponsor Message

"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.

Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.

Trump still hopes to meet KimTrump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.

In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."

Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."

Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.

Sponsor Message

Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."

Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

World.title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel. And, FCC violated ABC's free speech, judge says
World.content:
Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel. And, FCC violated ABC's free speech, judge says

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Severe storms sweeping across the nation threaten to cause widespread travel delays today, as millions of people gather with their loved ones. New York City officials announced that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled to Saturday due to the threat of powerful wind gusts that could reach up to 60 mph. This year marked the 100th procession, and the first time the iconic event is being postponed.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

🎧 Something is happening across almost every part of the country right now, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Extreme high tides are affecting the West Coast, snow is expected in parts of the Midwest, and in the South and Southeast, a major storm is advancing up the East Coast. Meteorologist Richard Bann with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center tells Lonsdorf the East Coast storm is the primary concern. Bann says the storm will become better organized throughout the day, bringing strong winds and heavy rain that could lead to coastal flooding. The good news: Forecasters expect the East Coast's major storm to move on, mostly wrapping up by Saturday, Lonsdorf says.

Sponsor Message

The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs targeting goods from 14 major U.S. trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union. Administration officials argue the measures counter unfair foreign trade practices, though critics question their ultimate effectiveness. Proposed rates may reach 40% on Chinese imports, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on products from other targeted nations. Additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft are also being suggested.



🎧 U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said that new tariffs could take effect within a couple of months. For each country, the White House has listed a "proposed" rate and a "deal" rate, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben says. For example, if talks with China progress positively, they may receive a deal rate of 20%, which is different from its proposed rate of 40%. Although the Supreme Court overturned President Trump's previous tariffs, the new ones fall under Section 301, a law meant to counter unfair trade practices. The administration says these countries exhibit "structural excess capacity" in various manufactured goods, a situation caused by policies that lead to overproduction, which can distort the global market.

Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in Eastern Iowa for lead contamination after the U.S. Army detonated thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown yesterday. Officials said the controlled explosion was the only safe way to dispose of the bomb-making compound.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio says the major concern is the potential release of lead into the air from the explosion. She adds that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has tested the area since the detonation and hasn't found lead in the air. The EPA has deployed around 300 people to sample the air, ground and nearby water. Lead is a neurotoxin that especially endangers children and pregnant people because it can impede childhood development. After a week and a half of delays and inconsistent communication from the Army, residents have grown hesitant about the Army and the EPA's initial findings, Billingham says. Residents want independent monitoring and the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois are conducting regional sampling. Results are expected in a few days and should show if their measurements align with the EPA's data, Billingham says.

A federal judge has blocked Trump from challenging the ABC television network's broadcast licenses. U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan ruled that the president retaliating against satire and commentary he dislikes is unconstitutional. AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction yesterday and dismissed the administration's request to throw out ABC and Disney's lawsuit challenging the review of the local license. Licenses typically last eight years and are rarely revoked. AliKhan's decision drew heavily on Trump's public statements and social media posts against ABC and Disney, as well as comments from Brendan Carr, the president's pick for chair of the Federal Communications Commission.

Life advice

toggle caption i J Studios/Getty Images

Holiday shopping season is in full swing. Before you spend, consider if you actually need what's in your cart. Sales are exciting because our brains are wired to seek newness. Retailers capitalize on that urge. To escape the cycle of constantly wanting more, shop intentionally and appreciate what you already own, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New. He shares his insights on breaking this cycle and finding joy in your current possessions with Life Kit.

Sponsor Message

🛒 Delete the app or remove your credit card info if you have one-click checkout with a company.

🛒 Add an item to your online shopping cart and leave it for 24 hours. Research shows that delaying a purchase decreases your interest in it.

🛒 Make intentional choices. Don't reject all new things. After you understand this, you can learn to say no to the wrong items and yes to the right ones.

🛒 Revisiting old things can provide you with untapped enjoyment in them, research has found. You can apply this by rereading a book or by traveling to a city you have visited before.

For more guidance on how to reclaim joy without seeking newness, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Picture show

Andrea Starr

Apple farmers across the Pacific Northwest are ripping out thousands of acres of orchards and grinding trees into mulch because growing the fruit no longer pays. Many say they're being crushed by soaring labor and equipment costs and international tariffs. Even multigenerational growers are leaving land unused rather than hemorrhaging money. Thousands of acres of fruit have been left to rot unpicked on branches, pushing some well-established farms into bankruptcy. Federal farm relief has also largely failed to reach specialty-crop growers. Take a look at photos and videos of affected farms, and read more about how the region that supplies the majority of the U.S.' fresh apples is handling the challenge.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Emilee Chinn/Getty Images

The Pittsburgh Steelers have cut quarterback Aaron Rodgers after he claimed in an interview that the team's head coach sleeps in meetings. The Ariston Cafe opened in 1924 along Illinois's Route 66, serving classic American diner fare. The National Register landmark attracts international travelers and hosts local milestones, from wedding proposals to 65th anniversaries. In this week's Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Emily Feng brings readers views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro. She was able to see it during a camping trip at altitude.

Sponsor Message

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: 'Memories of a Good Meal': How food made a difference during WWII
World.content:
'Memories of a Good Meal': How food made a difference during WWII

toggle caption i Denny Culbert; June Hersh and Alon Shaya

NEW ORLEANS — Chef Alon Shaya believes there's power in a meal.

"It's always been the way that I can start a conversation, build a relationship, disagree about things, but still be able to come together and break bread," Shaya, of the acclaimed Crescent City restaurant Saba, said one recent afternoon. "When you share a meal with someone, a lot of those barriers get broken down."

The Israeli American chef also believes food can be a source of inspiration even in the darkest of times. A few years ago, he spearheaded the Rescued Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and that got him digging deeper into the role that food played during World War II.

Sponsor Message

Now, he's collected those stories and the dishes they inspired in a new historical cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.

Shaya hopes home cooks use the recipes to inspire dinner table conversations about the deeper stories behind them.

"I want people to gather and cook and eat and put their phones down, and share a meal and recount these miraculous stories of survival, resilience and heroism," he told NPR.

Stories like that of Roddie Edmonds, a U.S. Army master sergeant, whose unit was captured in the Battle of the Bulge and imprisoned in a German POW camp. (Edmonds posthumously won the Congressional Medal of Honor earlier this year for his refusal to turn in his Jewish troops to be sent to concentration camps.)

One of the ways Edmonds and his fellow prisoners distracted themselves from the horror of the camp was to talk about the foods that reminded them of home, be it Sunday spaghetti sauce, hot cakes or cherry pie.

"They're eating up this idea that they were going to go home," Shaya said. "They were going to be free, and they were going to be able to sit around and dig into that filet mignon with creamy mushroom sauce."

Sponsor Message

The servicemen sketched out detailed plans for a dreamed-of restaurant called the Jolly Chef. There, they would serve all those yearned-for dishes, including candied yams with pecans and whipped marshmallow — one of the recipes in the new cookbook.

Another chapter highlights Polish partisan fighters who lived in underground bunkers and sabotaged the Nazis by derailing trains and blowing up ammunition plants. In a nod to the fire that ensued, a recipe from their chapter also includes smashed potatoes flambéed in vodka.

"Vodka was a form of currency for them," Shaya said. "They would use it to barter. They would use it to celebrate. And so each moment of that recipe helps to really tell the story of what they were going through."

The book has stories from around the world – Hungarian Jews whose non-Jewish cook salvaged the treasured family cookbook as they were being sent to Auschwitz; a French village that took in Jewish children and hid them from the Nazis; Navajo code breakers who changed the course of the war; and Japanese Americans, convicted of no crimes, who were incarcerated in military-style camps in the U.S.

June Hersh, a food historian and writer who worked with Shaya on the cookbook, said remembering and talking about favorite recipes was a form of resistance – turning a tragic situation into something triumphant.

"You can put me in a uniform, you can make me do hard labor, you can shave my head, you can starve me if you want, but I'm not going to let go of my food memory," she said. "It's something you can't take away from me."

World.title: At Albuquerque's Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course
World.content:
At Albuquerque's Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

There are plenty of kitschy diners and barbecue joints along Route 66, but just a couple of miles off the highway in Albuquerque, N.M., Native American dishes are the star at Indian Pueblo Kitchen.

Late on a weekday morning, the restaurant was already starting to fill up. Most of the tables were taken up by locals, like Merlyn Liberty and Rolf Pendall.

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

"I started with breakfast dessert. The blue corn waffles. And now I'm finishing up my sweetheart's plate of enchiladas and pinto beans," Pendall said.

The restaurant is attached to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, a museum and cultural center founded in 1976 by the 19 Pueblo tribes of New Mexico.

Sponsor Message

The center sits on land where the Albuquerque Indian School operated. Open from 1881 to the early 1980s, it was one of the hundreds of federally funded boarding schools designed to strip Native American children of their family bonds, languages, culture and spiritual practices.

The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center's president and CEO, Monique Fragua, said visitors can start in the museum's galleries and then visit the restaurant to experience Pueblo culture and hospitality.

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

"Whether that's through our exhibits, or our food, or in our gift shop, we can celebrate the art of our Pueblo communities," Fragua said.

Museum cafés are not a typical destination for foodies, but this one is.

The menu is all Native American and Southwestern-inspired. Dishes include blue corn enchiladas that you can get "Christmas style," one with red chile sauce and the other with green chile sauce. There's a chile posole with beef short ribs served on the bone, as well as Indian tacos on homemade fry bread. Then there's a dish that's really popular on social media: pickles marinated in cherry Kool-Aid and then deep-fried and served with a green chile ranch sauce.

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

Rita Toledo, from Jemez Pueblo, is Indian Pueblo Kitchen's star baker. One of her specialties is biscochitos — fragrant shortbread cookies spiced with anise and rolled in cinnamon sugar that are New Mexico's state cookie. Toledo has made some twists on the traditional biscochito, like making a chile pepper version that has just a little kick at the end with a nice balance of sweet and heat.

Sponsor Message

Indian Pueblo Kitchen's version of biscochitos is so popular that the restaurant also sells them at its café inside Albuquerque's airport. Toledo turns out at least 48 dozen biscochitos each week just for the airport location.

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

While we chatted, Toledo was wrestling to open a giant tub of one of her main ingredients — lard. These cookies can be made with butter or shortening, she said, but "lard's the only way to make good biscochitos."

Toledo said that she has been baking all her life and that her favorite part of her work is rolling out dough.

"It calms me. You know, your energy comes out on your dough," Toledo said. "I always tell my bakers, 'Come in happy and in a good mood. That way, your products will come out nice and everybody's gonna love it.'"

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

Along with locals flocking to visit, the restaurant is also a hit with tourists like Kathy Allio and Jeff Allen from Pennsylvania. While we chatted, Allio was finishing a bowl of bean chili with elk meat.

"The red chiles are just very flavorful without being hot," Allio said, "so it's delicious."

One thing Fragua, the center's president, is particularly proud of is that the Pueblo community can see itself reflected in the museum's galleries and programming and on the restaurant's menu.

"We're lucky to have that history here on our campus, that we've taken lands that were once created to really change the identity of Native people and change that story of who Native people are," Fragua said. "We've created a campus that's built on resilience, empowering our voices and truly telling the stories of who we are as Native people."

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

Additional reporting by Jeanette DeDios of member station KUNM.

World.title: Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed
World.content:
Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

Tens of millions of people are bracing for delays at airports and highways across the country on Thursday, as powerful storms across the United States threatened to disrupt travel for the Thanksgiving holiday.

On the West Coast, high tides have flooded streets along California's shorelines and knocked off a part of Pacifica Pier. The floods have also prompted evacuation warnings. On the East Coast, authorities are preparing to weather the impact of a storm making its way up into New England from the southeast with strong winds and heavy rain. Snow was also forecast in parts of the Midwest.

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Some 81.5 million people in the U.S. are expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA .

Sponsor Message

Hundreds of flights had already been cancelled or delayed by early morning Thursday, particularly on the East Coast, where authorities have warned people to stay home as the storm barrels through. The majority of people are expected to travel by car for the holidays, and the winter weather could affect their plans due to visibility issues on the road.

toggle caption i DANIEL SLIM/AFP via Getty Images

Richard Bann, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center, told NPR that the East Coast storm remained the main concern, calling it a "multi-hazard" storm.

"It's going to be getting better organized as we go through the day, and it'll be spreading a considerable amount of wind, heavy rain. The real concern with this thing is going to be coastal flooding," Bann said.

Meteorologist Matthew Cappucci with The Washington Post and MyRadar told NPR the storm's magnitude at this time of the year was "unusual."

"We would expect this in deep winter," Cappucci said.

The storm in the East Coast, however, is expected to mostly clear out by Saturday, easing weekend travel for those returning from Thanksgiving gatherings.

Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City delayed

Beyond travel, several Thanksgiving parades have also been affected by severe weather.

Sponsor Message

The incoming storm is expected to cause high winds in New York City, prompting Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday to delay the city's famous Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade. Organizers were already inflating the iconic giant balloons for the parade on Wednesday when officials announced the decision.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

The parade, which is now expected to take place on Saturday, will be the city's 100th, and while it was cancelled before during World War II, this is the first time that it's been postponed in the last century.

The parade's organizers said it took two years to prepare the elaborate celebration, which includes over 11,000 participants and volunteers, thousands of high school marching band musicians from across the country and hundreds of balloon handlers. In previous years, up to 2 million spectators have attended the parade.

"Safety is and will always remain our top priority, and this will be a heavy storm," Mamdani told reporters.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

He urged the city's residents to prepare for extreme weather conditions. He said the city expected sustained winds between 30 and 40 mph and possible gusts as high as 65 mph, with resulting floods and flash floods.

"Generation after generation has watched Spongebob and Spiderman soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down 6th Avenue. And I know this change of plans will cause inconveniences," Mamdani said. "Yet safety has to come first."

Philadelphia also grounded all balloons for its parade this year due to winds.

Steve Kastenbaum contributed reporting for this story.

World.title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
World.content:
FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million "orbital compute modules" (forming a data center constellation called "Starmind") would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing "the full power of the sun."

"America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move "opens a bold new frontier."

Sponsor Message

A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least "one authorized space station" by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.

The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns.

Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers "a fantasy."

"It's not going to happen," he said Wednesday.

Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun's energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult.

Sponsor Message

He and others also point to additional risks, such as atmospheric pollution through launches and reentries, as well as possible in-orbit collisions that could impact other essential satellites.

"You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions," said Becker, noting such crashes could create "a cloud of debris" in the low Earth orbit — where many weather and telecommunication satellites are also found.

In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. It also acknowledged that it had received a "substantial number" of public comments leading up to its authorization Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request. But the regulator maintained that deploying the satellites "serves the public interest" — and said that it dismissed topics that it didn't have authority over, such as environmental concerns.

The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space.

In a statement Wednesday, the AAS said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the FCC's decision. The organization said that SpaceX's proposed position of data centers in low Earth orbit would undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky."

"The proposed constellation involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," AAS said, noting that "these satellites would therefore be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky."

Becker echoed that sentiment. "It also is pollution of the night sky to the naked eye," he said.

Viasat, Amazon, SpaceX and the FCC did not immediately respond to The Associated Press' requests for further comment Wednesday.

World.title: Andy Taylor, guitarist of new wave icons Duran Duran, dies at 65
World.content:
Andy Taylor, guitarist of new wave icons Duran Duran, dies at 65

toggle caption i Jim Cooper/AP

Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, whose huge pop hits included "Hungry Like the Wolf," "The Reflex" and "Rio" and were inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.

Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.

"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed," the band said.

toggle caption i Lo Sai-hung/AP

On the night he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.

Sponsor Message

"I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band," he wrote. "You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one's own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible."

The two-time Grammy Award-winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the U.K. and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.

The band's 1981 debut album "Duran Duran" had their first hit single, "Planet Earth," but it was "Rio" that transformed them into trans-Atlantic stars. The Rock Hall explained their appeal this way: "They were new wave outsiders who became music video stars — 'Tiger Beat' fashion pinups who rocked arenas."

How music videos made Duran Duran massively famous

The band's imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as "Girls on Film" and "Union of the Snake" and the moody ballads "The Chauffeur" and "Save a Prayer." Other hits in the coming years included "The Wild Boys," "New Moon on Monday" and "Come Undone." Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song "A View to a Kill" and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.

Sponsor Message

Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesizers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people's walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labeled part of the New Romantics. Princess Diana was known to be a fan, which meant a lot to the band.

"It worked well for us," drummer Roger Taylor told Rolling Stone. "It was genuine. I don't think it was some sort of PR stunt. It was massive for us because she was the No. 1 icon of the early '80s."

The band's success was in large part due to their videos, including their Antigua-set song "Rio," which featured shots of the band in pastel suits sailing confidently on a yacht. For the album "Rio," they shot three music videos in Sri Lanka — including "Save a Prayer," which had John Taylor getting sprayed by an elephant — and two in Antigua, feeding MTV's need to have a stream of visuals, something classic rock didn't have.

"A lot of the success of the album is down to the power of the videos and the way it made the band omnipresent around the globe," Le Bon told The Daily Beast in 2012. Andy Taylor agreed: "I don't think we could have done it without MTV."

John Taylor and keyboardist Nick Rhodes started the band as teenagers in the northern city of Birmingham in 1978, with a name inspired by a character in the Jane Fonda-starring sci-fi movie "Barbarella." Roger Taylor, Le Bon and Andy Taylor joined soon after, with the British press referring to them as the "Fab Five." Andy Taylor answered an ad in Melody Maker music magazine for a "Live-Wire Guitarist." (None of the Taylors were related.)

"We all grew up on the same vinyl records and live gigs, from David Bowie to Roxy Music, The Sex Pistols and, of course, Chic. I could go to all those places as a player and developed a hybrid guitar style that fitted this amazing concept of a band," Andy Taylor wrote in a letter read by the band during their Rock Hall induction.

Sponsor Message

Behind massive success, Taylor and bandmates were distant

Duran Duran had the unenviable job of following Led Zeppelin at Live Aid in Philadelphia and performed "A View to a Kill," "Union of the Snake," "Save a Prayer" and "The Reflex." In his book, "Wild Child," Andy Taylor revealed the band was, as he put it, "falling apart at the seams."

"Everything should have been perfect, but privately we were screwed and in turmoil. When we came offstage in Philadelphia there were no congratulatory hugs or friendly smiles. It was like we were completely foreign to each other, and it would be the last time we played together for almost two decades."

toggle caption i Jim Cooper/AP

The various members all had some success with side projects: Le Bon, Rhodes and Roger Taylor recorded an album as Arcadia in 1985; John Taylor and Andy Taylor formed Power Station, a supergroup that included Robert Palmer, in 1984, having hits with "Some Like It Hot" and "Get It On."

In 1986, the band came together to record the hit album "Notorious," produced by Nile Rodgers — with hits including the title single and "Skin Trade" — but Andy Taylor made his second exit from the group after some early recording sessions for the album. He would stay away for such albums as 1997's "Medazzaland" and 2000′s "Pop Trash" — but returned for 2004's "Astronaut."

By 2007, Andy Taylor opted not to participate in the Timbaland-led "Red Carpet Massacre," an attempt to harness a more youthful rhythmic vibe.

"With Andy not turning up, it couldn't be a rock record, so that whole album was an attempt to patch over the cracks with Andy missing," John Taylor told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution in 2011.

Andy Taylor told The Scotsman in 2008: "People have wrongly assumed that I didn't want to be in the band, but the opposite is true. I always wanted to be in a band, but Duran Duran had ceased to function as a band."

Sponsor Message

At Duran Duran's height, they were as famously destructive as any rock band. Andy Taylor revealed in his memoir that he had a six-year cocaine habit and band members trashed hotel rooms, argued with management about money and had high-end shopping sprees.

Andy Taylor was the first of the Duran boys to get married, tying the knot with Tracey in 1982 and having four children — Andy, Georgie, Bethy and Izzy — and a grandson, Albie. He is survived by all of them, and they credited his devotion to them in a family statement.

"For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home," the family statement said.

In 2023, he released the album "Man's a Wolf to Man," his first solo release in over 30 years. On the title track, he sang: "Last night/I dreamt someone loved me/And life was not surreal/Someone's souvenir."

"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later when his own life is cut so short," Le Bon said in a statement Wednesday.

World.title: Data breaches are coming fast and furious. Are businesses doing enough to protect your data?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

First it was a data breach at Staples, with the company alerting staplesprint.ca customers Friday that some personal information was accessed in a recent security incident.

Then came a notice from Bell, saying an "agentic threat actor" had accessed personal information like names, phone numbers and email addresses, impacting customers of Bell, Bell Aliant, Bell MTS, Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile. Agentic usually refers to AI tools that can act independently.

The incidents are just the latest examples of breaches — Loblaws, Save-on-Foods, Montreal car-sharing company Communauto and telecomm provider Eastlink have all made headlines for data incidents in the past few months.

For Bell customers like Anna Stephenson, who received an email this week saying her data might have been compromised, news of another hack doesn't feel all that surprising anymore.

"It's kind of the world we live in now where we have to sort of deal with these things," she said.

Though she understands Bell's challenge in staying one step ahead of criminals, Stephenson wants to see companies do more to protect the valuable data they keep about customers.

"In my opinion, companies need to invest more in that security, and hopefully that's something that Bell's looking into," Stephenson said.

WATCH | Is AI making data breaches easier?: Bell cyberattack raises fear AI is making data breaches easier | Duration closed caption 1:49 Bell Canada has confirmed that an ‘agentic’ threat actor breached its systems on Nov. 17, which may have exposed personal information belonging to customers of Bell, Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile.

The experts agree. As AI tools make it easier to carry out hacks, lots of businesses are trying to keep up with the onslaught of attacks — but security and data experts say poor data management and security practices often leave consumer information more vulnerable than it should be.

Too much data, not enough protection

Canadian privacy laws require companies to follow 10 principles when collecting, using and safeguarding personal information. When a breach happens that creates a real risk of harm, businesses have to report it to the privacy commissioner, notify individuals as soon as possible and keep records about the breach.

Those rules put the onus on businesses to manage and protect consumer data, according to Sharon Bauer, a lawyer and founder of Bamboo Data Consulting.

"It is their responsibility to make sure that the data is secure," said Bauer.

While federal courts can fine businesses up to $100,000 if they fail to take certain steps, like report a breach, the federal privacy commissioner can't hand out fines itself. Bauer says that means the existing rules don't always have enough teeth to make companies feel like they need to comply.

Sharon Bauer is a Toronto-based privacy lawyer and founder of Bamboo Data Consulting. Often, businesses are keeping too much customer data they don't need, making it vulnerable to potential breaches, Bauer says. (Submitted by Sharon Bauer)

And best practices for keeping data aren't always followed. While lots of businesses have to keep some personal info on file, Bauer says many keep too much information that they simply don't need.

"It's probably one of the biggest risks that we find in almost every company that we work with," Bauer said.

She says companies might keep dates of birth that aren't being used, for example. Not storing data is the best way to prevent it from being stolen, according to Bauer, so keeping old or out of date customer information creates an unnecessary risk.

Terry Cutler, CEO of Cyology Labs, which provides cybersecurity services to small and medium-sized businesses, says many companies are often simply unaware of how vulnerable they are. He says some businesses he's worked with will use software that keeps part of their systems safe, thinking it covers their bases, while other parts of their network are exposed.

Cutler says a lot of companies currently "don't have the proper detection technology to know there's a hacker in their system, and they don't have a good response plan to get the hacker out once he's been detected."

And with AI making it easier for hackers to steal valuable data, the importance of taking cyber issues seriously is growing, too.

Brent Arnold, founder of cybersecurity and privacy law firm Capstan Legal, says hackers can essentially automate attacks using AI, as agentic tools can work on their own to solve a problem once they're given an end goal — like hacking into software.

He says he's seen a deluge of attacks by hackers moving at hyper speed in recent months, something likely being driven by AI.

"It all happens a lot faster before it can be detected," he said.

One in four malicious data breaches are now powered by AI, according to IBM's 2026 data breach report — a 56 per cent increase compared to the year before.

Arnold points out that the standard for protecting data isn't perfection, but that companies should take reasonable steps to prevent data theft.

WATCH | The massive Crime Stoppers database breach: Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database | Duration closed caption 1:52 A CBC News investigation found more than a million tips submitted to Crime Stoppers in Canada over the past 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach. About half the leaked Canadian tips obtained by CBC contained personal information.

However, as threats become more sophisticated, he says businesses will need to raise their prevention measures to match.

"The standard is always reasonable measures, but what that looks like is getting more and more sophisticated as the attacks get more and more sophisticated."

Some firms stepping up

While some companies might not be keeping up with cyber risks, Bob Gordon, strategy advisor for the Canadian Cyber Threat Exchange, says others are taking the issue very seriously.

The cyber exchange is made up of big and small businesses that share information about cyber threats, including how hackers might attack and what evidence they may leave. Sharing this intelligence is a big help to smaller companies, Gordon says, because they often have fewer resources to pour into security.

Gordon says the exchange has attracted new members in recent months. He says it's a sign that businesses are starting to realize cyber security isn't just a tech concern, but rather a major risk that can impact consumer trust or even temporarily shut down operations in a worst-case scenario.

Cutler says calls to his cybersecurity firm are up by about 40 per cent — mostly from companies wanting to know how hackable they are and how they can prevent breaches.

WATCH | What to know about the Communauto data breach: Communauto was hit by a data breach — here’s what you need to know | Duration 0:57 The Montreal car-sharing company says one of its employees tried to access customers’ personal information, including names, addresses and drivers’ licence numbers. Here’s what you need to know about the data breach.

Some companies have also stepped up prevention measures after breaches.

Communauto, for example, experienced a security incident earlier this year when it said an employee accessed customers' personal information. While a spokesperson said in an email that there's no evidence the stolen data was leaked, the company is still monitoring the dark web for it. Certain personal information will now be deleted or anonymized sooner, and access to customer data is now further restricted internally, the spokesperson said.

After its breach, Bell said it was investigating and had reached out to the RCMP's cyber crime unit. Staples said it was taking its breach "very seriously," and had also launched an investigation.

Cracking down with new rules

On top of those efforts, a new federal bill making its way through Parliament could bring tougher privacy rules.

Bill C-36 isn't yet law, but it would introduce stricter requirements about deleting customer data after it's been used — or whenever a person requests deletion — more measures about how it's stored and the ability to impose major fines in the millions of dollars if organizations don't follow the rules.

LISTEN | What to know about protecting your data: 54:36 The Value of Your Data and How to Protect It

Arnold says he's not sure stronger laws will have much impact.
