"The big problem is, companies often just don't even think about this," he said.

If the issue isn't on their radar, the threat of greater fines won't move the needle according to Arnold, meaning education about some of the free or cheap resources available to businesses could be a better place to start.

While Bauer says the new rules might not be perfect, they would up the ante for businesses to comply.

"I think that this is a wake up call for all businesses to start to think about how they handle … personal information and how they protect it."

World.title: Flood watch in place on Vancouver Island as king tide impact continues
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A flood watch is in place for eastern Vancouver Island as the B.C. coast continues to deal with a series of storms that are combining with unusually high tides on Thursday.

The B.C. River Forecast Centre issued the flood watch on Wednesday, along with a swath of high streamflow advisories for the South Coast and the rest of Vancouver Island, as between 50 and 100 millimetres of rain were predicted to fall on the island.

Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) said in an orange coastal flooding warning for Metro Vancouver that "moderate to significant flooding" was expected along coastlines and low-lying areas due to storm surge and very high tides.

A number of evacuation alerts were issued by the regional districts of Nanaimo and Comox Valley on Wednesday, adding to previous alerts from the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation and Parksville, with residents told to be ready to leave at a moment's notice.

A warning to stay away from the river, posted by the Regional District of Nanaimo, is seen on Wednesday. (Claire Palmer/CBC)

The B.C. River Forecast Centre said in its flood watch that residents should stay clear of running rivers and never drive across flooded roads.

"Significant storms earlier in the month have contributed to saturated soils and higher flows, increasing the potential for rapid runoff and flow response during this next storm," the Wednesday flood watch reads.

The king tides currently hitting B.C.'s coast — referring to a phenomenon where cosmic alignments can mean dramatic tides which can be about 0.3 to 0.6 metres higher than the average — are expected to end on Thursday.

ECCC said the water levels could elevate by as much as 0.7 metres during high tide on Wednesday and Thursday.

Grouse Grind closed

While the coastal flooding warnings covered nearly the entire B.C. coastline on Wednesday, high winds and rainfall were also an issue for many areas.

B.C. Ferries cancelled a number of evening sailings between Metro Vancouver and Vancouver Island, citing high winds in the Strait of Georgia, on Wednesday.

WATCH | 3 factors behind coastal flooding risk in B.C.: 3 forces are raising the risk of coastal flooding in B.C. | Duration 3:00

The Metro Vancouver Regional District said that the Grouse Mountain Regional Park in North Vancouver — which houses the popular Grouse Grind trail — would be closed on Thursday due to the heavy rain in the forecast.

"Park staff will assess and determine if trails are safe to reopen once weather conditions allow. Please stay out of the park for your safety, that of park staff, and first responders," the regional district said on Wednesday.

World.title: Police didn't initially search 18-year-old's devices after online exploitation and death, mother says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains references to suicide, abuse and graphic material that may be upsetting to some readers.

A grieving mother in St. John's says she and her family were left to find their own evidence after police didn't investigate signs her teen was being exploited by a sadistic online network, despite RCMP in the province being the first police force in Canada to warn parents about the threat more than two years ago.

The family — who CBC News is not identifying for fear of retaliation by online predators — reached out to the fifth estate earlier this year after seeing the program's investigative documentary about 764 — an online network of violent extremists that targets vulnerable minors. It also tries to coerce them into sending sexually explicit messages and images, doing self-harm — including carving their predators' names into their skin as a sign of devotion — and even killing themselves.

The mother says her teen, who we are referring to by the initial J, was being exploited in a similar manner and died by suicide in April at the age of 18.

J was an 18-year-old in Newfoundland who loved sunrises, sunsets, their family and their dog. They died by suicide in April. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Since their death, J's mother says she has been left to scour her child's devices and journals and has found evidence of multiple usernames exploiting her child, utilizing similar tactics used by members of 764, including sexual exploitation and pressure to self-harm.

While police were aware of J's victimization after J attempted suicide in June 2025, J's mother says police did not take J's devices for analysis then or after J died by suicide this past April.

WATCH | Mom questions police actions after teen's online exploitation, death:: Mom says police ‘asked for nothing’ after teen’s death, online exploitation | Duration closed caption 11:59 The mom of an 18-year-old in St John’s, N.L. who died by suicide believes the teen was targeted for years by 764, a global online child exploitation network. A joint investigation by CBC’s The Fifth Estate and The National looks into why the RCMP-RNC didn’t initially analyze the teen’s phones and computers, leaving the grieving mother to scour the device for evidence herself

Following an interview with the fifth estate, Sgt. Brent Perry, who runs the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary's integrated internet child exploitation unit, reached out to J's mother. He apologized for not "properly" communicating the force's "offer/ability to further this investigation" and has since taken the devices for review.

An inner world of exploitation

J's mother is speaking out now, she says, to find justice for J.

"I feel like this is my role now as J's mom … so the world can see what happens online because a lot of us are blinded to it and J's not here to tell the story themselves."

J left behind multiple phones and journals for their family in which they outline the extent of their online exploitation. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

J's vulnerability can be seen in journal entries, drawings and videos they left behind. In one recording, when J was 15, J speaks about their struggles with mental health, suicidal ideation and self-harm.

J's journal entries also reveal a window into a sadistic online world where J's vulnerability left them targeted and trapped.

According to their mother, J — who loved sunrises, their family and their dog deeply — was struggling with their gender identity during the pandemic and began to spend more time isolated in their room on their phone.

It was only after a suicide attempt in June 2025 that J ended up in hospital and disclosed they had been exploited online by several individuals who had pushed them to record and share images of them self-harming and attempting suicide.

J's mother said she was shocked by what her child shared.

"J explicitly said: ‘They told me to do this, they told to kill myself, they told me to cut myself. They told me, you know, they made me do it. I had no choice. They knew where we lived.'"

For what would have been J's 19th birthday in August, the family placed a purple bench in memory of the teen, at a spot where they enjoyed watching the sunset. (Submitted by J's family)

J's mom called Canada's national tipline, Cybertip.ca, which alerted police. An officer from the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary's integrated internet child exploitation unit came to the hospital and interviewed J.

But according to their mother, a few months later, an officer informed the family that without more information, the investigation was stalled.

Previous police warning

Just a year before, Newfoundland and Labrador RCMP was the first police department in Canada to warn the public about violent online networks that went by names like 764 or CVLT — groups targeting vulnerable children as young as eight on popular social media, gaming and streaming platforms.

At the time, police warned caregivers about how members of the group often invite minors to private chatrooms where they sexually exploit and groom them — for the main purpose of gaining clout within the group.

Since that advisory, the unit has been investigating at least half a dozen cases in the last year. In June, the unit held a news conference to alert the public of another 764 victim in the province.

Despite the growing awareness, and J's case bearing the hallmarks of 764's exploitation, J's mother says her child's online abuse was not flagged as another potential case.

J's mother says she can't understand why her child's case wasn't examined more closely given the RCMP had issued the 764 alert just a year before police became aware of J's exploitation.

"When it came to the 764 and knowing that my child was only a year after that and nothing was done — like it was basically dismissed and said: ‘This is it, there's nothing we can do….' Like, why didn't they take this more seriously? Why didn't they ask to see [the] devices?"

Instead, the family says after J's death, an officer told them to reach out if they found any evidence themselves.

J had several devices and in a note left behind included passwords and pointed to where the family could find phones, computers and journals documenting the abuse they endured.

With the help of family members, J's mother spent weeks poring through J's journals, combing through accounts and chats as well as images and videos and found evidence of multiple individuals exploiting her child.

"Why do I, as a parent who just lost my child, have to go through all of this looking for that explicit content? You know, like it's, to me that's torture."

J's mother has kept a number of J's personal belongings close, including the teen's baby blanket. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC)

When asked why a family in that situation would be left to gather evidence of their dead child's exploitation, Perry said he could not speak about individual cases. But he acknowledged his empathy for the family.

"I'm a father myself and that issue is very much alive to me," Perry told the fifth estate.

"I'll reiterate that if a family has information that they believe would be of interest to the police to investigate, our door is always open to investigate and hear what information they have."

764 offshoots continue to evolve

Understanding how to tackle the larger problem of 764 and its offshoots is still in its infancy, says Marc-André Argentino, an extremism expert with Public Safety Canada who has been tracking 764 and affiliate groups since 2022.

Argentino says 764 and its offshoots continue to evolve from a loose network urging minors to self-harm to pressuring members to commit acts of public violence.

"This is not fictitious. And it is as bad as we are saying. And actually it is worse."

764 and its related groups draw inspiration from a satanic neo-Nazi movement called the Order of Nine Angles (O9A). (CBC)

Argentino has spent much of his time in the last year training thousands of front-line workers around the world, including 2,000 police officers in Canada, to recognize signs of 764.

"We have a challenge talking about 764 and the network simply because of the type of harms and criminal acts that are perpetrated, the extreme nature of these acts," he said, adding that the fact youths are often behind the violence is hard for many to comprehend.

As the threat escalated, Canada was the first country in the world to designate 764 a terrorist threat in December 2025.

Since then, police have made multiple 764-related arrests across the country, including in Quebec City, New Brunswick and Saskatchewan, as well as identifying several victims in British Columbia.

In an email, a spokesperson for the RCMP said while it cannot share how many 764 cases are being investigated, the "threat is evolving and increasingly involves young people."

Calls for legislation

At a recent event in Ottawa, parents, young people and advocacy groups called on the federal government to implement its online harms legislation, the Safe Social Media Act (Bill C-34), which was tabled in June 2026.

The bill is designed to implement age-appropriate protections and safeguards for younger users, including safer design features and measures to reduce children's exposure to harmful material and high-risk online interactions. The bill is expected to become law next year.

J's mother says the legislation can't come soon enough.

She has spent hours going down dark online corners hoping to hold someone accountable and find justice for her child.

Police apologize, take devices

In the email to J's mother that was sent a day after the fifth estate interviewed Perry, he offered to support her analysis of J's devices "to further her search for answers."

Sgt. Brent Perry is in charge of the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary’s integrated internet child exploitation unit. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Perry added that "it has recently come to my attention that our offer/ability to further this investigation was not communicated properly and for that I offer my sincere apology."

The email, sent in June, was the first significant development since J's death in April. In that time, J's mother had found evidence to share, including images of who J claimed was their main predator and messages offering money in exchange for J to carve a name into J's skin.

The RCMP has since asked J's mother to bring in everything she found — including J's devices.

"I provided whatever information I possibly could," she said.

Her voice breaking, she added that she could feel J working through her "to keep me going, to push further and to keep searching. I so badly want justice."

Police have since copied most of the devices and told her the investigation could take months.

World.title: The 'unity' fight splitting Danielle Smith's party intensifies at UCP convention
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Loyalists to Premier Danielle Smith are spearheading massive get-out-the-vote efforts for this weekend’s UCP convention, in hopes of seizing firm control of the party board in the aftermath of Alberta’s separation referendum.

This includes offers to pay for meeting tickets and a surge of registrations by members from the party’s old Progressive Conservative wing, CBC News has learned.

On the other side, grassroots party activists are also spending money and organizing in hopes of electing more independence-friendly officials to the party board. But after several years of insurgent groups like Take Back Alberta holding sway at conventions, this could be the year that the party establishment strikes back.

“This is a similar effort that would happen for an actual leadership race,” one senior United Conservative told CBC News about the intensity of convention organizing.

However, Smith’s leadership isn’t up for a vote at this UCP annual general meeting, starting Friday in Calgary. It’s not the party president’s turn to be up for election either, but convention-goers will choose another eight of 18 voting directors on the UCP’s board, including chief financial officer and regional directors.

This weekend’s battle, insiders believe, could help tilt the board’s balance away from independence — or from the influence of Smith and her inner circle.

One party organizer trying to rally traditional Tories to the convention is Hal Danchilla, a lobbying firm partner who served as a key advisor to former premier Ralph Klein.

To explain his aims ahead of the convention, he hearkened back to the approach taken during the old Progressive Conservative dynasty, before its 2017 merger with the Wildrose Party to form the UCP.

“One of the fundamental pieces in the past was that we worked for the leader of the party,” Danchilla told CBC News. “The leader didn’t work for the party.”

At past UCP conventions, partisans have shown support for Smith. But they've also elected party board members that her loyalists are now trying to push out. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

How pitched are attempts to stack the convention, which a record 7,000 members are registered to attend?

One Tory in Calgary who hasn’t been active in the UCP told CBC News that of the many people who have urged her to attend this weekend, two separately offered to cover her registration fee, which after the early-bird discount runs $399.

The Tory, who spoke on the condition she not be named, declined the money, preferring to go on her own dime (and she wouldn’t say who offered). But the urgency got her concerned about the party’s health heading into next year’s provincial election.

“If you have to whip your own party like this at your own convention ... how are you going to run an election?” she said.

Multiple sources said the Smith loyalists’ goal is to bring thousands of supporters out to the convention, to outnumber activists’ efforts on the other side.

After 75 per cent of Albertans supported staying in Canada in the October referendum, the premier shifted from her long-standing tolerance for openly backing separatism within her UCP ranks.

She said she wants everyone speaking for her party to acknowledge and accept the referendum results, including all MLAs and election candidates next year. The party has issued a pledge for all board candidates and current riding association presidents to sign, saying they “abide by” that vote’s outcome — although several presidents have refused that demand .

New candidates for board posts include several UCPers who campaigned against a united Canada, including Chris Scott of the independence group Let’s Talk Alberta.

Other candidates have banded together on a slate dubbed Team Unity, including Patrick Malkin, a party vice-president whose day job is as the premier’s deputy chief of staff. This “team” professes loyalty to the premier and a commitment to a “strong Alberta within a United Canada.”

“It is eight like-minded, hard-working dedicated people who are running for the board that are unifying together,” Ken Engler, a candidate to be the party’s chief financial officer, said at a Calgary board candidates’ forum last week.

Part of an email sent to UCP members from board candidates calling themselves the party's 'Unity' slate. (United Conservative Party/CBC news graphic illustration)

The banner on this group’s campaign emails features the premier’s photo, but Smith has not endorsed any candidates.

“While the premier is not involved or associated with the creation of this group, it is great to see individual members from across our province organizing to keep our party united,” Smith spokesperson Ryan Fournier said in an email.

On Wednesday, a group of 21 Calgary business and community leaders sent party members a letter endorsing the slate's eight candidates to keep the "UCP strong and unified." It was co-ordinated by lawyer and veteran conservative fundraiser Brian Felesky, who said he backs Smith's efforts to "put the whole issue of separation to rest."

"I firmly believe in a united Canada, a united Alberta, and I don’t want this AGM to be hijacked," said another signatory, former Calgary police commission chair Mike Shaikh.

Not only is this slate taking on some of the pro-independence challengers like Scott — who willingly signed the post-referendum pledge — but it’s also running candidates against a few current directors with ties to the independence cause, including regional directors Brad LaForge and Mark Hunt , and CFO Jack Redekop .

“I don't need to be the establishment's choice, but I want to be your choice,” LaForge told the Calgary forum last Friday.

“I'm asking you to vote for the kind of party we can be, one where respect matters more than influence — where unity is something we build together, not something we demand from one another.”

The “unity” slate has also rankled the party’s board president, Rob Smith. In a social media post on Tuesday, he said it’s “extremely offensive” to suggest that other candidates aren’t for unity, and announced he’d endorse three contenders running against Team Unity members.

Danchilla’s view of the party working for the leader and not vice versa runs counter to the perspective of many UCP grassroots activists who prefer more of a bottom-up approach.

“The party doesn’t exist so that the leadership can use it to accomplish their goals,” Scott told CBC News this week. “The membership is supposed to be operating the party to make the leader and the government accomplish their goal.”

The party’s board will have particular importance with 2027 Alberta election looming. It holds influence over the UCP’s multimillion-dollar war chest and candidate selection, among other political matters.

Several current directors like LaForge and Hunt joined the board with the backing of activist groups like David Parker’s Take Back Alberta and Mitch Sylvestre’s pro-independence Alberta Prosperity Project, which sought to exert more heavy influence on the party and UCP government by controlling the board.

As those groups gained power at party conventions, those from the Tory side retreated or stopped coming. In the first post-referendum convention, there’s a big effort to bring them back into the fold to preserve the UCP as a staunchly federalist (and anti-separatist) party.

Elan MacDonald has helped reach out to hundreds of Tories and UCPers, urging them to come to the AGM. She was deputy chief of staff to former Tory premiers Ed Stelmach and Alison Redford — both of whom Danielle Smith opposed as Wildrose leader — but has emerged recently as a Smith backer, hosting a coffee party for the premier at her Edmonton house last July. MacDonald recently left a University of Alberta job to become a government-relations consultant.

“Conservatives are re-engaging with the UCP for this AGM because they see a small sliver of conservatives dictating an agenda that we don't share,” MacDonald said.

“We need a board that is very clear that this is not a separatist party. This is a broad-based conservative party that has broad-based conservative values.”

Elan MacDonald served as a key aide for two former Tory premiers, and is currently in government relations. (flyyeg.com)

Danchilla, who is working with MacDonald’s team, said the group is not offering to pay convention-goers. CBC was unable to confirm the identities of any organizations or individuals who are offering to cover costs of those intending to support the Unity slate.

On the other side of this board election battle, a pro-independence group named Next Step Alberta is offering to cover half the convention fees for like-minded supporters. Next Step head Nathan Steinke said he’s been getting referrals from APP to provide the subsidies to conservatives who bought their own tickets.

“I think that sovereignty-minded people need to be represented,��” Steinke said. He’s a former UCP cabinet aide and is married to Samantha Steinke, a veteran party board member who he says has accompanied him to some events where he’s touted his project.

Sylvestre, who has told APP backers he wants to get 1,000 of them to the convention, confirmed Nathan Steinke’s group is supporting him, and said repaying ticket-holders is “completely aboveboard.”

While party members must register individually for the AGM, the rules do not prohibit covering others’ costs, party spokesperson Dave Prisco said in an email.

Nathan Steinke said his budget for the effort is modest — under $15,000 — and he’s so far financially supported fewer than 100 AGM attendees.

He said he’s worried about what happens to the UCP if independence activists are shut out from the board and separatists don’t feel they have a home in the party.

“You know, if the establishment basically rolls in … and just steamrolls us, then I think that they are in some ways damaging unity more than sovereignty ever could,” Steinke said.

'Canada Guy' stages a small counter-protest at an October independence rally at the Alberta legislature. UCP Leader Danielle Smith has urged her party to stop talking about separatism. (Amanda May Erickson/The Canadian Press)

Chris Scott, who is confident he has enough supporters to get elected as the party’s central region director, echoed this sentiment

“If the rural and the grassroots folks smell funny business, that’s going to be reflected in the election,” he said.

“I think the party has to be really careful about the image they portray to the members, because there’s a lot of members that already feel disenfranchised.”

Concern about the next election and the UCP’s reputation is very much on the minds of many key party figures. The NDP’s byelection win in a former safe Calgary seat in September surprised organizers throughout the UCP, and party president Rob Smith told one podcast recently about the lesson it sent.

“What our door-knockers are hearing, not just in the official Calgary-Shaw byelection, but in door-knocking that’s happening across the province: there are an awful lot of Albertans who believe the UCP is a separatist party,” he told the show Unfiltered earlier this month.

Some in the party are bidding to deputize several hundred or thousand convention attendees to help dispel that image, and notch a comfortable win for Danielle Smith in her final convention before next October’s election.

World.title: Funeral boss 'The Undertaker' seen in police surveillance amid Toronto mafia probe
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When the U.S. slapped financial sanctions on a family-owned chain of Toronto-area funeral homes last week — alleging the company's president played a "senior" role in the Italian mob — the dramatic move likely surprised some clients.

But police records obtained by CBC News show Luigi (Lui) Vescio Sr. has been on the radar of Canadian and Italian investigators for nearly a decade.

Police in Ontario captured surveillance images of Vescio meeting in 2019 with visitors from Italy — purportedly leading figures in the notorious Calabrian criminal syndicate known as the 'Ndrangheta. Months later, Italian authorities sought his arrest on a charge of mafia association.

A news release issued last week by the U.S. Treasury Department identified Vescio, 55, as a key player in the criminal group's Canadian wing. The statement said the 'Ndrangheta in the Toronto area has "strengthened in recent years, becoming so powerful that they dictate events in Italy from across the ocean."

From left, Luigi Vescio Sr., his wife Rose and their children Laura and Luigi Jr. All four were recently sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department over alleged ties to the Italian criminal syndicate known as the 'Ndrangheta. (Vescio Funeral Homes)

The Treasury Department said the 'Ndrangheta in Canada is involved in drug trafficking, money laundering and murder. It named five other men reported to be leaders of the group in the Toronto area, including the purported top boss, Angelo (Don Angelino) Figliomeni.

The statement did not specify how the Canadian-born Vescio's businesses are suspected of fitting into the alleged conspiracy. One location in Vaughan, Ont., came into the spotlight in 2019 for hosting a Hells Angels funeral , attended by bikers from across the country.

Washington also sanctioned Vescio's wife Rose and their adult children Luigi Jr. and Laura "for acting on behalf" of Luigi Sr., who is also known as "The Undertaker." All three family members are listed as owners of Vescio Funeral Homes' three locations in the Toronto area, while Luigi Sr. serves as president.

The Vescio Funeral Home in the Maple district of Vaughan, Ont., north of Toronto. (Pelin Sidki/CBC)

The Vescios and their company did not respond to requests for comment. The allegations against them have not been tested in a Canadian court and the U.S. did not provide evidence for its findings.

No one answered when a reporter knocked on the door of the family's Vaughan home. Signs posted in front of the light brown brick house warned of cane corso dogs "on duty."

In a brief interview posted on social media last year, a smiling Vescio — who has tattoos covering his head and neck — said "we own service-oriented businesses," including the funeral homes and a limousine rental firm.

"I started [in the industry] when I was 15, and still pluggin' away," he said in the interview.

Pictured during surveillance operation

According to Italian police files and York Regional Police intelligence reports reviewed by CBC News, Vescio was seen picking up high-ranking Italian mob figure Vincenzo Muià at Toronto Pearson Airport on March 31, 2019.

Muià had travelled from Italy to confront other figures about the 2018 ambush killing of his brother in Siderno, Calabria, and to apparently seek permission to strike back against those he believed were responsible, the files say.

Luigi Vescio Sr. is seen in a 2019 police surveillance image, carrying a brown envelope outside one of his family's funeral homes. (York Regional Police)

Police noted that during his two-week visit, Muià stayed at the Vescios' five-bedroom home, which has a wine cellar, an in-ground pool and a black-and-white portrait from the movie The Godfather hanging in the den.

Records show investigators kept a close eye on Muià and his associates, including Vescio, during the trip.

A York police photo included in the surveillance report shows Vescio holding a brown envelope in the parking lot of one of his Vaughan funeral homes. In a separate image, he's seen with Muià and other suspected mob figures outside an Italian restaurant in Toronto.

Luigi Vescio Sr., far right, is seen with other men observed in a police surveillance operation in the spring of 2019. York Regional Police captured images of Italian mob figure Vincenzo Muià and his associates during his two-week visit to the Toronto area. (York Regional Police)

Italian authorities even managed to listen surreptitiously to Muià's conversations with Vescio and others after bugging the Italian's mobile phone — effectively providing them with a live microphone by his side at all times.

The eavesdropping became a key sticking point in Canada's efforts to deport Vincenzo (Jimmy) DeMaria, another one of the purported 'Ndrangheta leaders now facing U.S. sanctions.

WATCH | Bid to deport alleged mobster hinged on contentious wiretaps (from October 2022): Long investigation into alleged Italian mobster could collapse | Duration 5:53 A lengthy investigation into alleged Italian mobster Jimmy DeMaria is at risk of falling apart. The Canadian government’s case to deport DeMaria hinges on recordings obtained from wiretaps conducted by Italian police, saying the recordings prove he associates with the mafia, but DeMaria’s lawyer argues they were illegally obtained.

That came after Project Sindacato, a multimillion-dollar York police probe targeting the 'Ndrangheta, collapsed in 2021 following accusations that investigators illegally intercepted phone calls.

What do the sanctions mean?

The Trump administration moved to sanction 'Ndrangheta members last week because it said the organization provided "essential logistical and operational support" for major Mexican drug cartels, which the U.S. and Canada classify as terrorist groups.

The sanctions ensure the Vescios and their firms can't deal directly with U.S. banks or clients. In effect, it will mean they'll also be cut off from Canadian financial institutions, said Jessica Davis, president of Ottawa-based Insight Threat Intelligence.

"Because of the inter-linkages between the Canadian and U.S. financial systems, any Canadian financial institution doing business with those sanctioned entities is now going to look at them and say, 'your risk rating has really escalated,'" Davis said.

Staff at the funeral homes told callers on Monday that it's "business as usual," while avoiding talk of the ongoing turmoil.

Vincenzo (Jimmy) DeMaria, left, and Angelo (Don Angelino) Figliomeni are among several individuals and firms sanctioned in Canada by the U.S. Treasury Department, amid allegations they hold leading roles in the Toronto-area branch of the 'Ndrangheta. (U.S. Treasury Department)

By Tuesday, however, there were signs of trouble. Employees answering the phones at two locations confirmed the funeral homes could not process card payments.

Davis, a former CSIS analyst, said unless it can operate as a cash-only business, it's likely any such sanctioned entity would be forced to close.

The Bereavement Authority of Ontario, the funeral industry regulator, declined to comment directly on Vescio Funeral Homes, but said families can reach out if they have concerns about prepaid arrangements.

"All prepaid funds for arrangements are held within a third-party trust fund," spokesperson David Brazeau told CBC News in an email.

Both the RCMP and York police — which the Treasury Department said helped in the sanctions case — declined to comment directly on the Vescios or the sanctions.

World.title: What's at stake as Canada's top court ruling on Quebec secularism law looms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ahead of Friday's highly anticipated Supreme Court of Canada ruling on Quebec's controversial secularism law, which bars some public sector workers from wearing religious symbols on the job, there is optimism on both sides of the debate.

The big question now is whether the country's top court will rein in the use of the Constitution's notwithstanding clause.

Some legal observers say the decision could be studied by law students for generations to come, while others view it as a potential stepping stone toward lasting change rather than the final word.

"It will not be the end of the conversation on Friday," said Karine Millaire, a Université de Montréal law professor and lawyer who represents the International Commission of Jurists in the case.

"I would be very surprised if it would close all the doors and that it would answer all the questions," she said, noting the court is already scheduled to hear another notwithstanding clause challenge out of Saskatchewan in March.

That’s a fight about children's pronouns and names in Saskatchewan's schools, but here in Quebec, the debate is over the secularism law, known as Bill 21.

Canada's top court says its decision will be released at 9:45 a.m. ET Friday.

WATCH | Legal battle centres heavily on notwithstanding clause: Why all Canadians’ rights are at stake in the Supreme Court challenge of Quebec’s Bill 21 | Duration closed caption 5:41 Quebec’s Bill 21 bans religious symbols for some civil servants. Now, the legal battle has shifted from the ban itself to whether the province overstepped by invoking the notwithstanding clause in the text of the law, to bypass Charter rights.

Ruling felt across Canada

The decision is expected to reverberate nationwide and could carry major political consequences as the Parti Québécois, which has vowed to take Bill 21 even further, now holds a minority government.

The law, which applies to teachers and police officers among others, was adopted in June 2019 by the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government.

It quickly faced a constitutional challenge, with civil liberties groups arguing that the legislation discriminates against Muslim women who wear head coverings.

In April 2021, a Quebec Superior Court judge rendered a decision that described Bill 21 as a law that violates the basic rights of religious minorities in Quebec — but that those violations are permissible because the law invoked the Constitution's notwithstanding clause.

The notwithstanding clause allows governments, including provincial governments like Quebec, to temporarily shield laws from court challenges over fundamental rights violations.



In 2024, the Court of Appeal upheld most of the Superior Court's ruling and even overturned a previous exemption for English school boards.

Now, the notwithstanding clause is at the heart of the Supreme Court's upcoming decision, Millaire said.

While she doesn't expect the court to deliver a "black-or-white" ruling that either eliminates the notwithstanding clause or gives governments the power to override rights, she said the justices will have to weigh whether its use has limits — and whether courts can formally declare that a law violates fundamental rights even if the clause keeps it in force.

"At a minimum, people can expect to know if there is a violation of their rights — rights of many Quebecers,” Millaire said, noting that Quebec chose not to present evidence to justify the law, relying instead on the clause alone to shield it from scrutiny.

Both sides hopeful

Daniel Baril, president of the provincial secularism group Mouvement laïque québécois, said he is "reasonably optimistic" ahead of Friday's decision, pointing to a 2015 Supreme Court ruling his organization won against the City of Saguenay over prayer at city council meetings .

In that unanimous ruling, the court said the state must remain religiously neutral — a precedent Baril argues extends to public sector employees and forms the foundation of Bill 21. It means the law shouldn't even require the notwithstanding clause, he said.

"A unanimous ruling at the Supreme Court is very rare," Baril said in an interview Wednesday, noting Chief Justice Richard Wagner was a justice back then.

"He already signed off on that ruling, and today he is the chief justice. We hope he will have convinced the others."

However, in that 2015 decision, the Supreme Court did not rule out the presence of religious symbols, because it decided to limit the scope of its investigation to prayer only.

On the other side of the debate, Stephen Brown, the CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM), said he is also hopeful ahead of Friday's decision — but warned that the stakes extend far beyond Quebec, affecting the rights of millions of Canadians.

Stephen Brown, president of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, says the Supreme Court ruling extends far beyond Quebec. (Natalia Weichsel/CBC)

For Brown, the core question before the court is whether governments can unilaterally strip away fundamental Charter rights without justification or judicial oversight.

"Long story short: can politicians play wedge politics with the rights of Canadian citizens?" Brown said.

"If the answer to that question is yes, that is a massive problem for who we are as a country. Because if politicians can play wedge politics with our rights, we don't have rights — what we actually have are permissions."

Harini Sivalingam, director of the equality program at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA), said Friday's ruling will be one of the most consequential constitutional decisions in modern Canadian democracy.

With other provinces increasingly using or floating the notwithstanding clause on issues ranging from trans youth to homeless encampments , she said the stakes could not be higher.

"The implications extend far beyond Quebec and religious symbols," Sivalingam said.

World.title: How big U.S. unions view Trump's tariffs on Canadian goods
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

While U.S. President Donald Trump insists his tariffs will bring a boom in factory jobs, the unions who represent hundreds of thousands of manufacturing workers are largely skeptical of his approach.

Nowhere is that skepticism more apparent than organized labour's view of Trump's tariffs on imports from Canada.

Despite their long-standing support for targeted tariffs as a tool for protecting U.S. jobs, the leaders of some of the biggest unions in the U.S. are calling on the Trump administration to take a different approach to Canadian products.

Brian Bryant, international president of the IAM Union, formerly known as the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, says he'll take that message directly to Trump's point man on tariffs, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, at a meeting scheduled for early December.

"We're in favour of strategic tariffs where they're used appropriately to correct bad behaviour," Bryant told CBC News. "Canada's not the problem here."

Bryant says the Trump administration is applying tariffs haphazardly and should focus its attention on countries that pay cheaper wages.

WATCH | Carney government aiming for interim deal by end of year: Canada pursues tariff relief through interim U.S. trade deal | Duration closed caption 2:45 Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke briefly with U.S. President Donald Trump at the APEC summit in China as Canadian negotiators pursue an interim deal to secure relief from U.S. tariffs by the end of the year.

The IAM Union is particularly concerned about the Trump administration's tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, Bryant says.

"We have many manufacturers in aerospace, general manufacturing, shipbuilding that are dependent and reliant on that," he said. The Trump administration should not be "adding to their costs for those because that's going to jeopardize our members' jobs."

Progress in tariff talks

Canadian officials and their U.S. counterparts have said in recent weeks the two sides are making progress toward a trade deal.

While the Carney government is seeking as much of a reduction in tariffs as possible, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has said Canadians should not expect a deal that brings zero tariffs.

Unions in the U.S., some of whom represent significant numbers of Canadian workers, are watching the talks closely and urging the Trump administration to shift its position.

Roxanne Brown, international president of the United Steelworkers (USW), signed a joint letter with Bryant this summer calling on the White House not to impose the threatened 50 per cent tariffs on some $28 billion worth of Canadian goods.

The international president of the United Steelworkers, Roxanne Brown, centre, is surrounded by union representatives during a Sept. 15 news conference in Laval, Que., addressing tariff and trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

"We had great concerns about the impacts those tariffs were going to have on our members' jobs," Brown told CBC News. "We wanted to be on the record to really push back against those tariffs."

Trump went ahead with the additional tariffs, which apply to a range of Canadian products including wood products, alcohol, cheese and sporting goods.

Steel tariffs need study, says USW

When it comes to steel production, the USW supports tariffs on what Brown calls "bad actors," countries that unfairly subsidize their industry or engage in dumping of cheap steel.

"There should be a clear study into that dynamic between the United States and Canada. If it doesn't exist, the tariffs shouldn't exist," Brown said.

She says the environment between the Trump administration and Ottawa right now is "pretty combative" and her union has been asking the White House for months to take a more sensible, practical approach with its northern neighbour.

"That trading relationship has benefited both of our countries, it's benefited the jobs in both of our countries and for our union, that's a really important relationship to maintain," said Brown.

United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain delivers the keynote address at the annual national conference of the union's political arm, on Feb. 9 in Washington, D.C. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

One major union whose leadership has at times supported Trump's tariffs is the United Auto Workers (UAW). Its president, Shawn Fain, despite having urged his members to elect Democrats in 2024, strongly welcomed the Trump administration's initial sweeping tariffs, including those on Canada and Mexico.

"Tariffs are a powerful tool in the toolbox for undoing the injustice of anti-worker trade deals," the UAW said in a statement in March 2025. "We are glad to see an American president take aggressive action on ending the free trade disaster that has dropped like a bomb on the working class."

UAW president backs 'strategic and targeted' tariffs

Fain and the UAW appeared to buy into Trump's argument that auto tariffs would bring good-paying jobs back to the U.S., and the White House communications team amplified his support.

In the past year and a half, after several Michigan leaders of the UAW publicly broke with their union president, Fain has pulled back somewhat on his full-throated backing of tariffs.

He campaigned in the midterms for Abdul El-Sayed, the winning Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, where tariffs on Canadian exports became a key election issue. In a webcast conversation with El-Sayed on Oct. 16, Fain insisted his support for tariffs has always been restricted to "strategic and targeted" ones.

"The unfortunate side of this is this administration has just managed to do blanket tariffs on everything and try to use it as political leverage," Fain said.

Ford vehicles are shown on the assembly line at the company's assembly plant in Louisville, Ky. U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened threat to raise tariffs on automobiles and auto parts from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. 1. (Darron Cummings/The Associated Press)

The UAW did not respond to CBC's request for an interview this week.

Cathy Feingold, international director of the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of unions in the U.S., says the White House should be working with countries like Canada to address global trade challenges rather than punishing them.

"We completely oppose the chaotic nature in which the tariffs of the Trump administration have been imposed, especially on some of our closest allies and partners like Canada," Feingold told CBC News.

She says the AFL-CIO specifically opposes the 50 per cent tariffs imposed in August under Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act, the first time in nearly a century the section had been used.

"It's raised costs on both sides of the border. It disrupts cross-border industries. It's threatening union jobs on both side of the border," Feingold said.

She says she's hopeful the results of the midterms and the incoming Democratic control of Congress creates an opportunity for a shift toward trade policies that benefit workers in the U.S., Canada and elsewhere.

However, Trump has threatened to raise tariffs on automobiles and auto parts from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. 1, a move that would put significant pressure on the bottom line of the three big Detroit-based automakers, Ford, General Motors and Stellantis.

World.title: China, U.S. allies push back on latest round of White House tariffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

China, Japan and other U.S. trading partners protested planned tariff hikes by Donald Trump's administration and hit back at allegations they have excess manufacturing capacity.

The new tariffs, which are likely to take effect early next year, were announced Wednesday. They are intended to help reinstate tariffs for most of the economies after the U.S. Supreme Court ruling in February struck down most of Trump's sweeping tariffs implemented last year.

The new import duties followed a monthslong Section 301 probe. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he determined that practices of the 14 economies relating to excess capacity and production in manufacturing are "unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce."

Stock markets in Europe and Asia posted solid gains on Thursday as the latest salvo of tariffs looked less damaging than first feared. The new rates are also unlikely to be imposed until February or March.

"The macro impact from this increase is likely to be modest, particularly given the fact that the investigations have been telegraphed well in advance," said analysts at JPMorgan.

"Several key imports are still exempt from tariffs, including tech goods, and the administration has shown itself to be sensitive to market disruptions," they added.

Stocks in Europe gained 1.6 per cent in early trading, following on from gains across Asia.

Wall Street is closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday,

'Republicans have learned nothing': House Democrat

Canada was not subjected to the new tariffs. While Trump and Greer have raised a number of objections to what it portrays as unfair trade practices from Ottawa, excess capacity was not one of them.

Trump himself made no public remarks on the new actions, a marked contrast with his "Liberation Day" tariff announcement in April 2025 in the White House Rose Garden.

WATCH | Trade Minister LeBlanc says talks with U.S. to resume next week: Canada spared from new U.S. tariffs, but gaps remain in trade talks | Duration closed caption 2:09 Prime Minister Mark Carney calls Canada's exemption from a new round of U.S. tariffs 'good news' as both sides work toward securing an interim trade deal that would lower tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum and vehicles by year's end.

Trump has hailed the revenue that tariffs bring to the U.S. government, but the protectionist policies are unpopular with voters, who associate them with higher prices on many consumer goods, according to several polls. Republicans in Congress were quick to blame the president’s tariff policy for the party's stunning midterm losses earlier this month.

Several Democrats have argued that, by punishing allies, the policy did little to actual aggressive trade practices from Beijing.

"Republicans have learned nothing," incoming House Majority Leader Katherine Clark of Massachusetts said on X.

China calls tariffs 'pretext for political manouevring'

China, one of the biggest trading partners of the U.S., is facing a 20 per cent tariff. It slammed the notion of "overcapacity" as a "false premise."

"China opposes its use as a pretext for political manouevring," Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said at a regular press briefing.

China's commerce ministry urged the U.S. to "correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation." Ministry s pokesperson He Yadong also said China reserves the rights to retaliate to the measures if necessary.

The U.S. and China have extended by two months a trade truce that's set to expire on Jan. 10. The two countries also have agreed on tariff cuts on reciprocal lists of non-sensitive products worth about $60 billion.

Japan faces new U.S. tariffs of up to 15 per cent, matching the ceiling agreed in last year's trade talks in exchange for its commitment to invest $550 billion in the United States. The Japanese government said it protested to Washington.

"Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place," Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a regular news conference Thursday.

WATCH | Our CBC Washington correspondents on the latest out of the White House:

Follows 'forced labour' tariffs

Malaysia said it "does not have excess capacity in its manufacturing sectors that distorts or disrupts global markets," adding that it will continue to engage and consult with the United States. Malaysia said it will continue consultations with the United States to ensure total tariffs do not exceed 19 per cent, as it was one of the first nations to sign a trade pact with Washington.

On Wednesday, the European Commission expects any measures imposed by Washington needed to respect the previously negotiated 15 per cent tariff ceiling for EU goods imports. A spokesperson for the commission said it strongly rejected the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity.

Analysts say the 14 economies targeted by the Trump administration together account for roughly half of the global economy.

The latest U.S. tariffs are not as alarming as they look, said Stephen Brown, a chief economist with Capital Economics, as they are essentially broadly replacing, rather than adding to, earlier announced U.S. tariffs related to forced labour allegations announced in July.

Still, the new tariffs will likely help push prices higher and may "keep core goods inflation firm into next year," he said in a commentary.

World.title: The bizarre twists and turns of Colombia’s supermarket hostage siege
World.content:
Blackout drunk kidnappers, false statements by De La Espriella, and bogus accusations against hostages leave a trail of chaos and doubt.

Shortly after 76 hostages were liberated from the Exito Supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia, corporate media broadcast a video of two of the men they claimed were involved in the attack.

​The two men, Carlos Tapia and Daniel Díaz, appeared in handcuffs, being escorted by police from the scene of a tense 18-hour standoff between criminals and police.

The media, with information from President Abelardo de la Espriella, suggested that Tapia and Diaz were two of four surviving members of the gang that attacked the supermarket.

​De la Espriella praised the operation he said “came off perfectly,” and released a video of himself mocking two different men, who police say were the actual kidnappers, together with one more person who was killed in the operation.

The president also released a video of himself making demands into a walkie-talkie, falsely claiming that he was in charge of negotiations with the hostage-takers.

According to the indictment from the Prosecutor’s Office, all negotiations and communications with the three hostage takers were handled by Colombia’s anti-kidnapping police unit, the GAULA.

​Tapia and Díaz were released by police just a few hours later, and cleared of any wrongdoing after police confirmed the men were hostages rather than hostage-takers. De la Espriella confirmed shortly afterwards that the men were innocent of any crimes.

​The two men have since both spoken with Colombian media, in interviews in which both men claimed they were mocked by De la Espriella and treated badly by police before being cleared.

​A third man, Edgar Díaz, was also falsely accused by police. He released a video to social media as well, claiming that not only was he mocked and verbally abused by the President, but also robbed of a gold chain by police. Diaz says he was leaving a gym where he works as a personal trainer, in the same mall as the Exito, when he was grabbed by men who appeared to be armed.

The stories of the falsely accused hostages aren’t the only odd parts of the official story surrounding the stand-off between 3 nominally armed men and hundreds of marines, police, snipers, helicopters, and riot police in the city of Cali.

​One of the hostage-takers was killed by police when they entered the supermarket around 1 a.m., after the hostage-takers missed a deadline of 12:30 to release all hostages.

​According to police, the three men attempted to rob an armored car transporting money around 8 a.m., but the car had already left by the time the men arrived. For unclear reasons, the three decided to take nearly 100 people hostage in the Exito supermarket instead, which is part of the same “mega-mall” where the men allegedly intended to carry out the hijacking.

​Two of the men carried long guns that, again according to police, were “traumatic weapons” (similar to Airsoft rifles, the weapons fire foam bullets meant to be non-lethal), and one was armed with another that resembled a shotgun.

Early in the morning, before the men blocked windows in the supermarket, Colombian media captured one of the men from a distance clad in black tactical clothing, body armor, and what appeared to be a heavy steel helmet with a facemask.

​Many of those who were held hostage, speaking with media, said the men were drinking heavily throughout the day, with one witness going as far as to say they were “blind drunk” by the end of the day.

​Workers at the Éxito, who were also taken hostage, said the men set up large speakers, blasted music, and demanded to be given bottles of whisky.

​The two men who survived the police assault that liberated the hostages were asleep when police entered the Éxito, likely why they survived, according to multiple witnesses.

​Confusing matters even further, the wife of the man who was reportedly killed by police, Javier Humberto Muñetón Zapata, had spent the previous 14 hours speaking with local media in Cartagena, looking for her husband, who she believed to be among the hostages.

​She says they lived nearby and went to the mall every day, and that her husband had a membership at the same gym where Diaz works. She claims she began searching for her husband, who had promised to drive her to work and bring pastries from the supermarket, after he suddenly stopped replying to texts.

​She showed Blue Radio a text message at 8:12 a.m. from her husband that said, “Okay, I’m going to pop into Éxito, and I’ll pick you up right away.”

​She claims that her husband ran a small business, regularly drove her to work, and has no criminal record — a fact that has since been confirmed by Cartgena’s mayor. She has made multiple statements to the media asking for clarification and more information, claiming he could not have been involved in any crimes.

Early statements by police, shortly after the hostage situation began to unfold, put the number of hostages at 50. After two releases of hostages by the nominal gunmen, police stated they believed 20 hostages remained as evening approached.

​Shortly after the operation to enter the Éxito, police released details about their raid, claiming that they had “drilled holes in the walls and inserted cameras,” allowing them to identify the kidnappers and estimate the number of hostages.

​They also stated they had men on the roof, in the warehouse of the supermarket, and stationed at the interior entrance to the Éxito, which connects to the mega-mall.

​But more than 70 hostages remained when the raid was successfully carried out.

The attackers claimed in a letter to authorities that if the store was entered by police they would detonate explosives placed near the entrances, killing the hostages.

Police later revealed there were no explosives, and the men were bluffing.

​The two men who were captured alive (and reportedly asleep), Juan Camilo Torres Manco, 33, and Jhon Albeiro Mejía Blandón, 44, are both from Antioquia and have previous convictions for “violent” crimes, according to police.

​Both men appeared intoxicated in videos shortly after they were captured. De la Espriella released a video in which he berates the two men, telling them, “You thought you could just kidnap people and get away with it? Welcome to the miracle country.”

​The bizarre details of the event, as well as misreporting by the media, inaccurate and even contradictory statements by police throughout the day, and general confusion, led some critics of De le Espriella to claim the entire event was staged.

De la Espriella’s efforts to insert himself into the situation, and false claims made by the president, worsened that dynamic.

​There is no evidence currently to support those claims, but with a story that is just straight-up strange, we can see how some people came to that conclusion.

World.title: Colombia’s special forces liberate hostages from Cartagena supermarket
World.content:
Colombia’s security forces liberated some 20 people who were held hostage inside a supermarket in the northern city of Cartagena after a 15-hour stand-off.

The operation ended a tense situation that began around 8AM on Tuesday when the armed kidnappers entered the Exito supermarket in La Castellano, a residential neighborhood.

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who led the liberation operation, the kidnappers meant to rob an armored car that had already left with the proceeds of the day before.

The kidnappers subsequently kidnapped a group of 30 people, and demanded COP7billion ($2 million) and the possibility to escape the supermarket.

Throughout the day, at least five of the hostages were released from the supermarket cafeteria, whose windows had been covered with papers. One video showed a row of hostages sitting behind the window.

Riot police was deployed around midnight after family members and onlookers became restless.

The situation took a quick turn after 1PM when explosions were heard and special forces entered the building.

The security forces killed one of the kidnappers and detained the remaining four, De la Espriella said in a social media video.

Images that were shared on social media showed special police forces securing the Exito’s cafeteria and removing the paper from the windows.

De la Espriella said that all the hostages were released in an “extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the military forces.”

One agent would have been injured in the rescue operation, reported Caracol Radio.

The kidnappers “were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages, but they rejected that opportunity, so we took decisive action,” said the president.

In the morning, the prosecution said the kidnappers’ arms and explosives were fake and former hostages said the hostage takers spent most of the day getting drunk.

World.title: 22 injured after car bomb strikes central Colombia governor’s office
World.content:
Twenty-two people were reportedly injured and more than 80 buildings were damaged in a car bomb attack on the Governor’s Office of Meta in Villavicencio, central Colombia.

According to Meta’s Security Secretary, Franklin Olivos, the car that exploded carried approximately 100 kilograms of explosives and caused damage to buildings that were located more than 100 meters away from the blast.

Among the injured are five private security guards. One of them needed surgery, according to his employer.

Olivos blamed the attack on the 39th Front, a unit of the FARC dissident group EMC, which has opposed the peace process that started 10 years ago on Tuesday and controls large swathes of jungle territory in the south of Colombia.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said that “narcoterrorism is desperate because we are confronting it head-on. It seeks to intimidate us and force us to back down so we seek another sham peace process.”

De la Espriella, an opponent of the peace process, has been advertising an “iron fist” policy against organized crime and illegal armed groups.

The president’s alleged offensive has failed to produce any results and guerrilla groups have continued to attack State security forces and infrastructure.

World.title: Colombia strips key critics of security details
World.content:
Colombia’s National Protection Unit (UNP) has withdrawn the security details of journalist Daniel Coronell, a major critic of President Abelardo de la Espriella, after vowing to protect the freedom of the press.

Coronell’s local security detail was removed because he lives in the United States, which would make it impossible for the UNP to reassess his protection plan.

The Miami-based journalist frequently travels to Colombia for his work and was in Bogota to receive a lifetime achievement award from the national journalism prize.

While receiving the prize, Coronell sharply criticized De la Espriella for promoting self-promotion over governance. using state resources to censor critics, restricting public information to “friendly media,” and leveraging a history of aggressive lawsuits against reporters.

The journalist’s criticism triggered a clash with Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez, who accused Coronell of being angry for having State subsidies pulled.

After press freedom foundation FLIP responded to defend Coronell, Ordoñez claimed that “the freedom of the press enjoys full protection and guarantees from the government.”

We value and defend freedom of the press as a cornerstone of democracy. The press is free, but it is also responsible. It is not a license to abuse, slander, defame, fabricate stories, spread misinformation, or engage in politics. Nor is it a license to destroy democracy or its institutions with lies. Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez

Coronell played a key role in Colombian journalism since the late 1980’s and was forced to flee Colombia in 2005 after reports on the ties of former President Alvaro Uribe and paramilitary groups escalated death threats.

The journalist currently works with Noticias Uno and Caracol Radio, and has more than 700,000 subscribers on YouTube.

The UNP previously stripped former President Gustavo Petro and former presidential candidate Claudia Lopez of their security details.

World.title: Illegal armed group carries out first urban drone attack: three injured in northeast Colombia
World.content:
A couple and their 18-month-old baby were injured in a drone attack on a police station in Cucuta, the first major city to be struck from the sky by guerrilla explosives.

The attack damaged more than 60 homes near the Norte de Santander Police Department in the Tasajero neighborhood in the north of the regional capital, the province’s security secretary, George Quintero, told press.

As of now, the situation is as follows: more than 60 damaged homes located just 20 meters from the police headquarters, and three people injured. Security secretary George Quintero

The homes were hit because the police department’s signal-jamming systems reportedly caused the drones to miss their target.

An unknown number of drones were able to reach the interior of the Police Department’s compound, leaving only minor damage.

Guerrilla group ELN has been carrying out multiple drone attacks in Catatumbo, a nearby region with major coca cultivations, and exercises control in the peripheral slums of Cucuta.

The group was accused of attacking the same police department with home-made mortars in August. This attack injured seven policemen.

In a response to the guerrilla attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella in October ordered the militarization of the border city, which has been struggling with security issues for years.

De la Espriella vowed that he “will not allow narco-terrorism to continue sowing fear and threatening families” in Cucuta and the surrounding Norte de Santander province.

According to the authorities, the militarization of the city sought to “strengthen territorial control, protect citizens, and confront” the illegal armed groups that operate in and around Cucuta.

The president’s offensive against illegal armed groups and organized crime has been hampered by an increase in the use of drones that are equipped with explosives.

All kinds of illegal armed groups use the relatively new technology to push back the authorities from areas under their control.

World.title: Colombia asks X to suspend Petro’s social media account
World.content:
Colombia’s communications ministry said Sunday that it had requested social media platform X to suspend former President Gustavo Petro for “possible incitement to violence.”

In a statement that was published of X, the ministry said it reported Petro’s account to X’s Public Affairs, Safety, and Rules Enforcement Team.

According to the statement, the request to suspend the leftist former president, who has more than 9 million followers, was due to a November 21 post in which Petro asked “the people of Colombia to demand Abelardo’s resignation now.”

Petro has been trying to promote popular opposition against De la Espriella, who he has called an illegitimate president.

According to the ministry, Petro’s call to “take action in the streets” could constitute a call for violence against the government.

In a response, the former president said the De la Espriella administration sought to impose censorship on him, which is “expressly prohibited by the Constitution.”

The ministry’s request “demonstrates the extent of the current government’s illegitimacy,” added Petro.

The former president is now the leader of the Historic Pact (PH) opposition party and has actively been promoting a general strike in response to his successor’s controversial policy decisions.

Petro is a member of the PH’s more radical wing and can still count on a significant following among Colombia’s population.

World.title: The deteriorating press freedom in Colombia and the Americas
World.content:
I sat down with Joshua Collins of Pirate Wire Services to discuss the deteriorating press freedom situation in Colombia and the rest of Latin America.

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Havana Weather for November 26 to December 2
World.content:
Photo at a Havana bakery by Juan Suarez

Change in weather in western Cuba with rain followed by a drop in temperatures, bringing cooler conditions toward the weekend…

By Adrian Fuentes

HAVANA TIMES – The approach of a trough and the advance of a cooler air mass over western Cuba will bring an increase in rainfall in Havana over the coming hours, followed by a slight drop in temperatures toward the end of the week.

In the capital, rain and thunderstorms were expected to continue on Wednesday the 25th. A cold front will arrive between Wednesday night and the early hours of Thursday the 26th. Beginning Thursday, rainfall will gradually decrease, with partly cloudy skies and cooler conditions. Stable weather will prevail on Friday the 27th and Saturday the 28th, with temperatures slightly below normal for this time of year. Starting Sunday the 29th, temperatures will gradually rise again, although variable cloud cover will persist.

Winds will be from the southwest and west before and during the passage of the system, subsequently shifting to the northwest and north at speeds of between 15 and 30 kilometers per hour, with potentially stronger gusts associated with thunderstorms. Relative humidity will remain high during the first half of the forecast period, potentially exceeding 90% during rainfall, before decreasing slightly toward the weekend. Maximum temperatures will range between 24 and 29°C (75 and 84°F), with the lowest expected on Friday and Saturday, while the lows will range between 20 and 23°C (68 and 73°F). Sea surface temperatures will remain at 26 and 27°C (79 and 81°F).

According to the National Hurricane Center, the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season recorded 10 named storms and only one hurricane (Isaias), with activity well below average. No additional tropical cyclone development is expected in the basin before the official end of the season on November 30, and there are no active systems posing a threat to Cuba.
