World.title: A new Museum of Ritual Art in Indigenous Cultures is set to open in Oaxaca
World.content:
A museum projected to open in the city of Oaxaca before Dec. 1 will bring together about 4,000 masks, textiles and other objects from Mexico and more than 30 other countries in a former governor’s residence.

The Museum of Ritual Art in Indigenous Cultures — also called the Museo de las Máscaras, or Mask Museum — will house the collection of Oaxacan researcher René Bustamante in five galleries, with plans also calling for a restoration workshop, library and cafeteria.

It is separate from the Museum of the Cultures of Oaxaca, run by the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) in the former Santo Domingo convent, and the Oaxaca Textile Museum, run by the Alfredo Harp Helú Oaxaca Foundation.

State officials presented the new museum last week without formally inaugurating or opening it. In August, Gov. Salomón Jara had announced an October opening, but donation paperwork reportedly delayed things.

Officials have since switched to a late November opening without offering any specifics.

The state invested some 98.4 million pesos (about US $5 million) in the museum, according to reports. It covers converting the former governor’s residence into a museum, not the purchase of Bustamante’s donated collection.

The pieces will be installed gradually; officials did not announce admission prices or a director at the presentation.

Bustamante, 75, began documenting dances in Oaxaca some 53 years ago. His research initially focused on dancers’ textiles before expanding to masks and their ritual significance.

The collection will show how communities use masks to represent animals, ancestors, spirits and natural forces, preserving memories and conveying their histories through dance.

The collection includes historic pieces, among them a fishermen’s dance mask from coastal Oaxaca reported to be more than 170 years old.

The museum’s five galleries will focus on Mexico, Guatemala, Africa, Oceania and the wider world.

Other Mexican institutions devoted to masks include the National Mask Museum (Museo Nacional de la Máscara) in San Luis Potosí and the San Miguel Mask Museum (also known as Another Face of Mexico, or La Otra Cara de México) in San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato.

The latter is a private museum opened by an American, Bill LeVasseur, and his wife, Heidi, in 2006. It includes more than 500 masks, compared to about 1,300 at the National Mask Museum; the new museum should have at least 700 masks, based on a 2023 mask exhibition from Bustamante’s collection.

Bustamante has no university degree and calls himself a self-taught anthropologist. As a student in 1973, he traveled to Oaxaca’s Costa Chica to study textile symbolism and instead became captivated by the region’s dance traditions. He has since documented more than 80 dance themes.

With reports from El Universal, Oaxaca Media and El Heraldo de México Oaxaca

World.title: Job creation slows and unemployment ticks up in Mexico’s third quarter
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico added 122,348 jobs in the third quarter of 2026, according to official data, down from 487,434 in the second quarter.

The slower pace of job creation coincided with a slowdown in quarter-over-quarter economic growth. Mexico’s economy grew 0.9% on a sequential basis in the third quarter, compared to 1.4% in Q2.

The national statistics agency INEGI reported on Wednesday that 60,162,442 (60.16 million) people were in jobs in the third quarter, up from 60.04 million in the second quarter.

The total number of people in jobs was 628,993 higher in the third quarter than a year earlier.

Overall, the number of women in jobs increased by 157,009 between the second and third quarters, while the number of employed men fell by 34,661.

INEGI also reported on Wednesday that Mexico’s unemployment rate was 2.9% in Q3, up from 2.7% in the previous quarter. That’s the highest rate of any quarter since Q3 of 2024. Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, said that the higher unemployment rate and the high level of employment informality were signs of a “weak” labor market.

Mexico’s employment informality rate — the percentage of total workers employed in the informal sector of the economy — was 55% in Q3, down from 55.1% in Q2.

The newspaper El Economista reported that 78% of the jobs added in the third quarter were formal sector positions, causing the informality rate to decline slightly.

Of the more than 60.1 million people in jobs in the third quarter, 6.9% were underemployed, down from 7.1% in Q2.

Which sectors added the most jobs over the past year?

According to INEGI’s data, 722,566 jobs were added in Mexico’s tertiary or services sector in the 12 months to the end of September. The secondary sector added 179,297 positions in the same period, while the primary sector shed 270,633 jobs.

The industries that added the most jobs between the end of Q3 2025 and the end of Q3 2026 were:

Diverse services: 337,440

Construction: 166,384

Government and international organizations: 152,750

Professional, financial and corporate services: 150,431

Restaurants and accommodation services: 112,475

Social services: 55,599

Manufacturing: 20,799

The composition of Mexico’s workforce

Mexico’s economically active population (PEA) — the number of people in jobs and looking for work — numbers 61.96 million, according to INEGI’s third-quarter data.

The percentage of economically active people who currently hold a paid job (i.e., not seeking employment) is 97% (35.3 million men and 24.9 million women).

Of the 60.16 million people in jobs, 64.3% (38.71 million) work in the tertiary sector, 24.7% (14.85 million) work in the secondary sector and 10.3% (6.19 million) work in the primary sector.

The informal sector workforce is made up of 33.11 million people, or 55% of all workers.

Around 68.4% (41.14 million) of all workers are employees, while 6.2% (3.67 million) are employers.

Around 22% (13.33 million) of employed people work for themselves and have no paid staff. The number of independent, self-employed workers increased by more than 386,000 in the 12 months to the end of September.

Just over 3.2% (1.94 million) of workers are unpaid, according to INEGI’s latest employment data.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: A ‘unique’ human skeleton found during AIFA airport construction may date back 13,000 years
World.content:
A male human skeleton unearthed in 2021 during construction of the Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA) outside Mexico City has now been confirmed by the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to date back at least 11,700 years, making it one of the 23 oldest human skeletons found in the Basin of Mexico.

Foreign laboratories determined the age of the find by focusing mainly on the third molar. Isotopic Aging Inc., in Belgium, examined collagen and determined an age of between 12,987 and 13, 087 years before the present. The University of Georgia, in the United States, studied bioapatite — a non-organic substance in human bones and teeth — to come up with an age of between 11,700 and 12,050 years.

“Yotzin is one of the oldest human remains known to us from the Basin of Mexico,” said Culture Minister Claudia Curiel de Icaza, using the skeleton’s nickname from a Náhuatl word for “unique.” “Its dating brings us closer to a period in our history for which very little evidence exists, and it opens up new possibilities for investigating how those populations lived and where they came from.”

Three other human skeletons were found during the AIFA’s construction work, but according to INAH anthropologist Arturo Talavera González, Yotzin’s features are unique, as his nickname implies. He measures 1.75 meters tall and features high bone mass and a “tremendously robust” skeleton, showing characteristics of a hunter used to long-distance walking and combat.

As Yotzin’s teeth were examined, tooth wear was confirmed but there were no cavities. That absence reflects the fact that pre-ceramic hunter-gatherers did not consume sugars or simple carbohydrates. As Talavera explains it, instead they chewed many roots and tough barks, and used their teeth as a “third hand” for cutting and crushing, which accounts for the wear on its teeth.

Yotzin was discovered by archaeologist Israel Peña in the northwestern sector of AIFA, in sediments associated with ancient marshy environments and the remains of Late Pleistocene fauna – primarily mammoths and camels. Initially, Peña assumed they belonged to a camel. But as the excavation expanded, he identified them as human.

INAH expects to have the results of a genomic study from the University of Burgos, Spain, available during the first quarter of 2027. It should clarify the individual’s ancestry and provide information about the ancient populations of the Basin of Mexico, a geological region comprising four valleys, including the Valley of Mexico.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico’s new Animal Welfare Law officially reclassifies Mexico City roof dogs as municipal early-warning infrastructure
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Congress has formally approved the General Law on Animal Welfare, Care and Protection, landmark legislation that legally recognizes domestic animals as sentient beings while carefully preserving the constitutional right of second-story concrete roofs in the capital to serve as unregulated canine surveillance towers.

The sweeping reform, which amends five separate federal statutes and awaits publication in the Official Gazette, mandates that pet owners provide constant access to drinking water, suitable nutrition and shelter from harsh weather. However, legislative aides confirmed that the statute includes a critical semantic carve-out classifying a three-by-four-meter slab of sun-baked mortar in Colonia Narvarte or Santa María la Ribera as “an elevated, open-air security perimeter with panoramic street visibility.”

Under the new framework, failing to meet basic standards of pet care can result in administrative detention of up to 36 hours and steep fines. Yet legal analysts noted that the law’s enforcement mechanisms in Mexico City rely heavily on whether a territorial chihuahua barking at a passing tamales oaxaqueños loudspeaker at 3:14 a.m. constitutes “emotional distress” or “performing essential municipal infrastructure duties.”

“We are thrilled to align Mexico with the highest international standards of animal sentience,” said Hilario Padilla, a policy adviser to the Senate’s Joint Committee on Urban Ecology and Elevated Guard Dogs. “At the same time, we had to respect capital realities. If you take Solovino off a third-floor roof in Iztapalapa, who is going to alert a four-block radius that a gas truck or camote vendor has entered the neighborhood?”

The bill also cracks down on unregulated pet sales on social media platforms and prohibits aesthetic mutilations, though it stops short of defining whether an overturned plastic laundry tub wedged next to a tinaco water tank qualifies as “adequate protection from the elements.” Across Mexico City boroughs from Coyoacán to Azcapotzalco, residents reported that their local roof dogs had already reviewed the legislation and found it entirely satisfactory, largely because nobody climbed the staircase to tell them about it.

Lawmakers indicated that a follow-up subcommittee will convene next spring to determine whether a piece of corrugated fiberglass weighted down by a cinder block meets the federal definition of a “clean and safe environment,” provided the dog is left with at least some shade between noon and 4 p.m.

She noted Mexico has sent “94 criminals” to the United States, while “a lot” of its extradition requests, including ones related to the Ayotzinapa case, haven’t been granted. 💼 Sheinbaum’s husband didn’t go to China due to work commitments: Asked why Jesús María Tarriba Unger didn’t accompany her to the APEC Leaders’ Meeting last week, the president said he has his own job at the Bank of Mexico. She noted he often joins her on weekend working trips within Mexico.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At the start of her press conference, President Sheinbaum noted that today is the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.

Minister for Women Laura Itzel Castillo announced that Mexico would once again take part in the United Nations’ 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence campaign, which starts today.

Among the other notable issues discussed at today’s mañanera were the dispute between coffee growers in Chiapas and the Swiss multinational Nestlé, and the release of Inés Gómez Mont, a former Mexican television host, from immigration detention in the United States.

Gómez, who was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Oct. 30 for overstaying her U.S. visa, is wanted in Mexico for alleged tax fraud and embezzlement. On Monday, she was released from ICE custody and removed from the United States, according to a Department of Homeland Security statement sent to the newspaper El Universal.

Sheinbaum sides with coffee growers in dispute with Nestlé

A reporter noted that coffee producers in Chiapas protested against the low prices they are paid by Nestlé to grow coffee beans for Nescafé. The producers say they receive 43 pesos (US $2.20) per kilogram and are pushing for 60 pesos. The reporter asked the president whether federal authorities would speak with the coffee producers and governor of Chiapas about the issue. She also asked whether the government could provide additional incentives to coffee growers through the Alimentación para el Bienestar (Food for Well-being) program.

“I agree with the campesinos, with the coffee growers,” Sheinbaum said.

“Nestlé has to pay what it has to pay for a kilo of coffee,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that coffee producers say that Nestlé sells coffee for 580 pesos per kilo, but only pays 43 pesos for a kilo of beans.

“I think what they’re asking is for them to buy [a kilo of coffee beans] for between 50 and 60 pesos. We completely agree with what they’re requesting,” she said.

Sheinbaum said she had instructed the minister of agriculture to “support” the coffee growers in Chiapas in their negotiations with Nestlé.

“It cannot be that the international market sets the price of coffee for coffee growers through intermediaries … and that the price of Nescafé doesn’t come down,” she said.

“The coffee growers are right and we’re going to support them,” Sheinbaum said.

“And Nestlé has to pay [a fair price] and has to buy directly from the producers,” she added.

Sheinbaum questions why the US didn’t extradite Inés Gómez Mont to Mexico

Sheinbaum said that the release of Gómez Mont from ICE custody and her removal from the United States — but not to Mexico — is a “very important issue” in Mexico’s relationship with the U.S.

She noted that Gómez Mont was the subject of an Interpol Red Notice because a warrant for her arrest was issued in Mexico.

But the Red Notice — a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action — was “withdrawn” around a month ago, Sheinbaum said.

“So we have a very relevant complaint with Interpol. Why was this Red Notice withdrawn?” she said.

Sheinbaum said that Gómez Mont entered the United States on her Spanish passport and was consequently deported to Spain.

She questioned why U.S. authorities didn’t send her to Mexico given that “they know” there is an outstanding warrant for her arrest here.

“What we ask for in the relationship, as we have always said, is reciprocity,” Sheinbaum said, noting that her government has sent “94 criminals” — including a number of high-profile cartel figures — to the United States.

She said that “a lot” of Mexico’s extradition requests to the United States haven’t been granted, including ones for suspects in the infamous Ayotzinapa case involving the abduction and presumed murder of 43 students in Guerrero in 2014.

After reiterating that Gómez Mont’s case is an “important” issue in the Mexico-U.S. relationship, Sheinbaum said her government would send a diplomatic note to its U.S. counterpart.

She added that her administration has submitted a request to the government of Spain for Gómez Mont’s extradition to Mexico.

“We already requested it. But we’re interested in knowing why the Red Notice was withdrawn … because there is ample proof that she dedicated herself to fake invoices,” Sheinbaum said.

“So why wasn’t she extradited to Mexico?”

Sheinbaum explains why her husband didn’t accompany her to China

Asked why her husband, Jesús María Tarriba Unger, didn’t accompany her to China last week for the APEC Leaders’ Meeting, Sheinbaum explained that he had work commitments.

“My husband works,” she said before breaking into a hearty laugh.

“As you know, he works at the Bank of Mexico,” Sheinbaum said, referring to Tarriba’s employment at the central bank as a financial risk specialist.

“He goes to work every day. … That’s why he didn’t go with me,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that Tarriba does often accompany her on her weekend working trips to different parts of Mexico.

“But on this occasion, well, he also has his job,” she said.

World.title: MND Local BCS: Enjoying film and food festivals in Los Cabos, plus a guide to whale watching season
World.content:
Celebrities were synonymous with Los Cabos long before that moniker — a reference to the shared word for “cape” in both Cabo San Lucas and San José del Cabo — was officially coined for the newly minted municipality in 1981. When tourism began in the area in the late 1950s, celebrities were among the first guests at local hotels, including movie stars like John Wayne and Bing Crosby.

It’s not surprising, really, when you consider that Los Angeles has always been Los Cabos’ primary market for international arrivals, or that before the first scheduled flight from Los Angeles to La Paz was inaugurated in 1962, one needed either a boat or a private plane to reach Los Cabos’ early hotels.

But even as Los Cabos became more accessible in subsequent decades, celebrities continued to be among the destination’s most loyal visitors, a trend that has continued into the present.

However, it is only since 2012 that Hollywood A-listers have come to Los Cabos not just for pleasure, but also for business.

The Los Cabos International Film Festival returns in December

Numerous stars have walked the red carpet for opening night at the Los Cabos International Film Festival, or appeared to receive awards or talk up their latest films, including actors Monica Bellucci, Robert De Niro, Matt Dillon, Adam Driver, Gael García Bernal, Daniel Giménez Cacho, Nicole Kidman, Jared Leto, Diego Luna, Virginia Madsen, Ewan McGregor, Liam Neeson and Reese Witherspoon, and directors such as Terry Gilliam, Spike Lee and Oliver Stone.

Despite the movie star glamor, the festival is perhaps best known internationally as an industry platform that brings together filmmakers from the U.S., Canada and Mexico for behind-the-scenes dealmaking, and as a support network for Mexican filmmakers through its Gabriel Figueroa Film Fund (named for the acclaimed Mexican cinematographer). Locally, however, it’s the screenings that are the festival’s most beloved feature, including, through the years, the Mexican premieres for films like “Jackie” and “The Killing of a Sacred Deer.”

Screenings

For those planning to be in Los Cabos from Dec. 9-13, the scheduled dates for the 14th edition of the Los Cabos International Film Festival, headline screenings include “Elsinore,” a film starring Andrew Scott, Olivia Colman and “Mobland” villain Johnny Flynn, which will open the festival with an outdoor showing at the Puerto Los Cabos Marina.

Visit the festival’s website for a complete listing of screenings and events, including a Dec. 10 tribute to Dolores Heredia presented by fellow Mexican actor José María Yazpik. Like the majority of screenings, this retrospective will take place at Cinépolis in San José del Cabo, with tickets available to the public. The closing night outdoor screening, meanwhile, will be free in Plaza Mijares in San José del Cabo, although the film has yet to be announced.

Dates: Dec. 9-13

Location: Cinépolis, Mauricio Castro 1738, Campo de Golf Fonatur, 23400 San José del Cabo, B.C.S.

Cost: Not yet announced

Whale watching season approaching in Los Cabos

You don’t need to take a cruise to see whales in Los Cabos, as transiting cetaceans can be seen from virtually every coastal vantage during winter months. However, boat tours, particularly aboard high-speed inflatable Zodiacs, do offer the most intimate encounters once the season officially starts on Dec. 15, although “intimate” is relative, since regulations prevent boats from getting closer to whales than 60 to 80 meters (depending on the size of the boat).

For the benefit of first-time visitors, whale watching season essentially heralds the arrival of 5,000 or so whales, which have migrated from summer feeding grounds in the Arctic to their winter breeding grounds around Baja California Sur. Numerous whales make this annual journey, including gray and humpback whales, as well as blue, bryde, fin, minke, orca and sei species.

Gray whales are the main attractions in Magdalena Bay and the San Ignacio and Ojo de Liebre lagoons within the El Vizcaíno Biosphere Reserve, while in Los Cabos, transiting humpbacks, known for their spectacular breaching behavior, are typically the stars of local tours.

The season runs through April 15.

Foodie fest Sabor a Cabo returns

Sabor a Cabo was firmly established as the premier food festival in Los Cabos, at least before the COVID-19 pandemic, when the annual eat, drink and be merry fête featuring gourmet fare from international chefs and more than 50 local restaurants drew thousands of attendees, as well as a wealth of world-class musical talent, from Lila Downs to Earth, Wind and Fire.

This decade, though, the event sponsored by CANIRAC Los Cabos, the local restaurant association, suffered a long absence from annual event calendars during a three-year hiatus from 2020 to 2022 — although Sabor a Cabo Rural, a smaller gastronomic get-together held each spring in organic farm-to-table farming community Miraflores, has been more consistently scheduled.

The 18th edition of the main event, themed “La Verbena Sibarita” (“The Sybarite’s Fair”), should help restore Sabor a Cabo to its former prestige, particularly if organizers reach their targeted attendance of 3,500 on Dec. 5 at EDEA Venue, just outside Cabo San Lucas.

What to expect for the 2026 edition

The food and wine attractions will be abundant, highlighted by fare from 45 restaurants and a wine garden focused on Mexican vintners, with over 40 represented (many from Baja California’s Valle de Guadalupe). A producer’s market will also be held this year, along with a mixology garden; a chef’s plaza showcasing classes and presentations; a sybarite’s market spotlighting artisanal cheeses, chocolates and other gourmet goods; and “streets” focused on everything from seafood and tacos to coffee and desserts. The musical headliner is La Única Internacional Sonora Santanera.

Date: Dec. 5, 5 p.m. to 9 p.m.

Location: EDEA Venue, behind Viveros de la Baja, Puente Salto Seco, El Arenal, 23460 Cabo San Lucas, B.C.S.

Cost: General admission tickets are 3,250 pesos; VIP tickets are 5,600 pesos

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Lawmaker Says Pemex Abandoned Veracruz Wells
World.content:
A lawmaker of Mexico’s governing Morena party says Pemex left wells in northern Veracruz with no one in charge. The report carries no reply from the company.

A Pemex industrial workshops site at Naranjos, Veracruz, file photo from December 2021 (Photo: Isaacvp, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Energy: Mexico

On Wednesday 25 November 2026, federal deputy Xóchitl Zagal Ramírez said that state oil company Petróleos Mexicanos (Pemex) has left exploration wells abandoned in northern Veracruz state. La Jornada, a Mexican national daily, published her statements, which NVI Noticias, a Veracruz news outlet, carried on 25 November, and they are accusations, not established facts.

Zagal says the wells, in the Poza Rica and Papantla region, cause serious environmental damage and that Pemex has not done adequate remediation or compensation. The report does not include a response from Pemex.

Key Facts Who. Deputy Xóchitl Zagal of Mexico’s governing Morena party accuses state oil firm Pemex.

What. She says Pemex left exploration wells abandoned near Poza Rica and Papantla, Veracruz.

Open. The report has no Pemex reply; well numbers and sites are unknown.

A lawmaker of Mexico’s governing Morena party says Pemex left wells in northern Veracruz with no one in charge. The report carries no reply from the company.

Zagal says she toured the area “a few months ago” and documented a “lack of follow-up or responsibility” by Pemex. She calls the wells “huerfanitos”, or little orphans, meaning sites with no one in charge.

Some wells are conventional ones that sought crude oil, she says, while others sought gas by fracking. Fracking, or hydraulic fracturing, injects water, sand and chemicals into rock to free gas, and was planned under the 2013-14 energy reform of former president Enrique Peña Nieto.

She says the fracking wells date from the governments of Peña Nieto and Felipe Calderón, also a former president, and that companies left after community resistance. The report does not say how many wells are involved or who operated each.

File photo, 2008. A Pemex pipeline on a steel bridge over the Atoyac River in Puebla, Mexico. (Photo: Isaacvp, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Zagal says Pemex has “quite questionable and opaque mechanisms” to repair damage and compensate residents. After pipeline accidents or lack of maintenance, she said, tar “starts gushing out where there are cornfields or bodies of water, rivers or small ponds that supply the crops”.

“We eat that and it causes many health problems,” she said. The report quotes no one else.

She says she has two reform initiatives to ban fracking, one constitutional and one to secondary laws. They revive a similar initiative from former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador whose legal term lapsed, and “we reactivated and strengthened it”, she said.

Zagal says the two dictámenes, or committee reports, are under discussion, and she wants forums and social-environmental experts added to the group reviewing fracking’s viability. Nothing we found shows how far the bills have advanced.

A government document records similar grievances. SECIHTI, Mexico’s federal science and technology ministry, said in an August 2026 analysis that rural Papantla communities show “strong rejection of hydraulic fracturing” and grievance over Pemex impacts “that have never been repaired”.

The analysis says energy ministry assignments to Pemex in the Tampico-Misantla basin, an oil region spanning Veracruz and neighbouring states, cover 46 municipalities with 1,926,000 people. It adds that communities in the Huasteca and El Tajín regions have opposed fracking for more than 10 years.

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s scientific committee of 54 specialists presented its first report on Thursday 6 August 2026 with 10 recommendations, including public consultations where fracking is proposed. According to Crónica, a Mexican daily, and other Mexican outlets, it also recommended banning unconventional-gas extraction in the Tampico-Misantla basin, which includes the Papantla region.

The open points are how many wells exist, where, who operated them and whether Pemex or the energy ministry will answer Zagal. Until they do, her account stays an accusation by one lawmaker, carried by one outlet.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Zagal accusing Pemex of?

She says Pemex left exploration wells in the Poza Rica and Papantla region with no one in charge, and has not repaired the damage or compensated residents properly. The report carries no reply from the company.

Is a fracking ban on the way?

Zagal says two initiatives to ban fracking are under discussion, but her words are the only account of their progress that we found. The science ministry’s own analysis records local opposition in the Papantla region, and the government’s committee recommended banning unconventional-gas extraction in that basin.

World.title: Pemex Owes Banks US$14.6 Billion by 2030
World.content:
Almost three-quarters of Pemex’s bank debt falls due in four months of 2030, and three US banks are owed most of it. The company’s overall debt is falling, but the repayment dates are bunched.

Photo: ProtoplasmaKid / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

Business: Mexico

Pemex, Mexico’s state oil company, has 287.89 billion pesos (about US$14.6 billion) of bank debt due between June and September 2030. Zócalo, a Mexican daily, reported the figure on Thursday 26 November 2026 from Pemex’s latest quarterly report.

That is 74.23% of Pemex’s bank debt falling due in a window of four months, Zócalo calculated. Pesos are converted here at 19.66 per US dollar, the rate on 26 November 2026.

Key Facts Who. Pemex, Mexico’s state oil company, and its bank creditors in the United States and Mexico.

What. About US$14.6 billion of Pemex bank debt falls due between June and September 2030.

Share. That is 74.23% of Pemex’s bank debt, due within four months.

Power Index. Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 70.8 points (November 2026 edition).

As of. 26 November 2026, 13:45 GMT.

Almost three-quarters of Pemex’s bank debt falls due in four months of 2030, and three US banks are owed most of it. The company’s overall debt is falling, but the repayment dates are bunched.

Pemex’s bank debt stood at about 388 billion pesos (about US$19.7 billion) at the close of the third quarter of 2026. The rest is spread over 2028, 2029, 2031 and 2036, Zócalo wrote.

In August 2030, about 201 billion pesos (about US$10.2 billion) fall due to three big US banks: JPMorgan Chase Bank, Bank of America and Citigroup Global Markets. Mexican creditors for 2030 include the state banks Banobras, Bancomext and Nacional Financiera, plus the private lenders Banorte and Banco Azteca.

Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

File photo, 2009. Pemex Akal-C platforms in the Cantarell field in the Gulf of Mexico. (Photo: BoH, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Óscar Ocampo, economic development director of IMCO (Instituto Mexicano para la Competitividad, a Mexico City think tank), told Zócalo that Pemex cannot cover those maturities today. “However much the debt has fallen, Pemex today does not have the money to cover those maturities; I don’t know whether it will have it in 2030,” he said.

Ocampo said Pemex could issue long-term bonds as the dates approach, swapping current obligations for later ones. That would spread the pressure over a longer period, he said.

Pemex’s own numbers show a company whose total borrowing is shrinking. Its third-quarter results, reported at the end of October 2026, put financial debt at US$77.606 billion on 30 September 2026, the lowest in 12 years.

That is 9% (about US$8 billion) below the end of 2025 and more than US$28 billion below 2018, against a peak of US$113.227 billion in 2020. Elizabeth González, Pemex’s finance director, said the strategy is to keep additional net borrowing near zero, helped by capital contributions and federal government support.

Pemex still raised money during the year: Crónica, a Mexican daily, reports financing activities of 490.3 billion pesos (about US$24.9 billion) to 30 September 2026, including short-term bank credit. Repayments in the same period came to 34.5 billion pesos (about US$1.8 billion).

IMCO’s report Pemex en la Mira (Pemex in the Spotlight) counts all financial debt at 30 September 2026, bonds and bank loans together. It finds 8.1% due in late 2026 (about US$5.7 billion) and a further 39.0% from January 2027 to June 2030 (about US$27.4 billion).

The remaining 52.9% (about US$37.2 billion) falls due from July 2030 on. Because IMCO counts bonds and Zócalo counts only bank loans, the two sets of shares measure different things and cannot be added or compared.

US investors who hold Pemex bonds sit in IMCO’s all-debt measure, not in Zócalo’s bank-only figure. The US banks named for August 2030 are a separate, direct exposure.

In 2025 President Claudia Sheinbaum’s government, with the Finance Ministry and Banobras, built a financial vehicle of 250 billion pesos (about US$12.7 billion), Zócalo wrote. It was meant to pay Pemex’s project, supplier and contractor debts and to protect Mexico’s investment-grade rating, a credit grade that signals low risk of default.

Our report of 17 November 2026 covered Pemex’s bank loans and the US lenders’ share, and our report of 4 September 2026 covered a warning on Mexico’s rating tied to Pemex debt. Our explainer on Pemex sets out how the company and its debt work, and more coverage is in Mexico news.

Ocampo’s own view is conditional: he does not know whether Pemex will have the money in 2030. The 2025 vehicle shows that the government has stepped in before.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Pemex’s 2030 debt wall?

Zócalo and Expansión found that most of Pemex’s bank debt falls due within four months of 2030. Pemex’s total debt is falling, but the timing leaves little room for error.

Who is owed the money?

Three large US banks and Mexican lenders, including the state banks Banobras and Bancomext, hold the 2030 loans. Bondholders are counted separately.

Can Pemex pay it?

IMCO’s Óscar Ocampo doubts Pemex can cover the maturities today and says Pemex could issue long-term bonds. Pemex says it aims to keep new net borrowing near zero with government support.

World.title: Alpek Shares Jump 6% After Debt Buyback
World.content:
A discounted bond buyback has cut Alpek’s debt and pushed its maturities further out.

Monterrey, Nuevo León, the metropolitan area where Alpek is based. Photo: Daniel Escobedo (CC BY-SA 4.0). File photo.

Markets: Mexico

Alpek, a Mexican maker of polyester and plastics raw materials, saw its shares jump 5.99% to 14.69 pesos (about US$0.75) on Wednesday 25 November 2026. That was the day Alpek said it had extended its debt maturities after buying back US$500 million of its dollar bonds below face value.

Mexico’s main stock index, the S&P/BMV IPC, rose 2.99% to 71,372.25 points the same day. Alpek had closed at 12.33 pesos on Friday 20 November, so it is up about 19% in three sessions, including 7.2% on settlement day.

What. Alpek says it repurchased US$500 million of its 2029 and 2031 dollar bonds below face value.

On Monday 16 November 2026 Alpek told the Mexican Stock Exchange it would buy back up to US$500 million of two series of its senior notes (bonds). The offer covered its 4.25% notes due 2029, capped at US$300 million, and its 3.25% notes due 2031.

It priced the 2029 notes at US$957.50 per US$1,000 of face value and the 2031 notes at US$887.50, both below face value. Holders had until 5:00 p.m. New York time on 20 November to offer their notes, with payment expected on Tuesday 24 November.

The two series stood at US$495 million and US$553.3 million, so the maximum offer covered about 48% of the US$1.05 billion outstanding. The notes were sold under Regulation S and Rule 144A, the US rules for placing bonds with investors outside and inside the United States.

Alpek describes itself in its filings as one of the world’s main producers of purified terephthalic acid (PTA) and PET plastic resin, two raw materials for polyester and bottles. It says it runs 30 plants in nine countries, including the United States, and employs more than 5,000 people.

On Monday 23 November Alpek said holders had offered US$318.7 million of the 2029 notes and US$275.7 million of the 2031 notes. It accepted US$300 million of the 2029s and US$200 million of the 2031s, scaling offers back because they exceeded the caps.

On Wednesday 25 November Alpek said the repurchase came at a US$35 million discount to face value, before fees, and was paired with new bank financing at competitive rates. It said the average maturity of its debt had lengthened from 3.5 to 5.1 years.

That leaves about US$195 million of the 2029 notes and US$353 million of the 2031 notes outstanding, by subtraction from the two notices. Trading volume rose with the price, as 7.69 million Alpek shares changed hands on 25 November, against 4.29 million on 20 November.

Grupo México, a mining, railway and infrastructure group, rose 7.13% to 200.95 pesos on the same day, according to the market-data provider RT. Alpek’s gain therefore came inside a broad rally rather than on its own.

“We are taking concrete steps to strengthen our balance sheet and regain our investment-grade credit ratings,” Chief Financial Officer Rodrigo Prieto said in that release (translated from Spanish). He added that Alpek remains committed to cutting its total debt before cash in the short to medium term.

The filing prices tie out with the discount. US$300 million of 2029 notes at US$42.50 below face value per US$1,000, plus US$200 million of 2031 notes at US$112.50 below, comes to about US$35 million.

Alpek said the new maturity profile fits its expected operating cash flow and leaves more room to put future cash into paying down debt. Investment-grade ratings, the top tier of credit scores, lower a company’s borrowing costs, which is why Prieto named them as a goal.

Retiring bonds at 93 cents on the dollar saves about 7% of the principal. The release also notes that the credit rating agency S&P Global Ratings recently raised its outlook on Alpek to “stable”, while giving no rates for the new bank loans.

Why did Alpek shares rise on 25 November?

Alpek announced that day that it had bought back US$500 million of its bonds and lengthened its debt maturities. The main Mexican stock index also rose almost 3%.

What does the bond buyback mean for Alpek’s debt?

It retires part of its dollar bonds below face value and, according to Alpek, pushes the average maturity of its debt further out. The company has also said it plans to cut gross debt over the short to medium term.

World.title: Argentine Exchange Rule May Hit Small Firms
World.content:
A rule about collateral sounds technical, but it decides how easily companies can borrow for short periods. The wider stage, due in February, is the bigger test.

Business: Argentina

Argentina’s main stock exchange operator has changed which mutual funds can back short-term market loans, and one trader warns that small companies could be squeezed. The first stage took effect on Monday 2 November 2026, and a wider second stage follows on Tuesday 2 February 2027.

The operator is Bolsas y Mercados Argentinos (BYMA), and the change comes from its clearing house, BYMA Clearing, which settles trades and holds collateral. It covers “cauciones”, short-term loans in the stock market that are backed by collateral.

Key Facts What. BYMA Clearing, the exchange operator’s clearing house, is changing which mutual funds count as loan collateral.

When. Stage one began 2 November 2026; stage two reaches every approved fund on 2 February 2027.

A rule about collateral sounds technical, but it decides how easily companies can borrow for short periods. The wider stage, due in February, is the bigger test.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Argentina stock market Email address Follow

In October, BYMA Clearing told market participants it would update its admission criteria and its haircut method for the mutual funds used as collateral. A haircut, called “aforo” in Spanish, is the discount applied to an asset’s value when it backs a loan.

BYMA says the new scheme brings “objective and transparent criteria” and makes the haircut reflect each fund’s makeup “more precisely” (our translation). It adds that the three months between the two stages let market agents adjust gradually.

Stage one began on Monday 2 November 2026. Funds that failed the existing conditions were removed that day with no grace period, and new applications now face the new criteria.

Stage two arrives on 2 February 2027, when the new conditions apply to every approved fund. BYMA says the new haircut “may be higher or lower” than today’s, depending on what each fund holds (our translation).

The change has drawn criticism. One market operator, who was not named, warned that corporate bonds, financial trusts and promissory notes (short-term company IOUs) held by these funds would stop counting as collateral.

File photo: The Obelisco and the 9 de Julio avenue at dusk, central Buenos Aires.

That, the operator said, would sharply lower the value credited to collateral and force borrowers to post large amounts of replacement collateral. It could break the promissory-note financing that some small and mid-sized companies rely on, the operator added.

The same operator said the measure has unsettled business owners and provincial governors because of its possible effect on the real economy. These are the operator’s views, and BYMA’s statement, as quoted, does not address them.

Fernando Camusso, a market expert, said the change can create a liquidity problem even for sound companies. A project may be viable but not yet have the cash to repay a loan that must now shrink, Camusso said, which is a timing mismatch rather than insolvency.

Camusso also called it reasonable to require that short-term debt be backed by liquid assets. In his view the conflict lies in the transition, not in the principle.

BYMA’s statement rules out any grace period for the funds removed in stage one, and it leaves open how large the stage-two haircuts will be. Neither BYMA’s statement, as quoted, nor the operator gives a figure for how much collateral is affected.

For readers following Argentine companies, the date to watch is 2 February 2027, when BYMA applies the new conditions to all approved funds. Until then, market agents have the three-month window that BYMA describes to adjust.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is BYMA Clearing?

It is the clearing house of Bolsas y Mercados Argentinos, the operator of Argentina’s main stock market. It sets the collateral conditions for stock-market loans.

Why could the rule matter to small companies?

One market operator says some firms borrow against funds that hold promissory notes and bonds. If those funds stop counting, those firms need other collateral.

World.title: Regulator Blames Pemex for Gulf Oil Spill
World.content:
The regulator has put the blame on Pemex, but how much oil escaped and what it will cost are still unanswered.

Pemex offshore platforms in the Cantarell complex, Gulf of Mexico. Photo: BoH (CC BY-SA 3.0). File photo.

Energy: Mexico

Mexico’s safety and environment regulator told lawmakers this week that state oil company Pemex caused the Gulf of Mexico oil spill. Andrea González Hernández, head of the regulator ASEA (the Agency for Safety, Energy and Environment), blamed a crack in one of Pemex’s pipelines.

ASEA says 42,000 tonnes of hydrocarbon waste have been recovered since oil fouled more than 40 communities in the states of Veracruz and Tabasco. The spill is in the Gulf that Mexico shares with Texas and Louisiana, and the bill for it is still unknown.

What. A pipeline crack caused the spill, and ASEA has filed a criminal complaint with federal prosecutors.

Where. Gulf of Mexico, with oil reaching communities in Veracruz and Tabasco.

Greenpeace Mexico and other environmental groups had warned from satellite images that oil was spreading before any official named a source. On Thursday 16 April 2026 a government panel said the oil came from a 36-inch Pemex pipeline in the Abkatún offshore area of the Cantarell oil complex.

Then Pemex chief Víctor Rodríguez Padilla told that panel his company’s operating area had hidden the leak from him and resisted his requests for information. Three officials were removed: the subdirector for safety and environmental protection, the marine control coordinator and the head of spills and waste.

Rodríguez Padilla filed complaints with the FGR, the federal attorney general’s office, and with the anti-corruption ministry over the three, adding to a criminal complaint ASEA had already filed. Science Secretary Rosaura Ruiz said scientists used more than 70 satellite images to show that the slick drifted with ocean currents onto coasts and beaches.

Ruiz said the volume released was still unknown in April, and that Pemex’s operating areas had logged the leak since early February. Rodríguez Padilla said an overflight spotted the oil on 6 February and containment booms went up at once, while divers found the damage on 8 February.

Opposition parties pressed González repeatedly at a joint hearing of the environment and energy committees of Mexico’s lower house, the Chamber of Deputies. “Basically, the loss of containment refers to a crack in the pipeline,” she said, adding that the pipe is 36 inches wide.

“Unfortunately ASEA did not have the correct or timely information on what was happening,” González told the deputies, saying that delayed its on-site protocols until oil reached the coast. That fits the April finding that Pemex staff held back information.

González said the clean-up and waste collection are finished and, “according to what has been reported to us”, no new oil has reached beaches. ASEA has also imposed measures on how the waste is handled.

González also told deputies that ASEA keeps “constant monitoring in the whole Gulf of Mexico and in the whole country”. She said the agency works on a risk-based approach meant to prevent accidents before they happen.

ASEA carried out its own inspection and issued a ruling, but González said it “is not final”, so she could say no more about it. That leaves any penalty against Pemex unknown for now.

Greenpeace Mexico said after the April admission that Pemex still had not said how much oil spilled, and that the amount Pemex must pay for repairs was open. The group argues that support announced for fishing cooperatives does not replace full repair of the damage.

Greenpeace Mexico also calls the spill “not an isolated event”, part of a run of fires, leaks and spills tied to Pemex operations. For Pemex the exposure is on the coast: more than 40 communities in two states were polluted, and fishing families depend on that sea.

The next steps are the final ASEA ruling and the FGR case, and either could put a price on the spill. Until then, the cost stays an open question for Pemex.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who does the regulator say caused the Gulf of Mexico oil spill?

ASEA says Pemex did, through a crack in one of its pipelines. The government panel that investigated the spill reached the same conclusion in April.

Is oil still reaching Mexican beaches?

ASEA says clean-up work is finished and no new oil has arrived, based on reports it has received. It says it keeps monitoring the Gulf.

Has Pemex been penalised?

A criminal complaint is with the FGR, and ASEA’s own ruling is not yet final. Until those steps conclude, no penalty can be described.

Washington — tariff escalation · funding cliff Ottawa — unruffled · self-reliant Trade — cautious hope · ticking clock Montréal — tax anger · tactless Parliament — haste · exhaustion

Thanksgiving finds both countries in a mood of pressure, with Washington escalating its trade quarrels and Ottawa answering as a partner that refuses to plead. Washington speaks in proposals and public rebukes, and its Democratic opponents answer in kind on social media. Ottawa speaks in the language of responsibility, steady in tone and careful never to sound supplicant.

The through-line is a contest of patience in which each government wants to look able to wait. The calendar disagrees, because deadlines in December and January keep pulling both capitals towards a bargain.

Key Facts —Tariffs. The United States and Canada remain in talks on tariffs for steel, aluminium and autos. —Steel and autos. US tariffs on Canadian autos are 25%; Trump has said autos and steel go to 50% on 1 January 2027. —Rates. The Bank of Canada’s policy rate is 2.5%, and its next decision falls on 9 December. —Parliament. The committee on Bill C-39 sat more than 100 hours over seven days, finishing on 23 November. —Montréal. The proposed 2027 budget raises the average residential property tax bill by 9.8%, about C$515.

Ottawa: Responsibility As A Posture

CP24, citing the Canadian Press, reported on 25 November that a Pentagon fact sheet issued on 23 November said Canada’s defence spending limits its ability to help protect North America. Carney replied, according to CTV and CBC the same day, that Trump has not raised these complaints with him and that Canada is making “historic investments” in its military.

Defence Minister David McGuinty said, according to CP24 on 25 November, that he has not seen an allegedly leaked classified memo that reportedly restricts some military co-operation with Canada. The tone is calm and the substance firm, so a US reader should see a government that wants to be judged as an ally by its actions rather than lectured through documents.

Trade: Hope Under The Clock

Global News reported on 25 November that US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington wants a deal that “accommodates” Canada on steel, aluminium and autos. Carney and Trump met in Shenzhen the previous week, and Carney’s office said they agreed to keep working towards a “mutually beneficial” deal.

Global News added that chief negotiator Janice Charette told a federal advisory committee, according to sources briefed by the government, that multiple trade issues remain unresolved, the biggest being the auto tariff. The mood is cautious hope, and since the same report tied the renewed effort to Republican losses in the midterms, domestic price anger rather than goodwill looks like the engine.

Montréal: A Tax Bill And A Tactless Meal

Global News reported on 25 November that Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada suggested in an interview with Quatre95 that people may eat a little more Kraft Dinner because they cannot afford filet mignon, and later called the analogy “pretty tactless” on social media. The remark stung because it turned a tax bill into a question of dignity, and Projet Montréal and food-security groups criticised it.

Global News said a protest called “Soraya Dinner” is planned for 1 p.m. today outside city hall. For a US reader it is a reminder that cost-of-living anger is not only an American story, and that it can topple the reputation of a local leader in a single sentence.

Parliament: Haste As A Governing Style

The Canadian Press reported on 25 November that Bloc MP Gabriel Ste-Marie called the schedule for Bill C-39 “inhumane”, Conservative MP Branden Leslie called it “pretty brutal”, and NDP MP Heather McPherson said she had never seen anything like it in more than seven years. Carney countered that hours of clause-by-clause review are a better measure than days and that this is his government’s most consequential economic bill.

The Canadian Press added that the Senate has started its review before third reading and that its witness list already exceeds the House committee’s. The row shows a government in a hurry to build, an opposition that reads haste as disrespect, and a country in which speed itself has become the argument.

What This Means From Latin America

Mexico is the clearest beneficiary of the Canadian-American quarrel, since DesRosiers data reported by the Canadian Press on 25 November show its share of Canada’s light vehicle imports rising to 20.5% from 16.7%. For Latin America, the lesson is that friction between Washington and Ottawa can redirect supply chains toward Mexico.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Pentagon’s complaint about Canada?

CP24, citing the Canadian Press, reported on 25 November that a Pentagon fact sheet said Canada’s defence spending limits its ability to help protect North America. Carney replied that Trump has not raised these complaints with him and that Canada is making “historic investments”.

Where do US-Canada tariff talks stand?

Global News reported on 25 November that Jamieson Greer said Washington wants a deal that “accommodates” Canada on steel, aluminium and autos. The 25% US tariff on Canadian autos could double to 50% from 1 January 2027 if no deal is reached.

Why is Montréal’s mayor under fire?

Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada suggested people may eat more Kraft Dinner because they cannot afford filet mignon, then called the remark “pretty tactless”, Global News reported on 25 November. The comment came as the city proposes raising the average residential property tax bill by 9.8% in 2027.

What is the Bank of Canada expected to do on 9 December?

Global News reported on 25 November that economists expect a rate hike after the Bank raised its rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on 28 October. BMO’s Sal Guatieri expects at least 25 basis points more, which would take the rate to 2.75%.

Europe wakes on Thursday in a brittle, quarrelsome temper, with ambition on security colliding with a refusal to pay for it, as Euronews coverage of 25 and 26 November shows. The mood is less panic than a tired argument about who carries the bill, inside the summit hall and inside the parliamentary centre.

Leaders speak in ultimatums and deadlines, and the same outlet reported on 26 November that Chancellor Friedrich Merz threatens to veto the whole budget unless all 27 states back Ukraine support. Institutions sound defensive, with the EPP’s Siegfried Mureșan telling a press conference on 25 November: “Prime ministers shall not dictate to the European Parliament what we should do.”

The through-line is that Europe says it will pay for its security while arguing over who pays, and every capital answers in its own register. Brussels bargains, Warsaw hardens, Madrid polarises and Budapest tries a thaw, all within the same 24 hours.

Key Facts —Brussels. Council President António Costa proposes a 2028 to 2034 EU budget of about EUR 1.76 trillion, or US$1.93 trillion at today’s euro rate. —Parliament. The S&D and Renew groups suspended coalition talks with the EPP on 25 November. —Poland. Warsaw wants a no-fly zone along its eastern border by late December or early January. —Hungary. Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Volodymyr Zelensky met in Transcarpathia on 24 November. —Spain. Voters choose a new government in a general election on Sunday 29 November.

Brussels: Ambition Against The Bill

Costa’s budget draft answers the “frugal” states, including Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden. The same cut takes EUR 39 billion (US$42.8 billion), or 30%, from defence and space funding, according to the the same newsletter of 26 November, which makes the slogan of security first look thin.

Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius warned, the newsletter said, that the cut would jeopardise pan-European programmes, while Parliament’s April position set EUR 1.93 trillion (US$2.12 trillion) as its demand and MEPs say they will reject any deal built on the cut. For a US reader the signal is that European rearmament pledges still run into budget arithmetic, and a deal needs unanimity in the Council and an absolute majority of MEPs.

Strasbourg And Paris: A Centre Under Siege

The trigger was the passage of “Omnibus VIII”, a revision of environmental assessment rules, on which the EPP again voted with groups to its right, the same outlet reported on 25 November. The row shows a centre that no longer trusts its largest member, with a cooperation deal for the second half of the term at stake.

The same outlet said on 25 November that S&D and Renew want a written EPP pledge to stop voting with the ECR, Patriots and ESN, and Renew treats that pledge as a prerequisite for backing Roberta Metsola’s re-election as Parliament president next January. Marine Le Pen, absent from the summit and the frontrunner for next spring’s presidential election, has threatened to cut France’s EU contribution, the the same newsletter said on 26 November, which tells a US reader that the centre is squeezed from outside the chamber too.

Berlin, Bratislava And Budapest: Leverage And A Thaw

The same outlet said on 26 November that the Commission proposes a EUR 45 billion (US$49.4 billion) joint-borrowing loan for Ukraine, EUR 20 billion (US$21.9 billion) civilian and EUR 25 billion (US$27.4 billion) military, against a projected 2027 shortfall of EUR 70 billion (US$76.8 billion). Robert Fico called the linkage “a textbook case of blackmail”, and the same report says Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic oppose joining the loan.

The same outlet reported on 25 November that Magyar and Zelensky both called their talks substantive, and its Europe Today programme said Magyar asked for a “fresh start” with talks on trade and transport links. That is warmth on commerce rather than money, so Kyiv will want it to become votes, and Washington should watch whether Budapest’s tone ever reaches the summit table.

Warsaw: Alarm Turns To Assertiveness

Deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk said on 25 November that the zone would run “a dozen or a few dozen kilometres” deep, Notes from Poland reported, after three Russian missiles struck south-eastern Poland on 20 November and a Russian drone briefly entered Polish airspace on 24 November without troops firing. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski again said that shooting down Russian missiles over Ukraine could be self-defence at Kyiv’s request but needs NATO agreement, while PiS caucus head Mariusz Błaszczak called the plan cosmetic.

The same outlet said on 25 November that Russia denies its missiles hit Poland and accuses Warsaw of “stoking anti-Russian sentiment”, and that Sikorski called expelling the Russian ambassador “one of the options”. For a US reader, NATO’s approval of an AWACS deployment on 24 November shows the alliance answering in measured steps, while Polish politics rewards whoever sounds toughest.

Madrid: A Nation Counting Boats And Polls

The same outlet said on 26 November that feminist groups marched across Spain against violence, a reminder that the campaign closes amid a social argument as well as a political one. Final polls up to the 23 November blackout put the PP ahead, with PP and Vox possibly above 190 of 350 seats against a majority of 176, according to ANSA and the Majorca Daily Bulletin on 16 November.

Interior Ministry data to 15 November, carried by Artículo14 and EFE, show 96 boats arriving in November against 66 in the previous ten months of 2026, and El Hierro declared an emergency in early November. Whoever forms the next government inherits that pressure, and a win for the right could reshape Madrid’s line on migration and on Europe.

What This Means From Latin America

Spain’s vote on 29 November shapes Madrid’s role as a bridge between Europe and Latin America, including the EU and Mercosur agenda and the migration route fed by Atlantic crossings. A tighter long-term budget, as Costa proposed on 25 November, could also shrink the money available for EU Global Gateway projects in the region. Latin American diplomats will read the budget fight as a sign that Brussels has limited bandwidth for new partnerships while Ukraine absorbs the financing.

What We Are Watching

Frequently Asked Questions

What are EU leaders deciding at the Brussels summit?

EU leaders met in Brussels on 26 November, and the meeting may run into 27 November, to discuss the 2028 to 2034 budget and Ukraine’s financing, the same outlet said on 26 November. Costa has proposed about EUR 1.76 trillion (US$1.93 trillion), and Macron insists talks cannot run beyond December.

Why did the centre suspend talks in the European Parliament?

S&D and Renew suspended coalition talks with the EPP on 25 November after it again voted with groups to its right on Omnibus VIII, local media reported. They want a written pledge, and Renew treats it as a prerequisite for backing Roberta Metsola’s re-election next January.

What is Poland planning after the missile strikes?

Deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk said on 25 November that the ministry will ask the government for a no-fly zone along the eastern border, hoping to have it in place by late December or early January, that report reported. Three Russian missiles struck south-eastern Poland on 20 November, and NATO approved an AWACS deployment on 24 November.

When does Spain vote and who leads the polls?

Spain holds a general election on Sunday 29 November, and final published polls up to the 23 November blackout show the PP ahead. PP and Vox together could pass 190 of 350 seats, with a majority at 176, according to polls reported on 16 November.

Taiwan — tariff relief · vote jitters China — guarded · defiant Japan — brittle · short of capital South Korea — anxious · reassuring Myanmar — defiance · isolation Indonesia — waiting · vacant seat

Asia is in a mood of defensive bargaining on Thursday, after the US Trade Representative proposed Section 301 tariffs on 12 Asian economies, according to the law-firm summary published by Global Trade & Sanctions Law on 25 November. Capitals are reaching for ceilings, denials and procedure, while their own domestic quarrels carry on beneath the tariff headlines.

Leaders speak in the language of caps and consultations, and the Korea Herald’s headline on 26 November says Seoul expects to retain a 15% cap. Beijing answers with warnings, since Dawn reported on 26 November that China criticised the proposal and said it could take measures to defend its interests.

The through-line is a region that negotiates abroad while it quarrels at home, and the second struggle is often the louder one. For US readers, the proposal tests how much patience allies and rivals will show before the comment period closes.

Key Facts —Comments. Public comments on the proposed US tariffs are due 5 January 2027; hearings start 25 January. —China. Proposal lifts China’s effective rate on most goods from 37.5% to 45% if the truce runs past 10 January. —Genocide ruling. The ICJ ruled on 19 November that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, by 9 votes to 6. —Sanctions. . —Indonesia. Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigned on 12 November.

Taipei: Cautious Relief, Nervous Vote

Taipei is allowing itself cautious relief, with Agriculture Minister Chen Chun-chi saying 322 farm products stay exempt, according to Focus Taiwan. The government wants to be seen holding a negotiated line, because a promise of stability is the one thing it can offer voters before the local elections on 28 November.

That promise is competing with a campaign that has lost its footing, since local media reported on 26 November that the leading Taipei mayoral candidates cancelled major rallies over a road-use dispute. The South China Morning Post reported on 26 November that the KMT faces an uphill battle, so a US reader should expect Saturday’s vote to measure fatigue as much as loyalty.

Beijing And Tokyo: Guarded Outside, Brittle Within

Beijing’s public register is defiance, yet the local media reported on 26 November that the PLA is overhauling joint training and that Xi Jinping warned against a blind rush into technology. The posture suggests a leadership that wants to look unmoved by Washington while it manages its own limits.

Tokyo is brittle in a different way, because the local media said on 26 November that opposition parties want to censure the education minister over fundraisers and rent claims, which puts Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s bills at risk. The that report also reported a resident revolt against data centres on 26 November, and with the proposed Japanese rate of 15% up from 12.5%, according to Global Trade & Sanctions Law on 25 November, Takaichi has little room to absorb a fresh shock.

Seoul: Reassurance Over Anxiety

Seoul is selling calm while it feels exposed, with foreign minister nominee Lim Woong-soon saying the US alliance is “not so fragile”, according to the the same outlet on 26 November. The same paper reported that Homeplus will temporarily close all outlets from Friday amid liquidation fears, and Asia News Network noted scrutiny of the intelligence-chief pick over China ties, so a US reader should read the alliance talk as reassurance aimed at home. Markets are the mood here, since local media said on 25 November that the Taiex fell more than 1,900 points after heavy Wall Street losses.

Naypyidaw: Defiance From A Cornered Junta

The junta answers isolation with defiance, as the Irrawaddy reported on 26 November that Min Aung Hlaing told his cabinet the regime will not carry out measures it deems unacceptable. The opposition is urging ASEAN to shun the junta leaders, which turns the ruling into a test of the bloc’s patience.

The human cost lands next door, with Asia News Network reporting on 26 November that Rohingya refugees in Malaysia are asking for more time after the ruling, and the Irrawaddy saying on 25 November that Malaysia will repatriate thousands more Myanmar migrants. For a US reader, the gap between a legal verdict and any enforcement is the story, because the people in limbo are the ones left to absorb it.

Jakarta: A Country Waiting

Indonesia is waiting for a second-in-command, since the resignation came amid impeachment calls over Gibran’s academic credentials, according to the Jakarta Post on 13 November. The People’s Consultative Assembly is due to elect a successor on 9 December, after the date was moved from 2 December, and the wait keeps attention on President Prabowo Subianto.

Asia News Network said on 26 November that Gerindra backs Sugiono, whereas the Indonesia Business Post earlier reported regional Gerindra leaders backing Sufmi Dasco Ahmad. The nominee is not confirmed, so Washington should read the choice as a signal of how tightly Prabowo wants to hold his party’s factions.

What This Means From Latin America

In our reading, the Section 301 action puts Mexico’s probe in the same family, since Global Trade & Sanctions Law said on 25 November that Mexico and Norway have no determination yet. Tougher US treatment of Asian manufacturers may redirect goods and buyers toward other markets, which could bring both competition and opportunity for Latin American exporters.

Commodities offer a second link, since the the same outlet said on 26 November that Russia’s farm exports to China are at record levels but cannot fully replace US supply, which matters for Brazil and Argentina. Volatility in Asian chip-linked markets may also bear on copper and lithium demand, in our assessment.

What We Are Watching

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the US propose on 25 November?

The US Trade Representative published proposed Section 301 structural excess capacity tariffs on 14 economies, 12 of them Asian, according to Global Trade & Sanctions Law on 25 November. Proposed rates rise to a fallback of up to 40% for China.

What has Taiwan said about its rate?

Taiwan’s negotiated ceiling on US tariffs is 15%, with a fallback of up to 25% if talks fail. Which farm products stay exempt has not been confirmed.

How has Myanmar’s junta responded to the genocide ruling?

The Irrawaddy reported on 26 November that Min Aung Hlaing told his cabinet the regime will not carry out measures it deems unacceptable. The opposition is urging ASEAN to shun the junta leaders.

When does Indonesia choose a new vice president?

The People’s Consultative Assembly is due to elect a successor on 9 December, after the date was moved from 2 December. Asia News Network said on 26 November that Gerindra backs Sugiono, but the nominee is not confirmed.

World.title: Costa Rica Doctors Call a February Strike as Surgery Waits Average 449 Days
World.content:
Costa Rica’s largest doctors’ union is calling on general practitioners, specialists and medical residents across the public health system to prepare for a general strike starting in February 2027, a move that could hit hospitals, clinics and the waiting lists millions of patients already depend on.

The National Medical Union (UMN) announced the call on Wednesday at a press conference alongside the nurses’ union ANPE and Siprocimeca, which represents medical professionals at the Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS). The unions said the strike would cover both regular and overtime shifts. No specific start date has been set.

UMN president Randall Cabrera Garita said the union’s central demand is that the CCSS cancel a new set of rules on overtime pay. According to the union, the changes cut pay for work outside regular hours, including the extra shifts and on-call duty that keep many hospital services running, and could push more doctors out of the public system.

Cabrera also warned of what the union described as a creeping privatization of public health care. The unions argue that money meant for hospitals, clinics, local EBAIS health posts and new staff positions could instead flow to private providers, and they object to cuts in payments tied to programs meant to shorten surgery waiting lists.

A report published hours after the announcement brought that concern into focus. Massimo Manzi, executive director of the Costa Rican Health Chamber, which groups private providers, said the CCSS completed a market study last week on contracting private services for outpatient consultations, diagnostic tests and surgeries. Manzi said 24 providers took part. The CCSS had not responded to press questions about the study by this morning.

Manzi said the chamber wants providers outside the Greater Metropolitan Area included, and proposes contracts that would activate only when patients wait longer than the limits set by a Health Ministry decree. Any deal would have to follow Costa Rica’s public procurement law. The idea of paying private doctors to ease the backlog has been under discussion since earlier this year.

The scale of the backlog explains why both sides are pushing. The CCSS reported in late October that the average wait for surgery stood at 449 days, down from 535 days in April 2023. It also reported 816 people who had been waiting since 2021 or earlier, and an average wait of 769 days for a first orthopedic consultation.

The unions listed other grievances, including staff shortages, the departure of specialists, saturated emergency services and lagging infrastructure. They also cited the effects of the Public Finance Strengthening Law and the Public Employment Framework Law on pay. The UMN said the state owes the CCSS more than 4 trillion colones (about $9 billion), and complained that the government has blocked the appointment of a union representative to the CCSS board of directors.

Cabrera said the union has asked for a meeting with CCSS Executive President Mónica Taylor to discuss the demands before any walkout. The union said escalation can still be avoided if authorities open a dialogue, but that the strike call stands until the contested decisions are reviewed. Taylor had previously said the CCSS is reviewing its overtime payment tables. The institution had not issued a public response to the strike call by this morning.

The threat comes after a difficult year of labor conflict in the public health system, from a nurses’ strike at Hospital México in August to a nationwide health workers’ strike threat in September over unpaid salaries. Hospitals have also struggled with capacity, with some patients in Liberia waiting days in a chair for a bed.

The CCSS is the backbone of health care in Costa Rica. Workers, employers and legal residents, including foreign retirees and others with residency, are required to pay into the system, and most of Costa Rica relies on its hospitals and clinics. How the institution answers the unions over the coming weeks will help decide whether patients face a disruption in February, and whether more of their care ends up being delivered by private providers paid with public money.

World.title: Costa Rica Sloth Rope Bridges Reach 410 With 22,000 Crossings
World.content:
Costa Rica’s sloth rope bridges are drawing international attention, with The Associated Press publishing a feature yesterday on the conservationists and caretakers working to keep the sloths in the trees. The story begins behind a beachfront hotel in Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, where a small crew strings rope from one trunk to the next. To a passing tourist it looks like little more than a clothesline. To a sloth it can be the difference between staying safely in the canopy and coming down to the ground, where dogs, cars and power lines are waiting.

The work is led by The Sloth Conservation Foundation, founded by British zoologist Rebecca Cliffe, who has spent close to 20 years studying the animals on Costa Rica’s southern Caribbean coast. Her team has now installed roughly 410 rope bridges, most of them in places where roads, houses and hotels have opened gaps in the forest.

The design is deliberately simple, usually a single line. Cliffe says that for animals built to live in the trees that is enough, giving them a way over a gap they could not otherwise cross. Unlike monkeys, sloths cannot jump. Cliffe has a name for the problem, microfragmentation. A break of just 2 or 3 meters (about 7 to 10 feet) between neighboring treetops can force a sloth to look for another route, and the other route is often the ground or an electrical cable.

Making matters harder, sloths tend to stick to the paths they learned when young, even after the landscape around them has changed. Cliffe began experimenting with bridges nearly two decades ago after working at the Sloth Sanctuary of Costa Rica in Penshurst, where she kept seeing animals brought in after dog attacks, collisions with vehicles and electrocutions. With almost no funding, she started hanging single ropes.

Cameras mounted on some of the bridges have since recorded more than 22,000 wildlife crossings, and sloths are not the only users. Today the team responds to sightings at hotels and private properties, plants trees and works with neighbors to reconnect their lots. The ropes are not permanent. Tropical sun and rain wear them out in four or five years, and they have to be replaced.

The paradox is that Costa Rica is a celebrated reforestation success. A 2023 OECD report put forest cover at 59 percent of the national territory, up from about 21 percent in 1987. But geographer Carlos Morera Beita of the National University points out that much of that regrowth took place on old pastureland, in a countryside still divided up by farming. Sloths have proven more adaptable than scientists once believed, getting around through pastures with scattered trees, living fences and vegetation along rivers.

Those links matter, he says, because an isolated sloth has a hard time finding food, shelter and a mate. In his view bridges fix specific choke points, but lasting protection depends on keeping existing forest standing, restoring biological corridors and stopping further fragmentation. Back at the Sloth Sanctuary, founder Judy Avey-Arroyo cares for the animals that cannot go home.

Her work began when she and her husband took in an orphan named Buttercup, and today the sanctuary houses sloths with severe injuries or disabilities along with babies whose mothers were killed by cars, dogs or power lines. The smallest are raised in incubators and fed milk, while older juveniles move on to leaves, time outdoors and climbing practice. Avey-Arroyo says a mother cannot really be replaced.

A young sloth spends about a year learning which leaves are safe, which plants to avoid, how to move through the forest and even how to deal with parasites, and orphans that miss those lessons can struggle in the wild even when they look healthy. Accepting that some of her animals will never return to the forest, she says, is the hardest part of the job.

Climate change adds another layer. Small patches of forest heat up and dry out faster than continuous forest, and sloths control their body temperature by moving between sun and shade. Cliffe says extreme heat can drain their limited energy reserves while cold can interfere with digestion, so her group is planting shade trees alongside the bridges.

Scientists still lack reliable estimates of how many sloths Costa Rica has or whether their numbers are rising or falling. Cliffe’s team is testing thermal imaging drones, trained detection dogs and field surveys to find out. Two rescue centers in the region take in around three sloths a day, but without historical data no one can say whether that figure is climbing. Costa Rican conservation groups have separately backed a U.S. bill to ban sloth imports.

The idea is spreading beyond the Caribbean. On the southern Pacific coast, Alturas Wildlife Rescue Center and the state utility ICE are installing eight rope crossings along the coastal highway between Dominical and Uvita to cut down on wildlife being hit by traffic or electrocuted. Four were in place by late September.

The best outcome, Cliffe told the AP, would be for the bridges to become unnecessary once the trees grow close enough for sloths to move freely on their own. Until then she believes their future rests on many small acts, a tree planted here and a rope hung there. She calls it “the cumulative power of many individual actions” and says that is what keeps her hopeful.

World.title: Expect Two Weeks of Night Lane Closures on Costa Rica’s Route 1 Near Naranjo
World.content:
If you drive Costa Rica’s Route 1 at night, expect lane closures and a short detour near Naranjo for the next two weeks. Crews are demolishing the former Naranjo toll station on the Bernardo Soto Highway. Work runs from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. and started today. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) and the National Road Council (CONAVI) expect it to take about two weeks, with partial lane closures while crews are on site.

If you are heading from San Ramón toward Alajuela, you will be moved onto a temporary lane that runs alongside the old toll station. That is the direction drivers take toward San José and Juan Santamaría International Airport, so it affects night trips in from Guanacaste, San Carlos and the western Central Valley.

The overnight schedule keeps the work out of rush hour, but you should still leave extra time, especially if you have a late-evening or early-morning flight. Slow down as you approach the work zone, follow the temporary signs and do what the crews on site tell you. They will be working next to moving traffic in the dark.

The Naranjo station has not charged a toll since September 1, 2025. Authorities suspended collection that day at Naranjo and at Río Segundo de Alajuela, citing constant backups at Río Segundo and changes tied to the highway project at Naranjo. The booths stayed in place after the toll ended.
