The fresh allegations could again test the relationship between Bardella and Le Pen, who has said that the 31-year-old would become her prime minister if she came to power. Le Pen has worked to try to rid the party of the racist and antisemitic reputation it developed under her father, Jean-Marie, who was convicted multiple times for racist comments and downplaying the Holocaust.

This week, National Rally lawmaker Laure Lavalette also faced allegations she contributed to a student newspaper in the 1990s which contained antisemitic caricatures. Lavalette dismissed the accusations in a TV interview, saying she would not try to justify something that happened “30 years ago” in “a climate that was very different.”

World.title: EU leaders brace for a summit ‘bloodbath’
World.content:
EU leaders are gathering for two days of budget talks — but with little appetite for compromise, European Council President António Costa has his work cut out for him.

On today’s show, Ian Wishart and Kathryn Carlson unpack the sticking points in the EU’s proposed 7-year budget as leaders prepare to battle it out around the Council table. The clock is ticking: Costa wants countries to strike a final deal in less than a month’s time, despite the deep divisions over the proposal.

Next, Spain heads to the polls on Sunday as the ghosts of its brutal Civil War haunt the vote.

Finally, China has unveiled a new electric aircraft … and its latest tech breakthrough is making European plane manufacturers nervous.

World.title: Study shows stark differences in how much EU countries depend on US Big Tech
World.content:
“The explanation is an economic one: In a larger country, the domestic market is better able to support domestic alternatives or technologies that involve high capital investment and the high scale economies,” Lehdonvirta said.

Why size matters

In Europe, the picture of U.S. tech reliance follows similar patterns, reflecting market size and income, but is also more mixed thanks to a patchwork of national choices that complicates EU efforts to reduce strategic dependencies.

“By and large, you have this pattern where the small member states are using U.S. cloud and large member states aren't,” Lehdonvirta said. “Cloud is an example of a technology where there's a lot of upfront investment, and then the larger your scale of operation, the more efficient it is.”

The study’s methodology results in some limits in gauging overall reliance, as it only looks at where national-level public-facing services are hosted, not the local systems or the wider use of technology inside government. For example, Lehdonvirta said municipal bodies — school boards or swimming-pool ticketing systems — are more likely to rely on U.S. tech because digital sovereignty is not part of their mandate.

Size and income aren't the whole story either, with political choices shaping whether countries build up domestic providers.

In the U.K. — the fifth largest economy in the world — an estimated 50.9% of the country’s public websites are reliant on U.S. tech. Lehdonvirta said the British government “decided about 15 years ago to go all-in on cloud as a central government mandate for all government departments and agencies.” In the absence of domestic alternatives, “very quickly everything moved to U.S. cloud. Now it's hard to claw it back from there, even if they wanted to,” he added.

World.title: ‘Is James Bond conservative?': Trump gives verdict on Robert Pattinson – but asked about 007's politics first
World.content:
Everyone's got an opinion on the new Bond...

 

From Hollywood A-listers and Amazon bosses, ex-Bonds and former heads of MI6, we've heard from a lot of people about the casting of Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond... But one person had yet to give his two cents – despite having a track record for co-opting pop culture references and having previously weighed in on who should be the next Bond.

Now, Donald Trump has given Robert Pattinson his seal of approval as 007 and wished him "luck" as the seventh actor to play Bond. First, however, he had to check his political affiliation...

The New York Post asked Trump about Pattinson at an Oval Office interview this week.

Trump apparently needed to know where Pattinson stood politically before answering the outlet’s question about the British actor playing Bond. He reportedly called through the open door of the office to his aide Natalie Harper - who has been nicknamed the "human printer" for printing documents for him to review.

“Is James Bond conservative?” Trump asked.

“He’s been good,” she told the Trump, handing him papers detailing information about Pattinson.

One showed a 2012 tweet in which Trump urged Pattinson to dump his former girlfriend and Twilight franchise co-star, Kristen Stewart.

Indeed, Trump posted repeatedly on Twitter about the couple's break-up after Stewart admitted cheating on Pattinson in 2012. Pattinson has previously called Trump's interest in his former relationship "such a bizarre curiosity", and joked that he felt left out when the posts stopped.

One of Trump's many posts about Pattinson and Stewart Twitter / X screenshot

“Robert Pattinson should not take back Kristen Stewart. She cheated on him like a dog and will do it again — just watch,” Trump's tweet read.

Trump read the post aloud, telling the people in the room it was "a long time ago".

Trump was seemingly pleased as he continued looking through clips of himself and the actor.

“That’s cute,” he said, adding: “He says nice things” - without elaborating what those "nice things" were.

Trump added he “always” liked people who liked him and said Pattinson “looks nice”. He concluded by wishing him “luck” in his new role as Bond.

It is understood Pattinson has never publicly shared his political views. Then again, Trump could have been referring to 007 with his "Is James Bond conservative?" question – considering he has referred to Hannibal Lecter as a real-life person before.

To clarify, they're both fictional.

Pattinson, 40, will become the seventh actor to play 007, replacing Daniel Craig, who left the franchise in 2021 after No Time To Die.

In response to his casting, the actor, who has become one of the world’s most famous stars since his breakout roles in the Harry Potter and Twilight franchises, followed by Tenet, The Odyssey and Primetime, called the role the “honour of a lifetime” and “a dream come true”.

Production on the as-yet-untitled Bond 26 is due to start next year, with Denis Villeneuve directing and Steven Knight on script duties.

Before filming can start, Pattinson will have to complete filming The Batman Part II – production on which was temporarily paused after director Matt Reeves was faced with a personal issue. Steven Soderbergh has stepped in to help shoot the final few weeks.

This means that the earliest audiences will get to see the next Bond adventure will be in the second half of 2028 - making it seven years since Daniel Craig's swansong, and the longest gap between Bond films since 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye.

World.title: Kyoto's iconic autumn foliage draws crowds of visitors
World.content:
Japanese and international visitors gathered in Kyoto, Japan, on Thursday, 26 November 2026, as the city's autumn foliage reached its peak.

 

Maple leaves in shades of red, orange and gold framed rivers, gardens and historic buildings across the former imperial capital.

At the Yusai-tei Gallery in Arashiyama, reflections of colourful trees created striking displays, while tourists photographed the seasonal scenery in Maruyama Park and near Togetsukyo Bridge.

Known as 'koyo' in Japan, the autumn foliage offers a different experience from the famous spring cherry blossoms.

World.title: Civilian flights diverted as Kuwait army intercepts Iranian drone attack
World.content:
Flights on the key air traffic corridor between Europe, the Gulf region and Asia crossing Iraq towards the Gulf were suddenly redirected south on Thursday afternoon amid reports that Kuwait’s airspace was closed.

 

The Kuwait military has since issued a statement that four people were injured after "a number of hostile" Iranian drones were detected and intercepted in its airspace.

"The Iranian aggression targeted a vital facility, causing falling shrapnel that injured four people," said a statement by the defence ministry, adding that the injured were taken to a hospital for treatment while the incident caused unspecified "material damage".

Since the war in Iran broke out in late February, most international flights crossing Europe have been flying toward major hubs in Doha, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and other destinations via a route running through Turkey, Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and the UAE.

All flights on the corridor were given a new heading, prompting them to make a sharp turn ahead of Kuwait's airspace and move the entire international corridor toward neighbouring countries, including a flight on which Euronews reporters were travelling.

The drone attack on Kuwait comes just one day after the US Virtual Embassy in Iran said Tehran, Yemen's Houthis and other aligned groups may target US interests and citizens in the region, including companies and institutions.

Washington warned citizens across the Middle East to exercise heightened vigilance after Iran attacked US assets in Bahrain and Kuwait and Yemen's Houthi forces struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district, wounding 11 people.

US citizens in the region were urged to monitor airline and airport operations and prepare for possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.

The war has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.

The US and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran's attempts to close it.

Flights bound for the Gulf countries carry extra fuel for emergency diversions, in case they need to go into a holding pattern near their destinations if airports and airspaces are closed due to military activity.

This is a developing story and our journalists are working on further updates.

World.title: Fathers' antidepressant use tied to slight blood pressure risk in kids — but drugs may not be why
World.content:
Children whose fathers took antidepressants in the months before conception are at slightly higher risk of developing high blood pressure — but the fathers' mental health, rather than the drugs, may explain the link, a large new study suggests.

 

About 4.1% of men worldwide experience depression, and antidepressant drugs are a first-line treatment when it is moderate or severe. The share of expectant fathers taking these medications has risen over the past two decades in countries like Denmark, according to the study, which was published in The BMJ.

Researchers tracked more than 1.3 million babies born in Denmark from 2000 to 2023, and then followed them for an average of 12 years. About 18,400 children were diagnosed with a metabolic condition such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol levels, or overweight or obesity.

That includes 364 children whose fathers had used antidepressants in the three months before conception. They were slightly more likely to develop high blood pressure than children whose fathers did not take antidepressants, the study found.

The risks were not elevated for other metabolic conditions, and the extra risk disappeared when researchers compared them to children whose fathers took antidepressants during pregnancy, but not beforehand.

“The mental health conditions for which the fathers took antidepressants may partly explain the study findings,” Prasad Nishtala, a reader in the life sciences department at the University of Bath, said in a press statement. He was not involved with the study.

The findings offer “reassurance for men treated with antidepressants before pregnancy,” the researchers said.

They also accounted for mothers’ and fathers’ age, education level, other medication use, history of metabolic conditions and mental health history. Other factors, such as severity of illness, diet and exercise, may also have played a role.

Other large studies have found no link between fathers’ preconception antidepressant use and preterm birth, birth defects, autism or intellectual disability in their children.

“This study does not challenge the existing evidence. It extends it, cautiously, to metabolic outcomes,” said Alastair Sutcliffe, a professor of general paediatrics at University College London. He was not involved in the study.

“Men who need antidepressants should not stop them because of this study,” he added.

World.title: Farmers demonstrate in Brussels against EU budget cuts
World.content:
Cuts to the EU's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) could threaten farmers' livelihoods, food security and the future of European farming, according to Francie Gorman, president of the Irish Farmers' Association (IFA).

 

EU leaders meet in Brussels on Thursday to discuss the bloc's long-term budget. Farmers' groups say the current proposals "have not improved from an agricultural point of view".

Gorman also told Euronews that rising production costs and EU regulation remain a "huge issue" for farmers.

World.title: Judges in Netanyahu corruption trial urges dropping key charges
World.content:
Judges overseeing the long-running corruption trial of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have urged prosecutors to reconsider major parts of the case.

 

The Jerusalem District Court suggested prosecutors consider dropping the bribery allegation in one of the cases, known as Case 4000, which alleges Netanyahu used his position to provide regulatory benefits to telecoms company Bezeq in exchange for favourable coverage on the Walla news website.

It is the most serious of the three cases against Netanyahu and the only one involving a bribery charge.

In this instance, the court questioned the strength of the prosecution’s evidence, particularly testimony from former Communications Ministry director-general Shlomo Filber, citing inconsistencies and doubts over whether any quid pro quo had been proved.

In another case, known as Case 2000, concerning alleged negotiations with Yedioth Ahronoth publisher Arnon Mozes over favourable coverage, the judges questioned whether the conduct described actually amounted to a criminal offence.

The court also suggested that prosecutors seek an agreement over the remaining case, Case 1000, which concerns allegations that Netanyahu received expensive gifts, including champagne, cigars and jewellery, from wealthy businessmen.

The court stressed that its comments did not amount to an acquittal and no charges have yet been formally dismissed. Netanyahu has denied wrongdoing in all three cases. His trial began in May 2020.

Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said prosecutors would review the judges’ comments, while Netanyahu’s lawyer has called for criminal mediation.

Still no clarity over last month's election result

The intervention by the judges comes at a sensitive political moment in Israel, with the country still unable to form a government after the 27 October election.

Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot currently has the mandate to form a government, but his four-party bloc holds only 48 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, short of the 61 needed for a majority.

A weakening of the prosecution case could strengthen Netanyahu’s position in coalition negotiations and reduce one of the biggest legal uncertainties hanging over his political future.

World.title: Ashes to ashes: FC Barcelona reveals plans to let Camp Nou be fans' final resting place
World.content:
Liverpool's legendary manager Bill Shankly once famously said "Some people believe football is a matter of life and death. I am very disappointed with that attitude. I can assure you it is much, much more important than that."

 

Sentiments shared, it seems, by FC Barcelona as the Spanish Liga champions have recently unveiled plans for their fans to remain part of the club well into the afterlife.

Barça want to open up the Camp Nou columbarium complex at the end of 2027, a 1,500-square-metre space where supporters will be able to leave their ashes.

The project, called Memorial FC Barcelona, will have 26,000 columbarium niches and 9,000 commemorative plaques.

Presenting the plans, architect Quique Montoya said the design was inspired by the shape of a "trainer" and that the 26,000 niches represent as many supporters who will accompany the team in spirit.

A computer rendered Image of FC Barcelona's columbarium Courtesy: Memorial FC Barcelona

The Memorial will have its own entrance from the street, open on a permanent basis. On match days and on special dates it will also be accessible from inside the stadium, via gate 35. There is already a first name on the team sheet. Former club captain, Josep Vicenç 'Tente' Sánchez, has said that he wants to be laid to rest there.

There's a price to pay of course for such a coveted spot at a legendary club. Leases run for 10, 25 or 50 years for a niche of your own at the blaugrana stadium with costs starting from €2,490 euros for a decade, €4,990 for 25 years and €5,990 for half a century. To reserve one, you have to pay €500 up front, which is deducted from the total, and after that there is a yearly maintenance fee of €70.

The club is also offering a cheaper option by way of a commemorative plaques, which costs between €490 and €990 depending on how long you want your name on the hallowed walls. But even within these options there are surcharges, for example if you want a specific spot or to be seen close to the legends of the club.

Atlético de Madrid, the original

Barcelona are not however, the first Spanish side to offer fans a eternal place in a stadium. Similar ventures are also available to supporters of Espanyol, at Cornellà-El Prat, and Betis, which opened their own at the Benito Villamarín in 2011 with around 4,000 urns.

The Spanish pioneer in this 'field of dreams' was Atlético de Madrid which opened their Espacio Memorial at their former Vicente Calderón stadium back in 2008. It had space for 4,200 ceramic urns at a cost of €3,600 each, according to a study in the journal Disparidades.

The club itself boasted at the time that it was the first football stadium in the world with a space of this kind. As a result of its stadium's demolition, however, the remains of Atléti's deceased fans have sinced been moved to a final resting place at their new Metropolitano stadium, a process carried out "with the permission of the families".

World.title: Watch as rare cloud 'waterfall' cascades over Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro
World.content:
A rare cloud phenomenon took social media by storm, as thick clouds cascaded around Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, over the weekend.

 

The weather phenomenon occurs when moist sea air pushes up the slopes and cools, forming clouds that descend and create a water-fall effect.

Only the summit of the mountain, with the iconic statue, and the highest peaks remained visible above a white blanket that gushed down the slopes.

It has been described as Cidade Maravilhosa" (Wonderful City) - an epithet for Rio de Janeiro that gained popularity in the early 20th century and still lives up to the name.

Orographic clouds sweep over Christ the Redeemer

The moment was captured on a mobile phone by filmmaker and photographer Márcio Amaro, from the Santa Teresa neighbourhood, and quickly went viral on social media.

"I had never seen Corcovado like this", wrote Márcio Amaro, making it clear that "the image is real" and not produced by artificial intelligence (AI).

The scene looks as if it has come straight out of a film, but it is very real and has an explanation in atmospheric science. The technical term is orographic cloud, a rare phenomenon triggered by winds coming in from the ocean that push a mass of moist air against a natural barrier.

In this case, that air rose up the slopes of Corcovado. On its way up, it cooled very quickly, a change that leads to the condensation of water vapour and to the formation of dense cloud near the top of the mountain.

As it crosses the summit, the mist is projected over to the other side and, as it begins to descend, it follows the contours of the terrain, creating the illusion of falling water.

As it continues to drop, the air warms up again and the droplets evaporate, which reinforces the effect of a veil or curtain sliding down through the vegetation, until the mist eventually dissolves.

Given that Corcovado Mountain is close to the Atlantic Ocean and covered in Atlantic Forest, the orographic cloud phenomenon is actually frequent in Rio and the surrounding region, especially when cold fronts pass through or in the early morning.

Other photographers had already captured a moment like this in August 2026, showing Christ the Redeemer rising above a tangle of clouds at daybreak. However, that was only the result of static fog trapped in the valleys.

The moving waterfall image depends on a precise combination of factors: the height of the cloud, which has to be exactly at the level of the statue's feet, with Christ clear of the mist, the density of the vapour and a constant current of wind that drives the mass of air down the hillside without dispersing it immediately.

Rio de Janeiro was already an unmissable destination for nature lovers. After this spectacle, there really are no excuses left. You just have to get up early.

World.title: EU-Indonesia trade deal opens new markets, but challenges remain
World.content:
The agreement eyes new export and investment opportunities for Jakarta and Brussels. But can Indonesia turn Europe's growing interest in its markets and critical minerals into sustainable gains at home?

As the European Union seeks to deepen its presence in Asia and diversify its trade relationships, Indonesia is emerging as an increasingly important partner.

At a signing ceremony in Brussels last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the bloc's trade agreement with Jakarta as one of its "most ambitious deals" in the region, linking markets of 730 million people.

The deal, the culmination of nearly a decade of negotiations, reflects the EU's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships, secure access to critical raw materials and reduce strategic dependencies on China.

For Indonesia, it offers opportunities to attract investment, expand exports and strengthen its position in global supply chains.

The agreement will gradually scrap tariffs on more than 98% of product categories, covering almost the entire value of bilateral trade over 15 years.

Indonesia and EU finally seal landmark trade deal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Indonesia's strategic importance to Europe

For the EU, gaining better access to critical raw materials, particularly nickel, and diversifying its supply chains are central to its strategic partnership with Indonesia, said Philip Schleifer, an associate professor of political science at the University of Amsterdam.

"The main strategic interests are opening up a large and growing market for European companies, diversifying and deepening its economic partnerships, reducing strategic dependencies on China, and securing access to critical raw materials," Schleifer told DW.

Indonesia's mineral resources are particularly important for Europe's green and digital transitions. Nickel, for instance, is a key material for batteries and electric vehicles.

The agreement also creates opportunities for European investment in strategic sectors, including electric vehicles, electronics and pharmaceuticals.

But Indonesia has its own industrial ambitions. The government wants to move beyond exporting raw materials by developing domestic processing industries and retaining more value from its natural resources.

"The challenge for the EU is to reconcile its own interest in securing raw material supply with Indonesia's industrial development objectives," said Eline Blot, a senior policy analyst at the Institute for European Environmental Policy (IEEP).

Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Export opportunities and challenges for Indonesia

For Jakarta, the agreement offers opportunities to expand exports, attract investment and strengthen its position in global supply chains.

Yose Rizal Damuri, an economist at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said his institution's study estimates Indonesian exports could increase by around 60% in the coming years.

"Not only can Indonesia increase exports to Europe, but it can also become more strongly integrated into the global supply chains of European companies," Yose told DW.

Potential beneficiaries include labor-intensive manufacturing sectors such as textiles, garments, footwear and furniture, alongside other Indonesian commodities and manufactured products.

The agreement could also encourage European investment and create employment opportunities. However, Yose stressed that access to the European market does not automatically translate into higher exports.

He identified three priorities for Indonesia: raising awareness of the agreement among domestic businesses, strengthening production capacity and improving the country's business climate.

"Various trade agreements signed by Indonesia have relatively low utilization rates. The value of exports using these facilities remains limited compared with overall export values," he said, emphasizing the need for better information and outreach to producers.

Syafruddin Karimi, an economist at Andalas University, also highlighted the opportunity to diversify Indonesia's export markets and reduce dependence on major trading partners such as China, the United States and regional Asian economies.

However, he warned that Indonesian producers must improve their compliance with European standards.

"Products must be traceable, including whether their production involves environmental damage or labor practices that undermine human dignity," Karimi said.

He added that smaller businesses would need greater government support to meet requirements concerning raw materials, production processes and workers' rights.

Is Europe still a global power? The brutal free trade debate To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Environmental costs of economic integration

The expansion of trade and investment could also increase environmental pressures, particularly in nickel mining, palm oil production and manufacturing.

IEEP analyst Blot warned that increased production without stronger environmental safeguards could worsen pollution, ecosystem degradation and industrial emissions. "Nickel mining and processing can contribute to pollution and ecosystem degradation, while palm oil remains closely associated with deforestation," she said.

The growing importance of Indonesian iron and steel exports also raises concerns about emissions from energy-intensive production.

The EU's Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) presents another challenge for Indonesian producers, particularly small-scale farmers who may lack the resources, technical capacity and documentation needed to demonstrate compliance.

Blot acknowledged that these requirements could create disproportionate costs for smaller producers and potentially favor larger companies.

However, she cautioned against using smallholders' livelihoods as an argument to weaken environmental regulations.

Some Indonesian smallholder organisations, she noted, have supported the EUDR as an opportunity to improve accountability in the palm oil industry.

"Rather than weakening environmental requirements, the priority should be to ensure that smallholders receive adequate financial and technical support to meet them," she said.

Professor Schleifer at the University of Amsterdam also warned that growing global demand for Indonesian natural resources could create environmental and social problems previously associated with commodities such as timber, palm oil and coal.

While Indonesia has considerable bargaining power because of its mineral wealth, the challenge is ensuring that increased demand translates into domestic industrial development rather than simply expanding resource extraction.

How a leading EV supplier covered up toxic pollution To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can Indonesia turn market access into sustainable growth?

The agreement includes a dedicated Trade and Sustainable Development chapter covering climate change, biodiversity conservation, sustainable forest management and labor rights. It also provides mechanisms for cooperation and civil society participation.

However, there is no guarantee these commitments will be implemented. "Experience with other EU trade agreements suggests that there is often a big gap between sustainability commitments on paper and outcomes on the ground," Schleifer said.

Blot similarly called for a time-bound roadmap with measurable objectives, stronger monitoring and meaningful participation from civil society and local communities.

For Indonesia, the challenge also lies in preparing domestic industries to compete. Karimi stressed that the government, both at national and regional levels, must work with businesses to improve production standards, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises.

Yose also emphasized the importance of a predictable business environment, warning that frequent policy changes and regulatory uncertainty could discourage investors.

"Without improvements in the domestic business climate, this will not become a reality. Everything will remain good on paper but will not turn into real momentum for change," he said.

Ultimately, the trade agreement offers Indonesia an opportunity to strengthen its position in international trade and attract investment from Europe.

But whether the agreement delivers broader economic benefits will depend on the country's ability to develop competitive industries, move into higher-value production, and ensure that environmental protection and workers' rights are not overlooked.

DW's Muhammad Athif Aiman contributed to this article.

World.title: Joshua Kimmich critcizes Bayern bosses over Musiala health comments
World.content:
Joshua Kimmich has slammed Bayern Munich's leadership over comments about Jamal Musiala's health issues. The bosses have questioned whether the player can return to previous form – and is still worth his high salary.

Bayern Munich's disappointing 2-1 Champions League defeat at Lille on Wednesday night – in which Jamal Musiala came on for the last quarter of an hour – was overshadowed by comments the club's captain made afterwards.

"It must never happen that something like this is played out at a player's expense. Of course, the club always comes first and is bigger than the player, but it's not bigger than the person," Kimmich told reporters in the mixed zone.

"That's an absolute no-go and not Bayern-like," he added.

Kimmich was responding to recent comments made by Bayern supervisory board members Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge.

"If he (Musiala) doesn't return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation with his family, with the player, and, above all, with his agency – because, frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable," Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told Sky on Friday.

Honorary President Uli Hoeness has described the situation as a "dilemma" for the club, while CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen raised the prospect of talks with Musiala's management and family.

Neurological condition

While theGermany player has struggled with a number of injuries over the past couple of seasons, his health came into sharper focus in August, after he collapsed on the pitch in a couple of preseason matches. He subsequently revealed that he had been diagnosed with a neurological condition which causes him to suffer from occasional "absence seizures."

Kimmich added that criticism of a players' performances was legitimate, but that concerns about Musiala's situation should have been dealt with behind closed doors.

"That's something you should sort out internally, around a table, rather than trying to resolve it publicly," he said.

"It's not that he has problems because he's unprofessional. He's there every day trying to get the maximum out of himself."

Talks between two sides ongoing

Meanwhile, Bayern bosses met with Musiala's agents on Tuesday, and clarified the timeline of events, dismissing speculation that the player could have concealed the condition when he signed his last contract extension.

Bayern said the two sides agreed that he was first examined for seizure symptoms in April 2025, two months after he had signed his contract extension, which makes him one of the club's top earners and is to keep him in Munich until 2030. Discussions between Bayern management and Musiala's representatives are reportedly ongoing.

World.title: Crew member dies after diesel tanker sinks off Ibiza coast
World.content:
Authorities rescued 17 crew members but one later died in hospital after a diesel tanker sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza. A contingency plan against possible pollution damage is now in place.

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities said on Thursday.

The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, said in a statement.

According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.

The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it sank about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.

The last known position of the tanker Image: Vesselfinder/dpa/picture alliance

The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the sinking was not immediately clear.

Authorities monitor pollution risk

The Transport Ministry said the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.

Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.

Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest.

The Balearic regional government said it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

The importance of Ibiza for biodiversity

The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.

The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.

Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable."

Any pollution entering the sea could potentially harm Mediterranean seagrass ecosystems [FILE: February 8, 2020] Image: Dietmar Hasenpusch/Hasenpusch-Photo/dpa/picture alliance

But he said the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood."

"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he said.

Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.

World.title: What is the US permitting bill and would it actually help the climate?
World.content:
A sweeping US bill to speed up energy projects has rare bipartisan support. Supporters say it would unlock clean energy and lower bills, but critics say it's a gift to fossil fuels.

While the dust has barely settled on the Democrats' big midterm showing, lawmakers still have business to get done before a new US Congress takes office in 2027: namely, a permitting reform bill with rare cross-party support that could accelerate clean energy or fossil fuels — or both, depending on who's asked.

Permitting reform might sound like a snooze. But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) could have far-reaching consequences for the country's energy mix, household utility bills and climate goals.

BAAJA, which is backed by US President Donald Trump, has already cleared the Senate and now faces a vote in the House of Representatives. DW breaks down what's in the bill, the political fight playing out on the sidelines and what it could mean for consumers' pockets and the US energy transition.

What does the bill do?

Before many new solar farms, wind projects or power plants can connect to the electricity grid, they must first pass through an arduous and complex permitting process.

Getting the green light for an energy project can often take years and requires permits from multiple government agencies. If it manages to overcome those hurdles, a legal challenge can easily stop new infrastructure in its tracks.

It can take years until projects get the greenlight due to a complex permitting process Image: Getty Images via AFP

The nearly 500-page bill aims to overhaul that process. It would speed up environmental reviews, simplify the planning and construction of power transmission lines, make permits harder to revoke and require the growing number of data centers to pay for grid upgrades they need.

The bill is mostly technology-agnostic. So, the same reforms that would make it easier to build a lot of green energy infrastructure quickly could, in theory, be used to speed up oil and gas projects whose carbon emissions are warming the planet.

That's what's made BAAJA controversial, with some Democrats saying permitting reform is needed to get energy bills down and others saying they support provisions, like building more transmission lines required for transporting green energy, but not the whole package.

Would the bill cut emissions or raise them?

It's hard to estimate, and there's a lot of contradictory information out there.

The Rhodium Group, an independent research firm, found the bill would lower US greenhouse gas emissions in every scenario it ran, by up to 4% in 2040 compared with no bill. This is a fraction of the emissions reductions targets the US dropped when it withdrew from Paris climate accord this year.

Purdue University engineer Kevin Kircher reached the opposite conclusion. His analysis , which has not been peer-reviewed, estimates that domestic emissions would rise by about 2%, mostly because he assumes the bill would boost US fossil fuel production.

How LA is plugging hidden oil wells To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The difference comes down to a bet about what the bill ends up speeding up more: renewables and the power lines to carry them, or fossil fuels. That depends on which administration is issuing the permits.

Under Joe Biden's administration, for instance, renewables got a boost but since Trump took office, his administration has favored fossil fuels and spent billions paying developers to give up their offshore wind leases.

What would it mean for US household energy bills?

The White House Council of Economic Advisers, a team of economists that advises the president, estimates it would eventually cut the average household's electricity bill by $178 to $251 (€162 to €229) a year.

The logic is that long permitting delays discourage investment in infrastructure, which drives up prices. But that estimate considers only one part of the bill, faster environmental reviews, and doesn't say when the savings would arrive.

Independent analyses also found a drop in electricity prices for consumers, though a more modest one. The Rhodium Group estimates the bill's passage would save the average household $41 to $66 a year by 2035. That's largely because new transmission lines would let cheaper power reach customers and the costs of expanding the grid for data centers would no longer be passed on to households.

Critics point to the fact that those savings are relative. Electricity demand from data centers is expected to push up prices regardless, and permitting reform would only slow that rise rather than reverse it.

Data centers face backlash from US communities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Oil Change International, an advocacy group that opposes the bill, argues households will still end up paying more for energy than they do now, especially if the bill mainly speeds up gas projects, since US gas prices are expected to rise sharply over the next decade.

What do environmentalists say about it?

Most major US environmental groups oppose the bill as written, including the Natural Resources Defense Council , League of Conservation Voters and Earthjustice . The Sierra Club called it "fundamentally flawed."

Much of the criticism focuses on provisions making federal permits harder to revoke.

"It would prevent a future administration from reconsidering a prior administration's flawed decisions to authorize activities such as Arctic drilling, deep seabed mining, or development of data centers on public lands," Earthjustice wrote in a critique.

The reverse is also true. That provision also makes it harder for an administration to come in and halt clean energy projects, as Trump did with offshore wind.

Opponents warn the bill could weaken protection for water and habitats, and limit environmental lawsuits. One area that environmental groups praised is the overhaul of how transmission lines are planned and approved.

That matters because the windiest and sunniest places in the US are often far from the cities that need power, and building long-distance power lines to connect them can take a decade or more.

Still, many critics say they would rather wait until Democrats control Congress in January and pass a version more focused on clean energy. Though that approach is risky, any bill would still require Trump's signature to become law.

World.title: Health issues delay trial of Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia
World.content:
Prosecutors say the defendant used her political and military contacts to provide information on German defense and aid deliveries to Ukraine. Her arrest in January sparked a diplomatic row between Germany and Russia.

The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman on charges of spying for Russia due to start Thursday was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.

The arrest of the 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman triggered a diplomatic clash between Berlin and Moscow.

Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power.

Her full name has not been released due to German privacy laws.

She was arrested on January 21 and put in pretrial detention.

What is Ilona W. accused of?

She is accused of having contacts with current and former German defense ministry officials to provide information about defense industry locations, drone tests and planned drone deliveries to Ukraine.

She was also said to have been in contact with a man, her alleged handler, working for Russian intelligence at the Russian Embassy in Berlin since at least November 2023, prosecutors say.

On several occasions, she allegedly helped her contact at the embassy attend political events in Berlin under a false identity in order to establish contacts there. She is also suspected of having compiled background information on participants in high-level political events.

German spy chief warns of rising Russia threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Berlin summoned the alleged handler, who was identified by Der Spiegel magazine as the embassy's deputy military attache, over the incident and expelled him from Germany.

Ilona W. led an advocacy group for years that called for international cooperation, focusing particularly on German, Russian, Ukrainian relations.

In addition to her advocacy work, she also ran a small marketing agency.

Both positions allowed her to be active in Berlin's political circles and provided her with connections within the military.

Russia rejects the allegations

The Russian ambassador to Berlin, Sergei Nechayev, denied the allegations this week.

"The Russian Embassy has no connection whatsoever to this woman, and even if she happened to cross paths with one of our representatives, perhaps at some reception, that means absolutely nothing," Nechayev told news agency AFP.

Why Berlin remains an espionage hot spot To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He also said "he may have seen her himself at an event."

"But she is not a Russian citizen and, as far as we are aware, has no ties to Russia. She is a German and Ukrainian citizen, and, frankly, we do not associate with such individuals here," he said.

The trial is expected to run until May 2027.

World.title: Germany news: Final budget debate continues in Bundestag
World.content:
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has called for closer economic and political partnerships with African countries as he wound up what was probably his last trip to the continent as head of state.

Speaking in Kenya, Steinmeier said that there were great variations in the state of development between individual countries and even within some of them.

"But I believe it is worthwhile investing in Africa and in relations with African countries," he said.

He said this was not just meant with a view to possible investment by German companies drawn by Africa's mostly young national populations and developing markets.



"That is true, but we should not limit our view to that. Many African countries now have political weight and growing self-confidence and want a say in shaping the future of the world," he said.



"Africa, it has become clear, is a continent that requires patience if you want to discover it," Steinmeier said. "There is no single Africa, but very many."

Before Kenya, Steinmeier visited Ivory Coast and Ghana. On the final day of his trip, he went to the Crescent Island nature reserve on Lake Naivasha, an area under threat from climate change.

World.title: Germany: 2 arrested, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
World.content:
Federal prosecutors say they have ordered the arrest of two members of a pro-Iranian group on suspicion of planning an attack on a synagogue. They were detained in the cities of Heidelberg and Cologne.

Germany's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday said it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro-Iranian terrorist group.

It identified the men as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., and said that they were arrested in Heidelberg in Baden-Württemberg in the southwest, and in Cologne, several hours' drive to the north.

Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests.

Prosecutors also announced searches and raids of 17 sites in total across three separate states, saying these were ongoing.

What accusations do the men face?

Prosecutors said the two men were "strongly suspected" of membership in a domestic terrorist organization.

They said that Mostafa Al-R. wa an associate of a man in the US known as Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is accused of setting up a group with the acronym HAYI (Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya) that is thought to be "responsible for a series of attacks against US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026," in the aftermath of the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran.

Mostafa Al-R. and Al-Saadi allegedly "founded a separate organization to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and Europe at the end of 2025."

Police vehicles were spotted at the Federal Court of Justice on Thursday, apparently bringing the suspects to a hearing on being held in investigative detention Image: Rene Piebe/PR-Video/dpa/picture alliance

Prosecutors say Ameer J. joined this group. It gathered funds and "recruited several external people to carry out explosive attacks."

"On the group's orders, unknown assailants headed on two consecutive nights in late March 2026 — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city," prosecutors wrote. "The plan was, for reasons as yet unknown, ultimately not carried out."

Prosecutors said that intelligence behind the arrests could be traced back to the federal domestic intelligence agency, the BfV.

More than 250 police officers from various forces were part of Thursday's operation.

Both suspects were expected to appear before judges later on Thursday for a decision on them being placed in investigative detention.

One other person is being sought as part of the investigation, with several others not currently suspected of criminal offenses affected by it.

What happened during the series of antisemitic attacks in Europe in spring?

The stated date for the plot to attack Cologne's synagogue, late March this year, would have roughly coincided with a series of crimes in Europe targeting Jewish people or institutions in the weeks after the outbreak of war with Iran.

These included an explosion in front of Liege synagogue in Belgium on March 9, which caused property damage but no injuries.

Police in the Netherlands investigated a fire at Rotterdam's synagogue a few days later. An explosive device was set off outside a Jewish school in Amsterdam soon after, prompting heightened security across the Netherlands.

In London, a Jewish ambulance service was targeted in arson attacks in March, not long before two Jewish men were stabbed in broad daylight in what investigators treated as a likely act of terrorism.

Several months later, in September, police in Wuppertal in Germany arrested an Afghan national on suspicion of trying to set a fire at the city's synagogue.

World.title: Russia-Ukraine war extends to the Baltic and the Mediterranean
World.content:
By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Kyiv is trying to up the pressure on Moscow and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade?

First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.

Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.

What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?

It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.

And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.

Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.

Furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.

The Russian cargo vessel Sparta II was attacked off the Finnish coast Image: Finnish Border Guard/Handout/Lehtikuva/SIPA/picture alliance

Ukrainian attacks in Baltic Sea region

Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.

Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet."

Ukrainian special forces are also said to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria, well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.

Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.

The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.

Black Sea drone strikes put key global trade route at risk To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Could war become omnipresent?

"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.

"Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war."

Officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.

In an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia, despite the risks.

Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He said that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising."

Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea."

She said about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.

She added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: ¿Se ha movido el voto útil? Las opciones de izquierda y derecha en cada provincia con las últimas encuestas
World.content:
El modelo de EL PAÍS dice que hay 40 escaños en el aire. Consulta a qué partido le sirve más tu voto

Las encuestas tratan de predecir los votos del próximo 29-N, pero el modelo electoral que publicamos en EL PAÍS desde hace una década va más allá: estima los escaños en cada provincia, les asigna probabilidades, e incluso señala el llamado voto útil. A continuación mostramos sus pronósticos actualizados con las últimas encuestas, publicadas hasta el 23 de noviembre.

En el primer interactivo puedes ver los escaños seguros (99% de opciones), probables (75%-99%) y en juego (25%-75%) de cada partido. En total hay 186 seguros, 121 probables y 84 en juego (suman más de 350 porque varios partidos se disputan los escaños). También puedes elegir una provincia y ver nuestra estimación allí.

Voto útil: ¿qué voto ayuda a tu bloque?

Muchas personas votan para maximizar las opciones de un gobierno de izquierdas o de derechas. Quizás tienen un partido favorito, pero se hacen otra pregunta: ¿a qué partido de su bloque le sirve más su voto? Es lo que se llama voto táctico o estratégico. La respuesta cambia en cada provincia: por el método D’Hondt, un voto al PP y otro a Vox no valen lo mismo en escaños, porque uno de los dos suele estar más cerca de ganar el último diputado. Y lo mismo pasa con PSOE, Frente Amplio o BNG.

¿Cuál es el voto táctico en tu provincia? Puedes verlo en el mapa. Primero elige un bloque. Entonces el mapa mostrará, para cada provincia, el partido de ese espectro que tiene más probabilidades de ganar (o salvar) un escaño para su bloque.

Para un votante de derecha, existe voto táctico en 39 provincias. Hay 21 donde le conviene votar al PP (probablemente) y 18 donde le conviene hacerlo por Vox. A veces la diferencia es grande: en Gipuzkoa, Lugo y Ourense, un voto a Vox casi nunca decide un escaño, mientras que el PP se disputa el último con Bildu o el BNG. En Álava o Melilla, un voto al PP vale más de cinco veces lo que uno a Vox. Pero hay territorios donde un votante indiferente entre PP y Vox maximiza sus opciones eligiendo al partido de extrema derecha. Es lo que pasa en La Rioja, por ejemplo.

En la izquierda, el voto táctico favorece al PSOE en 34 de las 52 provincias. En 22 provincias es el único del bloque que mueve escaños en nuestras simulaciones, porque los Frentes y Podemos tienen números débiles en los sondeos. Hay excepciones en territorios con fuerzas locales: por ejemplo, en Lugo parece que un voto al BNG es mejor para los intereses del bloque, y en Ourense BNG y PSOE están casi empatados. Y ocurre algo parecido con Adelante Andalucía en Córdoba, con la Unidad del Pueblo Canario en Santa Cruz de Tenerife y con EH Bildu en Gipuzkoa.

En las provincias grandes, en cambio, el voto táctico se reduce. En Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia o Sevilla hay más de una opción dentro de cada bloque que puede ser competitiva.

Nuestra simulación también muestra otra cosa: mover un escaño es mucho más barato en las provincias más pequeñas. La probabilidad de que justo tu papeleta sea la decisiva es siempre minúscula (un voto cualquiera tiene una posibilidad entre 113.000 de decidir un escaño). Pero no es siempre igual de minúscula. En Lleida un voto al PP pesa casi seis veces más que la media: una posibilidad entre 20.000. Y en La Rioja o Ceuta, uno al PSOE pesa unas cinco veces más. En el otro extremo, un voto al PP o a Vox en Madrid vale la mitad de lo normal, en parte porque allí cada escaño cuesta más votos: hay unos 94.000 votantes por diputado, frente a 25.000 en Soria.

Una advertencia: esto no es una recomendación de voto. Es la aritmética de los escaños según las encuestas de hoy, que todavía pueden moverse y que son siempre una aproximación. Además, el voto táctico solo mide la probabilidad de mover un escaño, pero un voto puede tener utilidad para apoyar unas ideas o una formación incluso cuando no se traduzca en asiento del Congreso.

¿Cómo funciona el modelo?

El modelo parte de nuestro promedio de sondeos, lo proyecta a cada provincia con su historia y microdatos del CIS, y le añade la incertidumbre de las encuestas en el pasado. Después simulamos las elecciones 20.000 veces y contamos cuántas veces gana cada partido cada escaño. Así podemos clasificarlos en tres grupos: seguros, probables y en juego.

El siguiente gráfico muestra qué significan estas probabilidades. Puedes simular las elecciones una, dos, tres o cien veces para hacerte una idea intuitiva de cuántas veces se gana un escaño de cada tipo.

El modelo es sólido. Cada pieza la hemos puesto a prueba con otras elecciones generales. Por ejemplo, hemos probado varias formas de repartir el voto entre provincias, siguiendo técnicas habituales, y nos quedamos con la más precisa en votos y escaños.

El modelo es cauteloso. Y lo es por diseño: predecir cada provincia es difícil porque las encuestas pierden precisión a escala provincial. Un sondeo de 2.000 o 5.000 entrevistas no basta para estimar directamente el voto de Soria, Pontevedra o Castellón. Por eso no lo intentamos: lo que hacemos es usar el voto histórico de cada partido en cada provincia y lo que dicen en cada comunidad los microdatos del CIS, que acumulan decenas de miles de entrevistas. Además, las fuerzas locales no siempre salen en las encuestas y pueden sorprender al final: Teruel Existe gana escaño en una de cada cinco simulaciones. Y pasa algo similar con partidos pequeños en las provincias grandes: Podemos consigue un diputado por Madrid en el 60% de las simulaciones, y SALF, en el 24%. Si detectas cualquier omisión, escríbenos.

Y el modelo es confiable. Estas predicciones las hemos hecho muchas veces. Por eso sabemos que el modelo funciona y está bien calibrado. En 2023 dimos 189 escaños como seguros y se cumplieron todos, igual que en las dos elecciones de 2019 (156 y 153). Los que dimos como probables se cumplieron el 94% de las veces (365 de 388), en la parte alta del 75%-99% que prometíamos. Los errores de cada provincia se compensan en parte al sumarlos, así que el total es más fiable que cada provincia por separado. El modelo también acierta en el total nacional: en las generales de 2016 a 2023, los escaños de cada partido grande cayeron dentro de nuestra horquilla del 80% en 19 de 20 casos, más de lo prometido: es la cautela de la que hablábamos.

Si quieres seguir todas las encuestas del 29-N, apúntate el nuevo pódcast de Kiko Llaneras, en Spotify, YouTube, Apple Podcasts o iVoox.

Metodología

Las predicciones las produce un modelo estadístico basado en sondeos y en su precisión histórica. Es una versión renovada del que hemos usado en unas 40 elecciones desde 2016: en Andalucía, Castilla y León, Aragón, Extremadura, las europeas, las generales de abril y noviembre de 2019 y de 2023, y otras en México, Francia o el Reino Unido.

Funciona en cuatro pasos. 1) Un promedio de encuestas que pondera cada sondeo por su tamaño, su fecha y la precisión histórica de su encuestadora, según nuestro comparador. 2) Una proyección del voto a cada provincia con un modelo logístico, que parte de las generales de 2023 —y, para los partidos nuevos o que ahora concurren por separado, de las europeas de 2024 y las andaluzas de 2026— y se alimenta también con microdatos del CIS de cada comunidad. 3) La incertidumbre de las encuestas, calibrada con los errores de 44 elecciones en España desde 1986 y con una base internacional de miles de sondeos, según el tamaño de cada partido y los días que faltan para votar. Usamos distribuciones t de Student, con colas más anchas que una normal, y errores correlacionados entre partidos. Esos errores tienen una parte común a toda España, porque las encuestas suelen fallar en la misma dirección en todas partes, y otra propia de cada provincia. 4) 20.000 simulaciones de las elecciones, repartiendo los escaños según D’Hondt con barrera del 3% en cada circunscripción.

Un escaño es seguro si un partido lo gana en más del 99% de las simulaciones; probable, entre el 75% y el 99%, y en juego, entre el 25% y el 75%. En nuestras pruebas con las generales de 2016 a 2023, esas probabilidades están muy bien afinadas: los escaños en juego se cumplieron 202 veces, frente a las 195 que predecía el modelo.

Para calcular el voto táctico usamos las mismas 20.000 simulaciones. En cada una añadimos (o quitamos) un puñado de votos a cada partido en cada provincia, y miramos si su bloque gana (o pierde) un escaño. Solo contamos cuando el escaño cambia de bloque. El resultado es la probabilidad de que un voto decida un asiento para su bloque ideológico. Los bloques son derecha (PP, Vox y SALF), e izquierda (PSOE, Frente Amplio, Podemos, ERC, EH Bildu, BNG y Adelante Andalucía). PNV, Junts y CC quedan fuera.

En los gráficos nacionales agrupamos como Izquierdas a Frente Amplio, Podemos y las coaliciones Compromís-Front Valencià, Unidad del Pueblo Canario y Ara Més-Front Ampli; en cada provincia aparecen por separado.

Si quieres seguir todas las encuestas del 29-N, apúntate al nuevo pódcast de Kiko Llaneras, en Spotify, YouTube, Apple Podcasts o iVoox.

World.title: Sánchez: “Estamos tocando con la yema de los dedos la mayoría progresista, si llegamos al 75% la podemos tener”
World.content:
Pedro Sánchez llega sonriente. Viene de una entrevista y después de su conversación con EL PAÍS tendrá otra más. Se le ve poseído por el ritmo de la campaña electoral. Una y otra vez insiste en que del 29-N va a salir una mayoría de progreso y siempre que puede lanza un dardo a las derechas: “La última vez que gobernó la ultraderecha en nuestro país fue durante la dictadura franquista”, recuerda.

La entrevista, centrada en temas de actualidad electoral, se celebra el miércoles por la mañana en la sede del PSOE, en la calle de Ferraz (Madrid). El presidente y candidato socialista, de 54 años, viste traje azul, camisa blanca sin corbata y un lazo morado en la solapa. No rehúye ninguna pregunta ni pierde la calma ante las repreguntas. Tras seis campañas electorales y ocho años gobernando bajo todo tipo de tempestades, asegura que no está cansado: “Me siento una persona profundamente afortunada. Tengo 54 años y no voy a tener un trabajo mejor en mi vida. Queda todavía muchísimo por hacer”.

Pregunta. En los últimos días, el Gobierno ha aprobado una batería de medidas sociales. ¿Por qué ahora y no antes?

Respuesta. Desde hace ocho años aprobamos avances sociales en cada Consejo de Ministros. Lo importante no es el cuándo, sino el contenido. Ampliamos el permiso de duelo, de paternidad y maternidad, hay mejoras para los autónomos... Desde luego, es una declaración de intenciones.

P. ¿A qué se refiere con que se trata de una declaración de intenciones?

R. Es una declaración de intenciones sobre lo que quiere hacer un gobierno progresista durante los próximos cuatro años. Va a haber una movilización sin precedentes en nuestro país y, ante ello, el PP y Vox están poniendo en cuestión la limpieza del sistema electoral. Yo pido una movilización histórica. Necesitamos que el próximo gobierno progresista cuente con más fuerza para llegar más lejos en avances sociales.

Sánchez en Ferraz. Claudio Álvarez

P. ¿Pero no es electoralista aprobar tantas medidas a cinco días de la votación?

R. Así sería si fuera la primera vez que lo hacemos. Pero, insisto, todos los Consejos de Ministros a lo largo de estos ocho años han implicado avances. Hemos gobernado para la mayoría, con independencia de cuál fuera la orientación ideológica.

P. ¿Por qué no lo hicieron antes? ¿Se lo impedía Junts?

R. En el caso de los permisos de paternidad, Junts ha estado de acuerdo. Sin embargo, el PP y Vox andan diciendo que van a derogar muchas de estas medidas. La propia CEOE ha señalado que nos estamos acercando a la República Bolivariana de Venezuela. Yo incorporaría un matiz: nos estamos acercando a la República Bolivariana de Bélgica, donde hay también diez días de permiso de duelo. Se trata de medidas de sentido común que, si hay una mayoría de PP con Vox, se verían cercenadas.

P. Después de la traca final de este martes, ¿qué les queda para la siguiente legislatura si ganan?

R. Nos queda muchísimo. Por ejemplo, dar una respuesta más contundente al problema de la vivienda y blindar las pensiones y el derecho al aborto en la Constitución. El PP sostiene que el sistema de pensiones va a quebrar; eso es mentira, porque goza de una extraordinaria salud.

P. Pero hay una crítica creciente entre los jóvenes sobre la brecha generacional, con la idea de que los pensionistas están mejor que ellos. ¿Qué les contesta?

R. Yo diría tres cosas. La primera, que durante mi administración se han creado 900.000 empleos para gente joven. En segundo lugar, que los sueldos medios de los jóvenes durante mi administración han aumentado un 30%. Y en tercer lugar, que lo que necesitamos es precisamente reforzar el sistema de pensiones, que es la expresión de una solidaridad intergeneracional. Una de las pruebas de que estamos haciendo las cosas bien es que en 2018 yo heredé una hucha de las pensiones donde solamente había 5.000 millones de euros, y hoy hay casi 20.000 millones. Si continúa este gobierno progresista, en 2030 nuestra aspiración será que haya 50.000 millones. Subir los salarios, aumentar el SMI en un 75% y regularizar a migrantes para que coticen a la Seguridad Social son elementos de sostenimiento y fortaleza del sistema público de pensiones. Yo veo la inmigración como una gran oportunidad, no como un problema. Es evidente que tenemos que afrontar el debate de la integración, en el que también las comunidades autónomas y los ayuntamientos tienen mucho que decir. Pero la pregunta es muy sencilla: ¿queremos sociedades abiertas y, por tanto, prósperas, o sociedades cerradas y, por tanto, decadentes? El PP y Vox están en lo segundo. Buscan fórmulas que a mí me parecen contrarias a los principios de la Unión Europea, como estos centros de deportación que quieren hacer en terceros países.

El presidente del Gobierno en un momento de la entrevista, este miércoles. Claudio Álvarez

P. Vox culpa a la inmigración también de la crisis de la vivienda.

R. Nosotros hemos recuperado 300.000 empleos para el sector de la construcción durante estos últimos años. La pregunta que, estoy convencido, comparten muchos de los lectores de EL PAÍS es: ¿quién va a trabajar en la construcción para levantar las viviendas que necesitamos?

P. ¿Qué supone para usted el antisanchismo?

R. La derecha política, mediática y económica se ha lanzado a la deshumanización. Pero no me insultan solo a mí; también a las mujeres, a las que llaman “charos”; a los sindicatos, a los que denominan mafia; a los colectivos ecologistas o incluso a los medios de comunicación cuya línea no les gusta. Esto es común a toda esta internacional ultraderechista... Y creo que muchos medios tendrán que hacer una reflexión sobre el grado de mentira que han utilizado contra el Gobierno de España. ¿Se puede discrepar? Por supuesto. ¿Criticar? Claro, estamos en una sociedad democrática. Pero lo que no se puede hacer es utilizar la mentira como método.

P. ¿Son estas elecciones un plebiscito sobre su figura?

R. No. Son una disyuntiva entre el avance o la involución. Le pongo un ejemplo. Ramón Sampedro murió en 1998. Se tardó 23 años en aprobar la ley de muerte digna. Y ahora tanto el PP como Vox la quieren derogar. Se necesitan décadas para conquistar derechos que en un día se pueden esfumar. Por eso llamo a una movilización histórica de la España progresista.

P. ¿Cuánto daño les ha hecho el caso Ábalos en el voto femenino?

R. El voto femenino continúa siendo mayoritariamente favorable al progreso y particularmente al PSOE. Y estoy convencido de que el feminismo se va a movilizar de nuevo en estas elecciones. Ellas saben que, además de luchar contra la lacra de la violencia de género, reforzamos servicios públicos como la educación, la sanidad pública o la dependencia. Somos un Gobierno que apuesta por la ley de igualdad salarial y que regula la representación paritaria... Dicho esto, evidentemente, el caso Ábalos nos ha hecho mucho daño. Pero hemos respondido con contundencia. Se me puede reprochar haberlo nombrado, pero también puedo decir que lo hemos expulsado, hemos asumido las responsabilidades y hemos aprobado reformas internas para que estos casos no vuelvan a producirse.

El candidato socialista con el director de EL PAÍS, Jan Martínez Ahrens (a la derecha), y el periodista Carlos E. Cué, este miércoles en Ferraz. Claudio Álvarez

P. La práctica totalidad de las encuestas da como ganador a un bloque PP-Vox. ¿Se equivocan todas?

R. Feijóo y Abascal van a salir derrotados el 29 de noviembre. Y en el PP se va a abrir el debate sobre qué tipo de oposición quieren hacer. Que Vox cuestione nuestro sistema electoral es grave, pero que lo haga el PP de una manera tan abierta es extraordinariamente grave... Están practicando un trumpismo preventivo; están diciendo que si el PSOE y las opciones de progreso ganan por la mínima, será trampa. Por eso a los electores les pido esa confianza mayoritaria, porque si la victoria es rotunda e incontestable, tendrán menos excusas para poner en duda el resultado electoral.

P. No se cree las encuestas que en su mayoría dan ventaja a la suma del PP y Vox, pero ¿le parece serio que el CIS diga que usted ganaría por casi diez puntos al PP?

R. El CIS fue la única encuestadora que en el año 2023 dijo algo que parecía un sacrilegio: que el PP y Vox no iban a sumar. En esta ocasión va a suceder lo mismo: no van a sumar.

P. El PP dice que lo primero que hará es cesar a José Félix Tezanos. ¿Ha sido un error haber mantenido al presidente del CIS todo este tiempo?

R. El PP dice que va a cesar a Tezanos y también que va a poner a Eduardo Inda de director de informativos de RTVE. En fin, si es que este es el grado de involución en el que estamos...

P. Si logra ser la lista más votada, ¿pedirá al PP que se abstenga para su investidura?

R. Ya somos adultos. Sabemos perfectamente cómo es la derecha política española... Hay que pensar en lo posible, en una mayoría de progreso en las Cortes. La estamos tocando con la yema de los dedos. Si logramos esa movilización del 75% o más, podemos tener 176 escaños progresistas.

P. ¿Y volvería a pedir el voto a Junts?

R. El PSOE nunca ha puesto en cuestión el resultado electoral. Nunca. Cuando hemos perdido, lo hemos aceptado. El PP y Vox no están en ello, y eso es muy grave. Al señor Feijóo le hemos visto manifestar su inquietud por las urnas de cartón en los consulados. Pero lo que le preocupa al señor Feijóo es lo que hay dentro de esas urnas de cartón, porque lo que han hecho tanto el PP como Vox ha sido recortar el derecho a la participación política. Tengo dudas de que el PP y Vox, por lo que están diciendo, vayan a reconocer el resultado electoral. Y a partir de ahí, en el Parlamento que salga, yo tendré que hablar con los grupos parlamentarios que hayan sido elegidos. Lo que espero es que podamos tener 176 escaños progresistas.

P. ¿Por qué Carles Puigdemont le critica con tanta dureza? Dijo que tenía una ambición desmedida.

R. Eso no lo puedo responder yo; tendrá que responderlo él. En Cataluña hemos culminado un proceso de normalización de la convivencia que arrastrábamos desde el año 2017 y que ha sido apreciado, aplaudido y respaldado por la amplia mayoría de la sociedad catalana.

P. ¿Están la democracia española y sus instituciones preparadas para un gobierno que tenga componentes de extrema derecha?

R. La última vez que gobernó la ultraderecha en nuestro país fue durante la dictadura franquista. Yo he escuchado al señor Abascal decir que no quiere el Estado autonómico. Claro, es que la España preautonómica es la España predemocrática. Y cuando a Abascal le preguntan por Franco, dice que no tiene posición. Pero a mí me llama dictador...

P. ¿Y por qué la ultraderecha crece tanto con esos discursos?

R. En primer lugar, tiene el respaldo de la internacional ultraderechista, que empieza a mostrar síntomas de agotamiento en Argentina, Brasil y EE UU. La segunda razón está vinculada al algoritmo: hay tecnooligarcas que priman los discursos de odio. Y, por último, la derecha política, mediática y económica ha blanqueado a Vox.

P. ¿No tiene la izquierda ninguna responsabilidad en ese crecimiento de la ultraderecha?

R. La derecha y la ultraderecha basan toda su campaña en atacarme. Y yo hablo de los problemas de la gente y de las soluciones, de las políticas económicas socialdemócratas que hemos desarrollado estos últimos ocho años. Se podrá discutir sobre la vivienda, por supuesto; tenemos mucho que mejorar. Pero lo que es indiscutible es que hoy, como consecuencia de la reforma laboral, tenemos 22,6 millones de personas trabajando con unos índices de temporalidad que son mínimos. Y mientras otros en Europa no crecen, España sí lo hace, y reduciendo el déficit y la deuda públicas. La mejor respuesta son más políticas progresistas.

P. Por cierto, ¿cree que hay que entrevistar a los líderes de ultraderecha en la televisión pública?

R. Manifiesto mi sorpresa ante la apertura de un expediente a una periodista [Silvia Intxaurrondo, de TVE]. Sin periodismo no hay democracia. Y el periodismo es preguntarse y preguntar sobre debates que están encima de la mesa. A partir de ahí, creo que hay que escuchar todas las opiniones. Entre otras cosas, porque al oír a la ultraderecha se conoce exactamente el riesgo de involución que representa. Sin ir más lejos, en este mismo 25-N, Día Internacional contra la Violencia de Género, una concejala del Ayuntamiento de Madrid, una mujer de Vox, ha negado la violencia de género...

P. En el debate con Feijóo, en el que usted pidió varias veces perdón y admitió errores, ¿qué haría distinto si obtuviese otra vez una mayoría?

R. He nombrado a más de 55 ministros y ministras a lo largo de estos últimos ocho años y he tenido un caso de corrupción de un ministro. Rajoy y Aznar tuvieron 15 ministros imputados o condenados por corrupción. No resto gravedad a ese caso. Pero estamos a años luz en número de casos, en exigencia y en asunción de responsabilidades.

P. ¿Y se siente satisfecho con la estrategia del cara a cara? En casi todos los medios se le dio como perdedor.

R. No fue una estrategia; es una convicción. Con el insulto o la mentira no se discute. Al que insulta y miente se le gana en las urnas, votando por el respeto y por la verdad. Desgraciadamente, en nuestra sociedad y también en algunos medios de comunicación se ha banalizado la verdad.
