World.title: Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated rights of migrants sent back to Belarus, finds European court
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated the human rights of migrants from Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba who entered their countries illegally from Belarus in 2021 and 2022, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled. However, the ECHR did also recognise that states have the right to prevent the entry of migrants who have been “instrumentalised” by Belarus in order to create a crisis on the European Union’s eastern borders. That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation. 📽️ Watch a video explainer on the Grand Chamber cases concerning instrumentalisation of migration. 📽️ Regardez la vidéo explicative sur les affaires de Grande Chambre sur l'instrumentalisation de la migration. pic.twitter.com/ZhXqZ6lIur — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026 In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. Belarus engineered the migration crisis as part of the various “hybrid actions” undertaken alongside its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile. In response, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus. On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus. The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”. This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”. Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus https://t.co/7Gbsvs6I1e — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention. However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”. That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus. In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants. A court has found that Poland's border guard violated the law when sending two Afghan and Ethiopian men back to Belarus after they injured themselves crossing the anti-migrant border fence. One of them had made clear his wish to claim asylum in Poland https://t.co/42yOuGEgns — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2024 For Poland, the case concerned an unnamed Afghan national who had been part of a group that had crossed back and forth over the Polish-Belarusian border multiple times, as often happened in the early stages of the crisis. The ECHR noted that it had, at the time, issued an interim measure requiring that the Afghan man not be returned to Belarus. However, the Polish authorities did not take this into account, and sent him back to Belarus on 20 October 2021, thereby demonstrating they had not complied with their obligation to properly assess his need for protection, found the ECHR. The court also ruled that, in the case of that applicant as well as a fellow Afghan national, Poland had violated their rights by preventing lawyers from having access to them. It ordered Poland to pay the two men €20,000 (89,000 zloty) and €5,000 respectively as compensation. Two Afghan asylum seekers who crossed from Belarus into Poland have been awarded compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards. They were detained and driven back towards the border by officers, who did not accept their asylum applications https://t.co/M9bSHakS5j — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2025 In Latvia’s case, the ECHR ruled that the country had violated its obligations by sending Iraqi Kurdish children, some of whom were infants, back into Belarus, “disregarding the[ir] evident vulnerability”. At the same time, the European court dismissed further complaints by adult migrants against Latvia and Lithuania, finding that they had not demonstrated any vulnerability or risk. However, it did find that Lithuania had violated some Cuban migrants’ rights by failing to properly inform them of the reasons they were being held in a detention camp and thereby also of their right to legally challenge their detention. It also ruled that Latvia had violated the rights of migrants on its territory due to the poor conditions they found themselves in when camped out on Latvian territory, with no access to sanitary facilities and insufficient protection from rain and cold nighttime temperatures. ⚖️ Grand Chamber cases ➡️ Responding to realities of instrumentalisation of migration at Belarus border, European Court safeguards essential rights and reiterates limits of Convention protections. 🔗 Press release: https://t.co/nflEyCWKb1 — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026 In response to today’s ruling on Poland, the deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy, Maciej Duszczyk, hailed it as “very important and favourable for us”. He said that the ECHR’s findings regarding states’ rights to defend their borders from instrumentalised migration effectively endorsed Poland’s policies. The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a Warsaw-based NGO, also noted that the ECHR’s Grand Chamber had, for the first time, defined the scope of states’ obligations when another state has instrumentalised migration. “In the ECHR’s view, when migration is instrumentalised, states are not obliged to assess whether people being returned to the state instrumentalising migration will have access to an adequate asylum procedure there,” noted HFPC. Bardzo ważny i dobry dla nas wyrok Europejskiego Trybunału Praw Człowieka. Niezakwestionowano naszego modelu walki z nielegalną migracją. Trybunał odniósł się do instrumentalizacji jako sprzecznej z Konwencją i podkreślił prawo państ do obrony i ochrony swoich granic. — Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) November 24, 2026 A number of Polish courts have also found that the authorities violated the rights of migrants on the Belarus border. Last year, two Afghan asylum seekers were awarded 5,000 zloty compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards. In 2024, another court found that the border guard violated the law when sending Afghan and Ethiopian migrants back to Belarus after they had injured themselves while crossing the border. Last year, Poland’s government effectively formalised pushbacks by introducing a ban on asylum claims by people crossing the border irregularly from Belarus, who are now sent back without their applications being accepted. The measure has been criticised by human rights groups – including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Poland’s own human rights commissioner – as a violation of international law and Poland’s constitution. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Poland has also implemented a number of other tough policies, including easing rules for the use of firearms by uniformed officers protecting the border from illegal migration. This year has seen the migration crisis abate significantly, with Poland reporting a 98% decline in attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, as well as a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do cross. World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland in response to last week’s incident in which three Russian missiles struck Polish territory. Shortly after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone that entered from Ukraine. However, although the military was given authorisation to shoot the object down, they did not do so after the drone began to move back into Ukraine. Today, NATO Ambassadors met in the North Atlantic Council to discuss last week’s violations of Polish airspace. This was a dangerous incident and Russia bears full responsibility. NATO and Allied assets reacted quickly to the airspace violations, and the Supreme Allied Commander… — NATO Spokesperson (@NATOpress) November 23, 2026 On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeast Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border. The incidents took place amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine, and on Sunday Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. The missiles were in Polish airspace for around three minutes before striking the ground. Two Swedish Gripen fighter jets, which were patrolling Polish skies as part of a NATO air policing mission, received authorisation from NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre to fire upon the objects if certain conditions were met. However, the pilots were unable to confirm their identity in time due to poor weather conditions. On Monday, an extraordinary meeting of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s main decision-making body, took place to discuss the incident. Afterwards, deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski, who represented Poland at the meeting, announced that NATO had agreed to place an AWACS “at Poland’s disposal”. Later, NATO’s spokeswoman, Allison Hart, confirmed that “the Supreme Allied Commander Europe has authorised the forward deployment of a NATO AWACS aircraft” and is also “examining the deployment of additional assets as he continues to assess our deterrence and defence posture in Poland and elsewhere”. Poland has confirmed that the three objects which struck its territory last Friday were all Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. Preliminary findings indicate the missiles were recently manufactured at a plant in Dubna, Russia https://t.co/4N6k3eBUGN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 23, 2026 “This is a very serious capability that gives us enhanced situational awareness,” said Zalewski, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. “This is an immediate NATO response, and we are very happy about it.” “What I heard today is a great demonstration of the alliance’s unity with Poland in the face of Russian attacks,” he added. “It’s safe to say that the Russians have moved up the escalation ladder in their relations with NATO.This means…the need for an appropriate response.” Zalewski emphasised that “we’re not talking about offensive actions in any way, but about the ability to defend against all the attacks Russia is launching against NATO countries”. The aim is “not to escalate, but to…discourage Russia from attacks”. Wiceminister @ZalewskiPawel w Kwaterze Głównej #NATO: Do dyspozycji Polski będzie jeden samolot szybkiego ostrzegania #AWACS. To jest bardzo poważna zdolność, która daje nam pogłębioną świadomość sytuacyjną. I to jest natychmiastowa reakcja NATO. — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) November 23, 2026 On Monday night, after NATO had made its decision, Poland’s airspace was again violated, this time by a Russian drone that crossed the border from Ukraine. The operational command of Poland’s armed forces announced shortly before midnight that it had continuously tracked the object and granted authorisation to shoot it down. However, after the drone changed course and began to head east, back towards the border, a decision was made to refrain from engaging it, “taking into account the potential threat to civilians and the possible consequences of shooting down the object”, said operational command. W trakcie nocnego ataku Federacji Rosyjskiej na cele w zachodniej części Ukrainy, prowadzonego z wykorzystaniem środków napadu powietrznego, doszło do krótkotrwałego naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej przez rosyjski bezzałogowy statek powietrzny. W odpowiedzi na… pic.twitter.com/BhJN7UYg7m — Dowództwo Operacyjne RSZ (@DowOperSZ) November 23, 2026 According to a report by broadcaster RMF, based on unnamed sources, the vehicle was a jet-powered drone that flew 20 km into Poland and remained in Polish airspace for around nine minutes. Speaking to RMF on Tuesday morning, Zalewski said that “it is difficult to imagine that this was an accident; we assume it was an intentional action”. Russia has so far not commented on either its missiles hitting Poland last Friday nor the latest drone incursion. They are the latest in a series of airspace violations. In September this year, a Russian helicopter briefly crossed the border from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. In September 2025, around 20 Russian drones crossed Poland’s eastern borders in an unprecedented violation that prompted Poland to trigger NATO’s Article 4. The Netherlands will become the latest country to purchase Poland’s Piorun man-portable air-defence systems, which have been increasingly in demand following their successful use during Ukraine’s defence against Russia. On Monday, their Polish manufacturer, Mesko, which is part of state-owned defence group PGZ, signed an agreement adding the Netherlands to a list of countries that will buy Pioruns with funds from the European Union’s SAFE mechanism for financing defence spending. 🇵🇱🇳🇱⚡ HOLANDIA DOŁĄCZA DO DRUŻYNY PIORUNA! W @PGZ_MESKO_SA w Skarżysku-Kamiennej podpisano aneks do umowy ramowej, umożliwiający Holandii dołączenie do wspólnych zamówień zestawów PIORUN. ✍️ Dokument podpisali gen. dyw. Artur Kuptel, Szef @AgencjaUzbr, oraz Krzysztof Marwicki… pic.twitter.com/lVH0QgdD0t — Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa🇵🇱 (@PGZ_pl) November 23, 2026 Piorun (meaning “thunderbolt” in Polish) is a shoulder-mounted system that fires air-defence missiles capable of destroying aerial vehicles, such as helicopters, drones and low-flying planes, at short range. In 2022, Pioruns were among the large quantities of military equipment that Poland provided to Ukraine to help its eastern neighbour defend itself from Russia’s full-scale invasion. The systems have been successfully used to take down Russian aircraft. Since then, they have been in high demand, with Mesko receiving orders from the United States, Norway, Belgium and Sweden, as well as Ukraine itself. In August this year, Mesko signed an 8 billion zloty (€1.8 billion) agreement to supply further Piorun systems to Poland, Norway, Lithuania and Latvia, with the deal financed through SAFE funds. Precise details were not revealed. However, the agreement was said to involve the supply of “several hundred” launchers and “several thousand” missiles, with over 80% of the equipment going to Poland’s own armed forces. Now Mesko has signed an addendum to that deal, adding the Netherlands to the list of countries that are jointly ordering Pioruns. Deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who has overseen Poland’s participation in the SAFE programme, said after attending Monday’s signing ceremony that the Netherlands would not be the last country to join the procurement of Pioruns. “We promised that the list of Mesko’s buyers from all over Europe would grow, and today we have living proof of that,” said Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. “And I can reveal a secret: it’s not over yet.” She noted that Mesko has stepped up its production volumes in response to demand. Last year, it could produce “several hundred” systems annually; that has now risen to 1,500, and is set to grow even further. Last week, PGZ and the state assets ministry signed an agreement to support Mesko’s expansion with around 370 million zloty from the state Capital Investment Fund (FIK). It will help bring production capacity to around 2,500 per year. 🗣️ "Obiecywaliśmy, że lista kupujących z całej Europy będzie się powiększać i mamy tego żywy dowód. A mogę zdradzić sekret, że to jeszcze nie koniec. Dzisiejsza umowa to umowa w ramach zakupów w mechanizmie SAFE"@magdasobkowiak o zestawach Piorun dla Holandii ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/sTxG5SwnbZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) November 23, 2026 Growing demand for Pioruns resulted in Mesko last year posting the best financial results in its 100-year history. The firm’s revenues of 2.3 billion zloty in 2025 were up 33% year-on-year. The EU’s SAFE programme is providing a total of €150 billion in loans at preferential rates for member states to use on defence-related spending. Poland, with around €44 billion, is the largest single recipient. While most SAFE purchases are conducted individually by member states, some are also carried out jointly. Such joint procurement can also involve certain non-EU countries, such as Norway. World.title: Prague Christmas Markets Reveal Prices for Mulled Wine, Sausages and More
World.content:
Prague’s main Christmas markets will open on Saturday, November 28, with mulled wine priced at 100 CZK and sausages costing 180 CZK.

Organizers say prices for several popular refreshments have remained unchanged, while the sausage is the main item to have become more expensive.



The markets on Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will run until January 6, 2027, with stalls open daily from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

The company Taiko, which organizes the markets, says Prague remains among the most affordable Christmas market destinations in Europe for food and drinks.

The price of mulled wine has remained at 100 CZK since 2024. A hot apple drink will cost 70 CZK, the same as last year.

The price of sausages has increased, however. The item rose from 160 CZK to 180 CZK during the Easter markets and will remain at that level for the Christmas season.

The company also points to the ingredients used at its stalls. The sausages are made exclusively for the markets and contain up to 97 percent meat, while the mulled wine is produced from grapes supplied by the Moravian winery Chateau Valtice.

Prices at Prague’s main Christmas markets:

Mulled wine: 100 CZK

Hot apple drink: 70 CZK

Sausage: 180 CZK

Hot dog: 90 CZK

Sausage in a baguette: 180 CZK

Langoš with garlic, cheese and ketchup: 200 CZK

Draft Pilsner, 0.4 litre: 80 CZK

Hot chocolate: 130 CZK

Spiral potato: 100 CZK

French fries: 185 CZK

Record number of performers expected

The 2026 programme will feature a record 5,329 performers. Activities will include weekend workshops for children, a St. Nicholas Day event and the traditional Christmas Eve celebrations.

On December 24, festive soup will be served on Old Town Square from 11 a.m. A performance of the Czech Christmas Mass is scheduled for 9 p.m.

For safety reasons, the organizers have not announced the exact time of Saturday’s tree-lighting ceremony. They are also encouraging visitors to spread their first visits across the weekend and avoid bringing bulky luggage to the markets.

World.title: Expedia to Acquire Czech Flight Booking Company Kiwi.com
World.content:
American travel company Expedia Group has agreed to acquire Czech flight booking platform Kiwi.com, bringing a change of ownership to the Brno-based business.

The transaction is expected to be completed by the middle of 2027, although the companies have not disclosed its value.

The acquisition will see the departure of Kiwi.com’s current majority shareholder, US investment fund General Atlantic, which has controlled the company since 2019. Co-founder Oliver Dlouhý, who holds a minority stake, is also expected to exit.



Expedia said the deal would strengthen its technology and expand its position in the European air travel market. Kiwi.com generated approximately €227 million in revenue last year, equivalent to around CZK 5.6 billion.

Expedia said the acquisition would give travelers access to a wider selection of flights and provide new opportunities for growth across its brands, including Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo.

Kiwi.com was founded in Brno in 2012 by Dlouhý and his business partners. The company became known internationally for its search technology, which allowed it to combine flights from airlines that did not necessarily have direct partnerships with the platform.

The company has since developed into an international flight retailer, focusing on technology, automation and artificial intelligence to improve its operations.

The acquisition comes after several years of restructuring at Kiwi.com, which faced financial difficulties following the decline in air travel during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The company reduced its workforce by more than 200 employees in 2024. Earlier this year, it announced plans to cut approximately 250 jobs from a workforce of around 700.

Expedia Group was founded in 1996 as a division of Microsoft. It operates an online travel platform offering bookings for flights, accommodation, car rentals and activities, as well as technology services for corporate partners.

World.title: Christmas Trees You Can Replant After the Holidays Are Available in Prague
World.content:
Residents of Prague and Brno can choose a living Christmas tree this year and give it a chance to grow in the forest after the holidays.

Both cities are offering small potted firs that can be planted in spring with the help of foresters.

In Prague, the Forests of the Capital City of Prague are running their Christmas fir project for the tenth consecutive year. The initiative, known as A Christmas Fir with a Future, allows people to buy a young silver fir for 150 CZK.

The trees, approximately 50 centimeters tall, have been grown in a forest nursery in Čimický háj. Unlike cut Christmas trees, they retain their roots and can continue growing after Christmas.



The organizers acknowledge that the firs may not look like traditional Christmas trees. Their branches are often irregular, and each tree has its own shape.

The project also aims to support the return of silver fir to Czech forests. The native species (Abies alba) became scarce during the 20th century, partly because of air pollution, forestry practices and excessive numbers of wild animals.

Where to buy a living Christmas tree in Prague

The potted firs are available at several locations, including the Ďáblice Garden Center, the Prales eco-center and forest lodges in Hostivař, Chuchle, Šárka, Běchovice, Kunratice and Čimice.

How to care for a potted Christmas tree

A living Christmas tree needs more attention than a cut one. It should remain outdoors in a cool place, such as a balcony or garden, for as long as possible before being brought inside.

The tree should be gradually acclimatized to the warmer indoor temperature. The room should ideally stay below 20 degrees Celsius, and the soil needs regular watering. Spraying the needles with water can also help.

After Christmas, the tree should be moved back to a cooler environment gradually.

Even with careful handling, survival is not guaranteed. According to the Masaryk Forest Křtiny School Forest Enterprise, around 60 percent of the Christmas firs planted in previous years have successfully taken root.

World.title: Higher Prices, Fuller Hotels: Prague Is Becoming a Luxury City Break
World.content:
Prague is strengthening its position as a high-end tourist destination, attracting visitors willing to spend more on accommodation and services.

The Czech capital has ranked ahead of Vienna and Berlin in an international tourism index, while demand for luxury hotels continues to rise.

More than 2.3 million tourists visited Prague between July and September 2026, representing a three percent increase compared with the same period last year.



The city received a score of 92.7 out of 100 in the Global Tourist Perception Index, compiled by Data Appeal and Mabrian Intelligence. Vienna scored 85.6, while Berlin received 78.4.

The ranking assessed several aspects of the visitor experience, including satisfaction with accommodation, safety and the variety of tourist attractions.

According to František Cipro, chairman of the board of Prague City Tourism, the results reflect a shift in the city’s tourism profile.

“Prague clearly demonstrates that it is no longer a budget tourist destination, nor does it wish to be one,” he said.

The trend is also reflected in visitor spending. During the first half of 2026, Prague welcomed more than 3.8 million tourists, a one percent increase year-on-year. However, Mastercard payment data showed that spending by visitors from selected foreign markets rose by 18 percent.

Tourists from China and South Korea recorded the most significant increases in spending.

Accommodation figures point in the same direction. Almost two-thirds of guests staying in Prague hotels choose four- or five-star properties.

In 2025, the average price of a hotel room in the capital stood at around CZK 3,000 per night. In central Prague, the average rose to approximately CZK 4,100, while luxury hotels charged around CZK 5,800.

Demand for higher-end accommodation has remained strong despite rising prices. In September 2026, luxury hotels recorded an occupancy rate of 83 percent, their highest September result in seven years.

Germany Remains the Largest Source Market

Tourism continued to grow during the first nine months of 2026, with Prague recording more than 6.1 million visitors, a two percent increase compared with the same period in 2025.

Germany remained the largest source market for international visitors during the third quarter.

Some other markets also recorded notable growth. Visitor numbers from Taiwan increased by 27 percent, followed by Israel at 26 percent and Ireland at 23 percent.

World.title: How to Choose a High School in the Czech Republic: Open Days and School Fairs
World.content:
Choosing a high school is an important decision for students and their families.

School websites and brochures can provide useful information, but visiting schools in person offers a much better idea of what studying there is actually like.

Open days and high school fairs are two ways to explore the available options, meet teachers and students, and find out which school might be the right fit.



This is the first article in our series on choosing a high school in the Czech Republic.

Visit Schools During Open Days

Open days give prospective students and their parents the opportunity to look around a school before applying.

High schools open their doors to visitors, allowing them to explore classrooms, workshops and laboratories, meet teachers and current students, and ask questions about studying there.

An open day can help families find out more about:

Study programmes: What courses and specialisations does the school offer?

Admission requirements: What are the conditions for applying, and how does the entrance examination work?

Future opportunities: What options are available after graduation, including further education and employment?

School environment: What is the atmosphere like, and would the school be a good fit for the student?

Open days take place throughout the school year, with many schools organising them ahead of the application period.

Dates vary from one institution to another, so check individual school websites or use the online overview of high school open days to find upcoming events.

Compare Schools at High School Fairs

High school fairs offer another opportunity to explore different institutions without having to visit each one separately.

In Prague, one of the main events is SCHOLA PRAGENSIS, where visitors can meet representatives of secondary schools from different regions.

You can visit META stand at Schola Pragensis, Prague’s high school fair, taking place from 26 to 28 November at the Prague Congress Centre

– stand number 245 on the 2nd floor.

The META team of professionals will help you explore the options and answer all your questions.

Students and parents can compare study programmes, ask questions about admission procedures and learn more about individual schools directly from their representatives.

These events are particularly useful for students who have not yet decided what they want to study or are still considering several different options. Meeting representatives from multiple schools in one place can help narrow down the choices.

If you live outside Prague, you can also find a high school fair in your region.

Use Worksheets to Help Make Your Decision

Comparing schools, admission requirements and study programmes can quickly become confusing, especially when several institutions are under consideration.

Free worksheets are available to help students organise information, compare their options and think about what they want from their future school.

You can download the worksheets here.

World.title: EF English Proficiency Index: Brno Speaks Better English Than Prague
World.content:
Prague has improved its English proficiency score, but it still trails Brno, according to the latest EF English Proficiency Index (EF EPI).

The Czech capital gained nine points over the past year, while Brno recorded a slight decline. Despite the contrasting trends, the South Moravian city remains ahead.



The Czech Republic ranked 24th out of 117 countries and regions in this year’s global index, published by education company EF Education First. Its score of 569 points represents a drop of 13 points and one place compared with the previous year.

The country remains in the high-proficiency category, although several neighboring states performed better. Austria ranked second worldwide with 613 points, followed by Germany in fourth place with 611. Slovakia came 11th with 594 points, while Poland ranked 15th with 587.

Slovakia’s performance is particularly notable. The country has gained 49 points since 2016, making it one of Europe’s most improved performers over the past decade. Although its score fell slightly compared with last year, it still leads the Czech Republic by 25 points.

Brno Maintains Its Lead Over Prague

Brno scored 613 points in this year’s assessment, placing it 28 points ahead of Prague, which recorded 585.

The gap between the two cities has narrowed, however. Prague improved from 576 points last year, while Brno fell from 620.

Brno’s result is particularly strong in an international comparison. Its score matches Austria’s, which ranked second among the countries included in the global index.

The regional figures also support Brno’s position. The South Moravian Region recorded 606 points, the highest score among Czech regions.

Sweden Takes First Place in Global Rankings

The Netherlands has lost its position at the top of the global English proficiency rankings, with Sweden taking first place this year with 615 points.

The Dutch finished fifth with 609 points. Austria, Denmark and Germany occupied the places between them, scoring 613, 612 and 611 points, respectively.

The survey was conducted through the Ipsos Instant Research application and focused on respondents’ self-assessments of their language abilities.

World.title: Massive Attack to Headline Colours of Ostrava in 2027
World.content:
British trip-hop pioneers Massive Attack will perform at Colours of Ostrava on July 22, 2027, organisers have confirmed.

The band will take the main stage at the four-day festival, which runs from July 21 to 24 at the former Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex in Ostrava.

The announcement marks Massive Attack’s return to the Czech Republic after a nine-year absence.

The Bristol-born group, formed in 1988, is regarded as one of the most influential acts in the development of trip-hop.

The band is best known for songs including Teardrop, Angel and Unfinished Sympathy. Its music combines electronic sounds with elements of hip-hop, soul and dub, creating a distinctive style that helped shape British music in the 1990s.

Massive Attack’s live performances also feature large-scale visual projections, often incorporating political and social commentary.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Colours of Ostrava official 💛 (@colours_cz)

They join an already announced line-up for Colours of Ostrava 2027 that includes Robbie Williams, Ellie Goulding, Martin Garrix, 5 Seconds of Summer and David Kushner.

World.title: Leo Express Opens Prague–Munich Train Tickets From 49 CZK
World.content:
Leo Express has started selling tickets for its new Prague–Munich express service, which will replace České dráhy on the route from December 13.

The cheapest domestic fares currently available start at just 49 CZK for journeys between Prague and Plzeň.

The new service, known as Ex36, will be operated by Leo Express for five years after the company won a public tender. It will take over the route currently served by České dráhy’s Bavarian Express trains.



International tickets are not yet available. Although German stations already appear in the booking system, passengers can currently only book journeys within the Czech Republic. Leo Express says bookings for the full Prague–Munich route will open in the coming days.

The lowest advertised fare between Prague and Plzeň is 49 CZK. The same starting price applies to journeys as far as Domažlice. Business class tickets start at 199 CZK.

Prices will vary depending on demand and availability, so not all seats will be offered at the lowest fares. A second-class ticket between Prague and Plzeň will cost up to 236 CZK, equivalent to the standard OneTicket fare.

For comparison, České dráhy currently charges between 155 CZK and 235 CZK for the same journey, depending on the time of travel. Passengers can also use the cheaper Berounka express service by combining tickets from the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) and Plzeň Region Integrated Transport (IDPK) systems.

According to the booking system, most trains will have six carriages, including two business-class carriages. The operator will use former Deutsche Bahn carriages purchased by Spanish railway company Renfe and leased to Leo Express.

The trains will include both open-plan seating and traditional compartments. Eight services will run in each direction every day, matching the current timetable of České dráhy’s Bavarian Express.

World.title: Former UN chief Ban Ki-moon attends 1956 anniversary conference in Budapest Parliament
World.content:
Former United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon is attending an international conference at the Hungarian Parliament on 26 November, marking the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. The event examines the relationship between Hungary’s historic uprising and the United Nations, including the organisation’s response to the Soviet intervention and the fate of Hungarian refugees.

The conference, titled The 1956 Revolution and the United Nations, is being held under the patronage of Ágnes Forsthoffer, Speaker of the National Assembly. Opening speeches are being delivered by Anita Orbán, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, and Zoltán Tarr, Minister for Social Relations and Culture.

Initiated and organised by former Hungarian UN Ambassador Katalin Bogyay, the event brings together international diplomats, historians and researchers. Ban Ki-moon, who led the United Nations between 2007 and 2016, is the guest of honour.

Former UN chief Ban Ki-moon delivers a speech in the Hungarian parliament. Photo: Daily News Hungary

The opening speeches

In their opening speeches, the three Hungarian officials highlighted the continuing relevance of the 1956 Revolution and the principles underpinning the United Nations. Parliament Speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer recalled that around 180,000 Hungarian refugees were welcomed by 37 countries following the crushing of the uprising, with 100,000 resettled in less than ten weeks. She also paid tribute to Danish diplomat Povl Bang-Jensen, who insisted on keeping the identities of witnesses to the Soviet intervention confidential, a decision that cost him both his career and, ultimately, his life.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán stressed that the strength of the UN today, as in 1956, depends on how faithfully its member states uphold the principles of its Charter. She reaffirmed Hungary’s support for reforming the organisation and called for a Security Council that better represents its members and can respond more effectively to threats to peace.

Meanwhile, Minister for Social Relations and Culture Zoltán Tarr said the courage and solidarity of university students in 1956 had helped revive civil society. He argued that lasting peace requires autonomous universities, a freely operating civil society and organisations capable of holding those in power to account, adding that Hungary plans to adopt a national civil society strategy based on broad dialogue.

Previously restricted UN documents on 1956 opened in 2016

One of the most significant aspects of the conference is its connection to the release of previously restricted United Nations documents concerning the 1956 Hungarian Revolution.

Following the Soviet military intervention in Hungary, the UN Security Council discussed the situation and attempted to secure the withdrawal of Soviet troops. On 4 November 1956, however, the Soviet Union vetoed a US-backed draft resolution calling for their withdrawal. The Security Council subsequently adopted Resolution 120, calling an emergency special session of the General Assembly to address the crisis. The General Assembly also called for Soviet troops to leave Hungary and addressed the humanitarian situation facing Hungarian refugees.

In December 1956, the General Assembly established a special committee to investigate the events in Hungary. Its members collected testimonies from Hungarian refugees and other witnesses abroad, as the committee was not granted access to the country.

A particularly controversial chapter involved Danish diplomat Povl Bang-Jensen, the committee’s second secretary. He refused to hand over the names of Hungarian witnesses who had given confidential testimony, fearing that their relatives remaining in Hungary could face reprisals. The UN subsequently initiated disciplinary proceedings against him. He was found dead in New York in November 1959.

Some documents concerning the committee’s work and the Bang-Jensen case remained restricted for decades.

Photo: Daily News Hungary

If you missed it: Why 4 November is a day of mourning in Hungary: 70 years since Soviet tanks crushed the 1956 revolution

How Hungarian diplomacy helped unlock the archives

The efforts to make these historical records accessible began with research initiated by Hungarian historian András Nagy. In 2016, Katalin Bogyay, then Hungary’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, launched and led diplomatic negotiations involving the United States, Russia and UN officials.

The discussions included the countries’ then UN ambassadors, Samantha Power and Vitaly Churkin, as well as the leadership of the United Nations and Bang-Jensen’s son.

The diplomatic process resulted in approximately 1,500 pages of previously restricted documents becoming available for research in 2016. Around 400 pages of highly confidential material were held in the UN archives, while the remaining documents were kept in Columbia University’s Cordier collection.

The records include material relating to the UN special committee, witness testimonies and the Bang-Jensen case. Historian András Nagy was the first researcher granted access to the material and has since published his findings in both Hungarian and English.

Ban Ki-moon also has a personal connection to the events of 1956. As a school student in South Korea, he was chosen to read aloud a letter addressed to then UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld, appealing for international assistance for Hungarians fighting for freedom and democracy.

Later, as UN Secretary-General, Ban supported the release of the historical documents and the international commemoration of the revolution’s 60th anniversary in New York in 2016.

Zoltán Tarr. Photo: Daily News Hungary Anita Orbán. Photo: Daily News Hungary Ágnes Forsthoffer. Photo: Daily News Hungary

International experts examine the lessons of 1956

The Budapest conference also looks at the international significance of the revolution and the lessons it offers for the United Nations today.

In the historical section, András Nagy is presenting the findings of his research into the newly accessible UN documents. Mark Kramer, a Cold War historian from Harvard University, is examining the international context of the revolution, while historian Gusztáv D. Kecskés is discussing the UN’s role in assisting Hungarian refugees.

A separate session focuses on the organisation’s present-day crisis management challenges. Speakers include Vuk Jeremić, former President of the UN General Assembly, and Ambassador György Busztin, former Deputy Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Iraq.

The conference is organised by the United Nations Association of Hungary in cooperation with the National Assembly, Ludovika University of Public Service, Széchenyi István University, the Hungarian National Commission for UNESCO, the World Federation of United Nations Associations and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Institute for Cultural Diplomacy, based in Berlin and New York, is supporting the event.

The 70th anniversary conference brings the discussion back to the Hungarian Parliament, the historic location from which messages and appeals for international support were sent during the 1956 Revolution.

World.title: Debrecen ice rink named Europe’s most beautiful for the second time in a row
World.content:
The Christmas ice rink in Debrecen has been voted Europe’s most beautiful festive skating venue for the second consecutive year, retaining the title it first won in 2025.

Debrecen’s ice rink the most beautiful in Europe, again

The Hungarian city also secured a place among Europe’s seven best Christmas destinations in the 2026 European Best Destinations competition, making it the only Hungarian location to feature in that selection.

According to a statement from Főnix Event Organiser, which operates the ice rink, this year’s vote broke previous records, attracting almost two million votes from travellers from 176 countries. More than 6,400 Christmas markets across Europe were considered, with 27 shortlisted for the competition. The 20 destinations receiving the most votes were awarded international recognition.

Debrecen finished seventh overall, collecting 41,769 votes. It appeared alongside well-known European destinations including Zurich, Riga, Vienna, Paris and Madrid.

The organisers described the ice rink as one of the city’s most popular Advent attractions, combining winter recreation with a festive atmosphere. Retaining the skating title for a second year further strengthens Debrecen’s profile as a Christmas travel destination.

Advent season and skating dates

Debrecen’s 2026 Advent programme runs from 20 November to 23 December in the city centre, while the ice rink will remain open until 10 January 2027.

During the main Advent period, opening hours vary by day. The rink generally welcomes visitors from 8am on weekdays, with pre-registered groups given priority until 2pm, and from 9am at weekends. Special opening hours apply over Christmas and New Year.

The venue is also hosting public skating sessions and ice discos. The disco requires a separate event ticket, which is not included in the standard public skating admission.

Tickets and equipment

According to Csodálatos Magyarország, a standard skating ticket costs HUF 2,500 (EUR 6.72) per person per session, while an accompanying-person ticket is HUF 500 (EUR 1.34). Children under three can enter free of charge. Visitors can also rent skates for HUF 2,500 per pair, hire a penguin skating aid for HUF 1,500 (EUR 4.03) an hour, or have their own skates sharpened for HUF 2,500.

With its repeat European title and strong showing in the wider Christmas destination ranking, Debrecen is once again attracting attention among the continent’s festive destinations.

World.title: Ukraine pledges to accelerate minority rights progress for ethnic Hungarians
World.content:
Ukraine is ready to speed up the implementation of agreements designed to protect the linguistic, cultural and educational rights of ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has announced.

Ukraine’s FM Sybiha discussed the problem with Anita Orbán

Speaking at a press conference in Kyiv on Wednesday, Sybiha said the necessary legal framework was already in place and there was no reason to delay measures that could be introduced sooner. “Why delay measures that we can implement in a shorter timeframe, given that we already have a sufficient legal framework?” he said, according to Ukrainian news agency Ukrinform.

The minister confirmed that the issue had been discussed with his Hungarian counterpart, Anita Orbán. He added that further meetings were planned in the coming weeks and that bilateral mechanisms and commissions would resume their work to help both sides understand each other’s positions and agree on practical steps.

Sybiha described Ukraine’s approach as constructive and stressed that the Hungarian community was an integral part of Ukrainian society. He said Kyiv wanted to meet the highest European Union and Council of Europe standards for protecting national minorities.

Follow-up to talks between Magyar and Zelensky

The announcement came a day after Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Berehove (Beregszász), a town in Transcarpathia with a substantial ethnic Hungarian population.

Following the meeting, Magyar said Ukraine had agreed to Hungary’s request to accelerate the implementation of commitments concerning the minority’s rights. He had previously described significant progress in negotiations covering ten specific issues.

At their joint press conference, Magyar emphasised that passing legislation was not enough: the agreed rights must also be respected in everyday life. He cited the ability of ethnic Hungarians to use their mother tongue freely, including when requesting Hungarian-language guided tours at places such as Mukachevo Castle.

The two countries’ foreign ministers also held separate discussions in Berehove. Sybiha subsequently described the meeting as historic, saying it had brought progress on several issues, from minority rights to Ukraine’s EU accession.

Legal changes and EU accession

The dispute over minority rights has been a longstanding obstacle in relations between Budapest and Kyiv. Hungary has linked its support for further steps in Ukraine’s EU accession process to improvements in the treatment of ethnic Hungarians.

Ukraine’s parliament adopted amendments to minority-language education legislation in mid-October, subsequently signed by Zelensky. The changes allow minorities speaking official EU languages greater use of their mother tongues in education and provide for certain schools to receive national minority educational institution status under specified conditions.

The latest pledge signals a move towards putting those legal commitments into practice, although the practical impact will depend on the work of the bilateral bodies and the implementation of the agreed measures.

World.title: Germany’s Merz warns Russia wants more than Ukraine as he defends support for Kyiv
World.content:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that Russia’s ambitions extend beyond Ukraine, accusing Moscow of escalating threats to European security. He defended his government’s plans to increase defence spending and maintain financial support for Kyiv, arguing that helping Ukraine also means protecting Germany.

“Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine,” Merz told the Bundestag, Germany’s lower house of parliament, during a debate on the government’s draft budget for 2027, Reuters reported.

His remarks came after opposition parties, including the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the far-left Die Linke, again called for an end to military assistance to Ukraine.

Merz warns of growing Russian threats across Europe

The chancellor accused Russia of increasing tensions in several regions, including the Baltic area, Poland and the Black Sea.

“Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea; Russia is escalating in space, and Russia is by now also escalating massively here in our own country,” he said.

Russia has repeatedly denied seeking military confrontation with NATO countries, claiming that its actions in Ukraine are aimed at protecting its own national security. Moscow has also rejected accusations linking it to cyberattacks and sabotage incidents targeting critical infrastructure in Europe.

Merz argued that supporting Ukraine was not simply an act of solidarity, but also a matter of Germany’s own security.

“We are learning from Ukraine – technologically for civilian use but of course also in defence technology,” he said, referring to the lessons Germany can draw from Ukraine’s experience.

If you missed it: Magyar and Zelensky discuss energy, trade and EU membership as Hungary and Ukraine seek closer ties

Public support for military aid to Ukraine declines

Germany has been Ukraine’s largest military supporter in Europe since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022. However, public backing for the policy has weakened amid rising living costs.

A survey published on Tuesday found that a narrow majority of Germans now oppose providing military assistance to Kyiv.

During Wednesday’s parliamentary debate, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla challenged Merz over the government’s priorities, accusing it of supporting Ukraine while failing to provide enough relief to German citizens.

Germany plans to double defence spending

According to the draft 2027 budget, Germany intends to more than double its defence spending to over EUR 200 billion by 2030. The aim is to bring expenditure to 3.7% of national output by that year, in line with the country’s commitments to NATO.

Merz also addressed the European Union’s proposed budget for 2028–2034, presented by European Council President António Costa. The latest proposal would reduce the seven-year budget to EUR 1.582 trillion, around EUR 40 billion less than an earlier version presented by the Irish EU presidency in October.

EU leaders are due to discuss the proposal at a special summit on Thursday and Friday.

Merz said he wanted EU spending to be more limited and focused on priorities that would strengthen the bloc, particularly security and competitiveness. He argued that concentrating resources on these areas would provide additional protection for Germany and Europe as a whole.

World.title: 250kg WWII bomb recovered from Lake Velence with help of an amphibious icebreaker
World.content:
Hungarian military bomb disposal experts recovered a 250kg Second World War bomb from Lake Velence on 25 November after surfers spotted the unexploded device underwater.

Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi announced the operation on Facebook, saying soldiers from the Hungarian Defence Forces’ 1st Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Riverine Flotilla Regiment had safely removed the bomb.

According to the regiment’s own account, the German-made SC250 aerial bomb was recovered by specialist diving personnel. The operation was particularly challenging because visibility underwater was virtually zero. The divers had to identify the explosive device by touch and carry out the entire operation in these conditions.

Divers worked in near-zero visibility

The bomb was lying in shallow water, some distance from the shore. To recover it, the military enlisted the help of an amphibious vehicle belonging to the Central Transdanubian Water Management Directorate.

Ruszin-Szendi said the divers used the amphibious icebreaker to bring the 250kg bomb to the surface in around an hour and a half. It was then transported safely to a central collection site, where it will be destroyed at a later date.

The bomb was fitted with an electric detonator, but its power source had already run out, meaning the detonator was no longer operational, the minister added.

Ruszin-Szendi praised the soldiers for completing the operation despite the cold water and difficult conditions on the lakebed.

World.title: Budapest mayor proposes phasing out Airbnb rentals completely from the capital
World.content:
Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony has called for the complete phase-out of Airbnb-style short-term accommodation rentals in the Hungarian capital in the near future, arguing that the city needs a more sustainable tourism model that better balances visitors’ interests with those of local residents.

Mayor Karácsony wants Airbnb gone from Budapest

Karácsony outlined his position at the 64th general meeting of the Association of Hungarian Hotels and Restaurants (MSZÉSZ), where he also presented plans for a new tourism strategy and closer cooperation between the municipality and the hospitality industry.

According to Turizmus.com, the proposed strategy, including phasing out Airbnb and others over the next 10 to 15 years, entitled Budapest Flow, is intended to put the capital on a more dynamic development path after what the mayor described as a period of operating in survival mode. It could be discussed by the Budapest General Assembly at its final meeting of the year.

Karácsony said sustainable tourism must be something that residents themselves can support. While some parts of Budapest already experience overtourism, others attract too few visitors, he noted. The city wants to make better use of its attractions, increase tourist spending and demonstrate that Budapest offers more than nightlife and party tourism.

He also said he wanted to avoid a situation in which visitors are confronted with anti-tourism slogans such as “Tourists go home!”, as has happened in other popular destinations.

Short-term rentals under scrutiny

The mayor described short-term apartment rentals such as Airbnb as a particularly difficult issue because the interests of residents and tourism businesses can conflict. His personal position is that the practice should eventually disappear entirely from Budapest, provided those affected receive 10 to 15 years to prepare for the change.

Karácsony argued that hotels could accommodate visitors currently staying in privately rented apartments, provided the sector receives an appropriate regulatory framework. He said the combination of cheap flights and inexpensive short-term accommodation encourages a type of tourism that does not serve the capital’s long-term interests. New hotel developments could also be linked to the regeneration of former industrial areas, he suggested.

The proposal is not yet a municipal decision or an adopted citywide ban. Some Budapest districts have already introduced restrictions on Airbnb-like short-term rentals, including the Castle District and Terézváros, but the mayor’s proposal would go considerably further.

New tourism bodies planned

Karácsony also proposed establishing a destination management organisation jointly involving the capital and the state, as well as a tourism council bringing industry representatives together to help shape development priorities. He invited MSZÉSZ to nominate a representative.

Budapest accounts for around 38 per cent of Hungary’s GDP, and tourism plays a significant role in its economy, the mayor said. He argued that predictable policies and cooperation between businesses and residents would be essential to creating a tourism model that benefits both.

World.title: Daily cuteness: watch how Budapest Zoo’s Persian leopard cubs take their first steps
World.content:
Two Persian leopard cubs at Budapest Zoo are beginning to explore their surroundings after opening their eyes and attempting their first steps at around three weeks old.

Persian leopard cubs starting to explore their own

The young animals are being raised by their nine-year-old mother, Banu, in a quiet, protected indoor enclosure. She is caring for both cubs without human intervention, meaning zookeepers have not yet been able to examine them or establish their sex.

Visitors can currently catch glimpses of the family only through footage recorded by cameras inside the enclosure and shared on the zoo’s Facebook page. The zoo says the mother and her offspring need complete peace during this early stage, so neither visitors nor photographers are allowed near them.

Persian leopards are a subspecies of leopard (Panthera pardus tulliana). Like other leopards, their cubs are born blind, with their eyes usually opening at around one week of age. They generally begin trying to walk independently when they are two to three weeks old.

According to Blikk, the cubs are already showing signs of curiosity. While Banu gently carries one back to its resting place, the other may set off to investigate its surroundings.

Second litter for experienced breeding pair

The cubs’ father is Akhum, a ten-year-old leopard born in France. Banu was born in Jászberény and has family links to Budapest Zoo. The pair have now produced their second litter together.

As in the wild, only the mother takes responsibility for raising the cubs. Zoo spokesperson Zoltán Hanga explained that even weighing the newborns would require separating them from Banu, causing unnecessary stress.

Persian leopard cubs typically weigh between 500 and 750 grams at birth, but their exact weights will remain unknown until their first examination.

Meat introduced at around ten weeks

For now, the cubs feed exclusively on their mother’s milk. The nursing period for Persian leopards lasts approximately three months, although animals in zoos may continue suckling until they are around four months old. At about ten weeks, the cubs are expected to begin tasting solid food before gradually transitioning to a meat-based diet.

In the coming weeks, they should also become more confident at climbing and playing with one another. The zoo plans to introduce the cubs to visitors in December. Until then, their development can be followed through updates and videos on the institution’s social media channels.

World.title: Hungary could still reach EUR 1,000 minimum wage by 2028, despite missing another target
World.content:
Hungary is set to miss one of the key goals of its three-year wage agreement, as the gross minimum wage will not reach 50% of regular gross earnings next year. However, the country could still achieve another headline target: a minimum wage equivalent to EUR 1,000 by 2028.

Under an agreement reached last week by the government, employers and trade unions, the gross minimum wage will rise by 7.5% to HUF 347,000 (approximately EUR 930) in 2027. The guaranteed minimum wage, which applies to jobs requiring at least secondary education or vocational qualifications, will increase by 6.1% to HUF 396,000.

Minimum wage target falls short

The three-year wage agreement signed in 2024 originally envisaged minimum wage increases of 9% in 2025, 13% in 2026 and 14% in 2027.

However, economic conditions proved considerably less favourable than expected. The planned 13% increase for 2026 was reduced to 11%, while next year’s agreed rise is roughly half the originally planned 14%.

The agreement also aimed to bring the gross minimum wage to 50% of regular gross average earnings by 2027. Regular earnings exclude bonuses, rewards and 13th-month payments.

According to G7, the minimum wage represented 44% of regular gross average earnings in 2025. Although the full-year wage data for 2026 is not yet available, comparing the current minimum wage with the latest figure for regular gross average earnings, from September, gives a ratio of around 45%.

If you missed it: Official: Here’s how much minimum wage will be in Hungary in 2027

What could happen in 2027?

There are no specific forecasts for the growth of regular gross earnings. However, the Finance Ministry’s medium-term economic and budgetary programme for 2027–2030 projects average gross wage growth of 5.6% next year, while the National Bank of Hungary forecasts 5.8%.

If regular gross earnings increase by around 5% from their September level, the minimum wage would account for just over 46% of regular gross average earnings in 2027. Even if wages remained at September’s level, the ratio would approach 49%.

Jácint Hatvani, president of the LIGA Trade Unions, said the latest agreement had produced an unusual outcome: Hungary had met the expectation set by the EU minimum wage directive in terms of the net minimum wage, but not the gross minimum wage.

Is EUR 1,000 still within reach?

A separate political promise made in 2024 was for Hungary’s minimum wage to reach EUR 1,000 by 2028. Unlike the 50% target, this was not linked to an EU directive, but formed part of the previous government’s economic messaging.

The goal is still achievable, although it would require another substantial increase in 2028. A stronger forint would also help.

At the exchange rate prevailing recently, the new minimum wage of HUF 347,000 would be worth approximately EUR 930. By contrast, at the exchange rate of around HUF 350 to the euro seen in mid-June, the same wage would have been worth approximately EUR 990.

Reaching the EUR 1,000 threshold will therefore depend not only on future wage increases, but also on how the forint performs against the euro.

World.title: Serbia’s New Speaker Sets December Presidential Election, Vucic Signals Boycott
World.content:
New Speaker of Parliament Aleksandar Cupic on Thursday signed the decision calling a presidential election for December 27.

The election will follow the resignation in September of former President Aleksandar Vucic and the defeat in October 25 parliamentary elections of his long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS.

“Building democratic institutions is a task for all of us, particularly political actors and the media. Good laws are the walls of our society, while informed citizens are the true masters of the political community,” Cupic said on Thursday.

“I hope we will face a difficult choice between excellent candidates and their programmes. May public debates and a democratic electoral process encourage high voter turnout,” he added.

Vucic, who now heads the SNS-led parliamentary group, has called for a boycott of presidential elections, although his party has yet to announce its final decision. On Wednesday, Vucic described the upcoming election as “the most pointless election in history”, according to news agency Tanjug.

“There are different views within the party. Some want us to support an independent candidate, some want us to field our own candidate, while others, like me, want us to simply ignore the election and let them boast about having taken over everything and won 94 per cent of the vote,” Vucic said, adding that he would await the party’s decision.

Earlier, on Monday, Vucic also said he favoured boycotting a presidential election, but his party would make its final decision at its assembly on December 13. He said he personally leaned towards “not granting them that kind of legitimacy”.

Vucic claimed taking part in an election was pointless under conditions of “absolute terror”.

The Student List, which secured 140 of parliament’s 250 seats in October’s elections, has said it will unveil its presidential candidate shortly after the election is called.

The SNS’s 14 years of rule were marked by allegations of corruption, nepotism, electoral irregularities, a lack of the rule of law and restrictions on media freedom, among others. These issues were also highlighted in the European Union’s regular reports.

Following its defeat, it has accused the Student List of using “revolutionary terror” and seeking to arrest SNS officials and supporters, even though the SNS still officially controls the government, as the Student List has yet to form a new government.

So far, the Student List has only constituted the new parliament, where SNS representatives have also accused it of not providing the party with sufficient space and of denying it any leadership positions within parliamentary bodies.

World.title: EU Could Unlock Additional €338 Million for Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia
World.content:
The European Union could unlock another 338 million euros with the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans funds in the coming weeks for membership hopefuls Albania, Montenegro and North Macedonia, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday.

Speaking at a press conference after the EU-Western Balkans Summit in Brussels, von der Leyen said that this year implementation of the Growth Plan reforms “has shifted into high gear”.

“A year ago, partners had delivered 38 per cent of the reform steps due. Today, we have already reached 63 per cent. And these are reforms that make a difference. They could unlock another 338 million euros for Albania, Montenegro and North Macedonia in the coming weeks,” she said.

At the press conference following the summit, Council President Antonio Costa highlighted the progress towards membership made by Montenegro and Albania, saying that “enlargement is a realistic possibility, and it should be seized”.

Serbia did not attend the summit. Costa said he had spoken with Serbia’s acting President, Parliament Speaker Aleksandar Cupic, who had explained that he could not attend because of urgent parliamentary business in Belgrade.

“Of course, we understand, and we will have further opportunities to continue our engagement with the Serbian authorities to continue the accession process into the European Union,” Costa said.

Cupic declined the invitation to Brussels citing his parliamentary obligations amid the institutional transition following the October 25 parliamentary elections, which saw the opposition Student List defeat the long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS.

Serbia also skipped last December’s EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels after its then-President, Aleksandar Vucic, decided not to send a representative following the EU’s failure to agree on opening Cluster 3 in Serbia’s accession negotiations.

World.title: Protesters Across Balkans Demand Action to Curb Violence Against Women
World.content:
Seven women have been killed by partners or relatives in Kosovo this year. Protests were also held followed the killing of Arlinda Zekaj, who was killed in Peja/Pec minutes after police escorted her home after she had reported her former husband for domestic violence.

Zekaj had repeatedly warned the authorities that she was in danger. Kosovo’s Police director resigned after the protests, and 11 police officials and two prosecutors were suspended.

In September, after two women in Kosovo were murdered by their partners within days, BIRN reported on the institutional failures in Kosovo to protect victims who had asked for help.

World.title: Croatia’s War Victims, Mass Graves Documented by New Independent Research
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Nejra Mulaomerovic, Nikola Mokrovic, Tena Banjeglav and Vuk Tesija at the event in Zagreb. Photo: Documenta.

Civil society groups are carrying out the task of documenting wartime crimes and compiling lists of victims – a role that should fall to state institutions, an event at the Cultural and Information Centre in Zagreb on Wednesday was told.

The event showcased the new Croatia research conducted for BIRN’s mass graves database Bitter Land, and the online platform Croatian Book of Remembrance (Hrvatska knjiga pamcenja), newly published by the NGO Documenta – Centre for Dealing with the Past.

Establishing the facts about war crimes and their victims is important for their families, but also for society as a whole and for future generations, as it is the only way to counter nationalist manipulation, Tena Banjeglav from Documenta told the event, which was titled ‘Civil Society, Mass Graves and the Documentation of War Victims in the Former Yugoslavia’.

“We hope that the scope for distorting facts will diminish, allowing for the construction of a society based on trust, solidarity, respect for human dignity and peace,” Banjeglav said, adding that systematic work on such issues is impossible without cross-border cooperation.

The impetus for Documenta’s research was the fact that, when the organisation began work in 2009, no comprehensive list of war victims existed – and none exists to this day.

“Out of approximately 21,000 victims in Croatia, we have already published findings on 12,000, but data on only just over 1,000 victims has so far been made available on the platform,” explained Nikola Mokrovic, Documenta’s coordinator of research into human losses.

“Once all the data has been published on the platform, it will constitute the first comprehensive list of victims in Croatia from 1991 to 1995. For now, the amount of available data is limited, and the process will continue for some time,” Mokrovic said.

The platform includes victims’ names, basic biographical information and details about the research and methodology. In addition to individual data, such as full name, status, ethnicity, citizenship, place of birth, place of residence and location of death, the database also includes narrative accounts providing more detailed descriptions of the suffering endured by victims.

BIRN’s Bitter Land database is a complementary project, focusing on mapping wartime mass graves across the former Yugoslavia.

“The goal of the research is to show the extent of the crimes, make the archive and information available to the public, and bring the data together in one place to facilitate research,” said BIRN’s transitional justice project manager Nejra Mulaomerovic.

Research into mass graves in Bosnia and Herzegovina began in 2020, and the Bitter Land online database became publicly accessible in 2021, initially mapping more than 30 locations in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, including some of the largest mass graves discovered in the former Yugoslavia.

To date, 95 locations have been mapped in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo and Serbia – and most recently in Croatia.

The platform features contemporary photographs of the sites, archival photographs and footage of exhumations, as well as geographical coordinates, the number of identified persons, court judgments related to the crimes, brief descriptions of the crimes, survivor testimonies and links to sources.

Explore the Bitter Land database here.

World.title: Kosovo Privatisation Process Leaves Many Ex-Workers Out of Pocket
World.content:
Faridin Berisha waited more than a quarter of a century for the privatisation of the Union of Cooperatives of Kosovo, expecting to receive his part of the 20 per cent share of the sale price guaranteed by law to former employees.

The enterprise, which managed cooperatives and their credit operations but had been inactive since 1998, was sold in March last year for 800,000 euros.

Berisha, however, was informed last week by Kosovo’s Privatisation Agency that he was no longer eligible for a share of the proceeds because he had already reached retirement age at the point the enterprise was put up for sale. Indeed, none of the enterprise’s former employees were eligible, according to officials at Kosovo’s Privatisation Agency, PAK.

“The building was usurped by a political party and some warlords, and nobody dared to sell it,” said Berisha, 67. A court took years to rule on the status of the enterprise’s property, and by the time it could eventually be sold, the former employees had either died or entered retirement.

World.title: Letter from Washington: ‘Blue Tsunami’ Puts Trump’s Balkan Relationships in Disarray
World.content:
Greetings from Washington, where Congressional Republicans and President Donald Trump have entered a lame-duck period after being swept away by a “blue tsunami”. Democrats won convincing majorities in both chambers of Congress, including in states that have voted Republican for decades, such as Texas, Kansas, and Mississippi. Voters turned to the Democrats out of frustration with high fuel and food prices caused by the war in Iran, while watching the President and those close to him grow richer.

The midterms were a referendum on the President, but Trump does not see himself as responsible for the Republicans’ rout and remains combative. A confrontation with Democrats is all but guaranteed; once they officially take control of Congress in January, gridlock in Washington’s domestic politics is virtually certain. On foreign policy, Congress could pull in one direction while the White House pulls in another. This could have implications for the Balkans, too.

World.title: Albania’s Rebuild After 2019 Earthquake Still a Work in Progress
World.content:
Edi Rama called it “magic” - the 330 million euros in cash and 850 million in long-term projects and loans pledged at a Brussels donor conference to mitigate the impact of a devastating earthquake in Albania on November 26, 2019.

“This is a real wow and the fact that I don’t have a speech with me tells about my expectations,” the Albanian prime minister said. “Some magic has happened. This is beyond our wildest imagination.”

Seven years after the earthquake - which killed 51 people and razed 11,000 homes - 29 residents of the capital, Tirana, have died without ever receiving the keys to their new homes; hundreds more have been left in limbo by a stalled reconstruction effort.

As of December last year, according to a document prepared by Tirana Municipality, 463 earthquake-affected families were still waiting to be rehoused, some 80 per cent of them in the city’s Kombinat neighbourhood.

The Reconstruction Programme has absorbed more than 100 billion lek [1.1 billion euros] in state budget funds, but no clear deadline for completion has been set.

Speaking in late November during the presentation of next year’s budget to parliament, Rama described the reconstruction as a success story, while acknowledging a “problem” in Tirana.

World.title: The Limits of Illiberal Power: What the Defeats of Vucic and Orban Reveal
World.content:
An opposition that wanted to win

For years, Hungary and Serbia were characterised by fragmented and discredited opposition parties that struggled to challenge the governments beyond major cities. Successive elections saw them compete for a limited electorate, while failing to convince voters that they offered a credible alternative to the governing parties.

Tisza and the Student List broke with this pattern. Neither carried the political baggage of repeated electoral defeats or years of participation in a political system that many voters had come to distrust. They could therefore present themselves as a clear break with the existing order.

Both movements also understood that their supporters were primarily dissatisfied with the political system itself, rather than with particular government policies. Their campaigns focused less on ideological disputes and more on defeating the incumbents and putting their countries ‘back on the right track’. Mass demonstrations, marches and direct challenges to the governments’ legitimacy became central to their political identity. Although earlier opposition parties had also protested corruption, their continued participation in the political system made it harder for them to represent a genuine break with it.

Tisza and the Student List instead presented the elections as a choice between preserving the existing order and bringing it to an end. Perhaps most importantly, they gave voters a reason to believe that victory was actually possible. There was also something distinctly populist about their approach: they appealed to widespread frustration with the ruling political elite rather than offering a clearly defined alternative ideology.

Yet the two movements differed considerably in their organisation. Tisza developed into a highly centralised, professionalised party centred around Magyar’s leadership, while Serbia’s Student List emerged from a decentralised movement based on grassroots decision-making. Their shared success therefore cannot be attributed to one particular organisational model. What mattered more was their novelty, their ability to mobilise beyond established opposition circles, and their determination to win.

World.title: BNB: Loans to households in Bulgaria in October 2026 up 20.5% on annual basis
World.content:
Loans to households and NPISHs (non-profit institutions serving households) in Bulgaria added up to 33.635 billion euro at the end of October 2026, an increase of 20.5 per cent compared with October 2025, Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) said in a regular report on monetary statistics on November 26.

This followed 20.7 per cent annual growth in these loans in September 2026, BNB said.

At the end of October 2026, loans for house purchases added up to 20 billion euro, an annual increase of 24.1 per cent, following 24.8 per cent annual growth in September 2026.

Consumer loans amounted to 12.589 billion euro. Compared with October 2025, this was an increase of 16.3 per cent (16 per cent annual growth in September 2026).

Deposits of Households and NPISHs were 57.799 billion euro at the end of October 2026.

This was an increase of 15.4 per cent compared with October 2025 (16.2 per cent annual growth in September 2026), BNB said.
