World.title: Estonia to fund pneumococcal vaccines for children
World.content:
Estonia plans to add pneumococcal vaccination for children to its national immunization schedule starting in the second half of 2027, the Estonian Health Insurance Fund announced.

Pneumococcus is a bacterium that can cause serious illnesses, including pneumonia, sepsis and meningitis. Over the past decade, the number of pneumococcal infection cases in Estonia has tripled.

The necessary legislative amendments must be finalized before the plan can be implemented. Once the changes take effect, the Health Insurance Fund will begin funding pneumococcal vaccination for young children under the national immunization schedule.

The Health Insurance Fund currently funds pneumococcal vaccination for children in risk groups, while other families have been able to have their children vaccinated at their own expense. Adding the vaccine to the immunization schedule will make protection against pneumococcal infection available to all children, regardless of their families' financial circumstances.

"Pneumococcal infection can cause serious illness in young children and lead to hospitalization. By adding the vaccine to the immunization schedule, we are moving away from a system in which vaccination for children outside risk groups has been a matter of parental choice and expense, toward making pneumococcal disease prevention part of routine childhood vaccination," said Hanna Jäe, vaccination service manager at the fund. Existing vaccination arrangements for risk groups will continue as usual.

Under the immunization schedule, the vaccine will be administered in three doses: the first two at 2 and 4.5 months of age, followed by a booster dose at 12 months. The pneumococcal vaccine can be administered alongside other vaccines included in the immunization schedule, meaning parents will not need to schedule separate vaccination appointments.

According to Leelo Moosar, an infectious disease specialist at West Tallinn Central Hospital, pneumococcal vaccination is included in childhood immunization schedules in most European countries. Vaccination aims to reduce the incidence of and prevent severe pneumococcal infections, as infants and young children are the most severely affected.

World.title: Estonia quotes small-scale power producers millions for grid connections
World.content:
An investigation by ERR has uncovered cases across Estonia of small-scale electricity producers being quoted millions of euros by grid operator Elektrilevi to connect to the power network.

An investigation by ERR's "Pealtnägija" brought to light a case in Kõrveküla near Tartu where a man who wanted to sell electricity generated by solar panels he planned to install on his home's roof to the grid was quoted a connection fee of €13 million by distribution system operator Elektrilevi. The network operator attributed the error to a mistake made in haste and acknowledged that around 10 other customers in the same area had received similarly exorbitant quotes.

Apologies were sent to customers and that might have been the end of the story. However, following the broadcast, "Pealtnägija" received reports of similar cases from across Estonia. A couple of earlier cases emerged in Kõrveküla itself, along with others from the Tartu area and South Estonia. Viljandi County also stands out for its exorbitant grid connection quotes, with the same pattern evident in Märjamaa, Haapsalu, Anija and Saku, just outside Tallinn.

"Pealtnägija" does not know how many such quotes, some running into the tens of millions of euros, have been issued over the years, but there are likely more than the roughly 20 cases the show's team has been able to examine. Four Elektrilevi customers agreed to speak to "Pealtnägija" in greater detail about their experiences with astronomical connection fees.

Power line repairs. Source: Jaanus Tanilsoo/Elektrilevi

The case of forestry entrepreneur Silver Solba, for example, dates back to 2021. Solba wanted to build a 100-kilowatt solar farm on his Kubija property on the outskirts of the small borough of Võnnu in Tartu County. The investment would have cost him €120,000 at the time.

"I applied for a grid connection […] And the response was that I could connect, but the price would be €5.6 million plus VAT. I also had to pay €1,600 within a week for them to calculate the exact cost," Solba said.

The experience left him feeling as though Elektrilvi's parent company Eesti Energia feared competition and did not want these solar farms, despite previously encouraging people to build them and advertising the availability of government subsidies.

"The other thought, of course, was that some official there wanted a bribe. That they'd simply quote an outrageous price initially and then, if you did someone there a favor, perhaps the price would come down to something reasonable," he said.

Another example involves Ruve Visnapuu, whose work involves managing apartment associations and providing them with technical consulting services, among other things. In 2022, he was working with an apartment building in Soinaste, Kambja Municipality where residents wanted to use the building's roof to generate solar power and feed surplus electricity into the grid. Toward the end of the summer, a grid connection application was submitted on behalf of the apartment association of the townhouse-style building, which was built in 2016. The plan was to install up to 30 kilowatts of solar generation capacity on the roof.

"The quote was €5.6 million plus VAT. The reason given was that the regional substation's capacity to feed generated electricity into the transmission grid needed to be increased," Visnapuu added.

"Your bills and profits are already pretty substantial, yet ordinary apartment association members are supposed to rebuild all your power lines and substations for you. It seems like nonsense," Visnapuu said, criticizing the energy company.

Unsurprisingly, none of the building's residents were willing to pay such a sum.

The third case takes us to Märjamaa where businessman Marek Kosubenko, who works in shipbuilding and real estate and already had experience with solar energy, was confronted with a colossal grid connection quote.

"My brother and I were planning a grid connection for our rural property and since we'd already acquired a solar farm in Märjamaa in 2020, we wanted 50 kilowatts of capacity in both directions, so we submitted an application. The response was that the estimated cost of the work required for our project would be €6,395,000, excluding VAT," Kosubenko said.

"That was the end of that for us. Why should we go along with such a farce? There's no point. The payback period for our little power plant would be, I don't know, 100 or 200 years," Kosubenko added.

In the fourth case, however, the quote sent to the customer reached truly astronomical proportions. Peeter Sööt, who works in car restoration and repair, owns an old manor-era watermill in Õisu, Viljandi County, where the previous owner had already installed a small hydroelectric power generation system.

Power lines. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"I needed a little more generation capacity because during the spring floods, the water level would rise so high that I was generating a couple of kilowatts more than my existing capacity allowed. I thought the easiest way to resolve the situation would be to apply for three kilowatts of additional capacity, giving myself a little leeway," Sööt said.

"The response went beyond even the realms of satire or comedy for me. The initial quote was €24.7 million, or roughly €30 million including VAT. That's €10 million per kilowatt. At energy prices at the time, I reckon the payback period would have been somewhere around 200,000 years. I thought that might be a bit long and perhaps not worth it," Sööt said.

In Sööt's view, there is no point in issuing unrealistic quotes that no one would agree to anyway.

"It's the same in my own line of work. Whatever job I'm doing, I don't give someone a quote that's absurd to the nth degree. I simply tell them that I can't do it, don't want to do it, don't have the time or whatever the reason may be, or that I just won't do the job, and that's that. I don't literally mock people by throwing unrealistic figures at them."

While "Pealtnägija" cannot untangle every detail of each case, one recurring pattern is that of multimillion-euro connection fees that effectively deter prospective customers.

"Pealtnägija" also approached Elektrilevi to establish how many cases there have been in which grid connection quotes issued to microgenerators or small-scale electricity producers have been absurdly high from the perspective of an ordinary citizen.

Elektrilevi management board member Rudolf Penu said that since the beginning of 2024, a total of 87 grid connection quotes exceeding €1 million had been issued to electricity producers.

"Considering that Elektrilevi issues around 20 grid connection quotes every day, you can't say these constitute the vast majority," Penu said.

On last week's show, Elektrilevi's head of connection services, Marii Uduvee, said around 10 quotes had been issued erroneously in Kõrveküla near Tartu. This raises the question of whether those 87 quotes have been verified and whether any of them were similarly erroneous, astronomical quotes. According to Penu, that possibility certainly cannot be ruled out.

"Such errors do indeed occur. When these situations arise, which is regrettable, we contact customers and see what can be corrected," the Elektrilevi representative added.

According to Penu, however, there is little hope of a plan being implemented in the near future that would allow all household microgenerators to connect to the grid for a minimal fee or entirely free of charge. Doing so would require an additional €50 million annually on top of the money already being invested in network upgrades.

Penu pointed out that the situation was already critical at around 68 of the 135 regional substations.

"Unless you're an ordinary household consumer, it's very likely that you can no longer connect to the grid, or at the very least, doing so would require a very thorough analysis. And the situation is actually getting worse with each passing month."

"What we can certainly do, and what we are doing, is ensuring that there is a logical explanation behind these large figures, so that customers aren't simply presented with a huge number without any further justification," Penu pledged.

Elektrilevi logo. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

World.title: Finding purpose in rescue — the Saudi women saving abandoned animals
World.content:
RIYADH: By day, Manal Al-Assaf works as a partnerships consultant, while Faee Al-Malaq is a data analyst and an MBA student. Outside those roles, the two dedicate their time to rescuing abandoned animals, finding them warm homes in Riyadh and encouraging others to join their cause.

For both women, volunteering at Rahma Animal Rescue Shelter in Riyadh has become an act of self-fulfillment, a way of finding true companionship with animals and an opportunity to advocate for greater animal welfare in the Kingdom and worldwide.

An animal lover and pet owner who has always bonded with animals more than humans, Al-Assaf only started her animal rescue journey this year after seeing a Reddit post about an abandoned rabbit trapped on the street in a birdcage.

The rabbit had a broken bone, burns and fleas, and was severely malnourished. Unable to ignore his condition, Al-Assaf contacted the woman who posted the pictures, collected the rabbit and took him to a veterinarian. She then cared for him at home until he recovered and could be adopted and named him Iris after the national flower of Palestine, to symbolize his resilience.

Among the proposed ambassadors are Shams, a sociable rabbit, and Romana, a dog who was shot but remains affectionate towards people. (Supplied)

“I realized through him that really every life is worth saving. There’s not a single life that doesn’t deserve to exist. I don’t even kill bugs. That’s how dedicated I am to this. And because of him, I decided that I wanted to start my own shelter,” Al-Assaf told Arab News.

She initially planned to establish her own nonprofit organization to rescue different species, including cats, dogs, rabbits, birds and others that are harder to care for in general shelters. However, after meeting the founder of Rahma, she decided to volunteer and contribute her ideas and experience, hoping to extend its role beyond rescuing and treating animals and turn it into a community and advocacy space for animal welfare.

For Al-Malaq, animal rescue has been part of her life for 12 years. Her first rescue came at 18, when she found a cat with an injured eye beneath a car. With financial help from her grandparents, she arranged the cat’s treatment and eventually found it a warm home.

She continued to rescue cats and dogs and search for adopters independently for years, but the financial and emotional demands eventually led her to stop for three years.

“When I started here, it was the beginning of changing my life, because I had stopped rescuing animals for three years. But then I came back with Rahma. They gave me a lot. I wasn’t living through a good phase of my life. But when I came back, I came back to joy and peace,” she said.

Al-Malaq initially volunteered to care for the animals before taking responsibility for adoption management as well as coordinating volunteers. Al-Assaf describes her as “a jack of all trades.”

Among the animals Al-Malaq has cared for is Hope, a husky found in August at an open market in Riyadh, who had stopped eating and was in poor condition. For six months, she devoted herself to his recovery, feeding him, holding him and helping him regain his strength.

“I spent a lot of time, around six months, holding him. He was around 16 kg. I started having back injuries from holding him, but I didn’t care about any of this. I was hoping that he would survive. That’s why, after all, I named him Hope.”

Hope has been at the shelter for two years. Several potential adopters have been interviewed but none were considered suitable to meet a husky’s needs.

Al-Malaq says finding responsible owners is among the most demanding aspects of rescue work. She interviews applicants, assesses their ability to care for an animal and matches them with suitable pets. Despite her attachment to Hope, she hopes he will eventually find a permanent home.

“I am so passionate about giving more, and whenever I’m tired, I come back. I cannot stop,” she said, adding the experience has also helped her overcome social anxiety and develop confidence in dealing with people.

Beyond her own involvement, Al-Malaq is especially interested in encouraging young people to volunteer. She explained: “The young volunteers are the future. I want to influence them as much as I can because they are the future. If you invest in them, they will do great things. They will do good for people, and they will continue to influence more people. So, if you do all of this work with them, the future will be good.”

For Al-Assaf, volunteering also offers an exciting opportunity to bring her creative interests into animal welfare. She hopes to transform Rahma from a rescue shelter and veterinary clinic into a community space that brings people closer to animals through education, art and social activities.

The shelter already hosts a monthly cat cafe, where visitors can enjoy fresh coffee surrounded by rescued cats and potentially adopt them. With the support of partners and donors, she hopes to organize book clubs, art workshops and crochet circles where visitors can socialize with rescued animals and potentially adopt them.

She also plans to introduce educational school visits featuring selected rescued animals as ambassadors, teaching children about animal welfare, biology and conservation. Among the proposed ambassadors are Shams, a sociable rabbit, and Romana, a dog who was shot but remains affectionate towards people.

Other plans include a children’s book inspired by the animals’ rescue stories and a fundraising campaign offering hand-drawn pet portraits by Al-Assaf to donors or adopters.

A portrait sketch by Alassaf Of Shams, the rabbit animal ambassador. (Supplied)

Al-Assaf continues to encourage the establishment of more rescue organizations. She said: “The more organizations that come up and do the same thing we do, the more we see it as help, not competition. We cannot physically take every rescue case. It is very difficult and very financially draining. We need all the help we can get.”

The shelter relies on donations to support veterinary treatment, daily care and its trap-neuter-release program for stray animals.

Rahma is also on a mission to offer a symbolic adoption initiative through which donors could receive photographs and videos documenting the recovery of individual animals. Donors are also welcome to visit the animals in situ, so they can enjoy seeing them without the responsibility of taking them home.

Both Al-Assaf and Al-Malaq also call for the commercialization of animals to be stopped, emphasizing the health risks breeding can cause.

“Pay attention to the stray dogs (and cats) that we rescue. I know they’re mixed breeds, but they’re so special. People pay a lot of money because they want a particular breed, a poodle, a German shepherd, a husky, whatever. I always tell people to please adopt rescues, mixed breeds. They are the kindest, sweetest, most loving animals. They will give you a lot of hugs,” Al-Assaf said.

“At the end of the day, we only live one life, so why would you want to leave it without doing some good in the world?”

World.title: Saudi performing arts tour brings theater, traditional arts to Buraidah
World.content:
BURAIDAH: The Theater and Performing Arts Commission’s traveling tour, “Nuhyeeh wa Nuhayyeeh,” arrived in Buraidah on Wednesday, bringing live performances and interactive cultural experiences to Al-Noor Park.

The Arabic campaign slogan plays on words to convey the message: “We salute the arts and bring them to life.”

The opening evening featured traditional performances alongside contemporary puppet shows, highlighting the diversity of Saudi Arabia’s cultural heritage.

The main stage hosted two theatrical productions, “The Family,” a comedy exploring different perspectives on performing arts within a Saudi household, and “The Artist,” which follows a young man’s journey of artistic self-discovery.

Visitors are also invited to look deeper into the creative processes behind the theatrical productions, through interactive experiences such as exploring the costumes, props, puppetry and other backstage activities.

The initiative reflects the commission’s continued commitment to making performing arts and cultural experiences more accessible and enjoyable across the Kingdom. The tour, which started this month, blends traditional theater and folk performances into contemporary public spaces across six Saudi cities.

Running in Buraidah from Nov. 25-28, the four-day event features a diverse program, including nine interactive activities designed for visitors of all ages. This is the tour’s third stop, following Riyadh and Dammam, with shows scheduled for Hail, Taif and Jeddah before the end of the year.

World.title: French woman on trial for IS propaganda says ‘ashamed’
World.content:
PARIS: A French woman accused of becoming a propagandist for the Daesh group in Syria told a Paris court on Thursday she was “ashamed” of her actions.

Emilie Konig, a mother-of-five who is now facing up to 30 years imprisonment, is on UN and US blacklists of dangerous militants, accused of encouraging other women to join the militant group.

The case has been closely watched in France, which has been rocked by a series of militant attacks in recent years, including devastating Daesh shootings and suicide bombings in Paris in 2015 that killed 130 people.

Wearing a mustard jacket and appearing nervous, Konig, 41, apologized to her children, her mother and the “French nation.”

“I know the impact the jihadosphere may have had. I’m really ashamed,” she said at the start of her four-day trial for joining the group.

“People are judging me for things, but that person — I no longer feel that they’re there,” she said, arguing she had changed.

Konig, who hails from the Brittany city of Lorient, left two children behind in France to travel to Syria in 2012 to marry an Daesh member one year into the country’s civil war, remaining there for 10 years.

She lived under the so-called caliphate that Daesh proclaimed in 2014 across swathes of Syria and neighboring Iraq, appearing in the extremist group’s propaganda videos.

Kurdish-led forces fighting the militants detained her in late 2017, before France repatriated her from a detention camp in 2022.

Three of her children, born in Syria in 2015 and 2017, have also returned to France.

Prosecutors accuse her of acting as a “true icon” of the extremist group, who wielded considerable influence online, according to the charge sheet.

Her lawyer Emmanuel Daoud said Konig initially “found in Daesh a sense of validation that she had never known” after being “assaulted, abused, beaten throughout her childhood and adolescence.”

But since returning to France she has become a “model prisoner,” determined to become deradicalized, he added.

Her eldest child, who is now an adult, is expected to speak at the trial in her favor.

But the French region now in charge of her three younger children born in Syria has accused her of psychological and physical abuse against them, including subjecting them to atrocities such as public beheadings.

World.title: Saudi Arabia calls for continued human oversight over AI advances at UN
World.content:
RIYADH: Saudi Arabia wants to ensure human oversight remains a fundamental principle in the use of artificial intelligence, and seeks greater transparency and precautionary measures for AI’s safe and responsible application.

Fares Al-Otaibi, acting head of Saudi Arabia’s permanent mission to the UN in New York, delivered this message on Wednesday during a Security Council open debate titled “Conflict resolution in an era of rapid technological change.”

Al-Otaibi emphasized the need to clearly disclose the capabilities, operational limitations and potential risks of AI systems.

He added that rapid advances in military technologies require adherence to international humanitarian law, the protection of civilians and continued human oversight and accountability.

The debate, which began on Tuesday, examined the implications of emerging technologies for international peace and security, including their potential to strengthen conflict prevention, mediation, peacekeeping operations and civilian protection.

Al-Otaibi also warned against terrorist organizations exploiting emerging technologies to develop their military capabilities, urging international vigilance against this growing threat.

He called for stronger international cooperation, capacity building and the exchange of expertise to enable countries to benefit from technological advances without compromising their safe and responsible use.

The Kingdom has been committed to promoting the responsible use of emerging technologies through international cooperation and national initiatives.

In May 2025, Saudi Arabia’s Presidency of State Security and the UN Counter-Terrorism Centre organized a roundtable in Riyadh addressing the exploitation of emerging technologies by terrorist organizations, particularly in financing their activities.

The Kingdom has been a longstanding supporter of the center, which was established in 2011 through an initial $10 million Saudi contribution to advance international counterterrorism cooperation.

In September, the Kingdom co-hosted UNESCO’s fourth Global Forum on AI Ethics in Riyadh, bringing together 200 international speakers and 60 ministers and delegation heads.

It also presented its National AI Risk Management Framework for mitigating and monitoring AI-related risks.

World.title: Asian countries brace for tariff hike as US threatens fresh round of levies
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A host of Asian nations on Thursday protested to Washington as others pushed for more tariff negotiations, after the US announced plans to impose a fresh raft of duties set to impact a dozen countries in the region.

The Office of the US Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed new levies ranging between 15 to 35 percent on imports from 14 countries: China, the EU, India, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Vietnam, Taiwan and Bangladesh.

The new US tariffs are expected to hit Asia the hardest, with China facing the potential maximum rate of up to 40 percent, followed by Vietnam at up to 35 percent, when accounting for previous trade agreements.

The proposed measures do not have a clear timeline of implementation, and have to go through rounds of public consultation and potential hearings, with the listed countries also expected to hold more talks with Washington to lower the tariff rate.

According to the USTR, the 14 economies implemented acts, policies and practices “which create, sustain, or contribute to structural excess capacity and production,” leading to unreasonable burdens and restrictions on US commerce.

India, for example, was deemed unreasonable for its “industrial plans to expand manufacturing” and “failure to address global excess capacity and production,” among other things.

India, which could lower its tariff to 17 percent by reaching a deal or pay 25 percent without one, insisted it “does not have structural excess capacity in any sector” but “remains committed to working closely” with the US toward an “early conclusion” of a bilateral deal, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry said in a statement.

Tokyo, which faced similar accusations and more, has also protested to the US over its plans to impose a 15 percent levy on Japanese imports.

“Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity,” Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said during a regular press briefing on Thursday.

“It is regrettable that the US announced proposed measures targeting Japan, and we have already conveyed that view to the US side.”

China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said that the “issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist” and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation.

“Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests. Relevant issues should be resolved through consultation on the basis of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit,” he told reporters at a weekly briefing.

Singapore, faced with a maximum proposed tariff rate of 20 percent that could be lowered to 10 percent with a deal, has rejected the basis of the tariffs.

“Singapore disagrees with the USTR’s findings, and we are very disappointed with the proposed actions against Singapore,” the country’s Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said in a statement.

The city-state plans to continue engaging with US trade officials to urge them to “reconsider its proposed actions” and “to explore ways to reduce the tariff,” insisting that the USTR’s findings did not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.

Other countries, like Indonesia and Thailand, responded more positively to the US announcement.

“When assessing the impact of US tariff measures, it is crucial not only to look at the tariff rate imposed on Thailand, but also to compare it with competing countries exporting similar goods to the US market,” said Lalida Periswiwatana, deputy spokeswoman for the prime minister’s office, as reported by Nikkei Asia.

Thailand’s proposed rate of 18 percent, lower than several key trade competitors like Vietnam, India, China and Singapore, serves as “a key factor in preserving the competitiveness of Thai goods in the US market, as well as maintaining Thailand’s attractiveness as a manufacturing base for export,” she was quoted as saying.

Similarly, Haryo Limanseto, a spokesman for Indonesia’s Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs, said the 18 percent proposed rate on its goods still leaves a “significant tariff differential” compared with competing nations, which will give a “comparative advantage” for Indonesian companies.

This fresh round of tariffs was “completely expected,” said Anupam Manur, a professor of Economics at the Takshashila Institution in Bengaluru, adding that this was the Trump administration’s plan B after the Supreme Court ruled that his previously announced tariffs were illegal.

“The proposed rates mostly recreate last year's deals. Asia was always going to be the target. That is where the US runs its largest bilateral deficits, and it is where supply chains leaving China have moved since 2018,” Manur told Arab News.

Vietnam is considered the most vulnerable to the proposed tariffs, as the US buys one-third of its exports, followed by Cambodia and Bangladesh, as they rely on low-margin garments and footwear already subject to high US duties.

“China has less to lose at the margin than the headline suggests, because its direct exports to the US have already shrunk sharply,” Manur said.

“India is in an awkward middle: 25 percent is the second-highest rate on the list without a deal, which makes the trade deal urgent rather than just good to have.”

World.title: A nation that keeps building, with the citizen first
World.content:
On Tuesday in Riyadh, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman chaired the Cabinet session that approved Saudi Arabia’s state general budget for 2027.

It was not a routine approval of figures. It was a renewed declaration of a state’s confidence in itself, in its people and in its future at a time when wars surround the region and volatility shakes the entire world economy.

The crown prince summed it up in a single sentence: “The budget for the fiscal year 2027 embodies the government’s commitment to placing the elevation of the nation and the interest of the citizen at the forefront of its priorities and preserving the gains of development for this generation and for generations to come.”

The budget sets expenditure at SR1.39 trillion ($370.7 billion) against revenues of SR1.2 trillion. The expected deficit is SR190 billion, or 3.6 percent of gross domestic product, down from an estimated 4.9 percent in 2026.

That deficit is not a weakness but a deliberate choice. As Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan explained, the government accepts a deficit when the economic and social return on spending exceeds the cost of financing it. The estimates are also conservative: actual revenues have exceeded budget estimates for six consecutive years, he told the government press conference.

Al-Jadaan was clear that there is no ceiling on the Kingdom’s ability to finance its military and security needs Faisal Trad

After an oil-driven dip this year, the economy is expected to rebound strongly in 2027, with growth of nearly 11 percent, powered by higher oil production and the continued healthy expansion of non-oil activities. Inflation is forecast at just 2.3 percent, while global inflation exceeds 4.7 percent.

Al-Jadaan affirmed that “the citizen comes at the forefront of the government’s priorities.” Investing in people, improving quality of life and creating jobs, he said, are not slogans but commitments reflected in where the money goes.

The figures bear him out. SR544 billion is allocated to education, health, social development and municipal services: SR256 billion for health and social development, SR195 billion for education and SR93 billion for municipal services.

In other words, nearly 40 percent of the budget goes directly to what citizens and residents touch every day: their child’s school, their family’s hospital, their neighborhood street and support for those who are eligible.

Security, the foundation on which all development stands, receives SR263 billion, up on this year. Al-Jadaan was clear that there is no ceiling on the Kingdom’s ability to finance its military and security needs, to defend the nation and protect citizens and residents alike.

The minister offered a figure every citizen should pause at: non-oil activities have reached their highest share of GDP in the Kingdom’s history, at 57.7 percent.

This is the transformation Vision 2030 set out to achieve and it is happening now. Non-oil revenues have grown from SR166 billion in 2015 to SR505 billion in 2025 and now cover about 37 percent of government spending, compared with roughly 16 percent a decade ago.

Government reserves have risen by about 20 percent since 2022, with no current need to draw on them. Government deposits at the central bank stand at SR399 billion, foreign reserve assets at about SR1.7 trillion and nonperforming loans remain below 1 percent. Al-Jadaan called this resilience “extraordinary.”

Two-thirds of Saudi scholarship students now attend world-leading universities and more than 100,000 gifted students have won hundreds of regional and international awards.

The 2027 budget is a covenant that education, health, housing and employment are not items on a table but the citizen’s right Faisal Trad

Deaths linked to infectious diseases have halved and coverage has reached about 95 percent of the population. In 2027, the transfer of health cluster employees to the Health Holding Company will be completed.

In the first nine months of 2026, 90,836 Saudi families moved into their first homes. Homeownership has reached 66.24 percent, ahead of the interim Vision 2030 target and on course for 70 percent by 2030.

Some 2.7 million Saudis now work in the private sector. Unemployment among Saudis has fallen from 12.3 percent at Vision 2030’s launch to about 7.2 percent and women’s participation in the labor market has reached 35 percent. With 1.83 million small and medium-sized enterprises, ours is an economy of young entrepreneurs, not of large companies alone.

In 2025, the Kingdom welcomed 123 million tourists, more than 30 million of them from abroad, who spent over SR303 billion.

More than 97 percent of government services are digital, placing the Kingdom among the world’s top 10. At the World Smart City Awards 2026 in Barcelona this month, the Riyadh Infrastructure Projects Center and the Riyadh Metro were each ranked among the top four in their categories.

The Public Investment Fund’s assets have grown from SR720 billion in 2015 to more than SR3.4 trillion, with SR750 billion injected into the domestic economy over five years.

Preparations for the 2027 Hajj are well underway, with more than 520 entities from over 150 countries taking part in this month’s Hajj Conference and Exhibition in Jeddah.

The greatest achievement was not a figure but a real test. When the regional crisis erupted on Feb. 28 and the eastern ports were almost entirely closed, the government and the private sector redirected logistics in under 48 hours, shifting shipping to Red Sea ports, railways and northern crossings. Trucks leaving Jeddah Islamic Port rose from 2,000 a day to 10,000.

No commodity ran out, prices held steady and citizens did not feel fear. The Saned program was reactivated to protect Saudi jobs, government dues were made payable in flexible instalments and loans were rescheduled through the Public Investment Fund and the National Development Fund. That is what a strong state looks like.

For the citizen, this means a better job, an easier path to a home, a better school and hospital, support that reaches those who deserve it, and an economy that no longer shakes when the oil price does. For the resident, it means security, quality services, an open business environment and respect for their culture. The minister confirmed that basic care for residents is part of the government’s priorities. For future generations, it means continuity. “The Vision is the north star for the Kingdom,” Al-Jadaan said. Its objectives are fixed; only the mechanisms change.

Budget 2027 is not simply SR1.39 trillion to be spent. It is a covenant that education, health, housing and employment are not items on a table but the citizen’s right and that the Kingdom will remain a state that builds in time of war, grows in time of crisis and advances while others retreat.

As the crown prince said, the third phase of Vision 2030 “builds on the reforms and achievements accomplished during the previous two phases.” We have passed the phase of construction and entered the phase of harvest. And what is coming is greater.

World.title: White Friday and payday in Saudi Arabia: The behavioral economics of spending
World.content:
RIYADH: With Saudi public sector employees receiving their salaries a day before White Friday, this year’s shopping event presents an interesting test of consumer spending habits and the psychology behind purchasing decisions.

Known as Black Friday in the West, the annual shopping event takes place the day after Thanksgiving in the US. E-commerce platform Souq.com introduced it to the Middle East in 2014 as White Friday, recognizing the religious and cultural significance of Friday among Muslims in the Arab world.

Bassim Allaheeb, a behavioral economist and faculty member at Majmaah University, told Arab News that paying salaries on Nov. 26 could trigger what behavioral economists call mental accounting.

“The availability of money in one’s account may make an individual perceive it as an amount readily available to spend on White Friday,” he said.

Allaheeb highlighted the anchoring effect as one of the marketing strategies that brands use to attract customers, when retailers prominently display a product’s original price to establish a mental reference point.

“Research has demonstrated that the first number we read psychologically influences our assessment of the subsequent number,” he said.

Beyond influencing consumers’ perception of a product’s value, brands also put pressure on how much time consumers have to consider whether they actually need it, capitalizing on the psychological effects of scarcity and urgency.

“Some retailers use phrases such as ‘the offer ends in three hours’ or ‘only four items remaining,’ or even restrict the quantity available to each customer. Displaying such restrictions may suggest that the product represents an opportunity not to be missed.”

Even a product's desirability can be influenced by other consumers’ purchasing decisions, with brands capitalizing on the fear of missing out —FOMO — and our inclination to conform to social norms.

“Phrases such as ‘purchased 400 times’ or ‘bestseller,’ along with star ratings and the number of reviews, encourage purchasing decisions so that we do not feel different from others,” Allaheeb said.

But does the psychological pleasure associated with shopping during seasonal discounts stem from acquiring the product itself or securing a bargain?

“Seeing discounts may alleviate the pain associated with the price, meaning that the moment of securing a bargain may be more pleasurable than consuming the product itself later,” he said.

He referred to Nobel Prize-winning economist Richard Thaler’s distinction between acquisition utility, the value derived from acquiring a product, and transaction utility, the satisfaction of securing a favorable price.

“Some individuals may resort to shopping to improve their mood or alleviate psychological stress in the short term, but this behavior can become problematic when it involves borrowing, or when purchases come at the expense of essential goods, savings or potential investments.”

While discounts may give consumers a sense of saving money, instalment services may give them a sense of being able to afford more.

Amid concerns over inflation and rising living costs, Allaheeb challenged the notion that instalment services enhance consumers’ purchasing power.

“Buy now, pay later services do not increase purchasing power, as they simply divide the amount over a specified period of time. Such services can be beneficial if the purchase was already planned and falls within the consumer’s budget,” he said.

Otherwise, consumers may fall into what Allaheeb described as a threefold trap: “The illusion of saving, the illusion of securing a bargain and the reduction of the pain of paying.”

However, three polls conducted by social media platform Jodel across Saudi Arabia between Nov. 11 and 13 suggest there is scepticism and hesitation about the shopping season.

Some 48.1 percent indicated that they would not spend anything. In a separate poll, 36.2 percent said they would buy only if the offer was good enough, 33.5 percent were merely browsing, and 22 percent distrusted the offers. Only 8.3 percent had planned their purchases.

Misleading discounts were cited by 42.6 percent as the main reason for backing out of a purchase, almost identical to the 42.9 percent who said they did not need the product.

“There are offers all year. I only buy something if I want it. It’s not logical to buy just because they said it’s an offer,” one Jodel user in Jeddah commented.

Fashion and beauty were the most popular shopping category for consumers at 51 percent, followed by electronics at 32 percent and appliances and furniture at 17 percent.

For Lena Baabdullah, a 29-year-old mother of two, the appeal of this year’s shopping season extends beyond White Friday, with payday, the school holidays and preparations for Ramadan and Eid influencing her interest in seasonal discounts.

“I haven’t looked up White Friday offers in the years before, but since this season comes close to Ramadan and Eid, I have some items ready in my basket,” she told Arab News.

“While I enjoy shopping, I believe hard-earned money should be spent wisely,” Baabdullah said, adding that she only shopped from brands and online platforms she regularly purchased from, even outside the sales season.

World.title: Seven killed in Mexico in shootout with gunmen
World.content:
MEXICO CITY: Seven suspected gang members were killed in a shootout with the Mexican army in a turbulent region in the Latin American country, where criminal organizations are vying for control of drug trafficking routes, authorities said Thursday.

The defense ministry said those killed were members of Cartel de Los Reyes, a faction of the larger Carteles Unidos organization that the United States has classified as a foreign terrorist group.

Ten people were arrested and more than 30 weapons seized, the ministry said in a statement.

Army personnel were “attacked with firearms” by alleged members of the criminal organization while patrolling a rural area on the border between the states of Michoacan and Jalisco, according to the ministry.

The suspected leader of Cartel de Los Reyes was killed in September by Mexican soldiers, a month after his predecessor was arrested.

Michoacan is a leading exporter of avocados and a producer of limes.

But authorities say farmers face constant extortion by organized crime groups.

Several criminal organizations, including the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and La Familia Michoacana, operate in the state, vying for control of drug trafficking routes.

World.title: 10 French nationals sentenced to prison for joining ISIS
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Karkh Criminal Court sentenced on Thursday 10 French nationals to prison for joining the terrorist group ISIS.

Eight received life imprisonment, which equates to a 20-year term under Iraqi law, and two received 15-year prison sentences.

The 10 men are part of 47 French nationals transferred to Iraq from northeast Syria in 2025, whose trials in Baghdad began in September 2026 under Iraq’s anti-terrorism law.

Thursday’s rulings bring the number of convicted French citizens in this group to 26, as 16 had previously been convicted in earlier hearings. Another 10 defendants had their verdicts postponed to a later date.

Representatives from the French Embassy in Iraq and defense lawyers attended the hearings.

Iraq prosecutes ISIS members under its anti-terrorism statutes regardless of whether their alleged activities took place in Iraq or neighboring Syria.

France has repatriated hundreds of family members of jihadists while largely declining to bring back adult men accused of involvement.

Rights groups have criticized the pace and due process of Iraq’s terrorism trials, while Iraqi authorities continue processing thousands of detainees transferred from Syria.

World.title: Iraq in discussions with Apple to activate Apple Pay
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi authorities are holding official talks with Apple to introduce Apple Pay in Iraq as part of a broader push to expand digital payment services.

Head of the Communications and Media Commission (CMC) Baligh Abu-Kallal said in early November that Iraq is negotiating with Apple over launching Apple Pay, privacy policies, and gaming sector cooperation.

In August, Iraq accredited Apple as a verified digital platform, covering services such as the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Podcasts, Apple Arcade, and Apple Ads under local regulations.

Abu-Kallal stated that launching Apple Pay depends on completing technical, legal, and financial procedures, local news outlet Shafaq News reported.

Iraqi banks have also signaled interest in digital wallet expansion amid wider banking modernization and digital payment reforms.

Earlier in July, an Iraqi government source mentioned that the committee in charge of activating Apple Pay services met with Apple’s regional managers to make the service accessible in Iraq.

The initiative is part of the Iraqi government’s efforts to enhance the electronic payment infrastructure and boost the adoption of modern technology, thereby fostering financial inclusion and advancing digital transformation.

Iraq aims to make Apple Pay available to users, in accordance with the government’s strategy to expand the online payment sector and support the transition to a digital economy.

World.title: Iraq expands digital services for Iraqi Airways
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Transport has expanded digital services for Iraqi Airways to facilitate passenger travel and reduce airport congestion.

Travelers can complete check-in procedures and issue their electronic boarding passes online before arriving at the airport.

Passengers can also choose their preferred seats in advance during booking or check-in.

Users can now electronically change their flight schedules and destinations without visiting a sales office.

The airline enhanced its electronic reservation and online payment systems for both domestic and international flights.

A new pricing structure lets passengers select different fare classes with varying baggage allowances and modification terms.

Passengers can use these services through the Iraqi Airways official website or via the mobile app.

The step is part of the company’s strategy to grow its digital capabilities, improve passenger experience, and stay up with the latest standards in the aviation industry.

The service generally opens for check-in between 48 and 24 hours before the scheduled flight departure and closes up to two hours prior to takeoff.

World.title: Iraq’s judiciary rules that Baghdad can deploy forces along all borders
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the federal government in Baghdad can deploy troops to secure all international borders, including those in Iraqi Kurdistan.

The decision backs Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s push to assert central control over border crossings and oil fields across the country.

The court affirmed federal jurisdiction over international borders, customs oversight, and the auditing of oil and gas fields, while allowing shared management with regional authorities and provinces.

Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal takeovers of Kurdish-run border crossings and disputed oil fields following an oil smuggling investigation. The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) described the moves as constitutional violations and military threats, calling instead for dialogue.

The crackdown, which also targets militias with ties to Iran, is seen by analysts as part of Zaidi’s larger effort to consolidate power. As a result, the Supreme Judicial Council has called on all parties to uphold the 2005 constitution.

A day earlier, al-Zaidi ordered federal authorities to take control of all border crossings in Iraqi Kurdistan and directed the Oil Ministry to manage oilfields under Kurdish security control in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salah al-Din, and Nineveh provinces.

The KRG was instructed to approve crude oil and petroleum product exports only through the federal Oil Ministry.

The directives followed an investigation into smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company and a wider campaign against illicit oil networks—including alleged smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar linked to the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group, which denied the accusation.

World.title: Iraq presses OPEC+ to raise oil output
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is pushing OPEC+ to raise its estimated crude oil production capacity ahead of the group’s scheduled meeting on November 29 to set 2027 output quotas.

Baghdad rejected preliminary findings from OPEC+’s independent capacity review—conducted by consultant DeGolyer and MacNaughton—which put Iraq’s capacity at 4.9 million barrels per day, according to Reuters.

OPEC+’s review estimated Iraq’s sustainable production capacity at approximately 4.9 million barrels per day. However, Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair contends that Iraq can achieve a capacity of 5.2 million barrels per day.

Additionally, there are broader efforts within Iraq aimed at increasing this figure even further to support a larger production allowance.

Iraq’s current OPEC+ production limit stands at 4.43 million barrels per day. In OPEC’s November report, Iraq reported October output at 4.88 million barrels per day, while OPEC’s external secondary sources estimated it lower at 4.49 million barrels per day.

Capacity figures serve as a key benchmark for calibrating member quotas in 2027. Higher capacity estimates strengthen a member’s case to pump more oil or claim a larger share of group output.

To restore its economy and meet its financial obligations, Baghdad is looking for more oil earnings. Iraq threatened to leave OPEC earlier in 2026 due to the capacity assessment, but it subsequently dropped the threat when the UAE left OPEC and OPEC+ in May 2026 to increase output.

World.title: Iraq foils oil smuggling operations in Dhi Qar, Kirkuk
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi National Security Service (INSS) announced on Wednesday that it foiled oil smuggling operations across Dhi Qar and Kirkuk provinces.

The actions are part of a wider government crackdown led by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi against illicit oil trade and pipeline tampering.

Security forces uncovered an illegal tap on an oil pipeline in the al-Luhays area, which is administratively part of Basra province. Three hoses connected to illicitly installed valves were siphoning crude oil into tanker trucks.

With judicial authorization, INSS units intercepted and seized a vehicle illegally modified with side openings to offload fuel. Kerosene was found inside its tank, and a suspect was arrested.

Earlier in the week, Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council reported an organized crude oil smuggling ring using tankers near the Dhi Qar–Basra border, leading to detentions of a suspect and several Energy Police officers.

A committee completed fieldwork investigating alleged smuggling of Kirkuk oil through Iraqi Kurdistan toward Iran and Afghanistan.

The operations follow recent security deployments in Jurf al-Sakhar, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, in Babil province and arrests related to pipeline breaches in Najaf.

World.title: Kata’ib Hezbollah retains core Jurf Al Sakhar stronghold and absorbs 2,000 fighters into state payroll
World.content:
Bahjdad (IraqiNews.com) – Five days after federal security forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar (Jurf al-Nasr), informed sources revealed to Al-Mada newspaper—in a report on Wednesday, November 25, 2026—that the military operation has produced no substantive change to the balance of power on the ground.

According to the report, Kata’ib Hezbollah retains full control over the town center and its vital surrounding perimeter, including the areas of Abd Ways, Al-Farsiya, Al-Hujayr, and Al-Fadhiliya.

No federal security forces have entered this core perimeter—referred to by insiders as the “Kata’ib Hezbollah Square”—and the newly inaugurated joint control headquarters remains situated outside Jurf al-Sakhar’s administrative boundaries.

Rather than retreating, the faction utilized the official deployment announcement to absorb more than 2,000 of its previously off-roster fighters into the official payroll of the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF/Hashd al-Shaabi) under the 72nd and 79th Brigades, shifting their financial burden onto the state budget while securing institutional cover and legal immunity.

Field accounts indicate that the federal deployment touted by Baghdad was largely confined to peripheral sectors and routine troop rotations:

Iraqi Army: Deployment was restricted to the 38th Brigade of the 10th Division along the northwestern edge of Jurf al-Sakhar toward Anbar’s Amiriyat al-Fallujah axis and the canal linking Lake Habbaniyah to Lake Razzaza west of Karbala.

Federal Police: The only state force maintaining direct contact with Kata’ib Hezbollah zones simply rotated existing positions, replacing the 16th Brigade with the 17th and 11th Brigades without advancing into faction-held territory.

Counter-Terrorism Service (CTS): No CTS units deployed inside Jurf al-Sakhar, aside from a Karbala provincial regiment stationed at the garrison camp in Musayyib district outside the subdistrict’s borders.

Meanwhile, informed sources noted that Kata’ib Hezbollah leveraged the publicized “withdrawal” to execute a wide-scale military redeployment, transferring substantial weaponry and equipment to establish new positions in western Anbar and western Karbala in anticipation of a potential renewed military confrontation between the United States and Iran, while Iranian and Houthi advisors remain active inside Jurf al-Sakhar.

Political observers cited by Al-Mada suggest Tehran and allied factions orchestrated a nominal concession in northern Babylon—long targeted by Washington as a financial artery for Iran—in order to open a new security and political front against the Kurdistan Region.

According to these assessments, Tehran is pressing Baghdad to obtain a list of Iranian Kurdish opposition members residing in Kurdistan and relocate them to Samawah in southern Iraq to neutralize their potential involvement in any U.S.-Iran conflict.

This geopolitical maneuvering coincides with Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi’s announcement on Tuesday of heightened anti-smuggling measures around the Kurdistan Region’s perimeter, alongside Erbil’s denial of rumors regarding federal troop deployments inside the region or a return to the 1991 “Blue Line.”

Simultaneously, allies of Al-Zaidi view the nationwide crackdown on oil pipeline tapping as leverage to prosecute and imprison leaders of defiant armed factions by choking off illicit revenue streams. The anti-smuggling drive took a sharp political turn after Najaf MP Abdul-Hadi Al-Hasnawi stated that a farm implicated in oil pipeline tampering in Najaf belongs to the Harakat al-Nujaba militia rather than a private family, following arrest warrants issued for two of his brothers.

In Erbil, former Kurdistan Parliament member Abdul-Salam Barwari warned that actors implicated in Jurf al-Sakhar’s illicit economy are attempting to deflect scrutiny by manufacturing crises around the Kurdistan Region—effectively signaling that oil theft is not confined to northern Babylon.

While characterizing Al-Zaidi’s official rhetoric on state monopoly over weapons as generally measured, Barwari cautioned that commentary from aligned media and activists revives a 2017 Kirkuk-style mentality hostile to Iraq’s constitutional federalism, seeking to exploit internal Kurdish political tensions following the recent reactivation of the Kurdistan Parliament.

World.title: Turkey highlight urgent European demand for Development Road at Baghdad Transport Expo
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Minister of Transport Wahab Salman Al-Hasani announced on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, that Iraq is reclaiming its economic role as a vital transit bridge between East and West through an integrated infrastructure vision linking seaports, airports, railways, and highways, while Turkish Minister of Transport and Infrastructure Abdulkadir Uraloğlu revealed that European officials inquire daily with mounting urgency about the completion timeline for the Iraq-Turkey Development Road project.

Speaking during the opening of the Iraq International Exhibition and Conference for Transport, Airports, and Logistics at the Baghdad International Fairground.

Al-Hasani stated that the Ministry of Transport is modernizing its operational systems to convert Iraq’s strategic geography into an engine of economic strength.

He highlighted major milestones in southern Iraq, noting that core components of the Grand Faw Port are nearing completion as Iraq’s maritime gateway to global markets, reinforced by the recent inauguration of the Khor al-Zubair immersed tunnel to shorten transport distances and connect ports to inland road networks.

Al-Hasani confirmed that the strategic Development Road project has reached advanced stages in its engineering designs, establishing an overland economic corridor linking the Arabian Gulf to Europe via Iraq and Turkey to diversify national revenue, attract investment partnerships, and generate employment.

Alongside maritime and rail infrastructure, he noted that the ministry is upgrading air navigation systems, modernizing domestic airports, and expanding Iraqi Airways’ international route network to elevate aviation safety and global connectivity.

Addressing the conference alongside international partner firms and diplomatic envoys, Turkish Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu underscored that disruptions in global supply chains have made diversifying transport routes and enhancing corridor efficiency critical.

Positioning the Middle East at the crossroads of Asia, Europe, and Africa, Uraloğlu stated that complementing Turkey’s existing East–West transit lines with a North–South axis through Iraq’s Grand Faw Port creates an unprecedented commercial and logistics artery between Asia and Europe.

Uraloğlu emphasized that the success of the Development Road depends not only on physical rail and highway construction, but also on streamlining border crossings, accelerating customs procedures, and implementing digital transformation across transit networks so borders function as gateways rather than barriers.

Offering the international expertise of Turkey’s engineering and contracting sectors to support Iraq’s infrastructure rollout, he concluded by noting that European officials contact Ankara every day persistently asking when the Development Road will be completed—a testament, he said, to how recent developments in Europe have validated the corridor’s strategic necessity.

World.title: 'Abdul won't lay carpets': Chandrashekhar Azad, Asaduddin Owaisi promise Muslim deputy CM in UP
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Azad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram) chief Chandrashekhar Azad on Thursday promised a Muslim deputy chief minister if the Samajik Parivartan Morcha forms the next government in Uttar Pradesh after the 2027 assembly elections.

Addressing the alliance's rally in Lucknow on Constitution Day, Azad also said a leader from the backward communities would be appointed to the post.

"Bring our rule, and Abdul will sit alongside Chandrashekhar Azad as Deputy Chief Minister and become the strength of the underprivileged. Abdul will become Deputy Chief Minister; Abdul will not lay carpets for anyone anymore; he will sit alongside Chandrashekhar Azad," news agency ANI quoted Azad as saying.



"Power will be in his hands; he will resolve your grievances, and he will not lay floor mats for others. 'Asad bhai' (

) also wanted to know what Abdul will do. Alongside Abdul, we will also make a person from the most backward/backward communities a deputy chief minister, mark my words," he added.

Azad is the Morcha's chief ministerial candidate. He and AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi announced their alliance on November 12.





The combine plans to contest all 403 Assembly seats in the state.

Owaisi targeted SP chief Akhilesh Yadav asking him if he would "give a ticket to a Muslim from Karhal?"

âThose who have come after our beard, listenâyou keep one too. Bhaiya will talk about nepotism while working for his own dynasty. Will Akhilesh give a ticket to a Muslim from Karhal? You are losing because you people practice casteism. From places where Muslim MPs and MLAs used to be elected, Akhilesh Yadav is appointing his own family members," he said.

"You will have to give an answer, Akhilesh Yadav: when shameless dancing took place in Saifai and dancers came from Mumbai for two hours at a time, at that very time people in Muzaffarnagar were suffering and dying from the cold. Akhilesh Yadav has adopted the ideology of Hindutva; if you want proof, watch what is going to happen on 12 Decemberâhe is going out carrying the message of Hindutva. Listen Akhilesh Yadav, you are just getting Muslim votes and making Abdul lay out the carpets.

Now Abdul will not lay out the carpets; I am not going to be afraid," he added.

World.title: India's first museum dedicated to Chief Justices of India inaugurated at OP Jindal Global University in Sonipat
World.content:
India's first museum dedicated to the Chief Justices of India was inaugurated at OP Jindal Global University (JGU) in Sonipat on Wednesday, with 10 former Chief Justices of India attending the event in person or virtually.

The museum, inaugurated on the eve of

, documents the lives and contributions of former Chief Justices and traces the evolution of the Supreme Court and India's constitutional framework.

It has been set up across five galleries, featuring more than 280 busts of Supreme Court judges, models of 25 High Courts, 22 language tapestries, 20 interactive biographical pillars and displays on 20 landmark judgments.

The inauguration was attended by former Chief Justices MN Venkatachaliah, BN Kirpal, S Rajendra Babu, KG Balakrishnan, P Sathasivam, RM Lodha, Dipak Misra, Sharad A Bobde, UU Lalit and BR Gavai.



The event was held ahead of Constitution Day, observed on November 26 to mark the adoption of the Constitution by the Constituent Assembly in 1949.

Museum traces history of Supreme Court and constitutional law

According to the university, the museum seeks to present the office of the Chief Justice as an institution central to constitutional governance, while documenting the people, decisions and debates that have shaped the judiciary.

Its exhibits include a holographic courtroom, artworks, sculptures and installations, alongside biographical displays and recordings of former judges.





Former Chief Justice MN Venkatachaliah said the rule of law and democratic freedoms had played an important role in India's progress. He said the museum could contribute to legal education and help prepare future practitioners.

Former CJI BR Gavai said the museum documented the work of successive Chief Justices as well as the Supreme Court's contribution to constitutional law over the past 76 years. He also spoke about the Constitution's emphasis on inclusion and representation, referring to the participation of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, minorities and women in public institutions.

Former CJI UU Lalit said the museum traced the development of jurisprudence alongside the country's growth. He said the evolution of law was closely connected with economic development and the well-being of the population.

Former CJI Sharad A Bobde spoke about the responsibility of the judiciary to uphold the rule of law and recalled the Supreme Court's functioning during the Covid pandemic, including the introduction of online hearings.

Former CJI RM Lodha said the museum's displays included judgments that had shaped India's constitutional framework. He referred to the development of public interest litigation and the basic structure doctrine, while also acknowledging that the judiciary had faced periods of difficulty.

Former CJI P Sathasivam said the Supreme Court had grown in importance since it began functioning in January 1950. He identified independence from the executive, integrity and transparency as essential to maintaining public confidence in the institution.

Former CJI Dipak Misra said the museum could help students understand constitutional values, including liberty, equality and fraternity. Former CJI S. Rajendra Babu said the exhibits would be useful to law scholars and researchers by helping them understand the evolution of the judiciary and the issues it had addressed.

Former CJI KG Balakrishnan urged law students to study the Constitution and understand their responsibilities as future legal professionals.

Former CJI BN Kirpal also participated in the proceedings.

Five galleries feature judgments, judicial history and artworks

The museum is organised into five galleries: Pathways of Justice, Pillars of Justice, Hall of Constitutional Voices, Keystones of Justice and Ideas of Justice.

Pathways of Justice explores the historical and social foundations of justice through 10 marble plaques recalling trials from colonial India.

Its artworks address themes such as untouchability, dowry, bonded labour, education, transparency, workplace dignity and climate justice.

The gallery also features a model of the Supreme Court and a display titled 'Branches of Justice'.

Pillars of Justice focuses on the lives of former Chief Justices through 20 interactive pillars, each equipped with four screens. It also features 22 regional handloom tapestries representing the languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, along with models of 25 High Courts.

Hall of Constitutional Voices presents recordings of 11 figures associated with India's constitutional history.

It also includes an oral history project featuring conversations with former Chief Justices and other senior judges.

Keystones of Justice examines 20 landmark judgments and the principles behind them. Its exhibits include a holographic courtroom and an installation titled 'From Paper to Precedent', made using ceramics, paper and jute.

Ideas of Justice features a sculpture garden and busts of judges. Its installations include 'The Robe of Justice' and 'The Right to Fly', which refers to JGU founding chancellor Naveen Jindal's legal battle over citizens' right to fly the national flag.

Jindal said the museum extended the university's existing Constitution Museum by focusing on the Supreme Court's role in upholding constitutional values. JGU founding vice-chancellor C. Raj Kumar said the project aimed to bring together law, history, memory and public engagement to document the institution's constitutional role.

World.title: PDA quota, dole for jobless, caste survey: Decoding Akhilesh Yadav's big manifesto promises for UP
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Twenty-five lakh government jobs, Rs 5,000 a month for unemployed graduates, and 50 per cent reservation for the PDA communities in government contracts worth up to Rs 50 crore.

(SP) chief

's manifesto for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections is an ambitious, on-paper bid to build a winning coalition of voters against the BJP government led by chief minister Yogi Adityanath.

Unveiled on Constitution Day, 'Sattais Ka Sankalp: PDA Ka Pran Patra â Jan-Man Ka Manifesto 2027' has placed Akhilesh's PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) formula at its core. After losing back-to-back assembly elections in 2017 and 2022, the SP is seeking to expand beyond its traditional Yadav-Muslim support base by combining caste-based representation with welfare promises for youth, women, and farmers.



The PDA arithmetic

Focusing on SP's social justice pitch, the manifesto promises a statewide caste census and 50 per cent reservation for Dalit and PDA communities in government contracts. It has also promised a Dalit development council headed by the CM and 20 per cent of the state budget for Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe welfare.

The party has also promised a special recruitment drive to fill reserved vacancies and Samajwadi canteens offering meals at Rs 5 to women, poor people and PDA communities.





The promises are aimed at giving backward and Dalit communities a greater stake in government jobs, contracts and welfare spending. They also reflect Akhilesh's attempt to expand the SP's traditional support base beyond Yadavs.

Non-Yadav OBCs make up an estimated 33 per cent of the electorate, compared with around 8 per cent for Yadavs. Spanning Kurmis, Lodhs, Kushwahas, Jats, Rajbhars, Nishads and Most Backward Classes, these communities have been an important pillar of the BJP's electoral expansion since 2014.

Yadavs, meanwhile, remain the SP's most reliable support base. Akhilesh's challenge is to expand into non-Yadav OBC communities without alienating his traditional voters.

The caste census promise is central to this effort. By seeking to establish the population and socio-economic status of different communities, the SP wants to make representation and distribution of resources key electoral issues.

The party is seeking to bridge the divide between Jatav and non-Jatav Dalits, a constituency that has been central to the BJP's expansion in Uttar Pradesh.

The Muslim factor

The SP has placed Muslim outreach within its broader PDA framework, promising constitutional protection, equality, employment opportunities and representation rather than announcing a separate cash-transfer scheme for the community.

The prominent presence given to senior leader Azam Khan at the manifesto launch in Lucknow was also a political signal, reinforcing the party's effort to retain its Muslim support base.

Muslims account for around 19 per cent of UP's electorate and have a significant presence in 143 of the state's 403 assembly constituencies. Their estimated population share exceeds 30 per cent in 73 seats, rising to 60-65 per cent in Rampur Nagar and 55-58 per cent in Chamrauwa. Another 70 constituencies have a Muslim population share of 20-30 per cent, concentrated largely in Rohilkhand and western UP.

The SP's calculation is to secure Muslim consolidation while expanding the PDA coalition to other communities.

The challenge is to do so without giving the BJP an opening to turn the contest into one of religious polarisation.

25 lakh jobs, Rs 5,000 allowance: The Gen-Z pitch

Twenty-five lakh government jobs over five years, another two to three crore employment opportunities in other sectors and a monthly allowance of Rs 5,000 for unemployed graduates are at the centre of the SP's youth-focused pitch.

The party has proposed an annual calendar for government vacancies, with recruitment processes involving single-stage examinations to be completed within three months and those involving multiple stages within six months.

It has also promised a system free of paper leaks, with officials and ministers to be held personally accountable for irregularities.

To revive a signature scheme from its 2012-17 tenure, the SP has promised free laptops for students passing Class 12. Other education commitments include reopening 26,000 primary schools, increasing the monthly honorarium of Shiksha Mitras by Rs 5,000 until their regularisation process is completed, and providing Wi-Fi facilities in schools.

The party has also pitched technology-led growth, citing the establishment of HCL's facility and an IT City in Lucknow during its previous government.

"Delivering on the aspirations of Gen-Z and Gen Alpha will be part of our commitment," Akhilesh said at the manifesto launch.

The focus on young voters is significant. Those aged 18-29 accounted for 22.9% of the electorate, or around 3.44 crore voters, in the 2022 assembly elections.

By foregrounding recruitment delays, paper leaks and unemployment, the SP is seeking to turn the concerns of this sizeable constituency into an electoral challenge for the Yogi Adityanath government.

For 'aadhi aabadi'

An annual pension of Rs 40,000 for elderly women, including elderly women artisans, 33 per cent representation for women in new police recruitments and stronger surveillance in public places are among the SP's key promises to women.

The party has also announced a separate women-centric manifesto and proposed CCTV cameras, drone surveillance and dedicated cybercrime units in every district.

The pitch comes against the backdrop of the BJP's efforts to consolidate women voters through welfare delivery, including free rations, housing and cooking gas connections.

Women have emerged as an increasingly important electoral constituency, and the SP's challenge is to persuade them that its proposed financial assistance and safety measures offer a credible alternative to the BJP's welfare delivery and law-and-order pitch.

Relief promise across the rural belt

An immediate farm loan waiver, a legal guarantee for minimum support prices (MSP) on 23 crops and milk, free electricity for agricultural irrigation and up to 300 units of free power for rural domestic consumers form the core of the SP's agricultural package.

The party has also promised a price compensation mechanism for crops such as potatoes, tomatoes and onions that fall outside the MSP system. A Rs 15,000-crore corpus would be created to ensure sugarcane farmers receive payments within 24 hours, while sugarcane prices would be increased annually based on the actual cost of cultivation.

The SP has also proposed Rs 1.5 lakh crore for rural infrastructure.

The package seeks to appeal to farmers across caste groups, particularly in agricultural and sugarcane-growing regions.

The rural constituency is electorally significant. Of UP's 403 Assembly seats, 222 are classified as rural and another 131 as semi-urban in the constituency data used for this analysis. Together, they account for the overwhelming majority of the state's seats.

World.title: 'Rahul must apologise': Nitin Nabin targets Congress over Ambedkar at Patna event
World.content:
national president

on Thursday demanded an apology from Congress leader

over the insults allegedly heaped on Dr BR Ambedkar by the Congress. He accused the party of failing to uphold the constitutional values laid down by the architect of the Constitution.

Addressing the BJP's Samvidhan Gaurav Diwas event in Patna, Nabin accused the Congress of repeatedly undermining the Constitution for its political interests. He also questioned the party's record of dismissing elected state governments during its rule at the Centre, PTI reported.

"Congress dismissed 90 state governments while it was in power at the Centre," Nabin said, adding that former prime minister Indira Gandhi alone had dismissed more than 50 state governments during her tenure.



Nabin further alleged that the Congress had failed to follow the principles laid down by Ambedkar in the Constitution, while praising Prime Minister Narendra Modi for upholding them.

"Congress did not live up to the standards laid down in the Constitution drafted by Ambedkar, but Narendra Modi did," he said.

Invoking India's cultural and spiritual heritage, Nabin said the framers of the Constitution drew inspiration from the reign of Lord Ram.





"I feel that the framers of the Constitution drew immense inspiration from the reign of Lord Shri Ram," he said.

He also referred to the depictions of Lord Buddha and Lord Mahavira in the Constitution, highlighting Bihar's association with both figures.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

"When Lord Buddha and Lord Mahavira are depicted in Parts V and VI of the Constitution, the karmabhoomi of both is our own Bihar," Nabin said.

"The soul of this Constitution and its provisions were framed by carrying forward our culture and our heritage," he added.

Nabin also invoked Vande Mataram, recalling former president Dr Rajendra Prasad's recognition of the song as a symbol of the freedom struggle on January 24, 1950. He said the complete version of the song was sung at the Red Fort on August 15, 2026, adding that it made Indians proud of the Constitution's original spirit.

He further accused the Congress of sacrificing the Constitution for its vested interests.
