World.title: Muni Network: Newsrooms unite against AI disruption
World.content:
Facing the threats of AI-induced disruption and declining web traffic, Southeast Asian newsrooms unite through the Muni Network for the future of news

MANILA, Philippines – As artificial intelligence continues to squeeze traffic and revenue from independent media, the question of what path newsrooms need to take to survive the disruption has been at the forefront of many conversations within the industry.

Some independent newsrooms in the Philippines and other Southeast Asian countries are going a step beyond talking. From November 19 to 22, editors, technology leads, and newsroom strategists from these news groups gathered at the Rappler headquarters to confront the issue and explore approaches to addressing the AI enigma that capitalize on their collective strengths and communities.

Organized and hosted by Rappler, the event, Future of News (FON) Laboratory, aimed to build a collective approach to AI disruption, declining website traffic, and unfair policies by tech platforms, striving to secure, as its name suggests, the future of news.

“Since the launch of AI overview, we have seen a 50% to 70% drop in our organic traffic coming from the search engine,” said Wahyu Dhyatmika, CEO of Indonesia’s Tempo Digital. “We have to find other ways to ensure that we still can reach our audience, can still be impactful, and also build a new business model.”



Rappler CEO Maria Ressa stressed the need for a shared solution. “It doesn’t matter if one news group is moving ahead because we cannot fight these forces alone,” she said.

NEWSROOMS IN THE AGE OF AI. Nobel laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa discusses how artificial intelligence affects newsrooms during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

Ressa emphasized the need for newsrooms to find new business models and build audiences together. “That’s the other reason I wrote The Fight Back. The fight back literally is building our communities. It is bottom up with our communities, and then we have to work with our governments,” she explained.

Collective pushback

“The November 2026 sessions follow many preliminary meetings and one-on-one sessions where we confronted difficult questions that usually got in the way of collaboration,” said Gemma Mendoza, head of strategic programs at Rappler.

FORGING ALLIANCE. Editorial leaders and representatives from Kiripost (Cambodia), Katadata and Tempo (Indonesia), Malaysiakini (Malaysia), Mizzima (Myanmar), Mountain Beacon and Palawan News (Luzon), Daily Guardian and Sunstar Cebu (Visayas), and MindaNews (Mindanao) pose for a group photo during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

Newsrooms that sent participants to the Future of News Laboratory included Kiripost (Cambodia), Katadata and Tempo (Indonesia), Malaysiakini (Malaysia), and Mizzima (Myanmar), alongside Philippine community newsrooms Mountain Beacon and Palawan News (Luzon), Daily Guardian and SunStar Cebu (Visayas), and MindaNews (Mindanao).

Among matters discussed in preliminary sessions was Meta’s aborted effort to implement a clause in its commercial terms, which treated presence on its platforms as permission for the tech giant to scrape publisher content and use the same as training data for its AI products.

MUNI-MAXXING. Some representatives from Southeast Asian newsrooms engage in a workshop on how to set up, configure, and maximize MUNI in their workflows. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

“Meta’s recent decision to withdraw the planned website-crawling clause in its updated commercial terms proves that collective pushback works,” said Mendoza, who also leads Rappler’s Future of News initiative.

Representatives of participating newsrooms agreed that they cannot afford to lower their guard.

“They (platforms) steal data, they use data. And the irony is we buy data back from them,” said Redempto Anda, editor-in-chief of Palawan News.

Aryo Widhy Wicaksono from Indonesia’s Katadata also noted that because people now read news straight from social media and AI summaries instead of visiting news websites, fewer brands are buying ads from publishers.

“All the news that we produce, we took effort, we took time, we took a lot of work to do that. And then the AI just took an overview [of] it without really doing anything,” Wicaksono added.

Keeping humans in charge amid AI

While calling out unfair practices by AI companies, the FON participants also explored ways by which newsrooms can use AI safely to improve and enrich their daily work, as long as human editors stay in control.

At Cambodia’s Kiripost, AI is already helping small teams work faster.

“Recently, our data team, without any coding experience, started a few months ago with vibe coding,” shared Tharum Bun, its co-founder and managing editor.

THOUGHTS ON AI. Cambodian media company Kiripost managing editor Tharum Bun discusses his newsroom’s unique strengths and the impact of AI in their journalism. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

“Small web tool apps that we have never had before, now we can build in a few months, and we can produce more visual data and stories in a very effective way,” Bun added.

For Mildred Galarpe, editor-in-chief of SunStar Cebu, AI initially felt like a “shining, shimmering tool” that tempted newsrooms to adopt it without enough caution.

COLLABORATION. SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief Mildred Galarpe suggests community engagement efforts that newsrooms should implement, during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

Galarpe noted, however, that moving too quickly led to early mistakes, such as accidentally swapping the family names of the new and old governors in their coverage due to AI use. That experience taught them that while AI is an effective tool to fast-track work, it is not the editor.

“The human eye should always be there. Nothing should be published without your thumbprint,” Galarpe said.



Rappler’s Ressa further stressed that AI cannot replace humans because its models operate on probability instead of facts, meaning what many refer to as “hallucination” is actually just the system working as designed.



“You will always need a human in the loop…because news is anchored in facts, but the tech that is ruling our lives, they’re anchored in profit, so it’s corrupted the entire world,” Ressa added.

The Muni Network

To turn their stand into action, the participating newsrooms are joining forces through the Muni Network, inspired by the MUNI tab on the Rappler app.



The Muni Network will officially launch on December 10, coinciding with Human Rights Day, with plans to expand across the region soon.



For Anda, this network is essential for small newsrooms like theirs.

“I look at it as a startup venture, because this is something that is pioneering. You have newsrooms gathering together and figuring out a way to go around this problem of AI using our data [and] how we deal with social media platforms inundating and taking over newsrooms,” Anda added.

By combining their audiences and reach, smaller and independent newsrooms hope to achieve greater impact together, if not match the strength of global tech giants.

“AI doesn’t know boundaries,” Wicaksono said. “If we have a collaboration, we add those small sounds or small voices [to] become one.”

STATUS CHECK. Some Southeast Asian newsroom representatives put their ideas, capabilities, and ways to respond to AI threats on a whiteboard during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

The federation wants to change how newsrooms work together across Southeast Asia.

Dhyatmika added that publishers won’t stand a chance if they act individually in the era of AI. For him, newsrooms should not see each other as competitors but collaborators.

He emphasized that acting collectively would enable them to get a fairer share of the value created by their products in the digital ecosystem.

Alongside the workshop, the Future of News Laboratory participants also attended Rappler’s Social Good Summit centered on the theme “We, The Humans” — a timely reminder that humans (the journalists in this situation) must remain in control of technology and use its potential to drive meaningful action instead of being driven by it.

Initial collaborations

Before the November sessions, the group had also issued a joint statement to sound the alarm on the negative effects of AI on journalism, facts, and democracy.

Released last May for World Press Freedom Day, the joint statement highlighted issues such as algorithmic suppression of news, the economic challenges posed by Big Tech monopolies, and the rise of disinformation, which collectively threaten the survival of independent media.

Early collaborators have already launched public chat channels to strengthen local journalism and held community chats around newsroom-initiated investigations. Among those who participated were Daily Guardian and Sunstar Cebu. Both newsrooms have their branded chat channels embedded on their respective websites.

In September 2025, in time for World News Day, the collaboration also released an experimental video simulating Replica, an “AI-powered journalist.” The video aimed to send a dire warning about what could happen if independent newsrooms die and the only source of news would be AI, ending with a call for citizens to support real journalism. – Rappler.com

If you are interested in participating in the Muni Network and the Future of News initiative, email community@rappler.com.

World.title: Ex-Cale88 co-owner, BOC official to testify in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
World.content:
VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte talks to supporters as she prepares to leave the Quezon City Regional Trial Court after the postponement of the arraignment for her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.

Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada, who is also the Vice President's dentist, is expected to testify on Cale88's organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and financial affairs

MANILA, Philippines – A former co-owner of Cale88 Foods Corporation, who is also Vice President Sara Duterte‘s dentist, is expected to testify before the Senate impeachment court when her trial resumes on December 1.

The defense counsel submitted a manifestation dated November 25 asking the Senate impeachment court to issue subpoenas ad testificandum et duces tecum to Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada and direct her to participate during the proceedings scheduled from December 1 to 4.

Lebosada was also directed to bring certified true copies of the following documents:

Registration documents of Cale88 Foods Corporation, including relevant government records;

Documents relating to Cale88’s operations;

Documents relating to the company’s finances and business transactions; and

Other documents relevant to the foregoing.

Cale88, a banana chips production company co-owned by Lebosada and Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, came under scrutiny during the impeachment trial after Anti-Money Laundering Council records showed that it received P776 million in cash inflows despite having only P125,000 in paid-up capital and declaring P208 million in sales.

Lawyer Alex Cabrera, who prepared a forensic financial report on Duterte’s bank and financial records, described Cale88’s business model as “implausible” and likened its operations to a “revolving door,” which he said was indicative of money laundering.

Lebosada is expected to testify on Cale88’s organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and financial affairs.

The defense also sought a subpoena for Agaton Teodoro Uvero, deputy commissioner of the Assessment and Operations Coordinating Group of the Bureau of Customs. Uvero is expected to testify on Cale88’s exportation records under the custody of the BOC.

The impeachment court confirmed the issuance of subpoenas to both witnesses.

“As of this morning, Thursday, November 26, 2026, the Office of the Clerk of Court has completed service of both subpoenas — serving the Office of Bureau of Customs Deputy Commissioner Atty. Agaton Teodoro O. Uvero personally at 9:05 am, and serving Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada in Davao City via electronic mail at 9:54 am pursuant to the Court’s electronic service directive,” said impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol.

The impeachment trial is currently on hold to give way to Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget. Proceedings are scheduled to resume on December 1. – Rappler.com

World.title: When bicam convenes for 2027 budget, advocates want to be in the room
World.content:
BUDGET WATCH. Social Watch Philippines holds a press conference as the Senate conducts plenary deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget on November 26, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines – Budget watchdog Social Watch Philippines wants civil society groups to be present in person when the bicameral conference committee convenes to tackle the proposed 2027 national budget.

“Panawagan talaga natin…ay nando’n tayo mismo, on-site sa bicameral conference committee meeting para namo-monitor natin ang aktuwal na nangyayari,” Social Watch Philippines co-convenor Maria Victoria Raquiza said in a press conference on Thursday, November 26.

“Hindi ‘yong sa nangyari last year na livestreaming nga, open bicam nga, pero sa totoo lang, ang major decisions ay ginawa off-camera,” she added.

(Our appeal is for us to be allowed on-site at the bicameral conference committee meeting so we can monitor what’s actually happening. We don’t want a repeat of last year where there was livestreaming, it was supposedly an open bicam, but in reality, the major decisions were made off-camera.)

Play Video

Raquiza also said advocates want to have a voice during the proceedings.

Following the Senate’s briefing with civil society organizations in October, Senator Ping Lacson invited them to join the 2027 budget bicam. He also floated the idea of keeping the meeting open even if bicam members ask for session suspensions.

Raquiza said the Senate must publicize 2027 budget amendments so that civil society groups can scrutinize these changes before the bicam meeting.

Among the changes introduced by the Senate finance committee is the realignment of P19.8 billion from government assistance programs, including the Medical Assistance Program and the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations, to augment funding for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth).

This boosted PhilHealth’s budget from P73 billion in the House version of the general appropriations bill (GAB) to P94.2 billion in the Senate committee report.

Social Watch Philippines noted that the updated figure still falls short of the P244-billion funding requirement of the state health insurer next year.

The group added that while the budget for health promotion went up from P485 million in the House GAB to P1.55 billion in the Senate version, it is still lower than the minimum 1% of the total Department of Health budget of P273 billion, supposedly violating the Universal Health Care Act.

The Senate also introduced a P97-billion reduction in the allocation for over 3,400 “non-compliant” projects of the Department of Public Works and Highways. The funding would be realigned to foreign-assisted infrastructure projects.

“Ang mga tinanggal ng Senado sa ngalan ng paglaban sa korupsiyon ay hindi dapat palihim na ibalik sa bicam sa ngalan ng kompromiso,” Raquiza said.

(What the Senate removed in the name of fighting corruption must not be stealthily returned during the bicam in the name of compromise.) – Rappler.com

World.title: [OPINION] Slowly but surely, Washington drifts away from Asia
World.content:
What a difference a year makes!

When he made his whirlwind trip to Kuala Lumpur to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in late October 2025, Donald Trump had Asian leaders bowing and scraping before him like feudal vassals. He had imposed punitive tariffs on all the countries of East Asia, and none of their leaders dared to complain lest he take umbrage and raise the tariffs several notches higher.

Cambodian President Hun Manet told Trump he would nominate him for the Nobel Peace Prize for “ending” his country’s border war with Thailand, and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who had done the heavy lifting to bring Cambodia and Thailand to the table, graciously let him to take center stage and take all the glory for the fragile success of the negotiations.

Returning a year later, Trump was a significantly diminished figure.

He met briefly with ASEAN heads of state in Manila last week, the most significant news out of which were his announcing the conclusion of a controversial bilateral trade agreement with Thailand that was, in fact, still being negotiated — as well as his praise for the late president Ferdinand Marcos, the father and namesake of the incumbent president and the dictator who ruled the country from 1966 to 1986, saying the contemporary Marcos had “good genetics.”

Instead of cheers, Trump’s coming evoked jeers, with student-led mass demonstrations against the plan to include the Philippines in the US State Department initiative Pax Silica, which would incorporate the country into an artificial intelligence global supply chain aimed at countering a parallel initiative by Beijing.

There was no bowing and scraping this time. The assembled leaders probably smiled with secret satisfaction that the US Supreme Court had ruled in February of this year that Trump’s punitive tariffs against ASEAN and other countries were illegal; that he was trapped in a “forever war” with Iran; and that he had been dealt a massive blow by the results of the November elections, which saw the Democrats gain control of the Senate and House by very large margins, effectively rendering him a lame-duck president.

China’s shadow in Manila

As in previous years, China was a massive but unseen presence at the ASEAN summit. China has long been the number one trading partner of the Southeast Asian countries, its trade with ASEAN surpassing $1 trillion in 2025, with ASEAN being in deficit by $244 billion.

It has, however, trailed the US in terms of investments. Cumulative investment from the US in ASEAN hit $557 billion in 2025, while that of China was $199 billion.

However, while China’s economic relations with the region have remained relatively stable, things have been very rocky between ASEAN and the US under Trump. There is, for one, the administration’s push to impose punitive tariffs, motivated partly by strong suspicion that China has been using some countries, like Vietnam, as platforms to export Chinese goods to the US. Then, there is Washington’s drive to get information technology firms such as Taiwan’s TSMC and Korea’s Samsung to invest in facilities in the US owing to their being currently located in geopolitically vulnerable areas.

The pressure on IT companies to locate away from East Asia can only increase with the fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ‘s marital scandal, with the claim of US intelligence agencies that the Singapore-based cloud computing provider Megaspeed, of which Alice Huang was the CEO, has been a source of unauthorized shipments of advanced Nvidia chips to Beijing that had been banned by the US.

Trump’s ambivalent vibes

The US security relationship with the region has also come under stress. The Philippines has been the US’s main ally in the region, yet Filipino officials have been dissatisfied with what they consider Washington’s purely rhetorical denunciations of clashes between the Chinese and Philippine coast guard vessels in the South China Sea. Southeast Asian governments have also noticed how the Trump administration has not given clear signs of coming to Taiwan’s defense in the event of a China-Taiwan clash, in contrast to the Biden administration’s explicit commitment.

Also noted was Trump’s failure to back Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi when she asserted Japan would be involved in defending Taiwan in event of hostilities breaking out between Taipei and Beijing. In fact, there’s been a sharp decline in US warships transiting through the Taiwan Straits, with the number falling by some 56% from transits during the Biden administration, leading the rightwing Heritage Foundation to anxiously assert that “there is a real risk that American allies and partners — let alone Beijing — could misinterpret the Trump administration’s strategy as a retreat on American commitments. Perceptions of that kind, once formed, can become difficult to reverse.”

It has also not escaped Southeast Asia’s governments that Trump has been eager to have a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to lower tensions on the Korean peninsula, and that, despite the geoeconomic rivalry between Washington and Beijing, Trump wants to establish a friendly personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jin Ping. During Xi’s visit to Washington last September, Trump pulled out all the stops to butter up the Chinese leader, just as Xi gave him full honors during his visit to Shenzen to attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ last week.

Many commentators have said that unlike his predecessors, Trump’s attitude towards ASEAN and other Asian states has been “transactional” instead of being anchored on longstanding ideological and security considerations, pointing to his levying punitive tariffs on friends and foes alike as well as to his hectoring countries hosting US bases to raise their contribution to their defense to five per cent of GDP.

The triple whammy

What many observers fail to note is that rather than just stemming from a businessman’s whims, Trump’s attitude is rooted in the reality that the American economic and military presence in the Asia Pacific is becoming structurally unsustainable for the US.

A legacy of the US drive to defeat Japan during the Second World War, the US bases from Korea to the Philippines were repurposed during the Cold War to contain China and the Soviet Union. In return for their political loyalty in the struggle against Communism, the US not only provided security but also gave Japan first and later South Korea and Taiwan, very liberal entry for their goods into the US market while allowing them to maintain high levels of tariff and non-tariff protection against US products, allowing all three to achieve high-speed industrial growth.

In the late eighties and early nineties, the so-called “tiger cubs” of Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Singapore took advantage of the same liberal access to the US market while maintaining tariff walls against US products. From the early nineties on, China took the same route, eventually displacing its Asian neighbors as the source of cheap manufactures for the US market.

But China took the so-called Asian export-industrialization model one step further: it encouraged US manufacturers to relocate to China to take advantage of labor that was five per cent of its price in the US. It was an offer that many of America’s big name corporations could not resist, with Apple leading the way, contracting most it manufacturing operations to Foxconn and other firms based in Shenzen. By 2017, Apple admitted to creating 4.8 million jobs in China, or double the number it had created in the US.

Thus, before Trump’s first term in office, the US was suffering a triple whammy in its relations with East Asia.

First, it was running massive trade deficits with almost all the East Asian countries. Second, it was being deindustrialized as US firms moved their labor-intensive operations to China, even as cheap Chinese-made goods flooded the US market and rendered those firms that had not relocated non-competitive. And, third, it was spending over $11 billion a year to maintain its massive base structure in Japan, Korea, the Philippines, and Singapore. It was largely this unsustainable economic and military deficit that lay behind the radical reorientation of US strategic policy represented by the National Security Strategy 2025 that was released late last year.

A new grand strategy

In the 80 years prior to NSS 2025, Washington’s “Grand Strategy” was to meet challenges anywhere in the world that posed a threat to the national interest of the United States, and towards this end, it built a formidable military machine and system of forward bases, most of which were in the Asia Pacific. In the four decades between the late forties and late eighties, the strategy was justified by the ideology of containing Communism and supposedly promoting democracy in Washington’s client states.

The fall of the Soviet Union, followed by the dynamic ascent of East Asia, the rapid deindustrialization of the US economy, and the 2008 Global Financial Crisis made the old Cold War image of the US being Atlas carrying the world on his shoulders increasingly anachronistic to many Americans. Even as the Republicans and Democratic party elites remained stuck in a time warp, committed to the old Containment strategy in post-Containment times, Trump was able to seize on a large section of the population’s feeling that the US could no longer shoulder the costs of a dated strategy and wield it as a militant slogan that had popular resonance: that US allies in Asia and Europe had “taken advantage of US generosity” to build robust economies and saw the US military umbrella as a great excuse to spend very little for their own security.

The trenchant introduction of NSS 2025 was definitely one-sided, but it also contained a great deal of truth:

After the end of the Cold War, American foreign policy elites convinced themselves that permanent American domination of the entire world was in the best interests of our country. Yet the affairs of other countries are our concern only if their activities directly threaten our interests…Our elites badly miscalculated America’s willingness to shoulder forever global burdens to which the American people saw no connection to the national interest. They overestimated America’s ability to fund, simultaneously, a massive welfare-regulatory-administrative state alongside a massive military, diplomatic, intelligence, and foreign aid complex. They placed hugely misguided and destructive bets on globalism and so-called “free trade” that hollowed out the very middle class and industrial base on which American economic and military preeminence depend. They allowed allies and partners to offload the cost of their defense onto the American people, and sometimes to suck us into conflicts and controversies central to their interests but peripheral or irrelevant to our own. And they lashed American policy to a network of international institutions, some of which are driven by outright anti-Americanism and many by a transnationalism that explicitly seeks to dissolve individual state sovereignty. In sum, not only did our elites pursue a fundamentally undesirable and impossible goal, in doing so they undermined the very means necessary to achieve that goal: the character of our nation upon which its power, wealth, and decency were built.

NSS 2025 made it clear that under Trump, building a bastion of economic and military power in the western hemisphere would be Washington’s priority, and this was underlined by his brazen words about annexing Greenland, his implicit threat to take over the Panama Canal, and his kidnaping in broad daylight of Venezuelan President Francisco Maduro early this year.

While the NSS did say the US had a strong stake in the Asia Pacific, the stress was on reversing past policies towards China that were based on wrong economic assumptions by four successive administrations — assumptions that led to policies that has turned China into a “near peer competitor” of the United States. The priority was to “rebalance America’s economic relationship with China, prioritizing reciprocity and fairness to restore American economic independence.” Keeping the status quo on Taiwan is mentioned as is keeping the sea lanes in the South China Sea open, but it is formulaic. As for Southeast Asia, there is no mention at all of mainland and island Southeast Asia as a specific area of interest.

Will the Legions Sail Home?

Most Southeast Asian elites have taken very seriously NSS 2025’s message that their region is now of secondary, if not marginal, interest to Washington, and the Japanese and Korean establishments now have very serious doubts about the solidity of the US commitment to their defense if they are not seen as making progress in meeting Washington’s demand that they spend at least five per cent of their GDP on their defense and defray most of the costs of maintaining the US bases they host.

The realization is seeping in among the elites of the region that relying on the naval power and offshore bases of a power some 7000 miles away to provide protection is unsustainable in the long run, if not in the medium term. That the legions of America will eventually go home, as did Rome’s legions in Britain in the third century CE, is no longer dismissed as improbable.

Contributing to the apprehensions of the Asian elites has been Washington’s failure to subdue Iran after nine months of warfare. If a small country like Iran could successfully resist a massive joint US-Israeli to overthrow the their government, would not a bigger power be much more difficult for the US to take on? Also, the Asian elites know that the war has hardened the opposition of the American right, middle, and left to armed US intervention anywhere in the world. In other words, their staying power is no longer guaranteed by American military power.

In contrast, Asian elites have seen how simply by standing aloof from the Iran conflict, and allowing the US to expend its military resources and legitimacy in a war that has served mainly Israel’s interests, China has seen its status grow throughout the region. Winning the battle for influence without a fight might be an exaggerated way of putting it, but that is essentially what China has derived out of Trump’s ill-advised adventure in Iran. For Asia’s elites, the lesson is clear: China, not the US, is here to stay, so it is best to come to terms with this reality.

A revived ASEAN Regional Forum?

Here, it might be useful for Asian governments to look three decades back. There was a time, the 1990’s, when the governments of ASEAN, led by Malaysia’s Mohammad Mahathir, promoted the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) as a site where conflicts among countries in the region could be settled via diplomacy and not by force. It had its flaws, but the ARF was a step in the direction of a collective security system.

Yet the US boycotted the founding meeting of the ARF in Bangkok in July 1994 to register Washington’s disapproval of ASEAN’s ambitions. Then President Bill Clinton, in fact, explicitly denigrated the ARF and other multilateral security initiatives, saying they “are a way to supplement our alliances and forward military presence, not supplant them.” When the Asian Financial Crisis hit the region in 1997, Washington used it not only to try to resubordinate the ASEAN economies but also to delegitimize the ARF.

Today, with the US’s retreat from Asia, the ASEAN Regional Forum might be an idea whose time has finally come. The question is, does the current crop of ASEAN leaders have the courage and imagination to seize this opportunity to create what could eventually become a collective security order where governments from all over East Asia can come together to settle their differences?

Trump as today’s Nixon

And the US? For all his contradictions, haphazard behavior, and narcissistic tendencies, Donald Trump’s influence on the direction of the relationship between East Asia and the US must not be underestimated. His retreat from the region, justified and promoted by NSS 2025, may one day lead historians to compare him to Richard Nixon, the unlikely Cold Warrior who made peace with China and brought it into the mainstream of global politics and eventually into the global economy.

Trump dumped an obsolete Grand Strategy of global hegemony that the US could no longer sustain but which continued to command the adherence of both the fossilized Republican and Democratic Party elites, like Dick Cheney and Joe Biden, who knew what toll it was taking but lacked the nerve to abandon it. Indeed, the interminable war on Iran to which Trump was maneuvered by Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu simply confirmed for his MAGA base the correctness of the isolationist thrust of NSS 2025.

But what if a Democrat is elected president in 2028? Would they not bring back the old Grand Strategy? I’m very sure they won’t. In fact, the Cold War Democrats owe Trump the favor of doing the dirty work of cutting off a diseased organ that they did not have the guts to hack off. – Rappler.com



Walden Bello is co-chair of the Board of the Bangkok-based Focus on the Global South and co-editor, with Don Kalb, of Backlash: The Global Rise of the Radical Right (Pluto: 2026).

World.title: Lacson asks: Why settle unpaid 2024 DSWD guarantee letters in 2027?
World.content:
AYUDA PAYOUT. Drivers of transport network vehicle services queue at Quezon Memorial Circle in Quezon City to receive cash aid from the government amid oil price shocks, March 24, 2026.

Service providers reportedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents belatedly, which is why the special provision was only proposed in the 2027 budget bill

MANILA, Philippines – Senator Panfilo Lacson flagged the proposed special provision in the House of Representatives’ version of the 2027 budget bill to pay off unpaid guarantee letters (GLs) issued by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) three years ago.

Lacson raised the issue during plenary deliberations on the DSWD’s proposed 2027 budget on Wednesday, November 25.

He pointed out that the House version of the DSWD budget includes a special provision for the “protective services program for individuals and families in difficult circumstances.”

It states that the amount for the program “shall likewise be used for the payment of arrears to accredited and/or partner service providers arising from the issuance of Guarantee Letter (GL) in FY (fiscal year) 2024, subject to the availability of funds and compliance with applicable budgeting, accounting, and auditing laws, rules and regulations.”

The GLs are for the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS) program, which provides financial assistance for medical needs, burial, transportation, education, food, and other support services or needs of a person or family.

Lacson noted that the allotment of over P34 billion for AICS in 2024 was fully obligated.

“So you’re issuing guarantee letters over and beyond what is authorized under GAA (General Appropriations Act) or under the law to spend under AICS. Mahirap maintindihan (This is difficult to understand), Mr. [Senate] President,” Lacson said.

Senator Risa Hontiveros, the DSWD’s budget sponsor, said service providers belatedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents, which is why the special provision was only proposed in the 2027 budget bill.

“Nagulat din ang department. By the time dumating ‘yong mga GL, wala na pong pondo. Kasi hindi nila ino-obligate pagka-issue ng GL, pagka lamang ginamit na talaga at may billing na mula sa mga ospital,” Hontiveros said.

(The department was also surprised. By the time the GLs arrived, there were no available funds left. The department doesn’t obligate the funds when GLs are issued; only after the GLs are used and hospitals have sent the billing.)

The value of unpaid claims from the guarantee letters was not mentioned.

Asked whether the GLs were issued by lawmakers, Hontiveros clarified that it was the DSWD itself that issued the letters.

“Nagsi-signify ang department na handa sila kung sakaling hindi natin tanggapin na magkaroon ng special provision. Itutuloy ‘yong money claims process. Nga lamang, siyempre matagal ‘yon, at magkakaroon kaagad ng epekto na hindi tatanggapin,” she said.

(The department is signifying that it’s ready just in case the Senate won’t accept the inclusion of a special provision. It’ll just continue with the money claims process. It’s just that the process would be long and the possible effect would be the service providers may not agree with it.)

Learning from the ordeal, Hontiveros said, the DSWD will ensure early liquidation of guarantee letters moving forward, so there would be enough time to settle payments to service providers.

On Monday, November 23, the DSWD said it will temporarily suspend the issuance of guarantee letters for AICS starting November 30. The expected resumption will be on the first working day in January 2027.

This will not affect the availment of outright payment of cash aid to AICS beneficiaries.

“The DSWD will continue to accommodate individuals and families experiencing crisis situations who need immediate financial assistance through its field offices and satellite offices nationwide,” it said in a statement.

AICS funding for next year

Civil society groups criticize the AICS program as “soft pork” being weaponized for political patronage.

During his interpellation, Lacson said he wants to break down the funding for AICS into the DSWD’s sub-programs. He described AICS as “whimsical.”

“Kung sino ‘yong marunong lumapit sa mga politiko, ‘yon ang mga mauuna. Kaya nga minsan naka-hikaw ng ginto eh, hindi talaga nangangailangan, wala talaga sa crisis situations, nakakakuha sila ng biyaya galing sa AICS,” he claimed.

(Only the people who know how to approach politicians are being prioritized. That’s why sometimes those who receive aid from the AICS program are not really needy, not really in crisis situations, or they even wear gold earrings.)

Hontiveros assured Lacson that the DSWD has full control over the decision-making and disbursement of aid under the program.

Under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), AICS was allocated P33.29 billion. The House added P25 billion.

While the DSWD earlier appealed to senators for a P63-billion budget for AICS, the Senate finance committee only recommended P48 billion.

During a committee hearing in October, Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian said restoring the budget to P63 billion, the same level in the 2026 budget, will help them support Filipinos affected by El Niño, inflation, and other crises in 2027.

The Senate panel realigned the AICS budget to augment funding for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation or PhilHealth.

As a whole, the DSWD and its attached agencies have P253.34 billion for proposed general appropriations under the Senate committee report.

That figure is P12 billion higher than the P241.28 billion in the NEP, but P9.42 billion lower than the P262.76 billion in the House budget measure. – Rappler.com

World.title: 1Password customer data, source code taken in GitHub breach
World.content:
1Password says customer vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and unaffected as the platform does not have access to user passwords or secret keys

MANILA, Philippines – Password management software 1Password announced on Wednesday, November 25, that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account, stealing some customer data and copying source code from private repositories.

1Password, in its blog post informing the public about the incident, said it began investigations on November 19 following indications someone had taken over an employee’s GitHub account.

It added, however, that customers’ vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected because 1Password does not have access to user passwords or secret keys.

What was taken

The attacker downloaded account records of a subset of 1Password’s users.

These records include the following:

Names and email addresses

Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)

Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)

Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery

Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)

1Password also said the attacker copied source code from private repositories and gained access to a continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment system (CI/CD). The source code contains no customer data or user secrets, while the CI/CD holds “infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work.”

Mitigating the attack

In light of the attack, 1Password has triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed. It disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.

1Password also said it tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, adding new detections for this kind of attack. It also lengthened invitation codes from six to 10 characters as a precaution.

1Password also validated that no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise was done using any exposed account provisioning tokens.

It also asked help from independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment approaches and remediation efforts.

Be wary of phishing

While 1Password said there was no impact to its services, availability, or product security, it advised users to be wary of “phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.”

The company added, “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.”

It reminded users to keep their secret keys and passwords safe and invited users to report suspicious activity to support@1password.com. – Rappler.com

World.title: Excise tax on your coffee? House leader shuts down suggestion
World.content:
Previously, a group of liquor makers jokingly quipped that lawmakers consider taxing coffee, citing younger consumers’ apparent preference for it over alcohol

MANILA, Philippines – House ways and means chairman Miro Quimbo quickly shut down the idea of imposing an excise tax on coffee, after a group of liquor makers jokingly made the suggestion on Wednesday, November 25.

“The committee will not allow coffee to be taxed,” Quimbo, whose committee handles tax-related bills, said on DZBB Super Radyo on Thursday, November 26. “That (tax on) coffee, that will no longer be discussed.”

During the committee hearing on Wednesday, November 25, Distilled Spirits Association of the Philippines representative Olivia Limpe-Aw quipped that lawmakers might want to consider taxing coffee instead of alcohol.

She cited changing consumer behavior, as younger consumers — particularly Gen Zs — seem to prefer coffee over alcoholic drinks.

“We told Congressman Miro, maybe you would want to tax coffee because the (demand there) is huge, not alcohol. And coffee is expensive,” Limpe-Aw said.

Quimbo diverted the topic in his reply, saying: “Let’s talk about alcohol first. More people might get sleepy if we talk about coffee.”

On Thursday, Quimbo insisted there is no need to impose excise tax on coffee because it is not proven to be harmful.

“Besides, that is very difficult to administer. What kind of coffee? How heavy? With alcohol, you tax it when the alcohol content is higher. How about with coffee? Because it has more caffeine?” Quimbo said. – Rappler.com

World.title: [READOUT] What businesses can get out of ASEAN 2026
World.content:
From a landmark digital economy agreement to investment-ready energy projects, here's what businesses can take away from the Philippines' ASEAN hosting

The Philippines hosted the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from November 15 to 17. But aside from bringing world leaders to Manila, ASEAN also drew delegations of businessmen and investors hungry to make deals.

Let’s start with some of the biggest business developments to keep on your radar:

Digital economy. All 11 ASEAN countries signed the Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), which seeks to simplify cross-border e-commerce, digital payments, and data transfers across the region. With implementation targeted by May 2027, the Department of Trade and Industry plans to conduct trade shows and information campaigns next year to help entrepreneurs understand the agreement.

All 11 ASEAN countries signed the Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), which seeks to simplify cross-border e-commerce, digital payments, and data transfers across the region. With implementation targeted by May 2027, the Department of Trade and Industry plans to conduct trade shows and information campaigns next year to help entrepreneurs understand the agreement. Regional power grid. All ASEAN members signed an enhanced agreement on the ASEAN Power Grid that could eventually allow them to buy and sell electricity across borders. While construction remains some ways off, the International Energy Agency estimates that ASEAN will need $27 billion in cross-border power interconnection investments through 2040, on top of more than $300 billion to expand and modernize domestic grids, presenting opportunities for infrastructure developers and financial institutions.

While construction remains some ways off, the International Energy Agency estimates that ASEAN will need $27 billion in cross-border power interconnection investments through 2040, on top of more than $300 billion to expand and modernize domestic grids, presenting opportunities for infrastructure developers and financial institutions. Free trade agreements. Canada concluded negotiations for separate free trade agreements with the Philippines and ASEAN. The Philippine-Canada agreement, targeted for signing in 2027, covers goods, services, investments, and digital trade, opening another avenue for businesses looking to diversify their markets.

Canada concluded negotiations for separate free trade agreements with the Philippines and ASEAN. The Philippine-Canada agreement, targeted for signing in 2027, covers goods, services, investments, and digital trade, opening another avenue for businesses looking to diversify their markets. US trade relations. US President Donald Trump also flew to Manila for a special summit with ASEAN leaders and a state visit with Marcos, during which he announced what he called the “biggest trade deal” between the Philippines and the US. Although no formal agreement was signed, Trump claimed that the Philippines had agreed to source 100% of its agricultural and energy imports from the US, which Philippine officials have since questioned. Watch how discussions unfold, as even a partial shift toward US suppliers could reshape supply chains and introduce greater competition for local producers.

Beyond the high-level meetings, ASEAN-related forums also brought together an eclectic mix of business leaders and global personalities – from Tessie Sy-Coson, Martha Sazon, and Maria Ressa to Angelina Jolie – for discussions spanning inclusive growth, food and energy security, and artificial intelligence.

Among the businesspeople in the lineup, a recurring theme was how difficult it remains to do business across ASEAN, despite its long-held dream of being a single marketplace. Ayala Corporation chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala lamented differences in regulatory standards and investment approvals, while former CIMB Group chairman Nazir Razak criticized the slow pace of regional economic integration.

READ: From micro to massive, ASEAN’s entrepreneurs face regulatory hurdles

Yet ASEAN is still an attractive investment destination, with foreign direct investment reaching a record $246 billion in 2025, up 10%.

And there was no shortage of investment opportunities being pitched.

At the Fourth ASEAN Investment Forum, gathered in one room were Philippine Board of Investments managing head Ceferino Rodolfo, global infrastructure investor I Squared Capital, and representatives of sovereign wealth funds from Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, and of course, the Philippines’ own Maharlika Investment Corporation. Between them, these institutions oversee assets worth well over $100 billion – a dealmaking goldmine.

Here’s a peek at some of the Philippine projects being pitched to investors there, as detailed in an investment booklet distributed during the event and seen by Rappler:

Project SAFAL. ALCOM’s proposed $340-million sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) project is seeking $102 million in equity and $238 million in debt financing, with a projected equity internal rate of return (IRR) of 28%.

ALCOM’s proposed $340-million sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) project is seeking $102 million in equity and $238 million in debt financing, with a projected equity internal rate of return (IRR) of 28%. SPV Clark. SAFAsia’s proposed $226-million facility in New Clark City would convert locally available waste into jet fuel, targeting annual production of 20,000 tons beginning in 2028. The project seeks $67.8 million in equity and $158.2 million in debt financing, with a project IRR of 14% to 17%.

SAFAsia’s proposed $226-million facility in New Clark City would convert locally available waste into jet fuel, targeting annual production of 20,000 tons beginning in 2028. The project seeks $67.8 million in equity and $158.2 million in debt financing, with a project IRR of 14% to 17%. Burgos Solar Power Project. Zenith Renewable’s proposed 64.5-megawatt solar farm in Pangasinan, paired with 51.2 MWh battery storage, seeks $12 million for a 70% equity stake, with a target IRR of 13.4%.

Zenith Renewable’s proposed 64.5-megawatt solar farm in Pangasinan, paired with 51.2 MWh battery storage, seeks $12 million for a 70% equity stake, with a target IRR of 13.4%. San Pedro Agri-Solar Power Project. Another Zenith project combining agricultural land use with solar power generation seeks $2 million for a 70% equity stake, with a projected IRR of 17%.

READ: [Vantage Point] The ASEAN Summit’s billions: Who pays, who gains?

However, one investment opportunity conspicuously absent from every ASEAN discussion was the US-led Pax Silica initiative.

As officials had indicated beforehand, no Pax Silica deal was signed during the summit or US President Donald Trump’s subsequent state visit. Given the protests surrounding Trump’s arrival and opposition to Pax Silica itself, the administration had little political incentive to draw even more attention to the controversial project.

We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader.– Rappler.com

World.title: Couple shot dead in Bukidnon by one of victim’s ex-partner
World.content:
VALENCIA CITY, Bukidnon — A couple was shot dead allegedly by the former live-in partner of one of the victims in Bukidnon on Wednesday evening, November 25, police said.The Impasugong police station said that a 43-year-old woman and her 52-year-old live-in partner were shot dead inside their home in Sitio Ulayanon, Barangay Kalabugao, around 6:55 p.m.Police said the suspect is the woman’s former live-in partner, who remains at large.Initial investigation showed the victim’s daughter witnessed her biological father allegedly shoot her mother and stepfather.

Police said the killing stemmed from an unresolved dispute over ownership of a house and a motorcycle previously acquired by the suspect and the female victim.The matter had been brought before the Barangay Lupon of Kalabugao, but no settlement was reached.

World.title: Dangerous heat index hits 5 areas on Thursday
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — A dangerous heat index gripped five areas on Thursday as the El Niño phenomenon continues to affect the country, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa).

The highest heat index for the day was recorded in Dipolog, Zamboanga del Norte and Puerto Princesa, Palawan which peaked at 43°C, while Coron and Cuyo in Palawan and Butuan City, Agusan del Norte experienced a heat index of 42°C.

A heat index of from 42°C to 51°C is classified as dangerous byPagasa.

Article continues after this 

This is due to increased risks of heat cramps and heat exhaustion, which could then lead to heat stroke.

World.title: Senators warn agency heads: No show, less budget
World.content:
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri (Photo courtesy of Senate Public Relations and Information Bureau)

MANILA, Philippines — Senators on Thursday warned heads of government agencies that their offices may suffer budget reductions if they fail to attend budget deliberations.

The warning came as senators gave leeway to Philippine Sports Commission Chairperson Patrick “Pato” Gregorio, who missed the debates for the agency’s P1.9-billion proposed 2027 spending plan due to an overseas meeting with the Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA).

“Those heads of agencies who were not here, we’re forewarning them now that there’s a chance na mabawasan po yung budget nila kung hindi po sila sumipot dito,” Senate Majority Leader Sen. Juan Miguel Zubiri said.

Article continues after this 

(Those heads of agencies who were not here, we’re forewarning them now that there’s a chance their budget will be reduced if they don’t show up here.)

“I suggest that we just move their budget elsewhere. Or we just lessen their budget and give it to another department who are more willing to defend their budget,” the senator added.

READ: Gatchalian questions Duterte’s absence at OVP budget hearing

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian emphasized that it’s a time-honored tradition that the heads of agencies come to the Senate to defend and justify their own budget.

“Budget nila yan so dapat sila manindigan,” he said.

Article continues after this 

(That’s their budget so they should defend it.)

But Gatchalian also explained that Gregorio’s case is “an exception, rather than a rule” as FIFA has shown interest in investing into the Philippines’ sports industry.

Article continues after this 

According to Zubiri, the Senate accepted Gregorio’s reason for not showing up during the budget deliberation of his agency because a potential USD25-million football development initiative is on the line.

Gregorio has vowed to come to the Senate before the PSC’s budget is approved on second reading, Zubiri added.

READ: Sara Duterte arrives at Senate amid OVP’s 2027 budget deliberations

Likewise, Sen. Joel Villanueva reminded department heads not to normalize skipping budget debates, pointing to Vice President Sara Duterte’s attendance during the Office of the Vice President’s (OVP) budget deliberations on Thursday.

World.title: Impeach court subpoenas BOC exec, Cale88 ex co-owner as witnesses
World.content:
FIle photo of the Senate impeachment court. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court on Thursday confirmed that it has served subpoenas on two witnesses named by Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team, including a Bureau of Customs (BOC) official and a former co-owner of Cale88 Foods Corp., ahead of next week’s hearings.

Senate impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol said Presiding Officer Francis Escudero signed the subpoenas on Nov. 25, directing BOC Deputy Commissioner Agaton Teodoro O. Uvero and Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada to appear before the court and submit documents related to Cale88.

Cale88, a banana chip manufacturing company formerly co-owned by Duterte’s husband Manases Carpio, has figured in the impeachment proceedings over questions surrounding its business operations and financial transactions.

Article continues after this 

Duterte is being accused of amassing unexplained wealth, untruthful Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net worth declaration and non-divestment of her business interests while serving as the country’s vice president.

According to Tongol, the Office of the Clerk of Court completed the service of both subpoenas on Thursday, Nov. 26.

Uvero’s subpoena was personally served at 9:05 a.m. at the BOC office, while the subpoena for Lebosada was sent electronically at 9:54 a.m.

Uvero is expected to testify on matters concerning Cale88 Foods’ export records in the custody of the BOC.

He was directed to produce the company’s certificate of registration issued by the BOC, related government documents, and records concerning its exports.

Article continues after this 

It can be recalled that Cale88’s receipt of P319 million in inward remittances from China-based companies has drawn scrutiny from senator-judges, who questioned the source and nature of the transactions.

Meanwhile, Tingson-Lebosada is expected to testify on Cale88 Foods’ organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, financial affairs, ownership and related matters.

Article continues after this 

The Senate impeachment court is scheduled to resume proceedings on Tuesday, December 1, at 10 a.m.

World.title: Adiong tells Meta: Fake news is personal, impacts us, families
World.content:
Lanao del Sur 1st District Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong (Photo courtesy of House PPAB)

MANILA, Philippines — While social media companies like Meta may view disinformation and misinformation as issues that can be addressed through fact-checking, Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong reminded these firms that such activities have personal consequences for their victims, affecting not only individuals but also their families.

During a hearing of the House of Representatives’ Committee on Suffrage and Electoral Reforms, Alonto Adiong said he believes he is now being targeted by a disinformation campaign, referring to rumors circulating on social media about a supposedly unfinished flood control project.

READ: Facebook takes down accounts linked to Duterte’s ex-socmed strategist

Article continues after this 

According to the lawmaker, the rumors are not true because the people who posted it supposedly used old photos and videos, adding that the project did not start under his term, and that it has been finished.

“In my case ah, kasi parang targeted ako ngayon eh […] may mga post doon, so ‘yon ang example ko although parang unang-una mali-mali ‘yong mga pictures nila at saka mga videos nila, hindi ‘yon sa distrito ko, ‘di ba? […] Yeah, I mean, mga gano’n na example, nagbigay sila ng isang project, pinakita nila, that was the video (that) was I think was taped a couple of years ago,” Alonto Adiong said.

(In my case ah, because it seems I am being targeted now […] there are posts, this is my example, but it is outrightly wrong because the pictures and videos used were not from my district. I mean, that is the example, they will show one project, but that video, (that) was I think was taped a couple of years ago.)

“Binalikan nila sinabi nila na wala pang natapos, tapos walang gan’yan, tapos ang iniligay nila doon instead na ‘yong flood — flood control started way way back because part ang distrito ko ng NOAH ( Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards), kasi talagang may four major tributaries kami kami d’yan eh,” he added.

(They went back to say that nothing has been finished, and there are no projects there, but the flood control projects started way way back because my district is part of NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards), because there are really four major tributaries in our area.)

Article continues after this 

READ: 7 in 10 Filipinos see fake news as big problem

However, Alonto Adiong noted that while these images depict a fake story, it appears true to the people who cannot verify it — which affects their family deeply.

Article continues after this 

“These are things that I guess from the first glance, at first glance, you would see it is correct because but the facts are twisted. And then they do not know that it has been finished two years ago. Then it did not start during my time, I wasn’t even a congressman at the time when it started,” he said.

“But not all people… were able to verify what they saw, and that is harmful not only to my career, but to my own personal reputation […] It may not be personal to you but these individuals have families, I have my children, I have a wife, I have my own personal family, we’re affected. It may not be personal to Meta, but it deeply harms our personal lives,” he added.

Alonto Adiong did not mention who was behind the spread of misinformation against him, but he said that one of their colleagues in the House of Representatives shared it.

“The problem is one of our colleagues posted it also, believing in his own fake news.,” he added.

However, it was Davao City Rep. Paolo Duterte who shared on his official Facebook page a video of Alonto Adiong’s alleged projects in the second district of Lanao del Sur.

In his post, Duterte called out Alonto Adiong for being noisy about the impeachment trial of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, yet being silent about the flood control projects.

“You keep commenting on the unexplained wealth of VP Inday, but in your own district, you can’t even show a receipt of where all your billion-peso projects are headed,” Rep. Duterte said, as translated by Facebook.

“Don’t be stubborn, or else your district will be flooded,” he added.

Alonto Adiong’s reminder to Meta came as the committee on suffrage and electoral reforms — which he chairs — discussed the substitute bill to the proposed law on the fair use of internet and social media in relation to elections.

There has been a lot of discussions on proposals to crackdown on disinformation and misinformation. However, there were concerns from poll watchdog Legal Network for Truthful Elections (Lente) that any law should not hover around content regulation, as it has the tendency to result in censorship.

Lente warned during the hearing last October 5 that they want to avoid a chilling effect as defining misleading and false content will depend on the implementing agency, and may touch on protected speech.

One of the proposals on the topic, House Majority Leader Ferdinand Alexander Marcos’ House Bill (HB) No. 3691 or the proposed Social Media, Artificial Intelligence and Internet Technology Regulation for Fair Elections Act, seek to define various terms related to the internet like AI, bots, deepfakes, and coordinated inauthentic behavior (CIB).

HB No. 3691 would also allow “election propaganda on the internet and the social media” but will be “subject to the limitation on authorized expenses of candidates and parties, observation of truth in advertising, and to the supervision and regulation” by the Commission on Elections (Comelec).

As of now, no one has been penalized for engaging in CIB in the country, but the said activity has been observed several times by Facebook. As early as M arch 2019, then Facebook Cybersecurity Policy head Nathaniel Gleicher said they removed 200 fake accounts operating under the network of communication strategist Nic Gabanuda Jr. for CIB.

READ: PR group pushes ethics, training vs AI disinformation, trolls

Gabunada was the social media campaign of former president Rodrigo Duterte.

According to Gleicher, the taken-down accounts were made to appear as normal and legitimate accounts while boosting messages in favor of certain political candidates.

Then in September 2020, Gleicher announced that the social media platform had taken down two networks for CIB again, with one of the networks being traced to the Philippine National Police and the Armed Forces of the Philippines.

The other network taken down by Facebook was traced to a group of individuals in China’s Fujian province. This network had sites with posts in Filipino expressing support for President Rodrigo Duterte and the possible 2022 presidential bid of his daughter, then Davao City mayor and now Vice President Duterte. /jpv

World.title: Most of PH to have fair weather; expect rain in parts of Luzon, Mindanao
World.content:
Satellite image from DOST / Pagasa

MANILA, Philippines – Most parts of the country are expected to experience generally fair weather, while parts of Luzon and Mindanao may see cloudy skies and rain due to the effects of the shear line and easterlies, the state weather bureau said.

According to the latest weather forecast issued by the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa), the shear line will mostly affect Extreme Northern Luzon, particularly Batanes and the Babuyan Islands, on Friday.

Article continues after this

“Sa Metro Manila at nalalabing bahagi naman ng Luzon ay makakaranas ng partly cloudy to overcast skies and localized thunderstorms,” said Pagasa weather specialist Loriedin De la Cruz – Galicia.

(Metro Manila and the rest of Luzon will experience partly cloudy to overcast skies and localized thunderstorms.)

The easterlies will also bring rain and cloudy skies over the Caraga and Davao regions in Mindanao.

Davao City: 25 to 34 degrees Celsius

World.title: 2 sea turtles found butchered in Bohol
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — Two sea turtles were found dead, with their carcasses mutilated, on the shore of Barangay Tiguis in Lila, Bohol.

READ: Bacnotan, La Union records first sea turtle nest of the season

According to the Bohol Provincial Environment Management Office, the dead green sea turtles (scientific name: Chelonia mydas) were discovered on Nov. 18.

Article continues after this 

The office said the first turtle discovered—measuring 45 centimeters (cm) in length and 40 cm in width—had its carcass severely mutilated, with only its head, organs, and tail remaining intact.

Meanwhile, the second dead turtle—measuring 34 cm in length and 30 cm in width—was also butchered, with its meat removed and taken.

“This indicates that the primary purpose of the butchering was to obtain the turtle’s meat,” the office said in a statement.

Initial investigation showed that the first turtle was discovered around 5:30 a.m. by a farmer who immediately reported it to the authorities, while the second turtle was discovered floating near the shoreline just a few minutes later.

The Philippine National Police (PNP) said it had already identified a person of interest in connection with the incident after a boat was found with bloodstains on its fishing net, along with a piece of wood suspected to have possibly been used to strike and incapacitate the turtle before it was butchered.

Article continues after this 

“These observations are subject to further police investigation and verification,” the Bohol Provincial Environment Management Office said, quoting the PNP.

Meanwhile, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, in a separate statement, condemned the discovery, tagging it as a “deplorable act.”

Article continues after this 

The DENR said the incident was not only a direct assault on the country’s protected wildlife but also a violation of Republic Act No. 9147 (Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act).

Under the said law, marine turtles are a protected and threatened species whose killing is punishable under Section 28 by up to six (6) years imprisonment and/or a fine of up to P500,000.
