World.title: Myanmar’s Putschist President Shrugs at ICJ Genocide Verdict
World.content:
Myanmar’s putschist president, Min Aung Hlaing, hit back at the International Court of Justice (ICJ)’s genocide ruling on Wednesday, telling his cabinet that the regime will not implement “unacceptable” measures.

“As a responsible country, we will carry out measures we consider necessary but will not comply with those that should not be followed,” he said.

The World Court ordered Myanmar to implement several measures after ruling on Nov. 19 that it committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in Rakhine in 2016-17: Prosecute the perpetrators, provide reparations, ensure safe repatriation, guarantee non-repetition, and pass laws criminalizing genocide.

The junta chief claimed the ruling had damaged Myanmar’s national dignity, dismissing the case brought by the Gambia as a one-sided accusation.

“I will not accept anything that harms the country,” said the self-appointed president, who as military chief oversaw the 2016-17 Rakhine “clearance operations” now ruled as genocide. He also stands accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity following the coup he staged in 2021.

Legal experts noted that the ICJ ruling is legally binding, meaning the losing party cannot selectively choose which parts of the judgment to accept or reject.

“It was a final judgement from the international court — not a statement, recommendation or instruction,” human rights lawyer Zar Li Aye told The Irrawaddy.

“As per UN charter 94 (1), every member state is legally obliged to comply with orders from the International Court of Justice,” she stressed.

She added that Myanmar risked being found guilty of violating additional international laws if it failed to comply with the ICJ’s decision.

The ruling has drawn widespread international backing from Western and regional governments, the EU, UN officials, and major human rights organizations, which welcomed the landmark decision as a decisive step toward accountability for the Rohingya community.

Permanent members France and the UK requested a closed-door UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday to press members on Myanmar’s compliance with the ruling. The outcome of the meeting remains unknown.

Meanwhile, the judgement has triggered a chorus of denial from the regime and its allies. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected it as “a great disappointment delivered with dissenting opinions” and “not decided unanimously by judges,” referring to the 9-6 ruling.

However, it remains unclear what effect the judgement will have on the regime’s international standing.

“We may see no direct impact from the ICJ’s decision in the short term,” Myanmar political researcher Sai Kyi Zin Soe told The Irrawaddy.

“We expect to see different responses from different countries, depending on how Myanmar responds and to what extent it complies with the court’s decision,” he said.

World.title: Myanmar’s Economy Reeling as Kyat Nosedives
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of the kyat is tearing across Myanmar’s economy, disrupting imports, driving up production costs and raising fears of further economic shocks.

The kyat market rate steadily weakened since last month before nosediving to reach over 5,400 kyats to the dollar on Thursday.

Exporters as well as importers say their businesses are increasingly unprofitable, exacerbated by regime restrictions.

One exporter told The Irrawaddy that although businesses are officially allowed to exchange 85 percent of their export earnings at market rates, banks are often unable to offer them, plus the regime requires the remaining 15 percent to be converted at the fixed rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar, resulting in significant losses.

Rising operating costs and volatile exchange rates are forcing some exporters to scale back overseas shipments. Traders are also struggling to determine how to price imported goods as foreign-currency costs fluctuate sharply.

“Importers are finding it difficult to set prices because the dollar rate is so unstable. This problem needs to be resolved immediately or domestic consumption will also be affected,” said a trader.

The latest decline is due to several factors, not least that the regime has announced it will borrow over 2 trillion kyats from the Central Bank to pay plug the hole in its budget—essentially telling the bank to print money. The rubberstamp Parliament has already approved an additional budget for the Central Bank to churn out fresh banknotes.

At the same time, the regime recently issued new import licenses, driving up demand for dollars. Another factor at play is planned salary increases for civil servants in the next fiscal year.

The regime also relaxed the fixed exchange rate for remittances from overseas workers from 3,600 kyats per dollar to 4,600 kyats in a bid to encourage them to go through official banking channels—but that backfired and was read as a sign of weakness by the market.

Other currencies have soared apace, with 100,000 kyats falling from 700 Thai baht earlier this month to around 600 baht.

That is bound to make Thai consumer goods and clothing forbiddingly expensive, to say nothing of imported medicines, cooking oil and industrial raw materials.

As usual when the situation runs away from it, the regime is targeting currency traders to try and frighten the market into submission. Yangon money traders say officers from the Bureau of Special Investigation are roaming the markets in search of anyone to fine and arrest.

World.title: Myanmar’s Democratic Opposition Urges ASEAN to Shun ‘Genocidal’ Junta Leaders
World.content:
Myanmar’s democratic opposition has urged ASEAN not to reintegrate regime leaders accused of war crimes and responsible for genocide, following an ASEAN-backed stakeholders’ dialogue in the Philippines.

The two-day meeting, hosted by the ASEAN chair in Tagaytay on Nov. 22-23, brought together representatives from the National League for Democracy (NLD), the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), resistance organizations and civil society groups.

CRPH spokesperson Sithu Maung said participants warned against any ASEAN move to recognize Myanmar’s de facto military regime.

“We reiterated that ASEAN should no longer provide space for military leaders who have committed war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide,” he said, referring to recent remarks by Min Aung Hlaing that his administration is reconsidering ‌the country’s relationship with the regional bloc. The putschist president spoke out after ASEAN leaders at last week’s Manila summit reaffirmed the ban on regime leaders attending high-level regional meetings.

Singapore, which will assume the ASEAN chair next year, attended the stakeholders’ dialogue as an observer. Delegations from both the Philippines and Singapore received the SCEF’s policy paper on Myanmar during the meeting.

Also in attendance were representatives from Chin resistance forces, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front (ABSDF), elected lawmakers and other stakeholders. Discussions focused on the military situation, obstacles to delivery of humanitarian aid, implications of the Rohingya genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), and the regime’s escalating airstrikes against civilians.

SCEF said last week’s genocide ruling should spur stronger efforts to enforce accountability for the regime’s past atrocities and ongoing crimes in Myanmar. It urged the international community not to shield military leaders from responsibility or enable further violence.

Then-military chief Min Aung Hlaing oversaw the 2017 “clearance operations” against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine that the World Court said amounted to genocide.

The regime rejected the ICJ ruling as “unfair” and stated its repatriation of Rohingya refugees would continue on its own terms, ignoring UN calls to grant them citizenship rights.

The democratic opposition’s appeal comes amid growing debate over ASEAN’s approach to Myanmar. While the bloc continues to exclude Min Aung Hlaing and his leadership from top-level meetings, members including Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia have expanded bilateral engagement with the regime in recent months.

World.title: Myanmar Records Worst Landmine Casualties in the World for 3rd Year
World.content:
Myanmar recorded the highest number of casualties from landmines and unexploded ordnance in the world last year with nearly 1,900, according to the Landmine Monitor report released Tuesday.

The group’s research shows that Myanmar was the country worst affected by deaths from landmines and so-called “explosive remnants of war” for the third year running.

Worldwide, some 6,929 casualties were recorded in 2025, counting both civilians and military personnel. Myanmar accounted for a massive proportion of over 27 percent or nearly one-third with 1,891.

The military has regularly used antipersonnel mines since 1999 and increased their use notably after the coup in February 2021, the report pointed out.

Casualties soared as a result, from just 368 in 2021 to 1,003 in 2023 before doubling to 2,029 the following year.

They are regularly planted around military bases and outposts as well as mobile phone towers, mining operations and fuel pipelines.

One regime combat engineer reported that he was ordered to plant mines in Kachin and Rakhine states near populated areas, marked only by “Danger Do Not Enter” signs without mentioning mines.

“Often there are no signs,” said Thet Oo of the resistance Yinmabin–Salingyi Strike Committee in heavily mined Sagaing Region.

He said the regime frequently plants landmines when launching offensives or raiding villages, placing them at the entrance of houses.

They are designed to sever legs.

He admitted that the heartland resistance People’s Defense Forces (PDF) also used remote-controlled handmade landmines across the country after the coup. But when resistance governing bodies were formed, they banned mines near settled areas except for military purposes that require their authorization.

“The mines are meant to injure or delay the enemy,” he added. But he claimed they are always cleared before residents return.

The report says ethnic armed organizations reported seizing regime landmines almost every month between January 2022 and this September 2026, showing how prevalent their use is.

Regime-aligned ethnic Border Guard Forces (BGF) and the militias under the regime’s command also use landmines, it says.

“We urge all states to reject the production and use of antipersonnel mines, by any actor, under any circumstances,” Tamar Gabelnick, director of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL) told AFP.

Syria was the second-most affected country with an equally massive 1,602 casualties, trailed at a substantial distance by Afghanistan with 497.

World.title: Myanmar’s China Dilemma: Turning Beijing’s Need Into Leverage Requires Legitimate Leaders
World.content:
Anyone seeking clarity on China-Myanmar relations must first ask one crucial question: does China need Myanmar, or does Myanmar need China?

Some argue that Beijing’s often-cited desire for access to the Indian Ocean through Myanmar is overstated. Others contend that China barely needs Myanmar at all, and that the relationship matters far more to Naypyitaw than to Beijing.

The reality is more complicated.

The Malacca Dilemma

Some analysts state that China needs Myanmar to secure overland access to the Indian Ocean, bypassing the Malacca Strait chokepoint. Others dismiss this view, saying the chokepoint is no longer a problem for a country which now boasts the world’s largest navy.

Chinese leaders began wrestling with the “Malacca Dilemma” in the early 2000s under President Hu Jintao. Around the same time, Beijing and Myanmar’s previous junta began talks on pipelines to transport oil and gas from the Bay of Bengal to Yunnan Province. Agreements were reached in 2007-2008, and construction began in June 2010.

At that point, China had yet to commission a single aircraft carrier. Its first carrier — a Soviet-made ship bought from Ukraine in 1998 and modified — did not enter service until 2012. Today, China operates three aircraft carriers and is reportedly building a fourth, which is expected to be nuclear-powered.

In other words, the strategic calculations underpinning the China-Myanmar energy corridor were made before Beijing emerged as a major naval power.

More than one energy corridor

In reality, China has never relied on a single route to meet its vast energy needs. Myanmar’s gas and oil pipelines provide a direct energy corridor from the Indian Ocean, but are only one piece of a much larger network. Beijing also imports oil through the Kazakhstan-China pipeline and receives oil and gas from Russia via overland routes. Meanwhile, the Central Asia-China pipeline network pumps natural gas from Turkmenistan and other Central Asian states into western China. Additional pipelines from Central Asia and Russia are planned or under construction.

For a country the size of China, a single pipeline or supply source is never enough. Beijing’s strategy is diversification.

Why Myanmar matters

Those who argue that China does not need Myanmar often point to Beijing’s expanding network of rail, road and pipeline connections across Eurasia.

China has rail links with Laos, Vietnam, Russia, Mongolia and Central Asia. It has energy corridors stretching north into Russia and west into Central Asia. On paper, Myanmar is only one route among many.

Yet, China is not an economic monolith; its interests vary sharply from province to province. Here is where geography gives Myanmar a unique advantage.

For inland provinces such as Yunnan, Sichuan and Guizhou, Myanmar provides the most direct route to the Indian Ocean. It is also the closest overland entry for energy imports arriving from the Middle East and Africa.

A railway or trade corridor through Myanmar would offer southwestern China a global shipping link that is shorter, cheaper and likely more efficient than ports to the east.

It would also help bridge the yawning gap between the country’s wealthy coastal provinces and its underdeveloped inland regions. Coastal provinces like Guangdong have prospered through direct access to ports, global shipping networks and export markets, outpacing inland neighbors facing higher logistics costs and weaker international connectivity.

For Beijing, plugging southwestern China into international markets is not simply a foreign-policy objective, but part of a broader strategy to reduce economic inequality inside China itself.

This is where Myanmar enters the picture.

The China-Myanmar Economic Corridor, Kyaukphyu projects, road links, railways and pipelines are not intended for China as a whole. They are aimed at accelerating development in China’s southwest including Yunnan, Sichuan and other inland regions seeking easier access to the Indian Ocean and global markets.

A relationship of mutual interests

When it comes to foreign investment, countries only inject capital where they see strategic or economic returns.

During the so-called reform period between 2011 and 2020, Myanmar failed to attract large-scale investment from Western countries despite their stated commitment to the country’s democratization. They were reluctant to invest because the prospects of economic returns were low.

Beijing invests because it sees a tangible benefit — access to the Indian Ocean that will integrate China’s landlocked southwest into global trade networks.

In return, Myanmar gains infrastructure, jobs, technology transfer and improved connectivity. The ousted National League for Democracy government recognized the benefits in 2020 when it signed agreements for the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor.

A well-governed Myanmar could turn China’s need for access into an opportunity, negotiating terms that serve its national interests, and ensuring a win-win situation for both. The question is whether military-ruled Myanmar is in a position to do so today.

The real question

The argument over whether China needs Myanmar or Myanmar needs China misses the point. Both need each other.

China needs Myanmar as an Indian Ocean gateway, a trade partner and a critical link in the development of its southwestern provinces. Myanmar needs investment, infrastructure and access to the world’s second-largest economy. The ingredients for a mutually beneficial relationship are in place.

The real question is whether Myanmar has leaders capable of translating that potential into national gains rather than debt, dependency and unequal agreements.

A military regime lacking a public mandate, mired in corruption, and facing war crime accusations cannot negotiate from a position of strength — or ensure that Chinese investment serves Myanmar’s national interests.

China’s need for Myanmar is real. The challenge for Myanmar is ensuring that need works in its favor.

World.title: Arakan’s Next Battle Is for Legitimacy, Not Territory
World.content:
The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) November 19 ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during its 2017 military operations marks a historic moment for international justice. But its implications extend beyond Myanmar’s military and the courtroom in The Hague.

For the United League of Arakan/Arakan Army (ULA/AA), which now controls most of Arakan (Rakhine State) in western Myanmar, the judgment raises a fundamental question: Can a movement that has achieved remarkable military victories build a political system that protects the rights of all communities, including the Rohingya?

The ICJ judgment is legally binding on Myanmar, not directly on the ULA/AA, which was not a party to the case. Nevertheless, the organization now controls much of the territory from which hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. Its policies will influence the prospects for reconciliation, refugee repatriation and Arakan’s international engagement.

The ULA/AA’s next challenge is therefore not simply territorial control, but establishing political legitimacy through responsible governance.

The politics of identity

One of the most sensitive issues facing the ULA/AA concerns the terms “Rohingya,” “Bengali” and “Muslim.”

For Rohingya communities, their name represents ethnic identity, historical belonging and the right to recognition. Arakan political actors and the people of Arakan, however, reject the term “Rohingya,” preferring “Bengali” because of competing interpretations of the region’s history and migration.

The ULA/AA has sometimes encouraged the use of “Muslim” as a less politically contentious term in efforts to improve relations between communities.

Such an approach may help reduce tensions, but it cannot resolve the underlying disagreement. “Muslim” describes religious affiliation, while “Rohingya” represents ethnic self-identification. The terms are not interchangeable, and not all Muslims in Arakan identify as Rohingya.

The ICJ’s treatment of the Rohingya as a protected group under the Genocide Convention underscores the significance of their collective identity.

Yet peaceful coexistence does not require every community to agree on a single historical narrative. It requires accepting that disagreements over identity cannot justify discrimination or the denial of fundamental rights.

For the ULA/AA, respecting ethnic self-identification while ensuring equal treatment would demonstrate political maturity rather than weakness.

Social harmony requires more than symbolic gestures

Decades of discrimination, communal violence and displacement have created deep mistrust between Arakanese (Rakhine) and Rohingya/Muslim communities.

Some local initiatives under ULA/AA administration, including intercommunal meetings, sporting activities and limited Muslim participation in local governance, suggest efforts to rebuild relations.

These developments may be constructive, but genuine social harmony requires more than symbolic gestures.

It depends on freedom of movement, access to education and healthcare, protection of property, fair administration and meaningful participation in decisions affecting communities.

The ULA/AA also faces serious human rights scrutiny. United Nations reporting has raised allegations of abuses against Rohingya civilians in areas under Arakan Army control, including arbitrary detention, forced labor, forced recruitment and restrictions on movement.

The organization has disputed allegations of wrongdoing, while citing security threats from armed groups operating near the Bangladesh border.

Such threats require legitimate security responses, but they cannot justify collective punishment or discrimination against civilians. The actions of Rohingya/Muslim armed organizations must be distinguished from the rights of Rohingya/Muslim communities.

Credible investigations, accountability and transparent administration would do more to build trust than political assurances alone.

International engagement is not recognition

The ULA/AA’s territorial advances have transformed the political landscape along the Myanmar-Bangladesh border.

Bangladesh, which hosts more than a million Rohingya refugees, has publicly acknowledged communicating with the AA as part of efforts to address the refugee crisis.

This creates opportunities for practical engagement with regional governments, the United Nations and international humanitarian organizations.

China and India also have strategic interests in Arakan, particularly concerning regional stability, trade and infrastructure development.

However, practical engagement and formal diplomatic recognition are fundamentally different.

Governments and international organizations may cooperate with authorities exercising effective territorial control without recognizing them as sovereign governments.

The ICJ judgment does not confer international recognition or political legitimacy upon the ULA/AA. Nor does it guarantee that regional governments or the United Nations will recognize the organization.

Nevertheless, the ULA/AA could strengthen its international standing by demonstrating respect for human rights, facilitating humanitarian assistance and establishing credible policies for all communities.

The opportunity is significant, but international credibility must be earned through conduct rather than military victories alone.

Preparing for the Rohingya challenge

The Rohingya issue remains one of the most complex long-term challenges facing the ULA/AA.

Refugees in Bangladesh continue to face uncertainty over citizenship, security, freedom of movement, destroyed homes and the possibility of renewed persecution.

Although the ULA/AA cannot independently resolve Myanmar’s citizenship framework or confer internationally recognized Myanmar citizenship, it exercises considerable influence over local security, administration and conditions affecting eventual refugee returns.

Rather than waiting for formal international recognition or a nationwide political settlement, the ULA/AA should develop a comprehensive and transparent policy addressing the Rohingya issue.

Such a framework should prioritize equal protection, respect for ethnic self-identification, intercommunal dialogue and safeguards against discrimination.

It should also establish credible mechanisms to investigate alleged abuses, protect housing and land rights, preserve residency records and consult Rohingya representatives, including refugees in Bangladesh.

Cooperation with Bangladesh, relevant UN agencies and humanitarian organizations could help prepare the groundwork for future repatriation.

Any return process must be voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable. Premature repatriation without adequate security and rights protections would risk repeating past failures.

These steps would not immediately resolve historical grievances or guarantee international recognition. But they would demonstrate that the ULA/AA is preparing to govern a diverse society rather than merely administer territory captured through war.

The real test of Arakan’s future

The ICJ judgment concerns Myanmar’s legal responsibility for genocide. It does not determine Arakan’s constitutional future or confer recognition upon the ULA/AA.

Yet it presents the organization with an important political opportunity.

For decades, Arakanese communities have pursued greater autonomy, political rights and self-determination. Those aspirations remain central to Arakan’s political struggle.

But self-determination becomes more credible when it respects the rights and identities of other communities sharing the same territory.

The ULA/AA has demonstrated its military capabilities. Its next challenge is to establish institutions capable of protecting people regardless of ethnicity, religion or political affiliation.

International engagement may expand as the organization becomes increasingly relevant to regional security, humanitarian operations and the Rohingya refugee crisis.

However, lasting legitimacy will depend on whether it can translate territorial control into inclusive governance, accountability and peaceful coexistence.

The ULA/AA has won control of territory. Its next battle is to earn the trust of all the people who live there.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Leader to Attend Regional Talks in Vietnam
World.content:
HANOI, Vietnam—Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing will attend regional talks in Hanoi on Saturday, Vietnam said. It will be his first multilateral meeting since taking civilian office this year.

The event comes days after the UN’s International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar committed genocide with its 2017 crackdown on the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority.

Min Aung Hlaing was head of the armed forces at the time, before leading a 2021 coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and plunged Myanmar into civil war.

The prime ministers of Cambodia, Thailand, Laos and hosts Vietnam will also take part in the talks held under two regional cooperation mechanisms, ACMECS and CLMV, the Vietnamese Foreign Ministry said in a statement late Tuesday.

Min Aung Hlaing was installed as nominally civilian president in April following widely criticized elections in which pro-military parties won a landslide.

He has since been touring regional capitals, including in neighboring Thailand, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia, in what analysts say is a quest for legitimacy.

The four nations are part of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has frozen Myanmar out of high-level summits since the coup, but which agreed this month to seek “calibrated engagement.”

ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn will attend Saturday’s talks in Hanoi alongside Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung and Laotian Prime Minister Saleumxay Kommasith.

According to Vietnamese state media, the discussions are expected to focus on economic connectivity, notably infrastructure, logistics, trade and supply chains as well as the environment.

The meetings will comprise the 12th Cambodia-Laos-Myanmar-Vietnam (CLMV) summit and the 11th Ayeyawady-Chao Phraya-Mekong Economic Cooperation Strategy (ACMECS) summit.

Myanmar’s regime has always denied genocide, saying its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents, and described the ICJ ruling as “a great disappointment” and “not fair”.

World.title: Malaysia to Repatriate Thousands More Myanmar Migrants
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia—Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Tuesday the country will send more than 6,500 migrants back to Myanmar in a new round of repatriations.

The Southeast Asian Muslim-majority country has historically offered safe haven to those exiled from Myanmar by persecution or conflict but has been keen to resolve a long-running refugee challenge involving foreign asylum seekers.

Malaysia already sent back around 1,500 migrants back to war-torn Myanmar in late September in an opaque scheme that rights groups have raised concern about.

The fresh repatriation comes five days after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.

“The foreign minister has approved three naval ships to transport back on December 6 and 7, 1,500 Myanmar citizens,” Anwar told the Malaysian parliament.

“And for the month of December, 5,303 will be brought back by aircraft at the expense of the Myanmar government,” he added.

The UN’s highest court, based in The Hague, has ruled that Myanmar authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.

Kuala Lumpur said in late October it would seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country were being held in military detention.

Anwar did not mention the request for clarification, but he said Malaysia reiterated its stance over concern about the Rohingya and other ethnic groups, which was also underscored by the ICJ’s ruling.

Rohingya, a persecuted Muslim minority, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.

Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognize their status.

AFP fact-checkers have found that Rohingya refugees in Malaysia have been targeted by online disinformation campaigns that rights advocates say are fueling xenophobia and intimidation.

Turkey rebuffs Rohingya resettlement

Separately, Anwar said Turkey was not prepared to consider taking in 10,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, following an announcement by his deputy that was later rowed back.

Malaysia said Friday it was seeking to resettle the refugees in Turkey through a structured skills training program, but the statement was subsequently deleted from Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s Facebook page without explanation.

In his initial statement, Ahmad Zahid said the proposal aimed to address Malaysia’s Rohingya refugee situation in a more “coordinated, effective and humane” manner.

“So if they [Turkey] say that ‘we are not ready,’ I respect that decision,” he said.

In response to a lawmaker’s question on whether Ankara had agreed to take in 10,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, Ahmad Zahid said Turkey “is not ready to consider [the request].”

He added that Turkey is currently hosting “more than 4 million refugees from Gulf countries, Arab countries and several neighboring countries.”

Malaysia will explore third-country resettlement options, including among members of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, he continued.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Snow Leopard Population Nearly Doubles Since Early 2000s
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s snow leopard population has nearly doubled since the early 2000s, reaching around 200 animals in 2025, as the country expands habitat protection, scientific research and wildlife monitoring.

The population was estimated at 100–110 snow leopards in the early 2000s, according to the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources, which presented conservation results on Nov. 25 during a meeting between Kazakhstan’s Ecology Minister Alibek Kuantyrov and Azat Ziganshin, ecology and natural resources minister of Tatarstan.

The officials discussed biodiversity conservation, snow leopard protection and opportunities for joint scientific research, experience-sharing and the use of modern monitoring technologies.

Expanding habitat protection

Around 80% of snow leopard habitat in Kazakhstan is covered by protected natural areas, according to the ministry. In 2025, the Merke regional natural park was established in the Zhambyl Region to protect natural landscapes, including the snow leopard’s habitat.

Snow leopard conservation efforts involve the Institute of Zoology and staff of protected natural areas, who conduct research and monitor populations using camera traps and satellite collars.

As of 2026, 17 snow leopards had been equipped with satellite collars, enabling researchers to collect data on the animals and monitor their movements across their habitats.

Regional cooperation and research

The meeting also covered conservation initiatives in the region, including plans in Tatarstan to establish a Snow Leopard scientific center in the Altai Republic and the opening of the Ak Ilbirs research center in cooperation with Kyrgyzstan.

Snow leopards hold historical and cultural significance for Kazakhstan and Tatarstan, symbolizing strength, nobility and grandeur. Their protection remains a shared conservation priority.

World.title: Kazakhstan, China Explore Joint Energy Research Center and Grid Projects
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and China are exploring the creation of a joint energy research center, a 2-gigawatt transmission line and industrial energy storage projects as the two countries expand cooperation in engineering and energy infrastructure.

The initiatives were discussed during a meeting between Kazakh Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov and Ni Zhen, chairman of China Energy Engineering Group, during the minister’s working visit to China, reported the Energy Ministry on Nov. 26.

The talks focused on shifting cooperation from individual infrastructure projects toward broader scientific and technical partnership, including engineering expertise, energy system digitalization and solutions to improve the reliability of Kazakhstan’s power grid.

Joint research and hydrogen energy

Kazakhstan supported a proposal to establish a joint research center at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University. The center is expected to draw on Energy China’s research, analytical and engineering expertise to assess major infrastructure projects, develop technical and economic feasibility studies, digitalize energy systems and build industry databases.

The parties also discussed hydrogen energy development. Kazakhstan’s first hydrogen production facility has already been launched at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University, providing a basis for further research in the field.

“Today, our partnership with Energy China is moving to a new level toward joint scientific work, the exchange of engineering expertise and comprehensive planning for network development. The establishment of a research center at KazNU, the development of direct current technologies and energy storage systems directly contribute to improving the reliability and resilience of Kazakhstan’s energy system,” Akkenzhenov said.

Grid infrastructure and energy storage

The talks also covered the development of backbone electricity networks and balancing the national power system.

The parties discussed prospects for a 2-gigawatt high-voltage direct current transmission line along the Ekibastuz-Balkhash route. Kazakhstan has completed the necessary calculations and prepared a feasibility study for the project.

Industrial energy storage systems were another focus. Key substations and connection points for potential projects have already been identified, while a bill establishing mechanisms for investment returns on energy storage systems has passed its first reading.

Following the adoption of the legislative amendments, the parties are prepared to proceed with practical discussions on joint projects in the sector.

Renewable energy projects

The sides also reviewed ongoing renewable energy projects involving Energy China. The 300-megawatt Sauran solar power plant in the Turkistan Region is expected to be connected to the grid ahead of schedule, by the end of this year, according to the company.

Meanwhile, the parties are finalizing certain parameters of an investment agreement for a 500-megawatt wind power plant in the Karagandy Region to accelerate the project’s transition to the construction phase.

The negotiations concluded with both sides reaffirming their interest in expanding technological cooperation, exchanging expertise and implementing joint research and engineering initiatives.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Agricultural Exports Rise 34.7% as Processed Products Gain Ground
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s agricultural exports rose 34.7% in the first nine months of 2026, driven by growing shipments of processed products, including sunflower oil, flour and animal feed, as the country seeks to expand value-added production, according to the Agriculture Ministry.

Agricultural exports reached $6.4 billion between January and September, up from $4.8 billion in the same period last year. While grain remains a major export commodity, processed agricultural products are gaining a larger role in export growth, reflecting expanding capacities of domestic processing enterprises.

Growth in processed products

Sunflower oil exports increased from 470,900 tons to 661,500 tons during the reporting period. In monetary terms, shipments grew from $474.6 million to $731.4 million.

Exports of wheat and wheat-rye flour also increased to 1.59 million tons, up from 1.3 million tons a year earlier. Export revenue rose from $343 million to $462.2 million.

Animal feed exports demonstrated similar growth, reaching 2.85 million tons worth $662.3 million, compared with 2.02 million tons and $425.7 million in the same period of 2025.

Grain exports remain substantial

Despite the growing contribution of processed goods, Kazakhstan continues to export large volumes of grain. Exports of wheat and meslin reached 6.2 million tons worth $1.42 billion in January-September, compared with 5.5 million tons and $1.12 billion a year earlier.

Flax seed exports amounted to 881,700 tons, valued at $429.3 million. The growth in exports of vegetable oils, flour and animal feed reflects the increasing capacity of Kazakhstan’s agricultural processing sector, according to the ministry.

Expanding domestic processing allows the country to move beyond exporting raw agricultural commodities, create higher-value production chains, increase the value added within the domestic economy and strengthen the international presence of Kazakh products.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Infrastructure Ambitions Put Investment Climate in Focus, PM Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to allocate approximately 6.5 trillion tenge (US$13 billion) from the National Fund through 2029 to finance infrastructure projects, as the government seeks to attract foreign investment, technology and expertise to support nationwide modernization.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov discussed the investment agenda and cooperation with international businesses at a meeting of the Foreign Investors Council under the Kazakh President on Nov. 26.

The nationwide construction program, with 2027 declared the Year of Nationwide Great Construction, is expected to create opportunities for international partners in engineering, construction, infrastructure management and the production of materials and equipment.

Bektenov said the projects would lay the foundation for Kazakhstan’s long-term economic development, emphasizing the country’s interest in advanced technologies, modern construction standards and international management practices. The government also seeks to develop joint production of construction materials, equipment and components with potential for export.

New investment support framework

The government is working to improve its investment support system through a coordinated framework involving Baiterek holding. Kazakh Invest is expected to join the holding, while a unified front office will be established to support investment projects and facilitate access to financing.

The Foreign Ministry will continue working to attract investors through international outreach. Bektenov also highlighted efforts to strengthen legal protection for investors, including President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s initiative to establish an investment court in Alatau using international practices.

Foreign businesses raise regulatory concerns

Representatives of international companies raised issues related to taxation, customs procedures, energy regulation, labor legislation and digitalization.

Yerlan Dosymbekov, managing partner of EY for Central Asia and the Caucasus and chair of the Kazakhstan Council of Foreign Investors, highlighted concerns regarding the new VAT refund procedure for exporters, re-export taxation and customs transit.

Seger Hointink, managing director of Eni Kazakhstan, proposed introducing risk-based pipeline inspections and improving the distribution of additional greenhouse gas emission quotas in the oil and gas sector.

Gabriel Constantin, chief executive of Air Liquide Munay Tech Gases, highlighted the importance of developing highly qualified personnel, including recognizing international professional certificates and facilitating intra-corporate mobility for foreign specialists.

Predictable regulation remains key for investors

Predictable regulation, transparent tax and customs systems and the rule of law remain essential conditions for attracting foreign investment, said Zhanna Baidasheva, director of the Kazakhstan Council of Foreign Investors.

She said open dialogue between the government and businesses allows investors to raise concerns, find solutions and establish conditions for expanding cooperation. Such engagement matters for both international companies already operating in Kazakhstan and potential investors considering entering the market.

“For investors, clear regulations, clear rules of the game, a clear tax and customs system and, of course, the rule of law are fundamental. When the government is open to dialogue, investors understand that it is safe here and that any issues can be openly discussed,” Baidasheva said.

AI, productivity and human capital

Zhumashev also discussed AI adoption in business processes and the development of human capital, saying the main purpose of introducing new technologies should be to increase labor productivity.

“Sixteen companies participating in our council presented real-world cases of AI application. We discussed and examined how these solutions can be used today to bring greater benefits to Kazakhstan’s economy,” he said.

“We need to develop our young people and specialists. Then they will be able to contribute to the development of artificial intelligence in our economy, in the real economy,” he added.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First AI-Assisted Bill Targets Children’s Online Safety
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has used artificial intelligence to help develop a legislative draft for the first time, applying a specialized AI platform to prepare amendments to a proposed law on children’s digital and information security, according to Kazinform.

The AI-Quryltai platform, developed for the country’s parliament, combines data analysis tools with a legal AI model trained on a database of more than 800,000 regulatory legal acts. It was used to analyze existing legislation, identify potential legal inconsistencies and help formulate provisions for the draft law on Digital and Information Security of Children.

The platform also helped assess the current state of children’s safety online by analyzing large datasets, public appeals and concerns raised by parents, experts and civil society representatives, alongside international practices and emerging digital risks.

According to a co-author of the bill and Kurultai Vice Speaker Dinara Zakiyeva, the AI-assisted work resulted in more than 120 proposed amendments.

The proposals include introducing parental control mechanisms across platforms, filtering content accessible to children, restricting access to unmarked and unverified digital products, applications and games, and requiring platforms to label and verify digital products. Platforms could also be required to block products found to pose threats or violate regulations.

AI across the legislative process

AI-Quryltai is designed to support several stages of lawmaking, from identifying public concerns to assessing how legislation works after adoption. The ecosystem consists of five areas, including data analytics, legal analysis, expert review, regulatory impact assessment and monitoring of law enforcement and implementation.

Its analytical tools are intended to process public complaints, statistics, research and court practices to help lawmakers identify the scale and development of social problems. Consultations with constituents, regional visits and discussions with experts would also supplement the findings.

The legal module draws on a structured database of legislation to identify related provisions, potential conflicts, terminology inconsistencies and gaps. It can also help prepare draft provisions and comparative legal tables, reducing time spent on routine legal and technical work.

Another component focuses on preliminary assessments of corruption risks, conflicts of interest, legal inconsistencies and drafting deficiencies. AI-generated assessments are intended to complement existing expert reviews rather than replace them.

The platform also aims to help lawmakers assess the potential consequences of proposed regulations by identifying affected groups and the possible benefits, costs and risks for citizens, businesses and public institutions.

Following adoption, AI tools could analyze court decisions, public appeals and statistical data to identify recurring problems and evaluate whether legislation achieves its intended objectives.

Testing Kazakhstan’s AI model

AI-Quryltai is currently being developed and tested through a dedicated laboratory bringing together lawmakers, experts and developers. The laboratory has around 10 projects in its portfolio, including three legislative initiatives.

Each tool is expected to undergo testing for accuracy, reliability, legal precision and suitability for professional tasks. The system is also being developed using Kurultai’s institutional knowledge, including legislative records, expert assessments and the history of bill reviews.

Kazakhstan presented AI-Quryltai at the 2026 World e-Parliament Conference in Brussels, organized by the Inter-Parliamentary Union in cooperation with the European Parliament and attended by representatives from more than 100 countries.

World.title: Person Next to You May Need Help: Kazakhstan Launches Anti-Violence Campaign
World.content:
ASTANA – A person sitting next to you may be experiencing domestic violence without showing any visible signs. This is the central message of A Person Next to You, a public awareness campaign launched Nov. 25 in Astana as part of the annual 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, bringing together the United Nations, the European Union and local experts to discuss prevention, survivor support and shared responsibility.

The campaign encourages people to recognize their role as supportive friends, peers, neighbors and colleagues by listening without judgment, rejecting victim-blaming, respecting confidentiality and helping survivors access appropriate support. Its central message is that empathy and informed action can begin with the person sitting or standing next to us.

The campaign runs from Nov. 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, through Dec. 10, Human Rights Day.

A global challenge and local response

United Nations Resident Coordinator in Kazakhstan Sarangoo Radnaaragchaa emphasized that women’s rights are human rights and that freedom from violence is a right, not a privilege.

According to her, an estimated 840 million women worldwide, or nearly one in three, have experienced physical or sexual violence during their lifetimes. In a single year, 316 million women experienced physical or sexual violence by an intimate partner.

At the current pace, she said, achieving Sustainable Development Goal 5 on gender equality will take 171 years.

“Behind every number is a human life. A woman, daughter, mother, a friend, someone whose safety, dignity and future are at stake,” Radnaaragchaa said.

She acknowledged the important steps Kazakhstan has taken to strengthen protections for women and children, including legislative reforms in 2024 and 2025. However, she highlighted that legislation alone cannot eliminate violence.

“These are important steps forward, and they send a very clear message: violence has no place in our society. At the same time, as we all know, legislation alone is not enough. Violence against women and girls is persisting. Too many survivors still face fear, stigma and barriers to seeking help,” she said.

She called for stronger implementation of existing laws to ensure that survivors receive real protection and access to support.

As part of the campaign, seats at railway stations and Almaty International Airport will be turned orange. Orange is the global color of solidarity against gender-based violence.

Each orange seat will feature a QR code connecting people to a dedicated platform with helplines, support services and practical guidance on seeking help.

Radnaaragchaa urged the public to listen to survivors, believe them and respect their dignity and choices. She also highlighted the need for accessible, safe and confidential support, efforts to challenge stigma and harmful attitudes, and stronger accountability to ensure that laws translate into protection and justice.

The European Union Ambassador to Kazakhstan Aleška Simkić, said the campaign forms part of the EU’s broader gender equality agenda.

She identified three key areas of focus: supporting survivors of gender-based violence, improving the response of law enforcement and judicial institutions, and empowering women.

Simkić emphasized that stigma often prevents survivors from speaking openly about violence and seeking assistance.

“People do not talk about it openly. It’s connected to stigma. So, I think that with this campaign, we are trying to encourage the victims of domestic violence or gender-based violence to actually come forward, but they should know that there are people who care,” she said.

She also highlighted the importance of educating law enforcement officers and judges to ensure that cases are handled effectively and perpetrators are held accountable.

Women’s economic independence is another essential element of prevention, Simkić said, as it can help reduce financial dependence on abusive partners.

Simkić also pointed to the need to examine traditional values that may restrict women’s choices, including decisions about education, marriage and having children.

“We have to take a look at attitudes, the choices that women have and the way they can exercise their choices,” she said.

In February, the EU and the UN, in partnership with governments across Central Asia, launched an EU-funded program to strengthen efforts to prevent gender-based violence and advance gender equality across the region.

The program, titled Challenging Harmful Attitudes and Norms for Gender Equality (CHANGE), is jointly implemented by the U.N. Development Programme, the U.N. Population Fund, and U.N. Women, in cooperation with national authorities, civil society organizations, and the private sector.

“Access to social assistance, care services, employment opportunities and appropriate support can reduce economic dependence and contribute to women’s safety and resilience. The approach behind the EU-UN CHANGE program is simple: prevention starts with the person next to us, but it succeeds when compassionate communities are supported by responsive institutions and inclusive social policies,” said Katarzyna Wawiernia, UNDP Resident Representative in Kazakhstan.

Legal reforms and challenges in implementation

Dr. Muslim Khassenov, an associate professor in the Department of Private Law and a member of the National Commission on Women’s Affairs and Family and Demographic Policy, discussed the impact of Kazakhstan’s legislative reforms and the challenges that remain in their implementation.

Khassenov said the overall number of criminal offenses and murders had declined in absolute terms. However, one in five murders in Kazakhstan is still committed in the family or domestic sphere.

He also highlighted difficulties in bringing domestic violence cases to court. According to him, half of the cases under relevant provisions do not reach court because of reconciliation between survivors and perpetrators. A further 30% of cases that reach court are terminated on similar grounds.

He described criminalization as an important first step rather than a complete solution, arguing that Kazakhstan needs stronger prevention mechanisms to identify patterns of violence before they escalate.

“Government agencies and social services should be able to recognize systematic abuse, including coercive control within families,” Khassenov said.

“Of course, it is important to protect the victim and provide her with all the tools of protection and assistance. But it is very important to create a system so that violence does not happen again,” he added.

Workplace harassment was another issue he raised, describing it as difficult to identify and prevent because of employees’ economic dependence on employers and the imbalance of power between them.

“Amendments to the Labor Code are being prepared to define harassment, establish complaint mechanisms and require employers to introduce policies and confidential reporting channels. The proposed changes would also allow employers to dismiss employees found responsible for harassment,” Khassenov said

However, he argued that stronger accountability, potentially including criminal liability, is also needed to prevent offenders from continuing such behavior in other workplaces.

Economic independence as a tool for prevention

Anna Ryl, head of the Korgau-Astana Crisis Center, highlighted the importance of combining support for survivors with measures to prevent repeated violence.

She noted that the center’s work has evolved beyond legal and psychological assistance to include economic empowerment, helping women become financially independent and avoid returning to abusive relationships.

“The center provides training in practical and modern professions to expand women’s employment opportunities. Previously, its programs focused mainly on traditional services such as hairdressing and manicure. They now include digital skills, social media marketing and online work,” Ryl said.

With support from the driver company, the center also trained five women to drive this year, opening up potential employment opportunities in courier services and other fields.

Ryl emphasized that supporting women economically and helping families address the causes of violence are both essential to preventing abuse from recurring.

World.title: Tokayev, Putin Focus on AI Cooperation as Bilateral Trade Nears $30 Billion
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Russia are advancing cooperation in artificial intelligence and high-tech industries as bilateral trade approaches $30 billion, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Russian President Vladimir Putin said during a Nov. 25 meeting in the Kremlin ahead of the AI Journey 2026 conference.

Tokayev highlighted the growing importance of artificial intelligence and digitalization, recalling that Putin had outlined during the first AI Journey forum in 2020 that these technologies would soon become global priorities.

“Now everyone is talking about high technologies, artificial intelligence, and how it will behave in the future,” Tokayev said, emphasizing the significance of the upcoming forum.

According to him, Kazakhstan has made digitalization and artificial intelligence a national priority, with 2026 declared the Year of Artificial Intelligence Development. Tokayev said the country had made progress in digital transformation, citing its 16th-place ranking in the United Nations e-government and human capital development assessment, up from 24th.

Trade and investment cooperation

Tokayev said Kazakhstan and Russia were steadily moving toward a bilateral trade turnover of $30 billion. He noted that the intergovernmental commission was working to implement agreements reached during Putin’s state visit to Kazakhstan in May, which led to the signing of several important documents.

Tokayev also commented on the recent trilateral meeting involving the leaders of China, the United States and Russia in Shenzhen, noting that it took place amid a highly volatile geopolitical situation. He said Russia’s participation in the meeting as a major global power was a significant achievement for Putin.

“The declaration was adopted, and it is absolutely optimal in terms of its content and, of course, its significance, because it would be unrealistic to expect anything more in this modern world,” he said.

He also noted that the declaration’s wording and substance reflected ideas Putin had previously discussed, adding that the declaration represented a significant achievement for Russian diplomacy.

Expanding economic ties

Putin thanked Tokayev for visiting Russia and accepting the invitation to attend the AI Journey conference. He said the event would provide an opportunity to hear from specialists, meet with schoolchildren and university students, and discuss cooperation between Russia and Kazakhstan in high-tech industries, particularly artificial intelligence.

The presidents discussed further development of trade, economic and investment cooperation, as well as joint projects in energy, industry, agriculture, transport and logistics. They also exchanged views on current international and regional issues.

World.title: Kazakhstan Ranks 28th Among World’s Largest Steel Producers
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 28th among the world’s largest crude steel producers in January-September, with output reaching 3.27 million tons, according to a report by the Brazilian Steel Institute (Aço Brasil).

The country’s production increased 5.9% compared with 3.087 million tons recorded in the same period last year, according to the institute’s October statistical report, published in November and based on World Steel Association data.

In September alone, Kazakhstan produced 320,000 tons of crude steel, up 11.9% from 286,000 tons in September 2025.

Kazakhstan accounted for 0.2% of global crude steel production during the first nine months of this year. It ranked between Australia, which produced 3.541 million tons, and Argentina, with 3.22 million tons.

China remained the world’s largest steel producer, with 724.17 million tons, despite a 2.9% year-on-year decline. India ranked second with 129.96 million tons, up 5.6%, followed by the United States with 64.95 million tons, an increase of 5.8%.

Russia ranked fifth with 49.42 million tons, down 3.6%, while Türkiye and South Korea recorded increases of 6.1% and 2.9%, respectively.

Global crude steel production totaled nearly 1.367 billion tons in January-September, decreasing 0.7% compared with the same period last year.

World.title: Abkhazia introduces law to curb dumping by Russian tour operators
World.content:
The authorities in Abkhazia plan to introduce an anti-dumping law aimed at protecting small hotels from organised price-cutting by large Russian tour operators.

Abkhazia’s parliament has already passed the bill, titled “On Amendments to Certain Legislative Acts of the Republic of Abkhazia to Prevent the Monopolisation of the Tourist Accommodation Services Market”, in its first reading.

For several years, a trend has emerged in which large Russian tour operators buy up hotel rooms in Abkhazia at low prices ahead of the tourist season. They then sell them to tourists at even lower rates, offsetting the losses through other services.

The tour operators themselves describe this kind of dumping — offering a hotel room with three meals a day for 200 roubles ($2–3) — as a “special offer” designed to attract tourists to Abkhazia.

Small hotels suffer the most. They cannot afford to adopt such pricing policies and find themselves at a competitive disadvantage. As a result, they incur losses, and some even go bankrupt, selling their properties or renting them out to the same large tour operators.

Under the new bill:

Hotels will have to register contracts containing fixed room quotas with the Ministry of Tourism.

The register will record the number of rooms and the purchase price.

If a tour operator sells a room for more than 30% below its purchase price, the Ministry of Tourism will be able to issue a formal complaint.

If the violation is not rectified, sales may be suspended or the contract terminated.

The bill also introduces the concept of a “high season”, covering the period from 1 June to 1 September, during which all promotional discounts will be prohibited.

Abkhazia’s Tourism Minister Astamur Logua stressed that the aim was not to ban discounts, but to prevent dumping and market monopolisation.

If passed, the new rules could come into force on 1 January 2027.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Nakhchivan repeals 47 decrees by former leader: what decisions are affected?
World.content:
Azerbaijan: Decrees by former Nakhchivan leader repealed

Jabbar Musayev, prime minister of Azerbaijan’s Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic, has repealed 47 decrees signed by Vasif Talibov during his time as chairman of the Supreme Assembly and amended several others.

The autonomous republic’s official newspaper, Sharq Gapisi, reported the decision on 25 November. The text of the decision has not been made public, and the authorities have not explained the reasons behind it. The newspaper published only a list of the repealed decrees.

The decision came 20 days after the authorities abolished Nakhchivan’s permanent representation in Baku. We previously reported on how control over the autonomous republic had gradually shifted to Baku over the past four years.

Now another question arises: what does the list of repealed decrees reveal about the separate system of governance that Talibov built over 27 years?

What is on the list?

Most of the repealed decrees concern the establishment of autonomous republic institutions, the approval of their organisational structures and regulations governing their activities. The documents can be grouped into several categories.

Security and customs. Decrees approving the regulations and structure of Nakhchivan’s Ministry of National Security, the structure of the autonomous republic’s State Customs Committee, and social protection measures for customs officials.

Finance and economy. Decrees approving regulations for the Ministry of Taxes and the Ministry of Economic Development, as well as documents governing the activities of the State Procurement Agency, the Entrepreneurship Support Fund, industrial parks, the State Social Protection Fund and the Main State Insurance Agency.

Infrastructure. Decrees concerning Nakhchivan International Airport, the state-owned Nahavtoyol company, the State Motor Transport Concern, the Nakhchivan Oil and Gas Supply Enterprise, and the ministries of transport and communications.

Law, media and religion. Decrees concerning the activities of the Nakhchivan ombudsman, the Television and Radio Council, the State Committee for Television and Radio Broadcasting, the Office for Religious Organisations and the Civil Service Commission under the chairman of the Supreme Assembly.

Honorary titles. The first two items on the list concern the establishment of honorary titles in the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic and the approval of regulations governing them.

The repealed decrees also include those approving the “new structure” of the autonomous republic’s Cabinet of Ministers, the organisational structures of several central executive bodies and the Ministry of Education, as well as regulations governing the Nakhchivan branch of the Azerbaijan National Academy of Sciences (ANAS).

The legal foundations of a “state within a state”

Talibov served as chairman of the Supreme Assembly from December 1995 to December 2022. During his tenure, the autonomous republic had its own Ministry of Taxes, Customs Committee, Ministry of National Security, ombudsman institution, Television and Radio Council, and Civil Service Commission.

The list of repealed decrees shows that all these bodies were established or operated under decrees issued by the chairman of the Supreme Assembly. In other words, Talibov headed the parliament while also creating the autonomous republic’s executive bodies through his own decrees.

Now, however, the Cabinet of Ministers’ head — rather than the Supreme Assembly — is repealing these decrees. This became possible following constitutional amendments that took effect in March 2026. Under a law passed by the Milli Majlis in February, the article establishing the position of “highest official of the autonomous republic” was removed from Nakhchivan’s Constitution.

The Cabinet of Ministers is no longer subordinate to the Supreme Assembly and is authorised, in coordination with the president, to establish and abolish central executive bodies. The Constitution of the autonomous republic now recognises the president’s authorised representation in Nakhchivan as an executive body.

Almost four years have passed since Talibov’s resignation, but a new chairman of the Supreme Assembly has yet to be elected.

What will happen to the agencies?

The Sharq Gapisi newspaper’s report mentions only the repeal of the decrees. It does not clarify whether the agencies themselves will be abolished or which central government bodies will take over their functions.

Some changes took place even before the decision. Nakhchivan’s branches of the State Security Service and the State Customs Committee were transferred to the direct control of Baku. Following Talibov’s resignation, many officials in the autonomous republic came under investigation on charges of embezzlement and other crimes.

The fate of honorary titles remains another unresolved issue. It is not yet clear whether people who received honorary titles from the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic during Talibov’s tenure will retain their status and the associated benefits.

The future of the autonomous republic’s ombudsman institution is also uncertain. It remains unclear whether Nakhchivan residents will have to turn exclusively to the ombudsman in Baku if their rights are violated.

What does Baku say?

In August, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev said in an interview with AzTV in Nakhchivan that the autonomous republic would retain its status, but its system of governance needed to be “improved”. He noted that the model of special presidential representatives already operating in Karabakh and Eastern Zangazur also applied to Nakhchivan:

“In this way, we are effectively bringing these three regions together from an administrative point of view as well.”

Experts see the repeal of the decrees as another step towards strengthening central government control over the autonomous republic. Nakhchivan’s authorities have yet to provide any further explanation of the decision.
