World.title: “Attempted coup in focus”: Georgia’s State Security Service report
World.content:
Georgia State Security Service 2025 report

Head of Georgia’s State Security Service, Tamaz Borashvili, presented the agency’s 2025 activity report at a plenary session of the Georgian parliament.

The report covers internal and external security threats facing Georgia in 2025, including:

Challenges related to the territories occupied by Russia;

Hybrid warfare and the spread of disinformation;

Counter-intelligence and counter-terrorism operations;

Measures taken by the State Security Service to prevent and stop attempts to destabilise the situation inside the country.

According to Borashvili, the security situation underwent significant changes in 2025, both globally and regionally, and Georgia faced a number of internal and external challenges. He noted that several attempts were made throughout the year to destabilise the country.

The head of the State Security Service placed particular emphasis on threats stemming from the occupied territories and hybrid challenges.

He said Russia’s occupation of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) remained one of the main threats to Georgia’s national security, undermining the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Borashvili also said that throughout 2025 the SSS had continuously monitored propaganda and disinformation campaigns carried out as part of an “information war”.

Presenting the report, the SSS chief also addressed the events of October 2025, when a group of participants in mass protests in Tbilisi attempted to storm the presidential administration building. Borashvili said certain groups operating both inside and outside Georgia had planned to provoke civil unrest and destabilise the country in an attempt to overthrow the government by force.

“In coordination with other law enforcement agencies, this attempt was prevented,” Borashvili said.

He also briefed MPs on the results of measures taken in counter-intelligence and counter-terrorism, as well as efforts to combat corruption and official misconduct.

The SSS chief said that counter-intelligence operations had identified individuals involved in the activities of foreign intelligence services who had held operational and agent meetings in Georgia.

According to Borashvili, terrorist threats remain a relevant challenge for Georgia, although the country is considered to be at low risk of terrorist attacks.

He also outlined structural and institutional changes within the agency. During the reporting period, Georgia’s Intelligence Service, previously a state department, was transformed into an agency.

A decision was also made to turn the SSS training centre into a higher education institution, a legal entity under public law called the State Security Academy.

The report also covered measures to upgrade the agency’s equipment and facilities and improve working conditions for its staff.

At the end of his address, Tamaz Borashvili thanked SSS personnel for their work and daily efforts to ensure the country’s security.

Before the SSS chief’s address, the agency’s deputy head, Davit Archvadze, presented a brief overview of its 2025 activity report.

Notably, the brief statement published by the State Security Service refers to the issue of occupation only in general terms, while the events of 4 October 2025, described as an “attempt to violently change the government”, receive much greater emphasis.

It is also worth noting that just a few days earlier, on 19 November, Georgia’s Prime Minister’s special representative, Giorgi Zurabashvili, held his first meeting in Minsk with Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin.

This marked the resumption of informal direct dialogue with Russia, despite Moscow’s continued occupation of Georgian territories and its policy of recognising the so-called independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region.

According to the Georgian government administration, the meeting focused on trade and economic ties, cultural and humanitarian issues. Regional security was also discussed.

However, the Georgian side’s statement on the meeting did not specify what position was expressed on Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories.

News in Georgia

World.title: Construction of railway under Trump Route (TRIPP) project to begin in 2027
World.content:
Details of the launch of TRIPP in Armenia in 2027

Construction of a railway under the Armenian-American TRIPP project, which aims to unblock transport links in the region, will begin in 2027. Armenian Deputy Foreign Minister and Minister of International Trade Vahan Kostanyan told Public Television.

“The railway route has already been determined. Preparatory work to clear the site is now under way. This will allow us to begin construction itself next year,” he said.

Just two days earlier, the Armenian prime minister and the US president announced the start of the practical phase of the TRIPP project. Alongside statements by Nikol Pashinyan and Donald Trump, they also released a video filmed in Armenia’s Syunik region, through which the “Trump Route” will pass.

The footage shows heavy machinery clearing and levelling the area in front of a railway tunnel in Meghri.

Speaking about the railway’s technical specifications, Vahan Kostanyan said that a preliminary design was already ready.

“By the beginning of next year, the organisation conducting the study will complete its work and present us with the final results. These will clearly set out the engineering solutions and specify exactly what needs to be done.”

TRIPP (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) is a route that will connect Azerbaijan with its autonomous exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The project also aims to unblock regional transport links. It will give Armenia access to third countries through Azerbaijan. The 43km section running through Armenia will include a railway line. A highway, energy infrastructure and digital communications channels will also run along the same route.

On 28 October, Armenia’s parliament ratified a framework agreement on strategic cooperation under the TRIPP project. The agreement provides for the creation of TRIPP Development Company, which will oversee the project’s development and implementation. Initially, the US will hold a 74% stake in the company, while the Republic of Armenia will own the remaining 26%. After 49 years, if the parties extend their cooperation for another 50 years, Armenia’s stake will increase to 49%.

In the interview, the deputy minister also discussed other issues, including the integration of Armenia’s electricity grid with the power systems of Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Armenia’s relations with Russia.

Trump’s and Pashinyan’s statements

US President Donald Trump described the start of the practical phase of the TRIPP project as an “unbelievably exciting event” that he was very proud of. Recalling the Washington peace summit held on 8 August 2025, Trump stressed that progress would continue with the launch of the “Trump Route” and TRIPP Development Company. The company will oversee the project’s development and implementation.

“The partnership between the United States and Armenia will create new trade routes through the region for goods, energy and travel. We are responsible for making this a great, great success,” the US president said.

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan described TRIPP as the largest economic project in Armenia since independence. He said the “Trump Route” would have:

– “Exceptional importance for Armenia’s economic development:

It will significantly expand Armenia’s access to foreign markets, help develop the business environment and attract financial investment;

– Enormous regional and international importance:

It will give additional momentum to the viability of the Trans-Caspian Trade Route and strengthen East-West connectivity.”

The Armenian prime minister stressed that the “Trump Route” would make an important contribution to strengthening Armenia’s security:

“This will strengthen our country’s position and significantly expand the circle of stakeholders with an interest in Armenia’s stability and security.”

Explanations from Deputy Foreign Minister and Minister of International Trade Vahan Kostanyan

TRIPP will have global significance, including for the Middle Corridor

Vahan Kostanyan stressed that the US president does not issue special messages on every occasion. The launch of a project receives such attention only in exceptional circumstances. He therefore believes that Trump’s message:

demonstrates the project’s importance not only for Armenia but also for the United States;

confirms the US commitment to taking part in efforts to unblock the region.

“Developments over the past year indicate that TRIPP will have global significance, both in the context of the Middle Corridor and as part of much broader logistics networks. There is no doubt that both TRIPP and the Nakhchivan–Armenia railway link will have their place in these networks,” he said.

Speaking about the work currently under way, Kostanyan said that Armenia would officially register the TRIPP company soon, after which it would establish subsidiaries.

Each subsidiary will be responsible for specific infrastructure projects under TRIPP: railways, roads and power lines.

“We need to work with our American partners to develop an economic model for each subsidiary. We also need to engage with international investors and financial institutions,” he explained.

He stressed that TRIPP Development Company would manage the project. Armenia, meanwhile, would participate through separate entities that would carry out construction work on the ground.

Commenting on criticism that Yerevan should not discuss the Armenian-American project with Baku, Kostanyan said it was difficult to understand the logic behind what he called “unfounded” criticism:

“Since this infrastructure will enter and leave Armenian territory through our immediate neighbour, we must engage with Azerbaijan on this issue first and foremost.”

He said the two sides needed to discuss a wide range of issues, from technical specifications such as railway gauge and freight volumes to broader aspects of coordination:

“If the aim is also to achieve higher speeds along the Middle Corridor, we need to hold discussions with Azerbaijan, the Central Asian countries and our EU partners about the technical infrastructure we will provide.”

On 7 November 2026, Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Trade announced the launch of trilateral working groups involving Armenia, the United States and Azerbaijan. The groups will focus on technical planning for the development of the “Trump Route”.

“The parties agreed to establish the first two trilateral technical planning groups, covering transport and electricity transmission. The formation of these technical groups marks an important step towards resolving complex technical issues,” the statement said.

Integration with the energy systems of Turkey and Azerbaijan

Kostanyan said that Armenia was discussing the possibility of connecting its electricity grid to the energy systems of Turkey and Azerbaijan.

He stressed that Turkey’s energy system forms part of the European network. Armenia must therefore bring its own energy system into line with European standards to enable future synchronisation.

The deputy minister believes that establishing additional energy links with Turkey, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Iran would make Armenia’s energy system more resilient. He noted that Armenia was already working in this direction with Georgia and Iran.

However, Kostanyan gave no specific timeframe for the possible synchronisation of Armenia’s energy system with the European electricity network.

On 8 October 2026, Armenia’s Ministry of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure announced that representatives of the relevant Armenian and Azerbaijani agencies had held a technical meeting in the city of Goris. They discussed the construction of power lines under the TRIPP project.

No intention to burn bridges with Russia

Kostanyan also discussed the agenda for the meeting between Pashinyan and Putin scheduled for 3 December in Moscow. He said the leaders would discuss all the problems that had recently emerged in Armenian-Russian relations.

According to Kostanyan, the review would aim exclusively to “improve” relations:

“We have no intention of severing ties with Russia, creating a crisis or burning bridges. Russia remains an important partner for Armenia.”

The deputy minister expressed hope that his Russian counterparts were approaching preparations for the leaders’ meeting in the same spirit.

The Armenian prime minister announced that he would visit Russia on 3, 11 and 22 December. Under a preliminary agreement, Pashinyan will meet the Russian president in Moscow on 3 December. The Armenian prime minister also said that a meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council, bringing together the heads of government of the EAEU member states, was scheduled for 11–12 December. Annual meetings of the leaders of the EAEU and CIS countries will take place in St Petersburg at the end of the year.

World.title: Georgia to abolish State Grants Management Agency: What do we know about decision?
World.content:
Dissolution of Georgia’s State Grants Management Agency

According to a decision by the Georgian government, the process of dissolving the State Grants Management Agency must be completed by 1 January 2027. The relevant decree was issued on 24 November and signed by Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

Under the decree, the agency must fulfil its obligations under contracts concluded within the framework of the Law on State Procurement before its dissolution, and no later than 1 January 2027. It must also revoke an order issued by its chair on 18 July 2025, which established the rules for awarding state grants and monitoring how they are used.

A special liquidation commission will oversee the process of dissolving the Agency. Its responsibilities include conducting a full inventory of the Agency’s assets, outstanding liabilities and official documents, including archival records.

The commission will also determine which organisations will receive the Agency’s assets, liabilities and documentation. In addition, if necessary, it will appoint a body responsible for monitoring whether grant recipients fulfil their obligations under the relevant grant agreements.

Background

The Agency was established following amendments to the Law on Grants introduced by the Georgian Dream party. Under the changes, foreign donors must obtain prior approval from the Georgian government, or a body authorised by it, before awarding grants to organisations or individuals operating in Georgia. Under the law, receiving a grant without such approval carries a fine equivalent to twice the grant amount.

At the same time as adopting the amendments, the authorities announced a new state funding mechanism. According to the government, the Agency was intended to support civil society organisations whose activities aligned with the country’s development priorities. Georgia’s 2025 state budget allocated a total of 20 million lari (approximately $7.7 million) to establish and operate the Agency and implement its grant programmes.

In July 2025, the Agency announced its first grant competition. The maximum funding available for individual projects was set at 100,000 lari (approximately $38,615), while organisational development grants could reach 700,000 lari (approximately $270,306).

Critics of the Agency argued that the government intended to use state grants to fund organisations whose views aligned with its own political priorities, while restricting access to foreign funding – a move that hindered the work of independent civil society organisations.

In September 2026, Irakli Kobakhidze announced the decision to shut down the Agency. He said that non-governmental organisations served as instruments of foreign political interference and that the state should not establish or fund them.

Following Kobakhidze’s announcement, Nona Kurdovanidze, former chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association, noted that publicly available data showed that the Agency had awarded funding to 17 projects under its 2025 small grants competition, amounting to a total of 1,657,775 lari (approximately $640,153). She pointed out that some of the organisations receiving funding had been established shortly before the competition.

Under the government decree issued on 24 November, the process of dissolving the Agency must be completed by 1 January 2027.

Dissolution of Georgia’s State Grants Management Agency

World.title: Fake videos and leaked personal data: Georgian journalist Tornike Razmadze targeted in digital harassment campaign
World.content:
Georgia’s first AI smear campaign against an activist

Tornike Razmadze, a journalist and critic of Georgian Dream, has become the target of a smear campaign. Between 21 and 23 November, anonymous social media accounts circulated AI-generated videos portraying him as a drug dealer.

His phone number was also published, accompanied by suggestions that people could use it to buy marijuana. The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) described the incidents as a targeted harassment campaign.

Fact-checkers say this is one of the first cases in Georgian politics in which highly realistic AI-generated videos have been used in such a coordinated campaign against a government critic.

Tornike Razmadze is a journalist, blogger and civic activist. He regularly publishes videos criticising representatives of the Georgian Dream party, which attract large audiences. He also hosts two programmes on the Mismane YouTube channel.

What happened?

According to Myth Detector, on 21 November an anonymous Facebook page called Politikani published a video featuring Razmadze’s name. The page has previously been involved in smear campaigns against the opposition. The video shows a man who resembles Razmadze asking a drug dealer to hire him as a courier. It was accompanied by the caption: “Now it’s clear why he became friends with Akhobadze” (Giorgi Akhobadze is a Georgian doctor and activist who faced charges of illegally purchasing and possessing a particularly large quantity of drugs, but was later acquitted by a court – JAMnews).

On 22 November, a TikTok account called DaDash Pirveli published a video showing a man entering the stairwell of a residential building and bending down near the gas meters (apparently to leave a drug package – JAMnews). The video carried the caption: “Wasn’t it Tornike Razmadze who said, ‘It wasn’t me’?”

‘Threat of censorship’: What we know about Georgia’s new Interior Ministry department overseeing public communication

Georgian blogger says Interior Ministry wants to punish him for insulting Russian propagandists

On the same day, the Facebook page Ganulebuli Opozitsia published a photograph of Razmadze with a woman dressed in black. The post presented the woman as the mother of a young man who had died of a drug overdose. She blamed his death on “drug dealers like Razmadze”.

The Myth Detector fact-checking service concluded that the first two videos had been generated using artificial intelligence. According to InVID, there was a 96% probability that the video posted by Politikani was AI-generated. Sightengine put the probability for the TikTok video at 77%.

Fact-checkers note that both the anonymous pages and the TikTok account mentioned above had previously taken part in campaigns targeting government critics.

On 23 November, Razmadze’s phone number was also published on social media.

What does Razmadze say?

Razmadze has filed a complaint with the Interior Ministry. “The attacks against me have crossed the line into criminal activity. This is no longer just propaganda,” he said.

Speaking to TV Pirveli, he described the possible consequences of the digital harassment campaign: “This extremely dirty campaign could end with a physical attack on me or with someone planting something on me.”

Razmadze believes the authorities are behind the harassment. He says Dimitri Samkharadze, a Georgian Dream MP, discussed the possibility of physically attacking him in social media comments.

The activist links the campaign to his recent videos. In one, he recalls the case of Barbare Rapaliani (a 10-month-old girl whose tragic death in Georgia shortly before the 2012 parliamentary election became one of the country’s most high-profile and politicised unsolved cases in recent history – JAMnews). In another, he mocks comedians from pro-government television channels. Razmadze says both videos attracted widespread attention. He is now consulting lawyers.

How pro-government media covered the story

The campaign against Razmadze extended beyond social media to pro-government media outlets.

On 22 November, the Facebook page Pirveli Ambebi published footage of a residential building collapse in Batumi in 2021, presenting the incident as if it were happening at the time. The post claimed that hundreds of people were trapped under the rubble and that 30 had died.

The Interior Ministry denied the report, saying the post was intended to spread panic among the public.

Pro-government media outlets subsequently claimed that the Pirveli Ambebi page, which had circulated the false information, was allegedly linked to Tornike Razmadze. Their only evidence was that the page had previously published videos featuring him. None of the reports identified the people who ran the page.

Razmadze denies publishing the post and says he has no connection to the page. According to him, the page was created a long time ago and regularly published videos featuring other opposition figures. Razmadze has demanded that the Imedi, Rustavi 2 and POSTV television channels remove the false information and apologise.

What do human rights organisations say?

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) described the actions targeting Razmadze across various platforms as “a coordinated, targeted and systematic harassment campaign”.

The organisation says the materials published as part of the campaign amount to identity theft, as the videos reproduce Razmadze’s appearance and voice without his consent.

GYLA notes that the videos contain no elements of satire or parody, which “aggravates the negative impact on Tornike Razmadze’s rights – his rights to honour, privacy, identity and security”.

The organisation says the state has an obligation to assess such risks promptly, take protective measures and provide effective legal remedies for violations of these rights.

Reaction on social media

The story sparked widespread discussion on social media. Razmadze faced a wave of insults and accusations that echoed the narrative promoted by the fake videos. At the same time, many users expressed their support. Other bloggers and government critics voiced solidarity with Razmadze, warning the authorities that such campaigns could have dangerous consequences. YouTube bloggers and sports commentators also expressed their support.

Comedian Onise Okriashvili wrote on Facebook that this appeared to be the first case in Georgia in which someone had tried to discredit a person using hyper-realistic AI-generated videos rather than satirical ones.

Background: fined over remarks about Russian propagandists

A month before the campaign began, Razmadze was fined 3,000 lari. In September, the Interior Ministry opened administrative proceedings against him. The case concerned a Facebook comment containing obscene language directed at Kremlin propagandists Margarita Simonyan and Vladimir Solovyov. They had previously described Georgian King Erekle II as a ruler who “knelt down”. Razmadze’s video addressed those remarks.

A newly established Interior Ministry unit responsible for combating “hate speech” initiated the case. The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association described it at the time as a precedent for censorship.

Razmadze says he expected a campaign against him after the authorities opened the case.

What happens next?

Razmadze is discussing further legal action with his lawyers. The Interior Ministry has yet to say whether it has launched an investigation following his complaint.

Georgia’s first AI smear campaign against an activist

World.title: Georgia awarded contracts worth nearly $499m without competitive tenders – TI
World.content:
Non-competitive public procurement in Georgia

Between January and October 2026, almost half (45%) of tenders announced in Georgia attracted only one bidder. The lack of competition meant that these contracts cost the state around 150 million lari (approximately $57.5 million) more.

This is according to a new study by Transparency International Georgia.

According to the study, in the first ten months of 2026, government agencies awarded contracts worth a total of 4.09 billion lari (approximately $1.57 billion) through 16,222 electronic tenders.

A total of 7,364 tenders – 45% of all those announced – attracted only one bidder, either a company or an individual entrepreneur. The contracts were worth a combined 1.31 billion lari (approximately $499 million), accounting for almost a third of all public procurement spending.

According to the organisation, the winning bids in single-bidder tenders were, on average, just 4.3% below the initial estimated value set by the authorities. By comparison, prices in competitive tenders fell by an average of 15.4%.

TI estimates that if prices in non-competitive tenders had fallen by the same proportion, public contracts would have cost the state around 150 million lari (approximately $57.5 million) less.

The study also found that in 2,883 tenders, worth a total of 572 million lari (approximately $219.6 million), the winning bid exactly matched the estimated value set by the government in advance. In these cases, the state made no savings.

The largest public procurer using non-competitive procedures is the Special Penitentiary Service

According to TI, in 2026 the Special Penitentiary Service was the largest public procurer using non-competitive tenders. Through this mechanism, the agency awarded contracts worth a total of 203.7 million lari (approximately $78.6 million).

Almost the entire amount – 201.4 million lari – went towards two contracts for providing meals to prisoners.

In May 2026, the Special Penitentiary Service awarded contracts worth 152.4 million lari to Giorgi 2020 and 49 million lari to Delfood.

Both companies were the sole bidders in their respective tenders. Moreover, their bids exactly matched the estimated values set in advance.

The contracts were awarded amid a scandal over the quality of food served in Georgian prisons. Earlier, in March, the Special Penitentiary Service terminated its contract with Ili Group, which had been responsible for providing meals to prisoners.

According to TI, Giorgi 2020 had never previously won a public procurement tender.

On 3 April 2026 – the day the tender was announced – the company’s owners transferred 33% of its shares to Irakli Letodiani free of charge.

According to the TV Pirveli television channel, Letodiani is a former employee of the State Security Service.

Which sectors have the least competition?

According to the study, several sectors have particularly high proportions of tenders with only one bidder:

Transport services – 85%;

Software and information systems – 81%;

Repair and maintenance – 78%;

Medical equipment and medicines – 59%.

The proportion of construction tenders attracting only one bidder was relatively low, at 29%. However, construction ranked first in terms of the total value of contracts awarded.

Non-competitive construction contracts were worth a total of 517.9 million lari (approximately $199.8 million).

Tbilisi and Batumi account for the largest sums in non-competitive procurement

According to TI, 43% of tenders organised by municipalities – including those run by mayors and bodies established by them – attracted no competition. The figure for central government agencies and other state institutions was 48%.

Municipalities awarded contracts worth a total of 625 million lari (approximately $241.1 million) without any competition.

In monetary terms, Tbilisi ranked first, with 277 million lari, accounting for 38% of the capital’s procurement spending. Batumi came second, with 63 million lari, or 30% of its procurement spending.

In terms of the proportion of non-competitive tenders, the highest figures were recorded in Ambrolauri (61%), Terjola (59%) and Khulo (55%).

The risk of tailoring tender requirements to specific companies

TI notes that one possible reason for the high proportion of tenders with only one bidder is that authorities tailor procurement requirements to suit specific suppliers. The organisation cites several examples of this practice.

In June 2026, TI reported on five road repair tenders announced by Batumi’s Department of Infrastructure and Improvement.

Under the terms of the tender, bidders had to either own an asphalt plant within a 30km radius of the work site or provide a contract with such a facility. This requirement applied to a tender worth 29.2 million lari (approximately $11.3 million), in which Gza was the sole bidder.

Another example is a security services tender announced by Georgian Railway in 2023. To qualify for the contract, worth 7.8 million lari (approximately $3 million), bidders had to demonstrate at least 20 years of uninterrupted experience.

According to Transparency International (TI), only two companies in the entire country met this requirement. The sole bidder was Intersecurity Georgia LLC, owned by Ioseb Alavidze, a former head of the Tbilisi police. The company’s bid exactly matched the estimated contract value.

The organisation also cites a tender for the provision of social canteen services announced by Rustavi City Hall in 2022.

In that case, the company offering the lowest price was excluded from the tender because its revised price schedule listed figures to four decimal places instead of two. The contract was ultimately awarded to a company whose bid was 155,000 lari (approximately $59,800) higher.

The problem extends beyond large-scale tenders

TI says that a lack of competition in public procurement is not a new problem. The organisation refers to a 2024 study which found that half of the large tenders – those worth more than five million lari – announced between January and July 2024 attracted no competition.

Figures for 2026 show that the problem is not limited to large-scale procurement: only one bidder took part in half of all tenders worth up to 100,000 lari.

The organisation also criticises reports prepared by the State Procurement Agency. TI notes that although the agency’s reports point to an increase in competition, none of its annual reports published since 2019 has mentioned that almost half of all public tenders attract only one bidder.

Non-competitive public procurement in Georgia

World.title: NEST Centre: 408 Azerbaijani citizens killed while fighting in Ukraine for Russian forces. What is known in Baku?
World.content:
Azerbaijani citizens killed while serving in Russian army

At least 408 Azerbaijani citizens who fought in the ranks of the Russian army have been killed in Russia’s war against Ukraine. The figures come from a study published on 23 November by the independent think tank NEST Centre (New Eurasian Strategies Centre). The study draws on registered death records obtained through a data leak from Russia’s Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).

According to NEST Centre’s calculations, 6,947 foreign nationals who fought on Russia’s side were confirmed killed between 24 February 2022 and 29 September 2026. Azerbaijan ranks sixth in the number of fatalities, after Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.

Earlier this year, the authorities in Azerbaijan acknowledged that a “significant number” of the country’s citizens had died in the war between Russia and Ukraine, but did not specify how many. The leaked data help to fill some of this information gap.

What does the figure of 408 deaths tell us, what does it leave out, and how does Baku view the deaths of its citizens in this war?

How did the data leak happen?

In late October, the Belarusian hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian group Silent Crow said they had gained access to Rosstat’s information systems. The agency confirmed that it had come under cyberattacks between 29 October and 1 November, but denied that hackers had breached its databases or leaked confidential information.

Several international media outlets and research centres subsequently analysed the database. Janis Kluge, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said there was no longer any doubt about its authenticity. Bloomberg, meanwhile, reported that it had been unable to verify the data using cryptographic methods, but had found no signs of falsification.

Why could the death toll be higher than 408?

NEST Centre stresses that the list of fatalities is incomplete and that the figures do not reflect the true scale of Russia’s losses. There are several reasons for this.

First, the figure of 408 includes only Azerbaijani citizens. According to a Bloomberg analysis based on the same database, more than 6,000 of the 11,335 foreign-born servicemen killed had acquired Russian citizenship before their deaths. Russia offers foreigners a simplified and accelerated path to citizenship in exchange for military service. The figures for Azerbaijan do not include people born in Azerbaijan who died as Russian citizens.

Second, researchers say that if Russian civil registry offices did not register a foreign national’s death, the information may have remained only in the Ministry of Defence’s internal records. Third, the database contains no information about people missing in action. In 2025, the average delay in registering deaths exceeded four months.

How did they end up in the Russian army?

NEST Centre provides no specific information about how Azerbaijani citizens joined the Russian army. However, the study says that recruiters promised foreigners – primarily migrants from Central Asia – civilian jobs, help with paperwork or release from detention centres, before sending them to military units. In some cases, researchers say, recruiters used threats and physical violence to force migrants to sign military contracts.

There have also been individual reports of Azerbaijani citizens ending up on the front line under similar circumstances. In August this year, the Azerbaijani news website Modern.az published a video in which an Azerbaijani man serving in the Russian army claimed that authorities had unlawfully sent him to the combat zone.

What does Baku say?

Azerbaijan criminalises participation in armed conflicts abroad. On 3 February 2026, the State Security Service (SSS) said that “a significant number of citizens of the Republic of Azerbaijan have taken part in hostilities between Russia and Ukraine, been killed, gone missing or been wounded, while some remain in captivity”. According to the agency, in January that year authorities detained four Azerbaijani citizens suspected of fighting on the side of Russia or Ukraine. A court ordered their pre-trial detention.

The SSS warned citizens that “participation in such armed conflicts entails criminal liability in the Republic of Azerbaijan”. However, it did not specify how many Azerbaijani citizens had been killed, gone missing or been taken prisoner.

Azerbaijanis are also fighting on Ukraine’s side. In September 2024, Galib Osmanly, a representative of the United Azerbaijani Diaspora of Ukraine, told the Turan news agency that at least 60 ethnic Azerbaijanis had been killed while serving in the Ukrainian army since the start of the war. They included both Ukrainian citizens and Azerbaijanis who held residence permits in the country.

Against the backdrop of tensions with Moscow

The figures on those killed have emerged amid tensions between Baku and Moscow. The crash of an AZAL passenger plane in December 2024 and the disagreements that followed undermined trust between the two countries. In September this year, Azerbaijan placed three Russian propagandists on its wanted list.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry and State Security Service have yet to comment on the findings of the NEST Centre study. Russia’s Defence Ministry, meanwhile, does not disclose figures for the number of foreign nationals serving in its army or the casualties among them.



Azerbaijani citizens killed while serving in Russian army

World.title: Kyrgyzstan, TIF look to turn regional cooperation into investment opportunities
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kyrgyzstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Kyrgyzstan and the Turkic Investment Fund (TIF) have discussed expanding investment cooperation and the fund's role in supporting regional economic development, according to the Kyrgyz Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The meeting took place on November 26, 2026, between Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev and newly elected TIF President Kubanychbek Omuraliev.

Kulubaev congratulated Omuraliev on his election as TIF president and wished him success in carrying out his responsibilities.

The sides reviewed the fund's main areas of activity, ongoing and prospective projects, and opportunities to expand investment cooperation among member states.

Particular emphasis was placed on leveraging the TIF's potential to drive economic growth in participating countries, foster entrepreneurship, advance joint investment projects and expand trade and economic cooperation.

Following the meeting, both sides expressed interest in further developing ties and intensifying cooperation within the framework of the TIF.

Established by the member states of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), the Turkic Investment Fund is the first joint financial institution created by Turkic countries to mobilize capital, finance joint infrastructure and business projects, and promote intra-regional trade.

The fund focuses on supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), green energy initiatives, transport connectivity, agriculture, and industrial modernization across its member states, aiming to complement national development budgets and attract co-financing from international financial institutions.

World.title: Uzbekistan, AFoCO, South Korea's KT&G sign $350,000 forest restoration deal
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Uzbekistan's National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, the Asian Forest Cooperation Organization (AFoCO) and South Korean corporation KT&G have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on Thursday to cooperate on sustainable forest management and ecosystem restoration, with a grant-funded project worth $350,000 planned under the agreement.

According to Uzbekistan's National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, the project will focus on restoring degraded land, establishing forest plantations, promoting sustainable forest resource management, combating desertification and conserving biodiversity.

Additionally, the agreement provides for the exchange of international expertise, the introduction of modern technologies and training programs to improve the professional skills of specialists in the environmental sector.

Moreover, the parties plan to strengthen cooperation between government agencies, international organizations and private companies in implementing environmental initiatives.

Cooperation between Uzbekistan and AFoCO has expanded in recent years. During a visit by the chairman of Uzbekistan's National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change to South Korea in September 2026, the sides discussed forest restoration, measures to combat desertification and joint environmental projects.

Following those talks, they outlined plans to implement the Green Globe Project Uzbekistan Pine Forest in the Fergana region in 2027–2029.

To mark the agreement, the parties took part in a symbolic tree-planting event at Green University in Uzbekistan.

World.title: Alen Simonyan meets participants of fifth Peace Bridge roundtable (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Armenian Security Council Secretary Alen Simonyan met with participants of the fifth roundtable held under the "Peace Bridge" initiative.

The information was confirmed in a Thursday statement by the "Peace Bridge" dialogue platform.

"During the meeting, participants had the opportunity to ask the Security Council Secretary questions of interest to them. This was followed by a discussion of various views and proposals," the statement said.

The fifth meeting under the "Peace Bridge" initiative began in Armenia today.

A total of 60 representatives of Azerbaijani and Armenian civil society are taking part in the event.

As reported earlier, the roundtable will focus on the peace agenda agreed at the Washington summit on August 8, 2025, as well as initiatives aimed at strengthening and institutionalizing the Azerbaijan-Armenia peace process.

To note, the "Peace Bridge" dialogue platform was established to strengthen trust and foster sustained dialogue between representatives of Azerbaijani and Armenian civil society. Within the framework of the platform, the sides hold regular meetings to discuss issues such as the peace process, regional security, and the role of the media and civil society.

The first meeting took place in Yerevan on October 21-22, 2025, setting out the main areas of dialogue. Another key meeting was held in Baku on November 21-22, 2025, bringing together experts and NGO representatives from both countries.

The most recent meeting took place in Gabala on April 10-12. Discussions focused on promoting dialogue and direct contacts between representatives of civil society in the two countries.

World.title: Flight Centre investigating mass cyber breach
World.content:
Australian travel agency Flight Centre is investigating a cyber breach it says exposed a significant number of customer records, including some passport details.

In a statement to the ASX on Thursday, the Brisbane-based travel giant reported it had discovered "unusual activity" within the third-party accommodation system used by several of its booking agencies.

These included Flight Centre, Travel Associates and Cruiseabout, as well as some independent agents.

Flight bookings and corporate travel bookings were not affected, the company said.

Australians facing spike in data breaches Australians should expect an increase in future data breaches as a result of critical software flaws that have forced major government websites, education platforms and web hosts to go offline.

Early findings indicated "a significant number of customer records", comprising details such as names and some basic travel information, may have been accessed by "unknown persons", the travel agency said.

The company does not yet know how many customer records have actually been extracted.

A "very small percentage" of the compromised data included "limited passport details, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, or in rare cases health or mobility information", Flight Centre said.

Credit card, payment or banking details had not been affected at this stage.

Customers have been warned to exercise caution if they receive unexpected messages about their travel bookings. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

It is not clear exactly when the breach was discovered, but Flight Centre said it had responded by working with the third-party service to enhance its system security and contain the unusual activity.

The company said it was working with cybersecurity experts to understand the full "nature and extent" of the breach.

"FLT (Flight Centre Travel) is in the process of notifying the relevant authorities and has engaged external specialists to support in these investigations, including cyber security incident partner Mandiant," a statement to the ASX said.

Customers with existing accommodation bookings through Flight Centre's leisure brands can continue their travel plans without disruption, the company said.

Flight Centre declined to comment further.

Customers warned to be vigilant of dodgy messages

Flight Centre is warning customers to be cautious of "unexpected emails, calls or messages" about their bookings, and to "not click on links, open attachments or share personal information, passwords or payment details in response".

The company apologised to affected customers, noting "that an incident like this can be unsettling".

It said it would be contacting affected customers.

Flight Centre is the latest Australian company to suffer a major security breach, following incidents at Origin this year and Qantas in 2025. Both Optus and Medibank also experienced mass breaches in 2022.

In June, a rogue OpenAI agent hacked into an Australian Medicare data portal, fuelling concerns about the existential risks posed by autonomous artificial intelligence.

World.title: Report finds Support at Home co-payments should be reviewed
World.content:
Co-payments elderly Australians make towards the subsidised care they receive at home should be reviewed and clinicians should be able to override controversial assessment algorithms, a parliamentary committee has found.

A year on from the federal government's aged care overhaul, a Senate committee has recommended the Health Department review the amount elderly Australians pay towards their Support at Home services, such as cleaning, food preparation or gardening.

Senators from across the parliament also called on the government to "immediately" change the law to allow for humans to override "at the point of assessment" the algorithms used in the assessment process.

Taxpayer-funded cleaners not allowed to bend down Margaret Harvey is being charged for a cleaner who is not allowed to reach up to clean high places or bend down to clean low places.

The Coalition and crossbenchers, including the Greens, have been highly critical of the government's Support at Home program and the two algorithms used to determine the level of funding someone requires and how quickly they should be given that money.

Controversially, the algorithms cannot be overridden by human clinicians, prompting the government to establish an "escalation pathway" so people in "exceptional circumstances" can have their outcomes reviewed.

After staunchly defending the algorithms as a way to improve consistency, the government also announced in October it would review the algorithms.

Under the changes that took effect in November last year, older people are required to contribute more to the non-clinical care they receive at home.

Recipients cover between 5 and 80 per cent of the service, depending on the type of help and whether or not they are a full or part pensioner.

Services like cleaning and meal preparation demand a higher contribution, compared to remedial or respite care.

It suggests reviewing how the assessment model impacts older older people with varying incomes and needs. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

But the committee recommended the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing review this model to assess the impacts on older people with varying incomes and needs, and to determine if co-payments "discourage timely access to care".

The committee was supposed to deliver a final report, but has instead made an interim report and extended the inquiry until November next year.

On that basis, Labor Senators said they did not intend to comment on the content and recommendations of the interim findings.

"[We] instead reserve our consideration of the work of the committee until the time it presents its final report to the Senate," Labor Senators said in additional comments.

Coalition and Greens unite in criticising program

Inquiry Chair and Greens spokesperson for older people, Senator Penny Allman-Payne, said Labor had "botched" the Support at Home program and added "baffling layers of bureaucracy and complexity".

"Not only are providers jacking up their prices, the system rations and denies care, systematically underassessing need and priority and creating artificial scarcity by withholding packages," she said.

Inside the aged care algorithm Four Corners reveals the fullest picture yet of the secretive algorithm affecting the lives of tens of thousands of older Australians and their families.

Shadow Aged Care Minister Anne Ruston said many of the problems were either predictable or known to the government before the changes began.

"Labor dismissed them and now a Senate committee has confirmed every word," she said.

"The committee has backed what the Coalition has said from day one: an algorithm should never have the final say over an older person's care," Senator Ruston said.

"At a bare minimum, Labor must restore human override now, and stop short-changing older Australians with 60 per cent packages while hundreds of millions of dollars sit unspent," she said.

Government faces criticism for aged care underspend

During Question Time on Thursday, Centre Alliance MP Rebekha Sharkie echoed criticism from Liberal Senator Anne Ruston earlier in the week about the government not spending its full aged care budget.

Ms Sharkie asked Aged Care Minister Sam Rae why Labor underspent by $1.4 billion last financial year.

Sam Rae says as of June 30, more than 390,000 people were on ongoing packages. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"Ageing Australia stated they had capacity to deliver Support at Home to 30,000 additional older Australians," Ms Sharkie said.

Mr Rae said that was a "modest" part of the overall $44 billion budget, but nonetheless it had not been spent because providers were responding slower than anticipated to the need for more at-home packages and new residential beds.

"Since the Labor government was elected in 2022, we've effectively doubled the size of the aged care budget," Mr Rae said.

6,400 Australians die on home care waitlist More than 6,400 older Australians died while waiting to receive home care last year, an increase of more than a third on the previous year.

As of June 30, Mr Rae said more than 390,000 people were on ongoing packages, while more than 106,000 were waiting to receive their approved level of help.

According to data from earlier this year, more than 6,400 older Australians died while in the queue for their Support at Home funding.

Despite not securing the full $3 billion of savings the government was hoping to make from private health insurance rebate changes this week, Health Minister Mark Butler said Labor would still invest that full amount into aged care.

World.title: Councillor ordered to apologise over 'school short-skirt brigade' remarks
World.content:
Ipswich City Council voted to direct a councillor to make a public apology and undertake training and counselling after he made comments including that a female contractor was part of the "school short skirt brigade".

That was one of three allegations against Cr Andrew Antoniolli outlined in an investigation summary tabled at the council meeting today.

Cr Antoniolli excused himself from the debate, which was held in closed session, and the vote due to his conflict of interest.

The ABC has contacted Cr Antoniolli for comment.

Investigation summary outlines three allegations

The complaint was made by Ipswich City Council CEO Sonia Cooper to the Office of the Independent Assessor in February and then referred to the council for investigation.

The investigation summary stated the first allegation was that, on or around January 28, 2026, at a meeting with a council employee and representatives of a contractor, Cr Antoniolli referred to a female contractor as "being part of the school short-skirt brigade".

The second allegation was that, at the same meeting, when introduced to a female contractor, Cr Antoniolli "looked her up and down and said words to the effect that 'women do not normally work in facilities management'".

The third allegation was that, on or around January 29, at a councillor workshop at the Nicholas Street Precinct, in the presence of the council CEO and fellow councillors, Cr Antoniolli queried "whether they could find someone with Queensland Rail experience that had 'slept with the boss' when working at Queensland Rail to assist in dealing with property tenure issues".

The council spent multiple hours debating the item in a closed session before coming back to vote unanimously that "on the balance of probabilities" the first two allegations had been proven, and that Cr Antoniolli had admitted to the third.

It also required him to make a public apology and undertake training and counselling.

Mayor Teresa Harding did not speak in the public meeting on the matter.

Deciding on fellow councillor 'difficult'

Division 2 councillor Paul Tully said the council had "a very thorough discussion of the matters".

"It's probably been one of the most difficult decisions or recommendations for this matter to be raised," he said.

"I will say that the legislation has changed from the 1st of July. If these matters had arisen after the 1st of July, they would not have been referred back to council.

"[This is] probably the last matter in Queensland that will go to any of the 77 councils in Queensland for a decision.

"We've evaluated the evidence, evaluated matters which are in detail over a period of hours. It's not just a rushed decision.

"And in relation to the recommendation about the training and an apology, I think that is appropriate in all of the circumstances."

Concern some will 'misuse' decision

Division 1 councillor Jacob Madsen said the state legislation should not "ever include forcing councillors to make determinations about their fellow councillors".

"I gravely hope that people don't sort of misuse this to treat the subject councillor poorly," he said

"I do genuinely worry with how this may be potentially misused online and in media to do him harm."

Deputy Mayor Nicole Jonic, Division 4 councillor David Martin and Division 1 councillor Pye Augustine all echoed the comments that it had been unpleasant to make the determination, but praised the council's robust debate and unanimous decision.

The full investigation report, redacted to protect the identities of those involved in the investigation, will be published soon.

World.title: Hundreds of Sydney apartment buyers see $24m in deposits vanish
World.content:
More than $24 million in deposits from prospective apartment buyers has gone missing as a Sydney developer acknowledges "something has gone seriously wrong".

Almost 300 home buyers were due to get the keys to their newly-built apartments in Dee Why and Blacktown between this week and early next year but have been left in limbo.

Developer Landmark has launched legal action against Branston Neville Lawyers and solicitor Ken Neville to recoup the missing funds, after alleging only part of the deposits held in trust were transferred to Hendrix Legal as directed after the company changed firms.

The ABC has contacted Branston Neville Lawyers and Mr Neville.

The situation affects about 140 purchasers at the Casa Delmar development in Dee Why. (Supplied: Casa Delmar Dee Why/Landmark)

Purchasers in the Dee Why Casa Delmar complex were expecting to settle as early as Wednesday afternoon before receiving an email from Hendrix Legal that same morning that said their deposit had not come through.

In a statement, Landmark founder Arash Tavakoli said the situation was unprecedented.

"In over 25 years and thousands of homes delivered, this has never happened to us or our buyers," Mr Tavakoli said.

The situation affects about 140 purchasers at the Casa Delmar development at Dee Why and about 145 purchasers at the Second Avenue development at Blacktown.

Apartment buyers told the ABC they were devastated.

Developer Landmark is attempting to claw back $24 million worth of deposits. (ABC News: Quentin Theron)

'Don't have anywhere to go'

Wainwright Legal principal lawyer Clare Wainwright represents 42 affected Dee Why purchasers and said she was receiving "really limited information" about the "completely unprecedented" situation.

"Our position is our purchasers have done all the right things and ultimately settlement should be called for," Ms Wright said.

"We are needing to know what is happening and what the vendor's intention is because we have clients who don't have anywhere to go."

Clare Wainwright is representing 42 affected Dee Why purchasers. (Supplied)

Meanwhile, the Law Society of NSW confirmed it had suspended the practising certificate of Mr Neville and appointed a manager to Branston Neville Lawyers to "take control of the practice with immediate effect".

Mr Tavakoli wrote directly to affected apartment buyers to acknowledge "something has gone seriously wrong" and affirm the company's commitment to completing their contracts.

Calls to lift compensation cap

In the correspondence, he urged affected purchasers to write to NSW Premier Chris Minns and other MPs to encourage the Law Society of NSW to lift the cap on the compensation available through its Fidelity Fund.

The fund is administered by the Law Society to compensate people who lose money due to law firms acting improperly in relation to trust funds or property.

Do you know more? If you have any information about a story, contact Emily Baker at emlybkr@protonmail.com or emlybkr.53 on Signal.

It is capped at $1 million to a single law practice unless the Law Society authorises a greater payment.

"We would welcome the Law Society Council using its discretion to lift that limit, and the government looking at whether that limit still protects buyers in today's market," Mr Tavakoli said in his media statement.

The matter is due to return to the Supreme Court on November 30.

World.title: NSW train strike suspended at eleveth hour
World.content:
Industrial action set to impact regional and interstate passenger train services across NSW has been called off at the eleventh hour.

Workers with the Rail, Tram and Bus Union (RTBU) and Australian Services Union (ASU) planned to walk off the job at midnight, as part of week-long strike action over a months-long enterprise bargaining dispute.

Following a Thursday evening hearing with the Australian Rail Track Corporation (ARTC), which went to the Fair Work Commission in a bid to block the strike, the action was suspended.

Head of Intercity Services at Sydney Trains Magda Robertson told the ABC that Friday morning would be "business as usual".

"We can now run our timetable, particularly on the Hunter and the Southern Highlands," she said.

"Our customers will not be impacted and our timetables will be run as per their timetable order."

Ms Robertson said Sydney Trains would continue working with the ARTC.

Several regional and interstate services were expected to be replaced by coaches, and some North Coast and overnight Melbourne services were to suspend operations.

In a statement, the union said it would abide by the Fair Work Commission's decision but the ruling had only hardened members' resolve.

"Of course, we will comply with this decision but it's left our members furious and more determined than ever to take ARTC on, which risks more significant industrial action once the order lifts," said NSW RTBU Secretary Toby Warnes.

Earlier, Trainlink CEO Roger Weeks said most daily commuters would not be affected by any industrial action.

"It is important to note that the electrified line that is the Sydney Trains network will continue to operate," he said.

"All of the Mariyung intercity from Newcastle down into Sydney and the Illawarra will continue to operate as normal."

World.title: Authorities intercept more than 3 tonnes of meth on Pacific 'mothership'
World.content:
French authorities deployed to the Pacific have seized 3.3 tonnes of methamphetamine, bringing the total amount of drugs French armed forces have seized in the region this year to more than 15 tonnes.

The French military discovered the drugs after boarding a small unflagged oil tanker outside French Polynesia's maritime zone last Friday.

The operation was assisted by a maritime patrol aircraft from the US Coast Guard.

In a statement, the French Pacific Command (CPP) and French Armed Forces in French Polynesia (FAPF) said the vessel was spotted near Clipperton Island, an uninhabited French atoll about 1,100 kilometres from the Mexican coastline.

The vessel was tracked for several weeks, with assistance from international partners, before it was intercepted.

Some of the recent drug seizures in Fiji, New Caledonia and French Polynesia. (ABC News: Jarrod Fankhauser)

"The boarding team found 150 bales, weighing 3.328 tonnes, which tested positive to methamphetamine," said the statement translated from French.

The drugs were seized and transported to Tahiti for destruction, the CPP-FAPF said.

The crew and vessel were released in line with international law and flagged to international authorities.

Tanker a drug 'mothership'

The haul follows several other drug interceptions by French armed forces this year, including three cocaine seizures totalling more than 11 tonnes across January and February, much of which was bound for Australia.

Suspects released after 5 tonnes of Australia-bound cocaine dumped at sea French authorities intercept a ship carrying five tonnes of cocaine bound for Australia, before releasing the vessel and its crew.

But unlike those operations, which targeted smaller vessels, this interception involved what is known as a "mothership", said associate professor Jose Sousa-Santos, convenor of the Pacific Regional Security Hub at the University of Canterbury in New Zealand.

Mr Sousa-Santos said mothership vessels were intended to operate undetected until they approached a Pacific island, Australian or New Zealand waters.

"They are meant to travel underneath the radar undetected until it gets closer to Pacific island, Australian or New Zealand shores," he said.

The first semi-submersible vessel found at Arno Atoll, Marshall Islands. (Supplied: Arthmen Laukon)

Mr Sousa-Santos said motherships typically offloaded drug shipments onto smaller craft, including narco-subs, which then carried the cargo to smaller ports or remote locations.

In this case, he said the location of the seizure suggested the vessel was closer to its point of origin than its intended destination.

The operation also pointed to a higher level of cooperation between French and US authorities than had previously been seen.

"This would definitely be a hit and would send a clear message that trafficking in the region has become harder, especially because the seizure has happened so close to the port of origin," he said.

A shifting market

Mr Sousa-Santos said a series of large cocaine seizures this year had contributed to a shift in the Australian drug market, with traffickers increasingly turning to methamphetamine.

He said the most recent seizure reflected that shift, given it occurred in an area of the Pacific more commonly associated with cocaine trafficking.

"That market has grown, so you expect syndicates to increase the amount of methamphetamine moving toward the Australia and New Zealand market," he said.

The drugs were discovered on board, but authorities have not revealed the vessel's name or flag state. (Supplied: Marine Nationale)

Mr Sousa-Santos said transporting the seized drugs back to Tahiti, rather than destroying them at sea, could give authorities a greater chance of tracing the shipment to criminal syndicates.

"By taking the drugs back into port you can test the drugs, map where the point of origin is, map who the exporters are, which cartel and that makes a huge difference to understanding who is exporting to Australia and New Zealand," he said.

"When you're trying to disrupt markets in Australia and New Zealand, this information is critical."

World.title: Transport minister won't change mind on controversial Matilda Bay ferry terminal
World.content:
WA's transport minister has insisted she will not change her mind about the location of a controversial new ferry terminal at Matilda Bay, despite growing community backlash and projected cost blowouts.

The WA government promised to expand Metronet ferry services on Perth's Swan River during the 2025 state election campaign, at a joint Commonwealth-state cost of $107 million.

Two new ferry terminals were proposed, one at Applecross and one at Matilda Bay in Nedlands — directly opposite the University of Western Australia — to be serviced by five new electric ferries.

Rita Saffioti says Matilda Bay is simply the best choice for the Nedlands terminal. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Today the government confirmed the cost of the whole project had increased to about $150 million.

Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said the Matilda Bay section had incurred increased costs to "change the nature of the jetty and the length of the jetty"

Locals upset

The Western Australian Planning Commission approved the development for the new ferry terminals last December, but the government has continued to face opposition from locals, the Liberals and the Greens.

A petition tabled in WA's parliament today, signed by over 10,000 people, called for construction contracts to be suspended so more analysis of the Matilda Bay site could take place.

Ms Saffioti said a comprehensive analysis of five key sites in Nedlands had deemed Matilda Bay the best.

"We made a commitment at the election, we then went back and assessed all the different options again," Ms Saffioti said.

Row over plan for ferry terminal at Perth's Matilda Bay deepens A WA government-commissioned analysis finds the scenic and popular Matilda Bay is the safest spot for a ferry terminal, just as another report prompted by an advocacy group says it would put river users at serious risk.

She said "environmental experts" found alternative sites including Jojo's and Pelican Point were not suitable "because of the impact on seagrass, migratory birds and also impacts into some reserves".

Asked if the ferry site would be moved, Ms Saffioti said she was "not going to change [her] mind".

"There's no reason for me not to choose a better site if a better site was told to me," she said.

" It's not as if I'm just captured by this site, I took the advice. "

Save Matilda Bay spokesperson Megan Bagworth said her group would continue to lobby for the Nedlands ferry landing to be moved to Jojo's.

"Once it's built, it can't be undone," Ms Bagworth said.

"That's why the government needs to do the full and proper assessments now and review this decision."

'Yet another blowout'

Opposition transport spokesperson Steve Martin said Ms Saffioti had "blown another budget" at a time of cost-of-living pressures for West Australians.

Steve Martin is criticising the government for another cost blowout. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"Here we are, yet another blowout on the top of the Fremantle Traffic Bridge [Walyalup Bridge] that went from $230 million to $596 million and counting," he said.

Construction on the ferry terminals is expected to commence in the middle of next year, with the ferry services expected to start in late 2027.

World.title: Science cancelled and class numbers doubled as mouldy classrooms in WA shut
World.content:
Class sizes at a Wheatbelt school have doubled this term after mould forced part of the campus to close.

Five classrooms and a toilet block at Lancelin Primary School have been closed for nearly seven weeks, forcing multiple classes to share rooms and science lessons replaced with sport.

A longstanding issue

Parents and Community Association president and mother to two students, Jade Hamlyn said the school, 125 kilometres north of Perth, has about 150 students split between seven core classrooms.

Water damage is visible outside a classroom. (Supplied: Shane Love)

She said authorities had known about a recurring mould issue for more than a decade, and she could not believe it had been neglected to the point of closing facilities.

"It's appalling that the school and the school staff have had to advocate for 14 years to get anything to be done," Ms Hamlyn said.

She said many parents had health concerns.

"My daughter actually has been quite ill in regards to respiratory issues.

"Now I'm questioning whether this is a result of [the mould].

" I'd love to ask them [the state government] would you put your child in that classroom? "

Jade Hamlyn has six children, two of whom are currently attending the school and have been affected by the mould issues. (Supplied: Jade Hamyln)

Mixed classes disrupting students

Ms Hamlyn said the closures had forced multiple year groups to share the same rooms.

She said her pre-primary-aged daughter had refused to go to school for three weeks as the cohort shared a class with the kindergartens.

"She's finding that it's just too disruptive … she can't handle having so many students in one room," she said.

Ms Hamlyn said her older daughter in year 6 was learning in the library with another class, along with its regular users.

"There's three classes in this library at any one time," she said.

"You've got two of them actually trying to learn their lessons with book displays as borders [separating classes]."

An outdoor area was also closed during Shane Love's visit to the school. (Supplied: Shane Love)

Ms Hamlyn said science lessons had been replaced with physical education for the rest of the year as the dedicated facility was being used as a regular classroom.

"That's a huge concern because my child's a part of the graduating cohort, which then [science] won't be included in her school report," she said.

Like Ms Hamlyn, school board member and mother of three students, Casey Clarke said sharing classrooms was disruptive.

"There's like 35 to 40 little kids in one classroom," she said.

Ms Clarke said she knew of multiple families considering moving from Lancelin as they no longer wanted to send their children to the school.

"We've just got so many worried families," she said.

It's just a horrible situation."

Not a quick fix

Ms Clarke said staff had logged multiple incident reports to try and get the mould thoroughly removed, but were met with band-aid fixes each time.

"They [the Department of Education] can't have fixed the problem when they're not taking out cupboards or carpets to see the full ramifications of the moisture," she said.

" We are not comfortable to put our kids back into the rooms given they have not been sufficiently cleaned. "

Ms Clarke said her own children had frequent upper respiratory issues, which she thought could be connected to the mould.

Nationals WA member for Mid West Shane Love said the school looked "badly neglected" when he recently visited.

Shane Love says the classrooms' contents have been packed up. (Supplied: Shane Love)

He said the kindergarten classroom was in an "ancient" demountable building which had begun to deteriorate.

"The floor had basically rotted away and was all mouldy," Mr Love said.

He said a group of classrooms had visible water damage on their ceilings, and the pre-primary classroom's verandah had been cordoned off as it was mouldy.

"The department is saying that there's water damage. There's a bit more than water damage; you could smell the mould in there, Mr Love said.

"To have allowed this situation to develop, I think, is reprehensible by the Department [of Education]."

'Lessons continued as normal'

The Department of Education confirmed five classrooms were closed in October to inspect and repair moisture damage.

"Lessons continued as normal with students being accommodated in the school library and science room," a spokesperson said.

In November, four of the rooms were declared safe, but the school principal kept them closed for "unrelated work," including window cleaning, painting and installing new carpet.

The spokesperson said the fifth classroom would be replaced with a new transportable building next year due to a flooring issue.

They said the girls' toilets were closed as a precaution while contractors investigated potential water damage, but other facilities were available.

World.title: The cat’s out of the bag
World.content:

“We took our cat to a fete in a string bag (C8), to be entered into the pet show,” says Pamela Kerr of Moonta Bay (SA). “He was quite unconcerned and took out the prizes for longest tail, longest whiskers, largest cat and best cat. They changed the rules the next year to one prize per cat.”

“Geoff Carey spoke of the Christian brothers at his school not using the cane but opting for a leather strap (C8),” notes Mike Parton of Tamworth. “Doesn’t sound too drastic. I attended St Chad’s Marist College in Wolverhampton, UK, and they did use canes, but thoughtfully. Having been seen absent-mindedly touching (defined as ‘playing with’) a gas tap in the science lab, I was given ‘six of the best’ by the science brother, six by my headmaster and six by my housemaster for losing house points. However, they were given on three consecutive days, on my left hand, so my writing skills would not be affected. How thoughtful! I wonder how that would compare with ‘the strap’.”

“Ah, the good old days! We had a nun who insisted that every time she whacked us we had to say, ‘Thank you, sister’, because she was saving our six-year-old souls from eternal damnation,” recalls Peter Riley of Penrith. “And she kept whacking until you said it. I wonder how many Hannibal Lecters she produced in her ‘teaching career’?”

“Perhaps David Jones (C8) should change their name to Davy Jones (everybody’s favourite Monkee) as he rose to stardom in the early 1960s, causing the other DJ to assume Texan Jim’s surname,” says Colin Taylor-Evans of Lane Cove. “The Manchester department could be a tribute to Davy’s heritage.” Michael McFadyen of Kareela had the same thought but wondered, “Am I just a Daydream Believer?”

“My choice between DJs or Myer is made easy by the institution within the institution,” offers Howard Charles of Glebe. “Approaching Michael Hope (C8) at the piano means a seamless transition to a Gershwin, Porter or Ellington number, masterfully infused with a dose of Garner, Waller or Ellington swing, upon request.”

World.title: Why Clayton and Weatherald must be the two men considered for Test spot
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketTest cricket Why Clayton and Weatherald must be the two men considered for Test spot Nick Wright November 26, 2026 — 8:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Jack Clayton has issued Australian selectors one final reminder of why he warrants a maiden Test call-up, as he continued a trend which must garner serious consideration. The Queensland left-hander’s unbeaten 84 during the Bulls’ second innings of their Sheffield Shield clash against New South Wales at the Sydney Cricket Ground continued his tendency to score runs in precarious situations; a 109 on debut and counterpunching third innings century in the 2024-25 Shield final other examples. Jack Clayton has emerged as a possible successor for Marnus Labuschagne. Getty Images Trailing by 25 runs against a Nathan Lyon-led Blues attack, Clayton combined with Hugo Burdon (98) in a 132-run day four partnership, before Michael Neser (61 from 37 balls) wreaked havoc. Marnus Labuschagne’s declaration was nearly a masterstroke as NSW limped to 8/152 to force a draw – still 130 runs shy of victory as Kurtis Patterson’s 49 defied leg spinner Mitchell Swepson’s 11-wicket match haul.



The 27-year-old Clayton’s 449 runs at an average of 74.83 for 2026–27 – including a century and four half-centuries – trails only NSW opener Sam Konstas (479 at 68.42). He boasts 1554 runs at 48.56 since October 2024, building his game around solid defence and low-risk scoring options to thrust his name into contention for the four-Test series against New Zealand. “It was all about setting ourselves up in the first hour, giving ourselves a chance to then be able to explode,” a “proud” Burdon told this masthead. “I’ve played a lot with Clayto in the last five years – we’ve done a stint up in Darwin in the off season together, we’ve done a stint over in England together – so he knows my game really well, and I know his game really well. “I’ve got no doubt that if he gets his opportunity at the next level he’ll take it with two hands, and I know he’ll perform. His game is suited to Test cricket, and that’s where he belongs.



“He’s got the best numbers of anyone else besides those Test players playing at the moment, so he’s definitely ready for the next level.” Australia will name its Test squad at the end this Shield round, with Labuschagne a casualty of October’s South Africa fade-out – which included team capitulations of 99 and 111 in the second and third Tests – and Steve Smith to return after missing the third Test in South Africa with a neck injury. Allrounder Cooper Connolly, who replaced Beau Webster in Cape Town, is also no guarantee to be retained after scoring 29 and 0, before making nine on his return for Western Australia. His fate may be dictated by whether Cameron Green – who has battled abdominal, shoulder and concussion issues – can bowl. National selectors could opt to shift Travis Head back to the middle order and bring in an opener, with Konstas and Jake Weatherald the leading contenders.
