A Qantas plane was forced to abort its landing at Sydney Airport to avoid a potential collision with two aircraft crossing the runway, prompting a federal investigation months after a string of near misses on the tarmac. Pilots on QF426 from Melbourne were preparing to land on runway 16R on Wednesday morning while an Air New Zealand plane and another aircraft were on the tarmac. Qantas pilots delayed their landing as they awaited clearance from air traffic control. Wolter Peeters It prompted a last-minute “go-around”, which involved the pilots continuing to fly past the airport towards Sydney Harbour as the other aircraft crossed the runway. Air traffic control was yet to provide clearance to the Qantas pilots to land when they began the go-around. The flight landed safely at 10.25am about 10 minutes after the reported incident.



“Our pilots were following air traffic control instructions and elected to conduct a go-around as the other aircraft was crossing the runway,” a Qantas spokesperson said. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) began investigating the close call on Thursday. That inquiry will include interviewing flight crew and air traffic controllers to examine any potential errors that may have led to the incident. Qantas, through its spokesperson, said it would support the ATSB investigation. It comes less than two months after the ATSB released four preliminary reports related to six recent incidents at Sydney Airport. These included a near-miss involving a Qantas Boeing 737 that was cleared to cross a runway in front of a Qantas Bombardier DHC-8. The incident was ranked as the most serious on an international scale used to grade runway incursions. It was the third incident since Australian records began in 2003 assessed as a “Cat A runway incursion”.



The Boeing 737 (left) and the Bombardier DHC-8 involved in a breakdown of co-ordination at Sydney Airport in July. YouTube/@amyfoxtrot Other incidents probed by the ATSB include a Jetstar A320 suddenly braking to avoid a Qatar Airways Boeing 777 on August 9, causing a flight attendant to fracture their wrist. The same day, a Qantas Boeing 737 was cleared to cross the runway in front of a Virgin 737 that had just been cleared for take-off. Nine days later, a Qantas A321 had to brake to let a Qantas 737 pass in front of it. Strain on air traffic control staff was identified as an ongoing issue in the investigation of runway incidents at Sydney Airport, though the investigation didn’t determine whether waning staffing resources directly contributed to any error. The ATSB expects to release a preliminary report on Wednesday’s close call by January. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Victorian hot seats: ‘Stuff that’: The question about Joh Bauch’s past that One Nation refuses to answer
World.content:
“We’re not racist,” Joh Bauch says of One Nation when I first meet him. “Look at me!”

The son of migrants, Bauch is one of several Filipino-Australian candidates running in the Victorian state election for the populist party and hoping his heritage can challenge the beliefs many voters have about One Nation’s beliefs.

In person, Bauch is chatty and good-humoured (at least at first). He wears a giant novelty Australian-flag bowtie when we meet at a campaign event in St Albans. He bought an orange bowtie, he says, but lost it somewhere. “What’s more Aussie than an Aussie tie? We’ve got to fly our flag proud,” he says.

“We took our cat to a fete in a string bag (C8), to be entered into the pet show,” says Pamela Kerr of Moonta Bay (SA). “He was quite unconcerned and took out the prizes for longest tail, longest whiskers, largest cat and best cat. They changed the rules the next year to one prize per cat.”

“Geoff Carey spoke of the Christian brothers at his school not using the cane but opting for a leather strap (C8),” notes Mike Parton of Tamworth. “Doesn’t sound too drastic. I attended St Chad’s Marist College in Wolverhampton, UK, and they did use canes, but thoughtfully. Having been seen absent-mindedly touching (defined as ‘playing with’) a gas tap in the science lab, I was given ‘six of the best’ by the science brother, six by my headmaster and six by my housemaster for losing house points. However, they were given on three consecutive days, on my left hand, so my writing skills would not be affected. How thoughtful! I wonder how that would compare with ‘the strap’.”

“Ah, the good old days! We had a nun who insisted that every time she whacked us we had to say, ‘Thank you, sister’, because she was saving our six-year-old souls from eternal damnation,” recalls Peter Riley of Penrith. “And she kept whacking until you said it. I wonder how many Hannibal Lecters she produced in her ‘teaching career’?”

“Perhaps David Jones (C8) should change their name to Davy Jones (everybody’s favourite Monkee) as he rose to stardom in the early 1960s, causing the other DJ to assume Texan Jim’s surname,” says Colin Taylor-Evans of Lane Cove. “The Manchester department could be a tribute to Davy’s heritage.” Michael McFadyen of Kareela had the same thought but wondered, “Am I just a Daydream Believer?”

“My choice between DJs or Myer is made easy by the institution within the institution,” offers Howard Charles of Glebe. “Approaching Michael Hope (C8) at the piano means a seamless transition to a Gershwin, Porter or Ellington number, masterfully infused with a dose of Garner, Waller or Ellington swing, upon request.”

World.title: This election result will flow down through society
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters This election result will flow down through society November 26, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Photo: Fiona Katauskas To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Yes, life will go on for many after the election, as your correspondent writes (Letters, 26/11), but that depends who wins the election. There are many differences as Labor and Liberal are themselves vastly different in their beliefs. Labor has always been the champion of the ordinary working class. Liberal has always been for business and, as I see it, working more for the wealthy in the community. So life for many may go on but the ordinary folk are the ones who will suffer when there are cuts that affect the community. What happens after Saturday will make all the difference between a more or a less divided society.

Nola Cormick, Albert Park Here’s the mail: address these points

Dear Jess, thanks for your letter – I don’t get much snail mail these days. Quaintly addressed to “Mrs” too. I haven’t been called that since the ’70s. Given that we’ve never met, I don’t know how you guessed that I’m angry, but I am indeed, and there are certainly a couple of things you could do to help.

First, could you change your mind about abolishing the Treaty? It celebrates its first birthday in a couple of weeks and the sky most certainly hasn’t fallen in. Could you also change your mind about closing the safe injecting room in Richmond? I understand it’s saved hundreds of lives since it opened. If it’s the location that’s the problem, I’m sure you could find another spot nearby.

I look forward to your next letter (now you’ve had your little joke you could address it to Ms) to see if I’m still angry. If your party wins on Saturday, I suspect I may be. Cheers, Jo

Jo Bond, South Melbourne A candidate with old-time Labor values

As a life member of the ALP I was heartened to read of Mikaela Stafrace and her battle to win the seat of Caulfield (″⁣If Labor wants to know where it went wrong, start with diary of this loyalist″⁣, 27/11). She presents as one who fights for her beliefs which centre on old-time Labor values such as social justice, public education, honesty and transparency in government. Her reflections on why Labor is heading for a thumping need to be at the core of the soul searching that will follow this election. I fear for the social impact that will occur with a probable Liberal-One Nation victory, but I also worry that valuable lessons will not be heeded by state Labor.

Tony Ross, Bunyip



Pining for times now gone

I note the recent announcements from Jess Wilson to get rid of some of Labor’s better reforms such as the Treaty (which the Victorian Liberals once supported) and now the supervised injecting room. I’m now waiting for her announcement to bring back level crossings, which One Nation would also no doubt support as it would take us back to the “good old days” for which they yearn.

Craig Dickason, Heatherton Change deadline for releasing costings

It’s ludicrous for any party to release costings of its election promises just two days before the election. Most voters have already made up their minds, with pundits expecting Jess Wilson to be the new premier, without understanding what cuts she will make to balance the budget. Election reform is needed to require all parties to release all of their policies and verified costings at least four weeks before an election. Only then can the media and voters adequately consider who deserves their vote.

Guy Toner, Brighton Ruling some out, leaves just one

Jess Wilson seems down to earth, but I don’t want the Treaty to be revoked, and getting into bed with One Nation? Ben Carroll is under all the weight of Jacinta Allan’s baggage and I’m over the Big Build, but I love the Metro Tunnel. The Greens want Ukrainians to defend themselves without weapons – pompous ideology won’t protect civilians. I believe in democracy and I’m glad it’s compulsory to vote. I’ll be voting for the candidate I met in the park and who I feel safe to speak openly with – in my electorate that happens to be the Greens.

Lyn Pool, East St Kilda THE FORUM Rebuilding lives

The recent serious assaults on mental health staff and members of the community are very distressing. Occupational violence against health workers is a different problem from serious violent crime in hospitals or the community, and conflating them helps neither. Occupational violence is rising: WorkSafe claims for workplace aggression and violence in Victoria more than doubled in a decade, and health staff report higher rates than other public servants. That demands urgent action.

More than 93,000 Victorians were registered with public mental health services in 2024-25, and the overwhelming majority, including those with schizophrenia, are not violent. International research finds severe mental illness accounts for only a small share of violent crime, and the risk it carries is strongly linked to substance misuse. Reporting only tragedies fuels stigma and deters people from seeking help.

In 47 years as a mental health nurse, I have seen countless people rebuild their lives with excellent community care. That rarely makes headlines.

More funding is needed, including some acute capacity. But rebuilding psychiatric hospitals is not the answer. Evidence favours well-resourced community teams and stable housing. Housing First, backed by Australian and international research, helps people keep their homes and reduces hospital use.

Mark Thornett , Moonee Ponds



Fix the system

Patrick McGorry’s article “Broken social contract fuels crime” (25/11), highlights the failures in Victoria’s mental health care. Personal experience leads me to add my voice to his plea.

Earlier this year, a family member went from hospital to hospital seeking urgent help for severe psychiatric symptoms. The best he received was a few days of inpatient treatment with medication, followed by discharge to a motel for three nights. No community follow-up care was offered, and he was soon back on the streets, still very unwell.

His family had no idea of his whereabouts until a desperate phone call revealed that he was at a train station, so terrified that he was contemplating suicide or provoking police to shoot him. Police were called and he was taken to the nearest hospital emergency department. Another few days in a mental health unit followed, before he was again discharged into the community.

His acute illness eventually abated after he agreed to attend a series of appointments with a private psychiatrist.

In contrast, another family member was admitted to a public mental health unit for five weeks, stabilised on medication and discharged home under the ongoing care of a community mental health team.

The difference in the standard of care and the outcomes is stark.

Why is this standard of treatment not available to all people with severe mental illness?

Christine Stanton, Hawthorn Our good life

With this election, Australians should pause and appreciate the quiet, practical decency we have built – and think carefully before importing politics that could dismantle it.

Anyone who compares everyday life in Australia with the United States sees the difference immediately. Here, we take for granted universal Medicare, paid annual leave for workers, children walking into school without passing through metal detectors, and simple community touches like clean public facilities and free barbecues in our local parks. These aren’t luxuries; they are the result of a society that believes in looking after one another.

Yet segments of our media are increasingly amplifying figures like Pauline Hanson, who is echoing the hard-edged, American-style agenda associated with Donald Trump and Project 2025 – a worldview rooted in deregulation, division, and leaving ordinary people to fend for themselves.

We should be exporting Australia’s co-operative spirit to the rest of the world, not trading it away for imported culture wars and policies that weaken the social safety nets on which families rely.

When we cast our votes , let’s choose leaders who will protect our fair go, our public health system, and our peaceful way of life.

Clement Clarke, Warracknabeal Injecting room success

With Jess Wilson vowing to close the medically supervised injecting room – along with Yarra councillors’ recent inexplicable rejection of the installation of a 24/7 Naloxone dispensing unit in North Richmond – our community will, once again, be exposed to the trauma of an increase in public overdoses , discarded syringes and emergency service vehicles impacting the local shopping precinct, streets and laneways.

The MSIR is the most evaluated, researched, visited and probed medical centre in Victoria over the past eight years. Recent peer-reviewed research (July 2026) by Monash and Deakin universities, Ambulance Victoria and Turning Point revealed a 71 per cent decrease in ambulance callouts to opioid overdoses in the vicinity of the injecting room since it opened in 2018: surely an irrefutable indicator of success?

What evidence is there that recommends the closure of this facility?

Judy Ryan, Abbotsford Two options for RBA

I might be naive, but I thought it was the job of the RBA to keep inflation at a certain level (2 to 3per cent). But, if as it is reported, inflation is rising mainly due to outside events like wars and the interest rate that the RBA sets, then it seems dumb and counter productive to increase rates in order to increase pain because thepast pain we have inflicted was too high.

If that is the case, then it seems clear that the RBA can never achieve its supposed aim. In that case, there are only two ways of proceeding: 1) get rid of the RBA because it can’t do its job, or 2) change its tools and objectives so that it can do its job.

Dieter Liebrich, Swanpool Are loans being serviced?

I read the loans for building infrastructure are burdening the future generations.(Letters, 26/11). Just like paying a 30-year home mortgage, we are ″⁣burdened″⁣ or ″⁣crippled″⁣ by the debt when the loan cannot be serviced. Are we servicing the loans, should be the media’s focus?

Peter McGill, Lancefield



Debt is a good thing

Your correspondent (Letters, 26/11) bemoans Victoria’s high debt, at $160 billion. Victorian government revenue is $116 billion. Debt is 1.4 times revenue, and interest is 1 per cent of revenue. In contrast, average household mortgage debt is $730,000 against average household income of $110,000, ie, 6.6 times income. Average interest is getting towards 50 per cent of income. People would love to have the government’s debt ratios, as they buy homes despite the private debt they are getting into. Homes are an asset that will benefit their children now and eventually, just as the hospitals, schools and other infrastructure will benefit Victorian children now and in the future. No debt means no new infrastructure for future generations.

Louise Kloot, Doncaster More for workers

Ross Gittins (Comment, 25/11) sheds light on the vexed issue of productivity. He describes the powerful and often vocal business lobby constantly talking up what they will do if governments only give them more tax breaks and other favourable treatment.

The issue with this is it rarely puts more money in the workers’ pocket. We see this playing out constantly as rich businesses make millionaires and billionaires out of their owners, while real wages go backwards.

Sadly this kind of inequality is growing, especially when you consider that according to ACOSS reporting the average wealth of the top 10 per cent rose 84 per cent since 2003, from $2.8million to $5.2 million, and they actually own more than 50per cent of the total wealth. There’s something inherently wrong with this and it surprises me that more workers don’t kick up a stink about it. It’s about time more Australians shared in a greater percentage of the pie and rather than crying poor these profitable businesses could do a lot better by their workers starting with better pay and working conditions.

Michael Cormick, Carnegie Down after Epiphany

Concerning the traditions of Christmas (Letters, 25/11), in my family, the tree and the crib appeared on Christmas Eve and were packed away for another year on January 7, the day after the feast of the Epiphany. Not quite 12 days of Christmas but certainly a lot less than current practice which sees trees and other decorations appearing as early as mid-November and hanging around well into the new year. As for a crib, well that rarely gets a place. I suppose that’s what happens when the reason for the season is subsumed into a naked grab for profit.

Happy Christmas everyone.

Judith Taylor, Emerald On Twelfth Night

It is ″⁣de rigueur″⁣ to still have the tree up after New Year’s Day. The Twelve Days of Christmas run from December 25 to January 5. Traditionally January 5 (Twelfth Night) is the date to dismantle the tree and remove the decorations.

Brian Kidd, Mt. Waverley Imagine this . . .

In an attempt to understand the horror of Gaza. Let’s imagine two million people trapped in a contaminated toxic wasteland, according to a report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory, and between St Kilda and Frankston.

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood



Knitting just sew, sew

As a youngster, I bragged to my mother I was capable of knitting a jumper. After a tortuous couple of months, I would rather have gone to jail.

John Rawson, Mernda They are not our friends

Artificial intelligence companion apps are like the old imaginary friend we used to have only a thousand times more insidious.

Suzanne Palmer-Holton, Seaford Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING

Clever move by Jess Wilson to put out her costings after so many have already voted.

Marie Nash, Balwyn This is what constitutes good policy for a Jess Wilson-led government. Education: Build more elite government schools in the west. Housing: Extend the outer urban sprawl. Health: Provide taxpayer subsidies to private hospitals.

Gary Ross, Heidelberg Labor must not get re-elected on Saturday. Their bad behaviour simply cannot be rewarded.

Peter Venn, East Bentleigh Why on earth would an educated, intelligent person want to bring barbaric cage fighting to our state? Think about it again, Jess Wilson.

John Walsh, Watsonia One Nation’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering campaigns on a platform of ″⁣radical transparency″⁣. Meanwhile, many voters can see right through One Nation.

Annie Wilson, Inverloch



How ironic those letters correspondents pushing to maintain the Richmond safe injecting room aren’t from Richmond. Here’s a thought, nominate to have the injecting room next to your house.

Graham Stevens, Murrumbeena Whatever the result on Saturday. the sun will come up on Sunday .

Peter Randles, Pascoe Vale South Furthermore

We’ve known the risks of AI since 1968 at least To quote from 2001 A Space Odyssey, Dave: “Open the pod bay doors please HAL”. “Sorry Dave I’m afraid I can’t do that ... This mission is too important for me to allow you to jeopardise it.“

World.title: 'Neutral from the outset': Wellington mayor Andrew Little still holding back over rates controversy
World.content:
After weeks of controversial headlines and hours of public submissions, Wellington's mayor is still holding back from stating his position on the capital's major rating debate.

Andrew Little said he's forming a "very clear picture" of his view on the ratings system proposal, but didn't want to get ahead of the process with final submissions underway.

One long-standing Wellington councillor said the proposal to change the rating system from a land-value to capital-value system has caused the most concern she's ever seen in the city, with people stopping her in the street "worried sick".

The council received about 5700 public submissions and over 450 requests to speak on the city's rating review - which also includes proposals to decrease businesses rates.

The capital-value/land-value debate has struck a nerve, with some cinemas and central-city bars warning they are facing closure over rates increases, and supporters urging the change to stamp out land-banking in the city and saying other rates would decrease.

In an interview with RNZ, Little was asked what his view was on the controversial policy. He said he did not want to pre-empt the process.

"The whole issue of pre-determination does loom large in local government, so we are sensitive to it, particularly on big and controversial questions like this, so it is important we don't look like we've made up our minds before we've made a decision - otherwise people get cynical about the whole consultation process."

Little, however, said feedback from the community, and information received in the consultation process, would "weigh heavily" on the council's decision over its rating system, and suggested it would feature in his.

"I was neutral from the outset, although I'd met with people who were kind of, championing the cause, they could never explain to me what the impact would be, and until I was clear about that I didn't have a view one way or the other, but now I've got some good information to make a decision."

The campaign has involved vocal lobby groups on either side of the debate - Common Ground Aotearoa and Voice for Wellington, including donations for some councillors during the campaign from Common Ground Aotearoa and donations to other councillors from businesses or property developers.

Little said that was the nature of politics in New Zealand, where public funding wasn't provided for those who wanted to stand.

"There wouldn't be a councillor who hasn't had a donation from somebody who represents one view or another."

When asked whether the presence of these groups had influenced councillors, Little said he wasn't concerned.

"I'm not fazed by lobby groups, interest groups, pressure groups - whatever. It actually enriches our public debate. I think the job of those in elected public office is to use those discriminatory tools and understand that things said with the greatest passion or volume aren't necessarily correct."

'Most concern I've ever seen'

Independent councillor for the Pukehīnau Lambton ward, Nicola Young, said the ratings debate was "boiling over" in the city.

"I've been a councillor for 13 years, and never have I experienced the level of public concern that I have about this.

"I went to the orchestra, people came to me beforehand, during the interval and as I was going home. I'm getting emails all the time, people will stop me in the street - people are worried sick about it."

Nicola Young. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Hours of back-to-back public hearings held in council offices this week have canvassed a range of views on the different proposals.

Ngaio resident Michelle Rush said her rates would go up under a land value system, but she wanted the change, because it supported townhouse development.

Curbing expensive greenfield development in areas without existing infrastructure was crucial for the council, she said.

"It does help to contain urban sprawl, and spatial studies from both North America and Australia show that land taxation channels growth inward onto under-utilised, infill parcels near key infrastructure."

But architect and urban designer Graeme McIndoe, founding director of McIndoe Urban, told councillors he didn't believe a change to land-value rates would incentivise development, or efficient land-use.

McIndoe said inner-city development relied on market demand, interest rates, district plan controls - which had levers for intensive development.

World.title: Police search for family of boy found in Kaitaia
World.content:
Northland police are trying the locate the family of a little boy who was found by members of the public in Kaitaia on Thursday evening.

They said the child was about two years old and was found on Pukepoto Road just after 7pm.

He was wearing black shorts, a blue singlet with a picture of spiderman on the front and had ear-length brown hair.

He was also riding a small black bike with a blue seat.

World.title: Auckland mayor Wayne Brown says China trip was significantly under budget
World.content:
Auckland's mayor says the cost of his recent trip to China has come in significantly under budget.

Wayne's Brown's visit to six cities cost just under $20,000. The budget was for just over $25,000.

The visit made headlines back home after Brown claimed democracy had 'had its day', sparking a fiery response from US ambassador to NZ Jared Novelly, who called the mayor a boomer and questioned his intelligence.

Brown also appeared on Chinese television, saying New Zealand should sell its seat on the Five Eyes security alliance to Japan.

In a statement, he said an important part of his job as to open doors for Auckland businesses and promote the city on the international stage.

"There's a lot of value in getting in front of people, strengthening those relationships and looking at what other cities are doing well. Ultimately, it's about creating more opportunities for Aucklanders and our economy."

The Auckland mayor visited a number of cities while in China, including Changchun, Shanghai, Beijing and Auckland's sister city of 28 years Ningbo.

World.title: Poisonous invasive cane toad 'size of a guinea pig' spotted in Tauranga
World.content:
An invasive cane toad "the size of a guinea pig" was spotted in Tauranga this week.

Volunteer firefighter Annie Henley was training by the Tauranga Model Powerboat Club in Tauriko on Tuesday night when she saw the poisonous toad.

Henley said at the time she had no idea what she was seeing was a cane toad and thought it was just a large frog.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408910878112

"We were finishing up a training and pulling in some big hoses that were in the water and what I thought was a frog, jumped out of the water."

Henley said she and a friend went over to the toad and she began filming as she thought "it was the biggest frog I've ever seen".

She posted the video on Instagram and said a friend who was a conservationist messaged her and said she needed to contact the Ministry of Primary Industries (MPI).

"My friend got in touch and they [MPI] went to investigate. MPI called me the next day asking for exact coordinates."

Annie Henley is a volunteer firefighter. AnnieGProNZ / SUPPLIED

Henley said the toad had jumped into long grass and had been about the size of a guinea pig.

MPI Biosecurity NZ's manager of surveillance and incursion Wendy McDonald confirmed there had been a report of a single exotic toad sighting in Tauriko.

"We've sent staff to investigate.

"Cane toads can occasionally arrive here as hitchhikers, most commonly from Australia. The risk to the public is low, provided people avoid handling the toad and wash thoroughly after any contact."

Cane toads weren't established in Aotearoa, McDonald said, possibly due to our climate being cooler than Australia's.

"We're going to check the area thoroughly. From the video, it appears to be adult male cane toad."

If anyone thought they had seen a cane toad McDonald said they should report it to Biosecurity NZ immediately on 0800 80 99 66 or by emailing info@mpi.govt.nz or report.mpi.govt.nz

World.title: Shane Jones promises to pause and review $200 million Gas Security Fund
World.content:
Resources Minister Shane Jones has promised to pause and review the $200 million Gas Security Fund after officials said it was a fossil fuel industry subsidy.

Jones labelled that a "heretical conclusion" but said if he's returned to government he would look into it further to better understand the implications for international trade agreements.

The fund aims to bring gas to market more quickly and can support things like drilling in existing fields, exploration and storage.

Jones and other ministers have repeatedly denied it provided subsidies, and the Greens - who have long criticised the fund - are now accusing them of lying.

In September the government revealed the first investment: $23.5 million in loans for two projects run by Todd Energy which were expected to boost the country's gas reserves with enough to power 80,000 households annually.

The Greens circulated official documents - originally released to the New Zealand Herald - which showed foreign affairs staff advised the investments were "likely to be considered subsidies".

Officials drafted talking points (some of which are redacted) saying when the fund was established, investments were not expected to be subsidies.

"However, it has become clear that, in some cases, time-limited and targeted subsidies are needed to support energy security."

There were strong policy grounds for the investment, they said, pointing to the need to maintain reliable electricity supply during the transition to renewables.

Offering fossil fuel subsidies could breach the terms of some international trade deals, however officials noted the loans were consistent with such agreements.

In separate documents, Treasury officials warned the loans to Todd Energy were comparatively concessionary - that is, at a better rate than the commercial market would offer.

Jones told RNZ he did not accept the loans were subsidies.

"We could have invested equity into various options to boost oil and gas, but we entered into financial arrangements where the money has to be paid back," he said.

"That's a loan. A loan is not a subsidy."

Jones said officials had offered "narrow, globalist-driven interpretations", while the government wanted to accelerate the delivery of oil and gas to "rescue the economy", particularly while New Zealanders faced energy hardship.

"We are entitled to enter into arrangements with financial instruments that are loans," he said.

"We're not obliged to accept every word from Treasury, and it'll be a long day in hell before I ever accept every word from MFAT."

However given the potential trade implications, Jones said he would take a closer look if he was to govern again.

"It wouldn't be unreasonable for us to pause and and better understand why these heretical conclusions have been reached by MFAT and Treasury."

Greens accuse government of repeated lies

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the government had repeatedly made false claims about the fund by denying it was a subsidy.

"Ministers had once insisted these subsidies weren't subsidies because the Crown would be investing on commercial terms.

"But, in black and white, taxpayers are now lending Todd Energy 70 per cent of the cost of drilling these wells on terms cheaper than commercial lending."

In response, Jones said the Green Party was deeply hostile to the fossil fuel sector.

"I think you should just see it for political posturing."

The fund is designed to tackle swiftly dwindling gas supplies.

Government information about the two Todd projects said they expected to have gas flowing by the end of next year, using its existing fields and infrastructure.

World.title: Gastroenteritis outbreak at Waikato school camp
World.content:
There has been an outbreak of gastroenteritis (gastro) linked to a school camp in the Waikato, attended by more than 400 people.

A number of students, some parents and at least two staff have fallen ill with vomiting and diarrhoea after the Marian Catholic School camp, held between 18-20 November, Health NZ's National Public Health Service says.

About 360 students, 13 staff and 48 parents attended the camp.

Medical officer of health Kate Meerkerk said some people who didn't go to the camp but who live with someone who did have also been sick "which shows that gastro can spread from person to person at home".

Meerkerk said the cause wasn't yet known and the National Public Health Service was investigating and working to confirm how many people were affected.

"Public Health staff are working closely with the school and the camp to understand what may have caused it, including potentially food, water or the wider environment. Stool sample kits have been provided to the school, and we are asking people with recent vomiting or diarrhoea to help by providing a sample as soon as possible so we can find the cause."

The National Public Health Service's advice:

People with gastro should stay away from school until they have had no symptoms for 48 hours.

"Most people with gastro recover at home within a few days without needing medical treatment. If you are concerned, call your usual health care provider or Healthline on 0800 611 116, any time, for free. For more information visit info.health.nz."

World.title: French tourist Maëlle Favregros' fatal fall in popular alpine area prompts safety warnings
World.content:
Social media is leading some tourists to take risks and venture into the outdoors unprepared, a coroner says.

French tourist Maëlle Favregros died from blood loss after falling while crossing slippery, rocky terrain near the Brewster Glacier in Mount Aspiring National Park in February last year, findings released on Thursday said.

The 23-year-old was not wearing tramping boots or on a managed track and had discovered the Brewster Glacier trip on AllTrails.

Coroner Alexandra Cunninghame urged trampers to plan their routes using official sources - including the Department of Conservation (DOC) and Plan My Walk - be aware of hazards, stay on official marked routes and have the necessary skills and gear for alpine trips.

There were seven search and rescues in the area last year, six in 2024, seven in 2023, as well as another death in 2020.

Mountain Safety Council chief executive Mike Daisley said the coroner's findings aimed to stop such tragedies from repeating.

"Maëlle's death occurred in terrain beyond the managed DOC track network in an alpine environment where significant natural hazards exist and where visitor judgement, preparation and decision-making are critical factors in maintaining safety," he said.

Mountain Safety Council chief executive Mike Daisley. Supplied / Sarah Topliff

The Brewster Glacier area was reasonably quiet and not many people explored it until about six years ago when suddenly there was a spike in visits and a lot of interest, Daisley said.

Trampers should use social media for ideas but not for preparation, he said.

"Social media in itself is not the problem. Use that for inspiration, but don't consider that your plan. Do some investigating and find out about the environment that you've decided just because you've seen a picture of it, and it's great to be inspired by it, but do your research."

The Brewster Glacier is accessed via the steep Brewster Track which climbs about 1000 metres over about 2.8 kilometres.

An interagency group had been set up in April 2024 to help raise awareness of the hazards in the area after a rise in people getting into trouble.

It prompted a new Brewster Track safety video to be released last November highlighting the hazards.

The Department of Conservation carried out a review of Favregros' death and had made several changes to boost awareness of the hazards.

They included installing new signs at the carpark and at Brewster Hut warning of the risks, targeted social media advertising about safety and planning for the track, and working with AllTrails so people were aware of the hazards, risks and skills needed.

"The increasing use has been mirrored by an increase in visitor incidents requiring search and rescue involvement, mainly associated with visitors getting into difficulty when attempting to access areas off the DOC managed experience, such as Mt Armstrong and the Brewster Glacier," the review said.

The Department of Conservation's Central Otago operations manager, Charlie Sklenar, said beautiful pictures online were not showing the risks involved at the locations they drew people towards.

"Social media's inspiring people to visit some incredible places [but] our concern is people heading into challenging terrain without understanding what's required. We want people to be inspired by social media but we also don't want them to rely on that alone to plan their trips," Sklenar said.

She said the department had created its own social media messaging to direct tourists towards reliable information about the areas they were visiting.

"We've been working with the Mountain Safety Council to produce a safety video which has been really well received. We're also doing some geo-targeted social media to overseas tourists, as they're arriving in the area, to help them plan and steer them to where there is really credible and trustable information.

"It's really about knowing your limits, prepare properly and, if in doubt, turn around," Sklenar said.

Coroner Alexandra Cunninghame. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Brewster Hut was traditionally used as a base for alpine adventures and the department said it had been managed with the expectation visitors had the necessary skills, experience and capability.

The area had recently attracted "much lower skilled" visitors who wanted to visit Brewster Glacier, partly due to a surge in social media and visitor numbers, the department said.

The coroner did not make any specific recommendations to the department, saying it had already boosted safety messaging which would hopefully decrease the chance of similar deaths.

A long-awaited trip gone wrong

Favregros and her friend Arthur Boutillier had pitched their tents near the hut after walking up Brewster Track on 21 February 2025, the coroner's findings said.

They set out to explore the lake near the glacier about 5.30pm.

She was wearing shoes, not tramping boots, and carried a backpack and hiking poles.

Boutillier said his friend had grown up in the mountains and had experience hiking and trail running.

He described the area as "all ice and open rock" after arriving above the lake about 6.45pm, before they decided to get closer.

Boutillier took the route closer to the lake shore, while Favregros hiked up a long escarpment, where water flowed through cracks and moss and slime had attached on to smooth rock.

Brewster glacier. RNZ / Claire Concannon

Boutillier told the coroner they were tired but Favregros was happy to be there as she had been looking forward to the glacier trip for a long time.

"For me she was so [taken] by the glacier, she was always talking about, that she had been less vigilant about what she was getting into," he told the coroner.

Then he heard a scream and ran to find Favregros lying on the ground in a patch of water.

She lost consciousness and he tried to carry her, putting her into the recovery position when he could not take her further.

There was no reception and he realised he would have to leave her to go for help but told police she died before he left.

He ran back, taking about 40 minutes to get to the hut while trying to use his phone to call for help.

He called police on 111 at 7.48pm.

A helicopter was sent but low cloud initially prevented the crew from landing.

They were able to retrieve her body when the weather cleared.

World.title: 'Like your heart's been ripped out': Community protests sale of public housing in Lower Hutt
World.content:
It's been a night of reflection and waiata on Manderson Grove for a crowd of Lower Hutt locals protesting the sale of public housing.

Almost the entire street is on the market, pitched as an opportunity for developers, investors and landbankers, with a deadline sale of 8 December.

Kāinga Ora said it was selling properties that are costly to maintain, and that the units on Manderson Grove are old and no longer fit for purpose.

A spokesperson said the proceeds from the sale would be reinvested in social housing in the region, and selling the land provided the opportunity for new housing to be developed.

But some in the community say public land should stay in public ownership. On Wednesday night they took their protest to the site, camping out overnight among the empty houses on Manderson Grove.

Jade Hakaraia, a member of St David's Anglican Church, was one of those who took up the vigil overnight.

"I think it was 2 o'clock in the morning [on Thursday], and I just felt this prompting to walk around and look into the houses and I was imagining the cars in the carport, families walking into their homes through the gates, children on the street."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408889629112

She said she understood the stability and community that state housing provided.

"With the housing going elsewhere, it's like they have to rebuild that from the beginning. And that's really hard for anyone."

Former Manderson Grove resident George Wi Edward Crown said being told he and his grandkids would have to leave was "shattering".

"I was born and brought up in number 11 Manderson Grove from about five years old.

"My mum lived here. When my dad passed away in 1990, I moved back with my kids and my family to look after my mum. She just recently passed away in 2023. So she was here for 47 years."

He said it was hard to be back on Thursday morning.

"Oh, it's emotional. When you get taken out of a place you're brought up in all your life, it's not nice. It feels like your heart's been ripped out."

Crown said the community he'd known for decades had been broken up and dispersed.

"It doesn't get any easier," he said.

Former Manderson Grove resident George Wi Edward Crown said being told to leave was "shattering". RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Kāinga Ora said the agency had considered redeveloping the site but said "it did not represent good value for money compared with other opportunities to invest in social housing".

Protester and development manager with the Wellington Anglican Diocese, Nick Young, said the sections were prime real estate and he felt it made sense to continue the history of public housing.

"It's a fantastic bit of flat land in a beautiful little cul-de-sac grove in the middle of the Hutt Valley. What's not to like about this?" he said.

The land was likely to be among the easiest to develop pieces of land in the area, he said.

"If there's a need here ... why wouldn't you want to respond to that need by developing in this space?"

As of September 2026, 339 households were on the public housing waitlist in Lower Hutt.

World.title: Returning Matildas star Cooney-Cross wants to make late mum 'proud'
World.content:
When Kyra Cooney-Cross returned to the pitch for Arsenal in the Women's Super League in September, she shared a moving message from her mum.

Its essence is one that so many parents would have relayed to their kids in one manner or another in their sporting careers, whether they were as decorated as a Matildas' linchpin, or finding their feet for the first time in the under 5s.

"Kyra, try to remember what it felt like when you were little … when you just loved having the ball at your feet, playing with your mates, testing yourself against the boys or adults for the fun of it," the message read.

"Play because you love the ball at your feet, the rhythm of the game. Train because it feels good to move and challenge your body and feel strong.

"This is how you start doing it for you again — Mum."

Amongst the pain of losing her mother Jess to terminal bile duct cancer in July, Cooney-Cross has taken the message to heart, and three months after returning to club football, she's back for the Matildas.

Kyra Cooney-Cross returned for her club side Arsenal in August. (Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

The 24-year-old is in the squad for friendlies against Colombia in Canberra and Geelong, in a key test just seven months out from the Women's World Cup in Brazil.

"It's bittersweet. It's my first time back with the national team since everything that's happened with my mum and our family," she told ABC News Breakfast.

"But playing for your country, this is the highest level I can play at, and it's the highest level I can make my mum proud.

"So I'm really looking forward to it and being back at home in Geelong in front of my family and friends and just being back with the team."

Cooney-Cross last played for the Matildas at the Women's Asian Cup in March. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

Cooney-Cross's last international appearance was in March's Women's Asian Cup, and after her breakthrough tournament at the now fabled 2023 World Cup, she's eager to recreate those highs.

"It's definitely flown by. I don't think a lot of us players had even the time to process the World Cup and what we had done in this country and for women's football in Australia," she said.

"We're just going to work really hard. Stick together and focus on these next two games.

"The World Cup is obviously really important and we want to get really far."

McKenna making moves

Cooney-Cross will play a pivotal part in Brazil next year but others on the fringe, like midfielder Leticia McKenna, hope for their own breakout moment.

Leticia McKenna made her Matildas debut earlier this year. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

McKenna, 24, made her international debut in April, and starred for Melbourne City before securing a move to Nottingham Forest in the second tier of English women's football.

She was also recently named PFA Young Footballer of the Year.

"It's been very surreal. It's been a really big year, something I'm extremely proud of," she said.

McKenna's UK move made waves, setting an A-League Women's record with her transfer fee.

"It was a very, very hard decision to leave. It came up at quite short notice as well and I was very happy at the position I was in with Melbourne City and I was looking forward to the upcoming season in that regard," she said.

"But it was something I felt I was ready for. It was always in the back of my mind to make that step and move overseas."

Having made the most of her opportunities with the national side so far, and with only a handful of games left in the lead up, McKenna is eyeing off a berth in that final World Cup squad.

"You always gotta have a goal and aspirations and it's always been a dream," she said.

"Super grateful to be here and it's just making me even hungrier to keep dreaming."

World.title: NRL scraps All Stars game for 2027 preseason
World.content:
The NRL is looking at whether the All Stars clash could form part of an expanded grand-final week in 2027, after a cluttered preseason squeezed the annual fixture off the calendar.

The sheer number of players returning to training late from the World Cup, as well as early-season overseas travel, has left no room for the match next February.

The fixture has been part of every NRL preseason since 2010, except in 2014 and 2018, when it was skipped due to World Cups.

Earlier this year, NRL executive chair Peter V'landys floated permanently shifting the game to grand-final week, before the idea was talked down by Maori and Indigenous players.

The All Stars game has been a fixture on the NRL calender since 2010. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Chief among their concerns was the unavailability of players from teams in grand-final sides, and that players would be carrying injuries that could stop them playing.

But the nature of next year's schedule means an end-of-season fixture may be the only way the match could be fit in.

"Ideally, and it's a matter of getting everybody on the same page, we should be holding the All Stars at the end of the year," V'landys said.

"We want to give the All Stars a much greater profile. It doesn't get that profile at the beginning of the year.

"It should be right at the end in the grand-final week.

"What was proven from this World Cup: if you've got clean air, look at the ratings you get."

V'landys still has his sights set on the All Stars match being one of several in grand-final week, as part of an expanded carnival.

Part of that could still include the NRLW grand final being played as a standalone event, with V'landys leaving the door open to that in 2027.

The NRLW grand final could become a standalone event in 2027. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"You could have it at Allianz Stadium on a Friday night," V'landys said.

"Because I'm proud of how good the women are going, we want to take them to the next level at some point.

"We've got the best women's sport in Australia. Cricket has always been pretty high up there, but I think we've caught them.

"Our ratings show it. They got over a million viewers [for the World Cup final]. What did the Bleeding Cup [Bledisloe Cup] get? It got 600,000. The women beat them."

NRL to tweak rules again for 2027 The NRL will come down harder on hip-drop tackles in 2027 but has ruled out the possibility of rolling back the controversial set restart rule.

An underage State of Origin match has also been proposed as an option to be played in grand-final week.

A third-place playoff between the two losing preliminary finalists was also floated in August, before it was largely laughed down by critics and players.

"I know that it got, everybody wanted to pot it. But it was the highest-rating FIFA [World Cup] match," V'landys said.

"If you're a Tigers' fan and you're up against the Eels, you'll watch it. It's third against fourth.

"It's like anything else. You've got to market it properly and have prize money or sponsors involved.

"If we listen to all the traditionalists all the time, we'd be playing for a couple of hundred dollars a game because you wouldn't get the revenue."

World.title: Kurtley Beale back in Wallabies team for first time in five years
World.content:
Kurtley Beale's return to the gold jumper is no sentimental, one-off reward for the veteran playing a selfless backroom role and being a mentor to young Wallabies this past month.

Coach Les Kiss says Australia's great rugby maverick has won his place back at the age of 37 absolutely on merit.

There's not a soul in the Wallabies' camp who has not been enthusing about the 37-year-old's return to the starting 23 in Friday's (Saturday AEDT) Nations Championship finale against Ireland at Twickenham.

Players such as Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii have been gushing about how he has been an inspirational presence in the team room and on the training park following his shock call-up to the squad for the spring tour to the UK.

But Kiss was quick to make it clear on Wednesday that Beale's selection on the Test team's bench for the first time since he won cap number 95 for the Wallabies against Wales in 2021 was no sentimental end-of-tour present.

"This isn't a gift to Kurtley," Kiss said.

"I couldn't speak highly enough of him. He has been unbelievable and he's been selected on merit. He's earned it; that's the bottom line."

With Australia going for a six-two split of forwards and backs on the bench, Kiss felt Beale's remarkable versatility — he has played in five different positions in the Wallabies' back line over his 17-year international career — could be crucial on Friday.

It means he has jettisoned both Ben Donaldson and Filipo Daugunu, two of the rare Australian success stories off the bench on a trying trip this past month, with Kiss admitting it was tough on the pair.

"But if you saw Kurtley's Super Aus games [for the Western Force], he played at 10, then he went to 12. He helped engineer those wins,'' the coach said.

"He was kicking goals from everywhere, kicking corners. And that type of influence has come through in every session, every video session, every computer session on this trip.

"He's earned his call. He's been nothing short of exceptional, really, how he's worked with the group, brought his wisdom, been patient, and he's clearly earned his spot, not only in my eyes but in his peers' eyes."

Les Kiss has praised Kurtley Beale's contribution to the squad on tour, despite not playing a minute yet. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Jan Kruger)

Suaalii was among those singing Beale's praises.

"I grew up watching Kurtley. I've always admired him from afar,'' he said.

"I've enjoyed working with him, just sitting at computers, picking his brain off the field, and just seeing what he's like as a person and how much he loves the game.

"How he sees the game is different from a lot of people, and I've just been asking him different questions and just trying to grow my game as a player. He's a great man, and the crew love him."

Up front, Allan Alaalatoa will earn a 100th cap while, at the other end of the spectrum, winger James Ramm will make his debut.

Prop Alaalatoa is the 14th Wallabies centurion, having made his debut in 2016. He will line up with Isaac Kailea and hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa in the front row, with Harry Wilson dropping to the bench.

"We've taken some steps forward, grown our game and tested our squad depth this year and I know the team is highly motivated to put in a performance that reflects the hard work put in by everyone in our final test," Kiss said.

Ireland, meanwhile, has made two changes from the side that beat the Springboks last week in Dublin, with Australian-born winger Mack Hansen out of the squad.

Wires/ABC

World.title: David Warner takes aim at 'bullying' journalists
World.content:
David Warner has accused the media of "perpetuating speculation", intimating he is being bullied as the sandpaper scandal continues to simmer.

Warner has called for media to substantiate allegations that he used superglue and grit on finger strapping to tamper with the ball on the infamous 2018 tour of South Africa.

The claims, published by News Corp and SEN radio, were penned by prominent broadcaster Gerard Whateley.

"I'm not entirely sure where Gerard's assertions have come from, as they certainly do not align with my recollection of events," Warner posted on Instagram.

"In relation to the alleged use of superglue and grit, and the more recent claims regarding the finger, could I respectfully ask what credible evidence exists to substantiate these allegations?

"Before further unverified claims are circulated publicly, I would suggest establishing the facts rather than perpetuating speculation."

Australia's ball tampering with sandpaper during the 2018 Test series in South Africa is under fresh scrutiny following the release of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.

Khawaja's claims of the entire team knowing of the ball tampering have been backed by Warner and Cameron Bancroft, but rejected by current Test captain Pat Cummins and fellow bowlers Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc.

Usman Khawaja (left) and David Warner have been at the heart of the renewed speculation over the Cape Town Test. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

Khawaja completed a lengthy interview with The Grade Cricketer this week, where he revealed that he had issued a draft statement that hoped to find some "middle ground" between the two warring factions.

He doubled down though in saying that the whole squad knew about the ball tampering.

Khawaja also confirmed Whateley's report that a player had asked in Australia's first Test under Langer where the mints or red frogs were, with the ball not swinging.

Warner also replied to an Instagram user's comment that Whateley "is a long-time hater" of the internationally retired batsman.

Justin Langer's spray An Australian player suggested tampering with the ball in the nation's first Test after Sandpapergate before the intervention of then-coach Justin Langer.

"Refreshing to see someone willing to speak honestly," Warner replied.

"Education and eloquence are admirable qualities, but they should never be used to undermine those who weren't afforded the same opportunities.

"When someone uses their public platform to control a narrative without affording others the same voice, it raises a legitimate question about the distinction between journalism and bullying."

Steve Smith — who is yet to comment publicly amid the fresh furore — and Warner were banned by Cricket Australia for 12 months and lost the captaincy and vice-captaincy respectively for their role in the ball-tampering controversy.

Bancroft, who has admitted using sandpaper on the ball, was suspended for nine months.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: North star's path from family tragedy to a fourth AFLW flag tilt
World.content:
Football is emotional, and big games even more so.

It's something North Melbourne players are becoming veterans at understanding as their club heads into its fourth straight grand final this week. They are aiming for a third consecutive premiership.

But for Kangaroo star forward Jenna Bruton, there's an extra layer to it.

This season, she marked her 100th game in the qualifying final against Carlton.

She deeply wished her mum and aunt, who both died from brain cancer a few years before, could have been there.

"It made me pretty sad, obviously. But it is sad," she said of achieving her milestone without them.

"I want people to know that mum was a massive part of my journey."

Bruton's story is well known in AFLW circles. In late 2015 her mum, Suzy, was diagnosed with cancer. A top draft prospect, Bruton omitted herself from the historic inaugural 2016 draft to become her full-time carer.

Loading Instagram content

She didn't want to commit to anything if she couldn't manage her mum's treatments and help her where needed.

And with her mother's diagnosis, she "fell out of love with the game for a little bit".

"They did say mum, her life expectancy was probably lucky to get one year [after diagnosis], and she lasted five or six," she said.

During that time, Bruton made her way into the AFLW system after her partner and star player, Jasmine Garner, submitted her belated draft nomination for her.

"She did it for me," Bruton said. "I wasn't actually going to do it. She did the application and I didn't have a choice. I'm glad she did."

Bruton was taken with pick 11 by the Western Bulldogs in 2017, before signing with North Melbourne as an expansion player for the 2019 season.

Her mother died a week before the first game of the 2022 season.

Jenna Bruton is close with her family. (Getty)

Just three months earlier, her aunt Andrea, her mother's sister, died from the same cancer.

"You're more likely to win TattsLotto than two people in your family get the same brain cancer. So it was pretty hard on my nan and everyone," Bruton said.

"They said it's not genetic at all, which is crazy that it was both of them. They say it's just bad luck.

"We think about them a lot."

Bruton said her aunt's Facebook posts about her football journey now came up as memories.

If Garner had never put Bruton's name down, she would probably still be back in Trentham, working the 400-hectare potato farm she grew up on.

Jenna Bruton runs through the banner for her 100th match with niece Polly. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Her goal song, Hot Potato by The Wiggles, is a call back to this, along with being a favourite of her niece and nephew.

She is now a three-time premiership player; once with the Western Bulldogs and twice with North Melbourne.

A big part of that journey has been her family, Garner and their dogs Bronson and Honey.

"My mum's other sister is just up the road from dad, so I go up and see her a lot and she comes down to the footy. I feel like I'm closer to mum through them," she said.

"Then I've got a niece and nephew. Sort of feel like they're a part of mum. So, they've helped us a lot through losing mum.

Jasmine Garner and Jenna Bruton have been partners for 13 years. (Getty)

"Polly, my niece, she was born a couple of months before mum passed away. So mum did get to meet her, which was so good. She definitely keeps the family together."

She said her sadness during big games was also mixed with a lot of good emotions.

"I actually said to Jammin [Garner] after my 100th, it was probably like the best day," she said.

"Just with family and it was just so good. I don't really like the attention, but it was one of my favourite days."

The pair will be hoping those emotions come flooding back this Friday with another premiership, the club's third straight, if they are able to defeat Melbourne in the grand final.

World.title: Sydney Swans player has driving charge dismissed by judge
World.content:
Sydney Swans player Tom Papley has had a charge of driving while suspended dismissed in court.

Mr Papley was stopped on November 2 and charged with driving while suspended due to an unpaid parking fine, with a drug test later returning positive results for MDMA and cocaine.

The driving charge was heard in Waverley Local Court, with the court hearing Mr Papley had paid the fine two days earlier but had not checked whether the suspension had been lifted.

Judge Michael Barko dismissed the charge.

"I accept he genuinely honestly believed he was OK to drive," Judge Barko said.

"One can only say that he had the right attitude in relation to paying his fines. He should have simply waited until it was all clear before he drove."

The drug matter was not mentioned in the proceedings.

Outside court, Mr Papley apologised to his "family, the football club and my fans".

"My sole focus is earning their respect back," he said.

Banned by AFL

Police said at the time of the incident that the 30-year-old tested positive for illicit drugs, with a second sample confirming the presence of cocaine and MDMA.

NSW Police fined Mr Papley $722 and suspended his drivers licence for three months for that matter.

He was also banned by the AFL from the Swans' preseason game and the first three matches of the 2027 season due to "conduct unbecoming" under the league's Illicit Drugs Policy.

The league issued him a suspended $5,000 fine.

AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley last week said the sanction reflected the seriousness of the breach.

"AFL players are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with illicit drug use," Mr Harley said in a statement.

"The player is being held accountable for his actions and has acknowledged he made a grave mistake."

World.title: Jack Clayton draws on AFL draft experience to chase Test cricket debut
World.content:
Missing selection in the AFL draft has helped Australia hopeful Jack Clayton deal with the pressure of fighting for a Test debut.

Clayton made his final pitch to the selectors with an unbeaten 84 for Queensland on Wednesday, before NSW clung on for a draw at the Sydney Cricket Ground.

Australia will on Saturday name its squad for next month's first Test against New Zealand in Perth.

Clayton is considered an outside chance of a call-up, after starting the Shield season with 449 runs at an average of 74.83.

The 27-year-old was thrust into the spotlight in late October, as Australia's batting failed in its last Test in Cape Town at the same time as he was racking up 104 runs against Victoria.

While being talked up for international selection brings its own kind of pressure, Clayton has leaned on the experience he gained from being in the Brisbane Lions' academy before he was told by the AFL club in 2017 they would not draft him.

Loading Instagram content

"Something I learned playing AFL was about … thinking about getting drafted or things out of my control," Clayton said.

"As soon as I start thinking about what may happen, I don't play that well.

"I know as soon as I get into that mindset that it's taking me out of what I need to do and what I need to focus on. That's a skill I've developed over time."

Instead of worrying about what the future might hold, Clayton is focusing on his job of scoring runs for Queensland.

"And those things [such as selection], other people can control that; I can't control that," he said.

Clayton's hopes are likely to hinge on where the opening is in Australia's batting.

There could be just one change to the side from Cape Town, with the fit-again Steve Smith in at number three for the axed Marnus Labuschagne.

NSW draw against Queensland Thanks to a sporting declaration by Queensland and some exceptional bowling, the SCG was treated to one of the best Sheffield Shield finishes in years as New South Wales hung on for a draw.

And the option is there to shake up the openers, with Sam Konstas or Jake Weatherald selected.

But if Smith wants to stay at number four, Clayton is confident he can go to first drop if the opportunity arises.

"I've batted there before. I feel comfortable. I batted all my juniors there," he said.

After four seasons of first-class cricket with Queensland, Clayton is comfortable with his game.

"You never know if you're actually ready for Test cricket," he said.

"But I feel like I've been performing well, doing all the things I've been doing for the last three years.

"I try and take into account the shots I think are going to be low-risk scoring options and do that over and over again.

"That's what I've had success with."

AAP

World.title: The reason why North Melbourne dominates the AFLW landscape
World.content:
A North Melbourne victory has been a near certainty heading into almost every AFLW match of late.

The Kangaroos have lost just one game in their last 43, and boast a 96 per cent winning rate since losing the 2023 grand final.

At the opposite end of the scale, struggling teams Collingwood and GWS have winning percentages closer to just 15 per cent.

Tomorrow, North will play Melbourne in its fourth consecutive grand final, aiming to be the first side in competition history to secure a three-peat.

Despite the gap between either end of the ladder, AFL Hall of Famer and former Western Bulldogs coach Nathan Burke said it will benefit the league's competitiveness long-term.

"I think it's outstanding for the competition, because this is still a fledgling competition … to have North Melbourne so far out in front, it just means that everyone has to catch up," he said.

"The downside is that the competition becomes a little bit more predictable … and there are some people that just see that and think, 'Oh, North Melbourne are going to win,' and just turn off.

"They don't look at it closely and see the improvement that's coming from underneath because we're trying to catch North Melbourne."

The rest of the pack are trying desperately to chase down the Kangaroos. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

The Kangaroos have not been the only dominant side in the competition over the past 11 seasons.

This is the first year neither Adelaide nor Brisbane will feature in the AFLW grand final.

Want to win an AFLW flag? Club culture matters, data shows AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

The Lions have played in seven grand finals, yielding two wins, while the Crows currently hold the record for most premierships in the competition with three.

That record will be equalled if the Kangaroos salute at Princes Park tomorrow night.

AFLW commentator Chyloe Kurdas said a win would edge the Roos ahead when ranking the best sides across the competition's history.

"[They are] interesting comparisons because of the flags Adelaide have won. You look at the conversion rate for Brisbane [of grand finals into premierships], and you look at North Melbourne's conversion rate into their fourth grand final," she said.

"[To win] Three from four, I guess, on the conversion rate, North Melbourne — should they get over the line — will be the number one of those three sides."

Kurdas said the club is being rewarded for the efforts it put into a women's team well before the AFLW's inception.

Melbourne University Women's Football Club developed a partnership with the Kangaroos so players could train at Arden St, and remained the club's VFLW affiliate until 2019.

Emma Kearney has played over 100 games for North Melbourne. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Robert Cianflone)

"It's the groundwork North Melbourne did in 2009, 2010 to invest in the really early days, even before AFLW was on the radar … they used a lot of that intel to build a culture that was ready for women and girls to come into the game at a professional level," Kurdas said.

"And of course, how they built their list. They prioritised footballers at the time, really prioritised skills, and they were able to leverage the draft rules at the time and bring in a really strong group of players from day one."

Melbourne University alumni Emma Kearney and Ash Riddell joined North Melbourne in its first season in the AFLW and remain key pillars of the side leading into tomorrow's grand final.

This year, North lost its first match since the 2023 grand final and recorded its lowest score since that season, while still clearly remaining the premiership favourites.

"Slowly they're [other teams] catching up; it's not happening as fast as everyone would like," Burke said.

"I think Geelong made the biggest strides getting closest to North Melbourne … we'll see how close Melbourne get this weekend, but I do still think there's a bit of a gulf from those top three teams," Burke said.

The statistic in Melbourne's favour tomorrow is its win-loss record against the Roos.

The Demons are the only team in the AFLW to have a better head-to-head record against North since the two-time reigning champions entered the competition.

Tech.title: Waymo conquered city streets — why does it keep stumbling on freeways?
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Most people know not to try to pass highway patrol cars while performing a traffic break on a freeway. But on November 6th, a driverless Waymo on Interstate 280 failed that test.

Video shows the robotaxi attempting to overtake two California Highway Patrol cruisers during a traffic break, a moving violation that could get a human driver’s license suspended. For Waymo, it was the latest in a series of freeway blunders that eventually led to the California DMV last week banning its vehicles from all state interstates.

Construction zones have also posed a challenge. Between October and November 2026, the company reported a total of 11 instances in which its vehicles failed to recognize that a freeway lane was closed because of construction and drove into the restricted area anyway, according to a recently filed recall.

With all these violations piling up, Waymo decided last week to pause commercial freeway rides across all of its US markets. It was a bruising setback for the global leader of autonomous driving, exposing how easily its multibillion-dollar technology can still be tripped up by basic road rules.

For years, the autonomous vehicle industry assumed freeways would be the easy part — no jaywalkers, no unprotected left turns — while dense cities were seen as the ultimate battle. Yet Waymo has flipped that script, racking up millions of urban miles while repeatedly stumbling on the interstate.

It was a bruising setback for the global leader of autonomous driving, exposing how easily its multibillion-dollar technology can still be tripped up by basic road rules

This was neither the first time Waymo was forced to pause freeway operations nor the first time it had been caught blundering into construction sites. Earlier this year, the company temporarily halted freeway rides after its robotaxis entered active construction zones in Arizona and California. It issued a recall in June and gradually resumed freeway operations starting in late July after updating its software.

But experts note that the recall didn’t work, as evidenced by the subsequent violations.

”The most concerning part about this is now we have a pattern for Waymo: They issue a recall, it doesn’t fix the problem, but they keep scaling up anyway,” says Phil Koopman, emeritus professor in electrical and computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University and a researcher specializing in autonomous vehicle safety.

In an interview, Koopman says Waymo is using recalls as “Band-Aids,” which he argues doesn’t really address the root of the problem. In addition to the freeway snafus, Waymo also filed a recall related to the intersection crash where its vehicle failed to detect a police officer directing traffic. In short, the car followed the officer’s orders until passing traffic blocked its view, at which point its software lost track of the “stop” command and drove into the intersection on its own, the company said in the recall report filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Waymo later updated its software across its entire fleet so the vehicles remember manual traffic signals even when an officer is temporarily blocked from view.

There have been other recalls related to Waymo passing stopped school buses and driving through flooded roadways. This has led Koopman to theorize that rather than solving the underlying perception and reasoning flaws, Waymo is using “dynamic geofencing” to route around known flood zones or using real-time GPS feeds of school buses until a car encounters an unmapped situation.

“The most concerning part about this is now we have a pattern for Waymo: They issue a recall, it doesn’t fix the problem, but they keep scaling up anyway.” — Phil Koopman, Carnegie Mellon University

“It felt to me like they were really not being able to fix these problems,” he says. “They’re putting Band-Aids on and getting on with scaling.”

In response to the California DMV order, Waymo said it’s working closely with regulators on a solution, noting that its vehicles haven’t crashed or injured anyone while driving through restricted areas on the freeway.

“Our ridehailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week,” Waymo spokesperson Chris Pappas said last week. “We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”

Since its inception, Waymo has typically avoided highways, opting instead for longer routes that stick to local roads when ferrying passengers. This has not gone unnoticed by the company’s customers, who often complain their trips can take longer because the vehicles are prohibited from using routes that travel on highways. But in late 2025, Waymo said it was ready to hit the highway.

“Freeway driving is one of those things that’s very easy to learn, but very hard to master when we’re talking about full autonomy without a human driver as a backup,” Dmitri Dolgov, co-CEO of Waymo, said in a November 2025 briefing with reporters. “And at scale. So it took time to do it properly with a strong focus on system safety and reliability.”

“Freeway driving is one of those things that’s very easy to learn, but very hard to master.” — Waymo Co-CEO Dmitry Dolgov

Now it seems as if Waymo may have jumped the gun. The company’s decision to pull back from the freeway, twice in one year, reflects the enormous stakes of operating driverless vehicles at high speeds. At 10 to 25 mph on a city street, applying the brakes solves almost any confusion, and crash lethality is drastically lower. At 60 or 70 mph, stopping distances stretch out, and any mistake involving a roadside worker or stranded motorist is nearly 100 percent fatal. And if the vehicle gets confused and needs to ping a remote operator for assistance, the latency of that connection and the time it takes to receive a reply becomes a major liability.

Koopman thinks that subtle edge cases — like a gap in construction cones or a cop’s hand gesture — are tripping Waymo up right after its transition to end-to-end machine learning. Unlike older modular systems where engineers could write explicit rules, statistical models struggle when familiar objects appear in unfamiliar contexts.

“If you’ve trained on the individual elements, their combination presents a special meaning that is different than usual,” he says. “A stop sign folded out on a school bus is completely different from a stop sign on a post... Everything I’ve seen is consistent with the hypothesis that it’s having trouble with subtle contextual clues.”

For Waymo, solving for the freeway is essential if the company wants to continue expanding its service area to include popular ridehailing destinations, like airports. Waymo’s future reliability will depend on it. While safety engineers want to do the right thing, executives face massive market pressure to ship “good enough” fixes and apologize later, Koopman argues. And because traffic tickets and standard fines don’t deter well-capitalized tech giants like Alphabet, regulators need mandatory public transparency — not quiet software patches via recalls.

“If DMV gets a neutral look without political pressure, they’re going to say, ‘Fool me once, shame on you,’” Koopman says. “They can’t just accept Waymo saying, ‘Trust us, bro, we fixed it this time for sure.’”

Tech.title: X is finally getting its first parental controls
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

X is finally rolling out parental controls that allow parents and guardians to manage teens’ accounts on the platform. While teens will retain ownership of their own account, parents and guardians will be able to see how much time their child has spent on X, set daily limits, require approval for new followers, and limit For You recommendations to accounts a teen already follows.
